Introduction to KimTay Pet Supplies and StayWell Student Accommodation Databases

What a database is, why it beats a pile of files, and a first look at the two databases used throughout this course.

Module 1

  • 1-1. What Is a Database?
  • 1-2. The KimTay Pet Supplies Database
  • 1-3. StayWell Student Accommodation Database

1-1 What Is a Database?Objective 1

Every organization — including KimTay Pet Supplies and StayWell Student Accommodation — has to keep track of things: customers, products, invoices, properties, students, payments. The question this lesson answers is: where should that data live, and why does it matter?

Before a database, KimTay's office kept business data in separate files — the kind of setup most small operations start with:

📄

customer_list.xlsx

Customer name, address, and phone — kept by the front office.

📄

rep_commissions.xlsx

Rep names and the customers they call on — kept by sales, also lists each customer's address.

📄

invoices_2026.docx

Printed invoices — each one repeats the customer's full name and address again.

Access Pet Center is one of KimTay's customers — a retail pet store that buys from KimTay, not KimTay itself. When Access Pet Center moved to a new building, someone had to find and fix its address in three separate files — and if even one got missed, KimTay now has inconsistent data: different files disagreeing about where their customer, Access Pet Center, is actually located.

In a database, the customer's address is stored in exactly one place — the CUSTOMER table — and every other part of the system (rep assignments, invoices, reports) refers back to that same table instead of copying it. Just one table this time, not three separate files — the three cards below all describe that single table, in order: what it is, how the rest of the system uses it without duplicating it, and what that buys you.

📊

1. The one CUSTOMER table

Name and address live here, once, with a unique CUSTOMER_NUM. This is the only copy that exists anywhere in the system.

🔗

2. Other tables just reference it

A separate table, INVOICE, doesn't get its own copy of the name/address — it stores only the CUSTOMER_NUM and looks up the real data in CUSTOMER when needed.

✅

3. Result: update once, done everywhere

Change the address in CUSTOMER and every invoice, report, and query that looks it up sees the new address immediately — there's no second copy anywhere to forget.

Toggle between the two approaches above using the same KimTay scenario, then look at the vocabulary every database course builds on:

Data

Click / press Enter to flip
Raw facts — a name, a number, a date — before they've been organized into something meaningful.

Field (Column)

Click / press Enter to flip
The smallest named unit of data in a table, such as CUSTOMER_NAME or PRICE.

Record (Row)

Click / press Enter to flip
One complete set of field values describing a single entity — one customer, one item, one invoice.

Table (File)

Click / press Enter to flip
A named collection of records that all share the same fields — e.g. every row in CUSTOMER.

Database

Click / press Enter to flip
A structured, shared collection of related tables, designed so the data can be queried and cross-referenced.

DBMS

Click / press Enter to flip
The software layer (MySQL, Oracle, Access, PostgreSQL...) that creates, secures, and manages a database.

Why the file-system approach breaks down

As a business grows past a handful of files, four problems show up again and again:

🔄

Data redundancy

The same fact (a customer's address, an item's price) is copied into multiple files, wasting space and inviting mistakes.

⚠️

Data inconsistency

When a copy gets updated but the others don't, different files disagree about the same fact.

🔒

Data isolation

Related data is scattered across incompatible files, making it hard to answer questions that span more than one file.

👥

Limited sharing & security

Files are typically used by one program or person at a time, with little control over who can see or change what.

What a database (and a DBMS) fixes

A database is a structured, shared collection of related data. A database management system (DBMS) — MySQL, Oracle, and Microsoft Access are all examples — is the software that lets many people and programs create, read, update, and delete that data safely and consistently, while enforcing rules about what the data is allowed to look like.

💡
How to think about it

A spreadsheet asks "where do I put this fact?" A database asks "what is this fact, and what else does it relate to?" That shift in thinking is what Module 2 is all about.

Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
Q1The address that only half-changed

Access Pet Center moves to a new building. KimTay's front office updates the address in customer_list.xlsx, but nobody touches invoices_2026.docx, which still prints the old street. Using the four problems named in this lesson, which one has that missed update just created?

  • ✘a. Redundancy was already there before anyone moved - it is the pre-existing condition that made this failure possible, not the new problem the missed update created.
  • ✘b. Isolation is about being unable to combine data from separate files; here the address can be found in both files, it just disagrees.
  • ✔c. Correct - the lesson defines data inconsistency as one copy getting updated while the others do not, so different files disagree about the same fact.
  • ✘d. Sharing and security is about who is allowed to open or change a file; nobody's permissions caused this, a missed update did.

Remember: Redundancy is storing the same fact twice; inconsistency is what happens when one of those copies is updated and the others are not.

Q2The question nobody could answer

Before the database, KimTay's owner asked, 'Which of Valerie Kaiser's customers ordered anything in June?' Rep assignments lived in rep_commissions.xlsx, customer details in customer_list.xlsx, and orders in invoices_2026.docx, with no shared code linking them. Which of the lesson's four file-system problems does this show?

  • ✔a. Correct - the lesson calls this data isolation: related data scattered across incompatible files makes questions that span more than one file hard to answer.
  • ✘b. Inconsistency means the files actually disagree about a fact; nothing here says any file is wrong, only that they cannot be joined up.
  • ✘c. Redundancy is about storing one fact more than once and wasting space; the owner's trouble is pulling facts together, not storing them.
  • ✘d. The lesson's sharing and security problem is about weak control over who may see or change files; the owner can open all three, he just cannot connect them.

Remember: When a question needs data from more than one file and nothing links those files, the problem is data isolation.

Q3What exactly did we just buy?

KimTay decides to move off spreadsheets. A consultant installs MySQL on the office server, then loads the REP, CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE tables into it. In this course's vocabulary, what is MySQL?

  • ✘a. The database is the structured, shared collection of related tables; MySQL is the software that manages it, which this lesson calls the DBMS.
  • ✘b. A database is not one big file - it is a set of related tables, and the DBMS is separate software that manages all of them at once.
  • ✘c. A DBMS does far more than print: it creates, secures, and manages the stored data itself, so the old files are not needed at all.
  • ✔d. Correct - the lesson names MySQL, Oracle, and Microsoft Access as examples of a DBMS, the software that lets people create, read, update, and delete data safely.

Remember: The database is the data; the DBMS - MySQL, Oracle, Access - is the software that manages it.

          1-2 The KimTay Pet Supplies DatabaseObjective 1

          KimTay Pet Supplies is a small distributor of pet food, toys, habitats, and grooming supplies. A handful of sales reps each manage a set of customers (independently owned pet stores, clinics, and boutiques). Customers place orders that become invoices, and each invoice lists one or more items from KimTay's catalog.

          📖
          Meet the database

          KimTay Pet Supplies is headquartered in Maple Grove, OH. The schema below is an original design built for this course — it teaches the same ideas your book's KimTay chapters cover, but the exact columns and sample rows are not transcribed from any publisher's text.

          Primary key (underlined, bold)Foreign key (italic)One recordMany records (crow's foot)
          📝
          Reading the diagram

          Bold, underlined attributes are primary keys (the column, or columns, that make each row unique). Italic attributes are foreign keys (a column that points back to another table's primary key). The crow's-foot end of a line means "many"; the single tick mark means "one." Primary/foreign keys and crow's-foot notation get a full lesson in 2-3 and 2-6.

          Five tables capture that whole story, each with a clear, single job. So why five separate tables instead of one giant spreadsheet with every column crammed in? Walk through the design one table at a time:

          1

          REP stands on its own

          REP_NUM is REP's primary key — a short code like "20" that belongs to exactly one sales rep and is never blank or repeated. A primary key is simply the column you use to look up one specific row, the same way an employee ID badge number identifies one person without re-typing their whole file every time.

          2

          CUSTOMER points back to its rep, instead of copying it

          Every customer has exactly one assigned rep. Copying that rep's full name, address, and commission rate onto every customer row would recreate the exact redundancy problem from Lesson 1-1. Instead, CUSTOMER stores just the rep's REP_NUM. A column that stores another table's primary key purely to reference that row is called a foreign key — CUSTOMER.REP_NUM is a foreign key pointing back at REP.REP_NUM.

          3

          INVOICE points back to CUSTOMER the same way

          An invoice belongs to exactly one customer, so INVOICE stores that customer's CUSTOMER_NUM as a foreign key too — the identical pattern from the last step, one link further down the chain: INVOICE → CUSTOMER → REP.

          4

          One invoice, many items: a single foreign key isn't enough

          An invoice can list several items, and the same item shows up on many different invoices, so there's no single ITEM_ID column that could live on INVOICE. The fix is a connecting table, INVOICE_LINE, with one row per (invoice, item) pairing. Its primary key is a composite key — INVOICE_NUM and ITEM_ID together — because neither column is unique by itself.

          5

          Putting it back together

          Splitting the data five ways avoids repeating anything, but it also means a real question — "what did Access Pet Center order, and who's their rep?" — needs pieces from three different tables at once. Reassembling them is not guesswork, because the foreign keys above already record which rows belong together: a customer row and a rep row belong together when they carry the same REP_NUM, and an invoice row and an invoice-line row belong together when they carry the same INVOICE_NUM. Following those shared values from one table to the next is how any question gets answered here — same key value, two tables, matched back up. In Module 3 you'll get a single command that does it in one step; the reason it can is the design work in this lesson.

          Two relationship shapes came out of that walkthrough: REP–CUSTOMER is one-to-many (one rep, many customers, tied together by a single foreign key), while INVOICE–ITEM is many-to-many (resolved by the INVOICE_LINE connecting table). You'll meet both relationship shapes again, formally named, when Module 2 covers keys and ER diagrams in depth.

          Q1Whiskers and Wags gets a new rep

          Customer 1420, Whiskers & Wags Boutique, is currently assigned to rep 65, Juan Perez. KimTay reassigns the account to rep 35, Richard Hull. Using the design walked through in Lesson 1-2, what is the correct edit?

          • ✘a. REP holds one row per sales representative, not one row per customer; Hull already has his row, number 35.
          • ✔b. Correct - CUSTOMER.REP_NUM is a foreign key holding only the rep's number, so reassigning the account is a one-value change in one row.
          • ✘c. Copying Hull's details onto the customer row recreates the exact redundancy this design exists to avoid; the foreign key already reaches that data.
          • ✘d. INVOICE stores only CUSTOMER_NUM and has no REP_NUM column at all - the rep is reached through the customer.

          Remember: A foreign key means changing a relationship is one small value change, never a copy of the other table's data.

          Q2The intern who wanted one less table

          An intern argues that INVOICE_LINE is unnecessary: just put an ITEM_ID column on INVOICE. But invoice 50712 already carries two items, AV07 and FT88, and item CF21 appears on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711. Why does the intern's idea fail?

          • ✘a. Tables routinely mix text and number columns; ITEM_ID and INVOICE_NUM already sit side by side inside INVOICE_LINE.
          • ✘b. Cramming several values into one column makes them impossible to count, total, or filter one at a time - which is precisely why the connecting table exists.
          • ✘c. ITEM stores the catalog price, but it cannot record that invoice 50712 bought one AV07 at 64.99 - that fact belongs to the order, not the product.
          • ✔d. Correct - invoice 50712 has many items and CF21 sits on many invoices, so INVOICE_LINE carries one row per (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) pairing.

          Remember: A many-to-many relationship is resolved by a connecting table with one row per pairing, never by adding one more column.

          Q3The invoice that changed by itself

          Invoice 50710 sold 3 units of CF21 at 42.50 each on June 14. In July, KimTay raises CF21's catalog PRICE in ITEM to 46.00. KimTay's bookkeeper reprints invoice 50710 and it still bills 42.50 per unit. Why?

          • ✔a. Correct - QUOTED_PRICE is a value stored on the invoice line itself, which is why history stays accurate when the catalog price moves.
          • ✘b. Nothing locks ITEM.PRICE; prices are supposed to change, and the design protects old invoices instead of freezing the catalog.
          • ✘c. A foreign key points at another table's primary key and always shows that row's current value - it would have changed the total, not preserved it.
          • ✘d. No database reconstructs past prices on its own; the old price survives only because someone chose to store it at sale time.

          Remember: Store a value that must not move later, like QUOTED_PRICE, rather than looking it up from a table that keeps changing.

                  1-3 StayWell Student Accommodation DatabaseObjective 1

                  StayWell Student Accommodation manages off-campus housing near Millbrook University. Each property has a manager and is divided into rooms. Students sign a lease for a specific room, and make rent payments against that lease over time.

                  📖
                  Meet the database

                  StayWell is a fictional company built for this course, headquartered in Millbrook, OH. As with KimTay, this schema is an original design meant to teach the same concepts your book's StayWell chapters cover.

                  Primary key (underlined, bold)Foreign key (italic)One recordMany records (crow's foot)

                  StayWell's six tables follow the same reasoning you just walked through for KimTay in Lesson 1-2: give every table one clear job, and connect them with foreign keys instead of copying data around. A few StayWell-specific design choices worth noticing:

                  • ROOM uses a composite primary key: PROPERTY_ID + ROOM_NUM together, because room numbers repeat across properties (both buildings have a "Room 101").
                  • LEASE stores its own MONTHLY_RENT even though ROOM already has one. That's intentional — rent can change for future tenants without rewriting history for a lease that was already signed. You'll revisit exactly this design decision when Module 2 covers normalization.
                  • PAYMENT is where the one-to-many relationship really pays off: one lease, many monthly payments, each on its own row.

                  🔍 Knowledge check: the StayWell tables

                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                  Q1Room 101, twice over

                  StayWell's ROOM table holds room 101 at Millbrook Commons (P100) renting for 595.00 and room 101 at Sycamore Court (P200) renting for 610.00. The developer building the table first tried to make ROOM_NUM the primary key on its own. Why does that fail?

                  • ✘a. PROPERTY_ID is text as well and it is part of the key; a primary key value only has to be unique and always present, not numeric.
                  • ✔b. Correct - a composite primary key is used exactly when no single column is unique on its own, and (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) is unique for every room StayWell owns.
                  • ✘c. A column can be a foreign key and part of the primary key at the same time - ROOM.PROPERTY_ID is both.
                  • ✘d. Renumbering real rooms to rescue a weak key changes the business to fit the table; the composite key lets each property number its own rooms freely.

                  Remember: When one column's values repeat across rows, combine it with another column into a composite primary key instead of forcing the business to change.

                  Q2The rent that should not have moved

                  Trang Nguyen signed lease L001 for room 101 at Millbrook Commons at 595.00 a month. For next year StayWell raises that room's MONTHLY_RENT in ROOM to 640.00. A new developer on the project says LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT is duplicated data and should be deleted. What does Lesson 1-3 say?

                  • ✘a. Deleting it would rewrite history - the signed lease would silently jump to 640.00 the moment the room's rate changed.
                  • ✘b. STUDENT describes the person, not the agreement; putting rent there is real redundancy that serves no purpose.
                  • ✔c. Correct - the lesson calls this intentional: rent can change for future tenants without rewriting a lease that was already signed.
                  • ✘d. A DBMS does not compare unrelated columns in different tables; these two numbers are allowed to differ because they mean different things.

                  Remember: Two columns holding the same number are not automatically redundancy - LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT records what was agreed, ROOM.MONTHLY_RENT records what is charged now.

                  Q3Two checks, one lease

                  Lease L001 has two PAYMENT rows so far: 595.00 on August 1 and 595.00 on September 1. Millbrook Commons manager Diane Ortiz asks why StayWell does not just keep one AMOUNT_PAID of 1190.00 on the LEASE row instead. What is the best answer?

                  • ✔a. Correct - the lesson calls PAYMENT the place where one-to-many really pays off: one lease, many monthly payments, each on its own row with its own date.
                  • ✘b. PAYMENT_ID is PAYMENT's primary key; LEASE_ID is a foreign key, and it is supposed to repeat once for every payment made.
                  • ✘c. Both payments belong to lease L001 and therefore to the one student who signed it - the repetition here is across months, not across students.
                  • ✘d. Totals are easy to calculate from stored rows; the rows exist to preserve the detail that a single total would destroy.

                  Remember: On the many side of a one-to-many relationship, each event gets its own row so no detail is lost.

                  Q4Who manages Layla Ibrahim's building?

                  Layla Ibrahim is student S003 and holds lease L003. StayWell needs to know which manager to call about her building. Which chain of tables gets there, following the foreign keys stored on each table?

                  • ✘a. STUDENT holds only the student's own details - ID, name, email, home state - and has no link to a manager.
                  • ✘b. PAYMENT points back up to LEASE and stops there; it holds no property or manager information at all.
                  • ✘c. ROOM describes the physical room - type, rent, occupancy - and carries no MANAGER_ID; a manager belongs to the whole property.
                  • ✔d. Correct - LEASE holds PROPERTY_ID as a foreign key and PROPERTY holds MANAGER_ID, so the chain is STUDENT, LEASE, PROPERTY, MANAGER. The diagram routes LEASE through ROOM to PROPERTY, but because LEASE stores PROPERTY_ID itself, PROPERTY is reachable in one step.

                  Remember: To answer a question, follow the foreign keys table by table - each one names exactly which table it points at.

                  Summary Module Summary

                  A file system stores data as separate files that different programs manage independently, which invites redundancy, inconsistency, and isolation as an organization grows. A database, managed by a DBMS, stores related data once in structured tables so it can be shared, cross- referenced, and kept consistent. You met the two running examples for this course:

                  • KimTay Pet Supplies — REP, CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE.
                  • StayWell Student Accommodation — MANAGER, PROPERTY, ROOM, STUDENT, LEASE, and PAYMENT.

                  Next, Module 2 dives into why these tables are shaped the way they are — functional dependence, keys, and normalization — before Module 3 has you build them yourself with SQL.

                  Continue to Module 2 →

                  Terms Key Term

                  Database

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  A structured, shared collection of related data, organized so it can be queried and cross-referenced rather than duplicated across files.

                  DBMS

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  Database Management System — the software (MySQL, Oracle, Access...) used to define, secure, and manipulate a database.

                  Table

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  A named collection of records sharing the same set of fields, e.g. every row of CUSTOMER.

                  Record

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  One row in a table — a complete set of field values for a single entity.

                  Field

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  One named column of data within a table, e.g. CUSTOMER_NAME.

                  Data Redundancy

                  Click / press Enter to flip
                  The same fact stored in more than one place, increasing storage use and the risk of inconsistency.

                  🔍 Knowledge check: key terms

                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                  Q1Naming what you are pointing at

                  A tutor opens StayWell's STUDENT table, points at the EMAIL column holding tnguyen@example.edu, and asks what this course calls that named column. Which answer uses the course's key terms correctly?

                  • ✘a. A record is a whole row - the student's ID, last name, first name, email, and home state together - not one column of it.
                  • ✔b. Correct - the course defines a field, or column, as the smallest named unit of data in a table, such as CUSTOMER_NAME or EMAIL.
                  • ✘c. A table is the named collection of records that all share the same fields; STUDENT is the table, EMAIL is one of its fields.
                  • ✘d. A database is the whole structured collection of related tables - MANAGER, PROPERTY, ROOM, STUDENT, LEASE, and PAYMENT together.

                  Remember: Field is a column, record is a row, table is all the rows sharing those fields, and database is all the related tables.

                  Q2Is this redundancy or not?

                  KimTay's new bookkeeper is asked to hunt for data redundancy in the database. She notices that CUSTOMER_NUM 1120 appears on the CUSTOMER row for Access Pet Center and again on invoice 50710. Using this course's definition of data redundancy, what should she conclude?

                  • ✘a. Every foreign key by definition repeats a value that also exists in the table it points at - that shared value is the link itself. Redundancy is about repeating a fact such as a name, address, or price.
                  • ✘b. Without storing CUSTOMER_NUM, an invoice would have no way to say whose order it is; the key is the minimum needed to make the connection.
                  • ✔c. Correct - the name, street, and balance for Access Pet Center exist in exactly one place, which is what the definition of redundancy actually asks about.
                  • ✘d. The definition says the same fact stored in more than one place, so two copies already qualify; the count is not what makes this case different.

                  Remember: Repeating a key value to link tables is a reference, not redundancy; redundancy is copying the underlying facts.

                  Review Review Questions

                  Ten questions across everything Module 1 covered — why databases replaced files, the vocabulary, and the two case schemas. Nothing here is graded, so answer freely: the explanation opens the moment you choose, and it tells you why every option is right or wrong, not just the one you picked.

                  🔍 Module 1 review: files, vocabulary, KimTay and StayWell

                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                  Q1Software or the data itself?

                  A KimTay manager says "we bought a database last year — it cost more than the server." A student corrects her, pointing out that what the company actually bought was the DBMS. Using this module's definitions, what is the difference?

                  • ✘a. That is exactly backwards. The tables are the database; the software around them is the DBMS.
                  • ✔b. Correct — MySQL, Oracle, Access and PostgreSQL are DBMSs. KimTay's actual customer and invoice data is the database.
                  • ✘c. The module defines them separately on purpose. One is a product you install, the other is your organization's data.
                  • ✘d. Neither term has anything to do with how many machines are involved.

                  Remember: The DBMS is the software; the database is the data it manages.

                  Q2Naming one row

                  In KimTay's CUSTOMER table, the line reading 1120 / Access Pet Center / 215 Foster Ave. / Maple Grove / OH / 44601 / 3512.50 / 7500.00 / 20 is one complete set of values describing one customer. What is the correct term for that single line, and what is CUSTOMER_NAME on its own?

                  • ✘a. These are swapped. A field is one column; the whole line across all columns is the record.
                  • ✘b. A table is the whole collection of these lines, not one of them.
                  • ✔c. Correct — a record is one complete set of field values for a single entity, and a field is the smallest named unit of data.
                  • ✘d. "Data" means raw facts in general, and a DBMS is software, not a column.

                  Remember: Field = one column. Record = one row. Table = all the rows together.

                  Q3The question no one could answer

                  Before the database, KimTay's sales manager wanted a list of every customer in Brookville together with the total they had been invoiced this year. Customer cities lived in customer_list.xlsx and the invoice amounts lived in invoices_2026.docx, and there was no practical way to combine them. Which of the four file-system problems is this?

                  • ✘a. Redundancy is the same fact stored twice. The problem here is that the two facts are apart, not repeated.
                  • ✘b. Inconsistency is two copies disagreeing. Nothing here disagrees — the data simply cannot be combined.
                  • ✔c. Correct — isolation is data scattered across incompatible files, making questions that span more than one file hard to answer.
                  • ✘d. Nobody was blocked by permissions; the manager could open both files and still could not answer the question.

                  Remember: Isolation is about data being unreachable together, not about it being wrong.

                  Q4Why CUSTOMER does not store the rep's name

                  Every KimTay customer has exactly one assigned sales rep. CUSTOMER stores only REP_NUM — not the rep's last name, address or commission rate. Why was the design done that way?

                  • ✘a. The design assumes exactly one rep per customer. Reassignment is not the reason for the choice.
                  • ✔b. Correct — the rep's details are written once in REP, and CUSTOMER just points at that row with a foreign key.
                  • ✘c. Saving space is a minor side benefit. The real point is that one fact lives in one place, so it can only be wrong in one place.
                  • ✘d. There is no such rule. The same value appearing in two tables is exactly how foreign keys work.

                  Remember: A foreign key stores a reference instead of a copy, so a fact is recorded once.

                  Q5Two columns for one key

                  INVOICE_LINE's primary key is INVOICE_NUM and ITEM_ID together. Looking at the sample rows — invoice 50710 has lines for CF21 and DG04, and CF21 also appears on invoice 50711 — why can neither column be the primary key on its own?

                  • ✘a. There is no such rule. A composite key is used when it is needed, not because a table connects two others.
                  • ✔b. Correct — 50710 appears on two lines and CF21 appears on two invoices, so only the pair identifies one line.
                  • ✘c. A column can be both. INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM is a foreign key to INVOICE and part of the primary key here.
                  • ✘d. Data types have nothing to do with it. Uniqueness does.

                  Remember: A composite key is used when no single column is unique on its own.

                  Q6One invoice, many items — and back again

                  An invoice can list several items, and the same item can appear on many different invoices. How does KimTay's design handle that, and what is the relationship called?

                  • ✘a. A single ITEM_ID column on INVOICE could only ever record one item per invoice, which is the problem being solved.
                  • ✔b. Correct — INVOICE_LINE holds one row per (invoice, item) pair, which is how a many-to-many relationship is resolved.
                  • ✘c. One-to-one would mean each invoice had exactly one item and each item appeared on exactly one invoice. Neither is true.
                  • ✘d. Repeating the invoice would reintroduce the redundancy the whole design exists to avoid.

                  Remember: Many-to-many relationships are resolved with a connecting table.

                  Q7Room 101, twice

                  StayWell's ROOM table uses PROPERTY_ID and ROOM_NUM together as its primary key. Looking at the sample data, what makes that necessary?

                  • ✔a. Correct — P100 has a room 101 renting for 595.00 and P200 has a different room 101 renting for 610.00. It takes both columns to say which.
                  • ✘b. STUDENT, MANAGER, PROPERTY and LEASE all use single-column keys. The composite key is used only where it is needed.
                  • ✘c. Text columns can be primary keys — MANAGER_ID and STUDENT_ID both are.
                  • ✘d. Lease history lives in LEASE, not ROOM. ROOM has one row per physical room.

                  Remember: Room numbers repeat between buildings, so it takes the property and the number together.

                  Q8A copy that is not a mistake

                  ROOM already stores a MONTHLY_RENT, and LEASE stores a MONTHLY_RENT of its own. That looks like exactly the duplication this module warns about. Why is it deliberate here?

                  • ✘a. The lesson calls it intentional and says you will revisit the decision in Module 2, where it is defended rather than removed.
                  • ✘b. Speed is not the reason given, and it would be a poor justification on its own.
                  • ✔c. Correct — rent can change for future tenants without rewriting history for a lease already signed.
                  • ✘d. Both columns hold a monthly amount. Compare L001's 595.00 with room P100/101's 595.00.

                  Remember: A stored value that records what was agreed at the time is history, not redundancy.

                  Q9One lease, many payments

                  Student S001 signed lease L001 and has two payment rows against it, dated 2026-08-01 and 2026-09-01. Which relationship does PAYMENT illustrate, and what would go wrong if the payments were kept as extra columns on LEASE instead?

                  • ✘a. A lease does not have a fixed number of payments — L001 already has two and will collect more.
                  • ✘b. Each payment belongs to exactly one lease, so it is one-to-many. No connecting table is needed.
                  • ✔c. Correct — one lease has many payments, and giving each one its own row is what makes the number of payments open-ended.
                  • ✘d. Cramming several dates into one column is precisely the problem Module 2 opens with; it is not a workable fix.

                  Remember: One-to-many means the "many" side gets its own row per fact, not extra columns.

                  Q10Following the keys

                  A KimTay clerk is looking at invoice 50710 and needs to know which sales rep to notify. Using the sample data and the foreign keys in the schema, which path gets there, and who is the rep?

                  • ✔a. Correct — the chain INVOICE → CUSTOMER → REP is followed by matching the same key value from one table to the next.
                  • ✘b. INVOICE has no REP_NUM column. It stores CUSTOMER_NUM, and the rep is reached one step further along.
                  • ✘c. Items have no rep. ITEM stores catalog details only, and CF21 is on invoice 50710 but tells you nothing about staffing.
                  • ✘d. They are connected, just not directly. Two foreign keys in a row link them.

                  Remember: Tables are reconnected by matching the same key value from one table to the next.

                  Exercises Case Exercises

                  Original practice items for this module — work through each one, then click to check your thinking.

                  1. KimTay's owner wants to know: "Which of our customers currently owe us more than $2,000?" Which table(s) would you query, and which single column holds the answer?

                  Look in the CUSTOMER table and read the BALANCE column: every customer whose balance is above $2,000 belongs in the answer. No second table is needed — the balance is stored directly on the customer record, not derived from invoices.

                  2. A StayWell manager asks: "How much rent has student S002 actually paid so far?" Which table(s) are involved, and why isn't LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT enough on its own?

                  You need PAYMENT together with LEASE, matched on the LEASE_ID they share, adding up AMOUNT for that student's lease. MONTHLY_RENT only tells you the agreed rate, not how many payments have actually been made — that history lives in PAYMENT.

                  3. In your own words: why would KimTay keep QUOTED_PRICE on INVOICE_LINE instead of always looking up the current PRICE from ITEM?

                  Prices change over time. If INVOICE_LINE only pointed at ITEM.PRICE, an old invoice's total would silently change every time KimTay updated a price. Storing the price at the time of sale keeps historical invoices accurate. This tension — convenience vs. historical accuracy — comes up again with StayWell's LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT in Module 2.

                  2-1 Database ConceptsObjective 2

                  Objective 2 for this course asks you to tell these four ways of organizing data apart, and to see how each one represents entity relationships — how one kind of record relates to another. Click through each model below; all four illustrate the same real-world idea (a property, its rooms, who's responsible for them) so you can compare them directly.

                  Data is arranged as a strict tree: every child record has exactly one parent. A property's rooms belong to that property alone. Fast to traverse top-down, but a record that genuinely needs two parents (a room serviced by both its property and a separate maintenance team) doesn't fit cleanly. Historically used by systems like IBM's IMS.

                  A generalization of the hierarchical model: a child record can have more than one parent, forming a graph instead of a strict tree. This fixed the "two parents" problem, at the cost of more complex navigation — you had to know the path through the graph to find your data. Standardized as CODASYL in the 1970s.

                  Data lives in independent tables (relations), and tables are connected not by rigid parent/child pointers but by matching key values — a CUSTOMER row relates to a REP row simply because they share the same REP_NUM. This is far more flexible: you can query any relationship you need with SQL, without the schema having to anticipate it in advance. This is the model MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Access all use, and the one this entire course is built around.

                  Data and the behavior (methods) that act on it are bundled into objects, organized into classes that can inherit from one another — a GradStudent is-a Student with extra attributes. Popular for applications with complex, deeply nested data (CAD systems, multimedia), though most business systems — including KimTay and StayWell — are still better served by the relational model.

                  Quick comparison
                  ModelStructureRelationship styleStill common today?
                  HierarchicalStrict treeOne parent per childNiche (some legacy & XML-like systems)
                  NetworkGraphMultiple parents allowedRare (mostly historical)
                  RelationalIndependent tablesMatching key valuesYes — MySQL, Oracle, Access, PostgreSQL
                  Object-orientedClasses & objectsInheritance + object referencesSpecialized use cases

                  🔍 Knowledge check: the four data models

                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                  Q1The room with two owners

                  StayWell's legacy filing system stores every room record underneath exactly one property, so the record for Millbrook Commons' Room 101 hangs under that one property and nowhere else. The maintenance office now needs each of those rooms to also be reachable from the crew that services it, and the old system simply cannot do it. Which data model was created as the fix for this exact two-parent problem?

                  • ✔a. Correct - the network model is the generalization of the hierarchical model in which a child record may have several parents, standardized as CODASYL.
                  • ✘b. A hierarchical database is a strict tree: every child gets exactly one parent, so there is no legal place to hang that room record a second time.
                  • ✘c. Hierarchical and network systems stored records too; what makes relational different is linking by matching key values, and it was not the historical answer to this problem.
                  • ✘d. Inheritance means one class is a kind of another class, not that a record has two owners; a Room is not a kind of maintenance crew.

                  Remember: Hierarchical gives every child exactly one parent; the network model was the historical fix that allowed a record to have more than one.

                  Q2The question nobody planned for

                  KimTay's sales manager suddenly asks something nobody anticipated: which customers of rep 20, Valerie Kaiser, have ever bought item CF21? No path for that question was built into the database when it was designed. Why can a relational database answer it without anyone redesigning the schema?

                  • ✘a. Stored parent-child pointers are the older hierarchical and network approach; relational tables hold no pointers, only shared key values.
                  • ✘b. Having to anticipate every access path in advance is precisely the limitation of the hierarchical and network models that the relational model removed.
                  • ✔c. Correct - a CUSTOMER row relates to a REP row simply because they share a REP_NUM value, and an INVOICE_LINE row reaches an ITEM the same way, so any relationship can be joined later.
                  • ✘d. Relational design deliberately keeps REP, CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, and ITEM separate; cramming every column into one wide table is the redundancy problem from Lesson 1-1.

                  Remember: Relational tables link through matching key values, so the database can answer questions its designer never planned for.

                  Q3The class that borrowed its parent's fields

                  A StayWell developer sketches a Lease class that stores the lease data and also owns a monthsRemaining() method that computes an answer from that data. She then adds SubletLease, which reuses everything Lease has and adds a subtenant, and RenewalLease, which adds a priorLeaseId. Which model is she sketching, and what feature is doing the work?

                  • ✘a. A hierarchical tree links stored data records such as PROPERTY and ROOM; inheritance shares attributes and behavior between class definitions, which is a different idea.
                  • ✘b. A method is behavior that belongs to a class, not a second owning record; the network model is about one record having more than one parent record.
                  • ✘c. Storing the idea in tables is what you would do to keep it relationally, but a sketch with methods attached to the data is object-oriented by definition.
                  • ✔d. Correct - the object-oriented model bundles data with the behavior that acts on it, in classes that inherit from one another.

                  Remember: Data bundled with its behavior, in classes that inherit from other classes, is the signature of the object-oriented model.

                          0 / 8 placed

                          2-2 Functional DependenceObjective 3

                          Functional dependence is the idea underneath every key, every table split, and every normalization rule you'll use for the rest of this course. It has an intimidating name and a simple idea inside it, so start with the idea.

                          One question, asked about two columns

                          The whole concept is this question:

                          ❓
                          The only question you have to ask

                          If I tell you this, do you know that — every time, with no guessing?

                          If the answer is yes, you have found a functional dependency. Try it on your own campus.

                          If I tell you a student's ID number, do you know their name? Yes. An ID belongs to exactly one student, so there is nothing to guess. The ID determines the name, and you write it with an arrow:

                          STUDENT_ID → NAME

                          Now turn it around. If I tell you a student's name, do you know their ID number? Not for certain. There could be two students called Sam Rivera. So NAME does not determine STUDENT_ID.

                          That is the most important thing on this page: arrows point one way. Reading one backwards is the single most common mistake students make with this topic.

                          Why the word "functional"?

                          This is the only genuinely confusing part, and it is just borrowed maths vocabulary. A function is a machine: you put one value in, and you always get the same one value out. Put an ID in, get a name out. Put the same ID in tomorrow, get the same name.

                          So do not read "functional" as "it works" or "it is useful". Read it as one in, exactly one out. Once you hear it that way, the phrase stops being strange.

                          The arrow gets read out loud several different ways. They all mean the same thing, and your textbook will use all of them:

                          • "A determines B"
                          • "B is functionally dependent on A"
                          • "If you know A, you know B"
                          • "A is the determinant of B"

                          Two things that trip everyone up

                          1. It is about sameness, not scarcity. CUSTOMER_NUM → CUSTOMER_NAME does not mean customer 1120 shows up only once. It can appear on a hundred invoice lines. It means every one of those hundred lines shows the same name. A determinant is allowed to repeat as often as it likes, so long as what follows it never changes.

                          This also tells you how to catch a broken dependency — look for one value on the left with two different values on the right:

                          ✅ The dependency holds

                          CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME
                          1120Access Pet Center
                          1120Access Pet Center
                          1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets

                          1120 repeats, and that is fine. Both of its rows give the same answer, so "what is customer 1120 called?" has exactly one answer.

                          ❌ The dependency is broken

                          CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME
                          1120Access Pet Center
                          1120Riverside Pet Clinic
                          1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets

                          Now 1120 answers to two completely different names (highlighted). Anyone who asks "what is customer 1120 called?" has to guess, so CUSTOMER_NUM no longer determines CUSTOMER_NAME.

                          One value on the left with two different values on the right is the only thing you are looking for. In Lesson 2-5 you will run exactly this check as a query, on real data.

                          2. Sometimes one column is not enough. If I tell you an item ID, do you know how many were ordered? No — someone ordered 3 of CF21 on one invoice, and someone else ordered 2 on another. But if I tell you the invoice and the item, now you know. That needs two columns on the left of the arrow:

                          (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) → NUM_ORDERED

                          A left side made of more than one column is called a composite determinant. Keep it in mind, because second normal form in Lesson 2-5 is entirely about tables whose determinant is composite.

                          The formal definition

                          Now that you have the idea, here is the same thing in the words your textbook and your exam will use:

                          📖
                          Functional dependence, defined

                          Column B is functionally dependent on column A (written A → B) if, for every possible value of A, there is exactly one associated value of B. A is called the determinant. If A can be more than one column, that's a composite determinant.

                          Read that against the question you started with. "For every possible value of A there is exactly one associated value of B" is the careful way of saying if I tell you A, you know B, with no guessing.

                          Some real functional dependencies from the KimTay and StayWell schemas:

                          Determinant → Dependent
                          DeterminantDependent(s)Why
                          ITEM_IDDESCRIPTION, CATEGORY, PRICEEach item id names exactly one product, at exactly one catalog price.
                          CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME, REP_NUMEach customer number belongs to exactly one company record and one rep.
                          (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID)NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICEOnly the combination of which invoice and which item pins down a single quantity/price — ITEM_ID alone repeats across many invoices.
                          (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM)ROOM_TYPE, MONTHLY_RENTRoom 101 at Millbrook Commons is a specific room; PROPERTY_ID or ROOM_NUM alone isn't enough.
                          ⚠️
                          A dependency is a business rule, not a coincidence

                          In the small CUSTOMER sample from Module 1, every city happens to map to exactly one state (Maple Grove → OH, Northfield → OH). That might tempt you to say "CITY determines STATE." But that's just an accident of a small sample — nothing stops a real database from having a Springfield, OH and a Springfield, IL. A true functional dependency has to hold for every possible row the business could ever store, which is why designers rely on something like ZIP → CITY, STATE instead (real ZIP codes do genuinely pin down one city/state).

                          So the question has a second half hiding in it. Not just "do I know that?" but "would I still know it if the business grew to a million rows?" The data can show you a dependency is false. Only the business can tell you it is true.

                          Run the test yourself: for each pair below, ask "if I tell you the left one, do I know the right one, every time?"  (a) ROOM_NUM → MONTHLY_RENT  (b) REP_NUM → LAST_NAME  (c) CATEGORY → ITEM_ID  (d) LEASE_ID → STUDENT_ID

                          (a) No. Room 101 exists at Millbrook Commons for 595 and at Sycamore Court for 610. Tell me only "101" and I still have to ask which building, so ROOM_NUM alone determines nothing. It takes the composite determinant (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM).

                          (b) Yes. Each rep number belongs to exactly one person, so 35 always means Hull.

                          (c) No, and it fails in the other direction. Habitat contains both AV07 and FT88, so telling you a category leaves you guessing between items. The arrow works the other way round: ITEM_ID → CATEGORY.

                          (d) Yes. A lease is signed by exactly one student, so L003 always means S003. Note that the reverse is not guaranteed — a student could sign two leases over two years — which is another reminder that arrows point one way.

                          🔍 Knowledge check: functional dependence

                          Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                          Q1The pattern that was only a coincidence

                          StayWell's four sample students are Nguyen, Carter, Ibrahim, and Park, and no two last names match. A StayWell design intern concludes that LAST_NAME pins down exactly one student, so she writes LAST_NAME -> STUDENT_ID as a functional dependency. Is she right?

                          • ✘a. A pattern that holds across four sample rows is a coincidence, not a business rule; the next Park who enrolls destroys it.
                          • ✔b. Correct - a true functional dependency has to hold for every possible row, which is why designers trust ZIP -> CITY, STATE but not accidental patterns in a small sample.
                          • ✘c. Any column or set of columns can be a determinant; ZIP is the lesson's example and it is not a primary key anywhere in these schemas.
                          • ✘d. Data type is irrelevant here - ITEM_ID and ZIP are both text-like, and both genuinely determine other columns.

                          Remember: A functional dependency is a business rule that must hold for every possible row, not a pattern that happens to hold in a small sample.

                          Q2Two rooms numbered 101

                          Millbrook Commons rents its Room 101 for 595.00 a month. Sycamore Court has a Room 101 of its own, and that one rents for 610.00. On her design worksheet the same intern writes ROOM_NUM -> MONTHLY_RENT. Which statement correctly captures the real dependency in the ROOM table?

                          • ✘a. The value 101 sits on two different ROOM rows, one carrying 595.00 and one carrying 610.00, so one determinant value points at two dependent values and the definition fails.
                          • ✘b. The arrow runs from determinant to dependent, and two rooms can easily charge the same rent, so a rent amount cannot pin down one room.
                          • ✘c. Millbrook Commons alone charges 595.00 for room 101 and 450.00 for room 102, so one PROPERTY_ID value is attached to several different rents.
                          • ✔d. Correct - only the combination of which property and which room determines a single rent, which is exactly what a composite determinant means.

                          Remember: When one column's value repeats across genuinely different things, the determinant has to be a combination of columns.

                          Q3One lease, two payments

                          The same design intern moves on to PAYMENT, which stores PAYMENT_ID, LEASE_ID, PAYMENT_DATE, and AMOUNT. She claims LEASE_ID -> AMOUNT because each lease has one rent figure. Lease L001 already has two payment rows recorded against it - both of them happen to be 595.00 - and StayWell is about to start recording security deposits and partial payments in the same table. Does the dependency hold?

                          • ✔a. Correct - one LEASE_ID can sit on many payment rows, and although today's two rows for L001 both happen to be 595.00, nothing stops a deposit, a partial payment, and a full month's rent from carrying three different AMOUNT values under that same LEASE_ID, so only PAYMENT_ID determines one amount.
                          • ✘b. Being a foreign key says a value must match a row in another table; it says nothing about determining the rest of this row, and here it clearly does not.
                          • ✘c. Single-column determinants are perfectly normal - ITEM_ID -> DESCRIPTION and CUSTOMER_NUM -> CUSTOMER_NAME are both single-column dependencies.
                          • ✘d. Storing the same kind of value is not a dependency; a lease can take a deposit, a partial payment, and a catch-up payment, all different amounts.

                          Remember: A -> B only holds when one value of A never sits beside two different values of B - and it has to be impossible, not merely absent from today's rows.

                          2-3 Primary KeysObjective 3

                          A primary key is the column (or set of columns) a table's designer chooses to uniquely identify every row. It's really a special case of the idea you just learned: a primary key is a determinant that determines every other column in the table, and does so uniquely — no two rows may share the same key value, and a key value may never be missing (this is called entity integrity).

                          Candidate key

                          Any column (or column set) that could serve as the primary key — it's unique and never null. A table can have more than one candidate key.

                          Primary key

                          The candidate key the designer actually picks to identify rows and to be referenced by foreign keys elsewhere.

                          Alternate key

                          Any candidate key that wasn't chosen as the primary key. The designer can still require it to stay unique, so no two rows ever repeat the same value.

                          Composite key

                          A primary key made of two or more columns together, used when no single column is unique on its own — like ROOM's (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM).

                          💡
                          A fast test for "does this need a composite key?"

                          Ask: could this single column's value repeat across rows that are genuinely different things? ROOM_NUM repeats across properties (every building has a "101"), so ROOM_NUM alone fails the test — pair it with PROPERTY_ID and the combination becomes unique.

                          🔍 Knowledge check: primary keys

                          Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                          Q1The invoice with no number

                          A KimTay clerk saves a new invoice for Access Pet Center but leaves INVOICE_NUM blank, planning to type the number in later when the paper form comes back from the warehouse. In the spreadsheet she used before, a blank cell was harmless. In a DBMS that enforces entity integrity, which rule does the blank primary key break?

                          • ✘a. A NULL in an ordinary column is fine - STUDENT.EMAIL is declared EMAIL VARCHAR(30) with no NOT NULL, so it may legally be empty - but a NULL primary key leaves a row that no query and no INVOICE_LINE row can ever point to.
                          • ✘b. The composite key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) belongs to INVOICE_LINE; the INVOICE table is identified by INVOICE_NUM alone.
                          • ✔c. Correct - entity integrity means the primary key is unique and never missing for every row in the table.
                          • ✘d. Entity integrity has two halves, no duplicates and no missing values, so a single blank key breaks it even if it is the only one.

                          Remember: Entity integrity means every primary key value is present and unique - a blank key value is never acceptable.

                          Q2The email column nobody constrained

                          STUDENT stores STUDENT_ID and EMAIL, and the shipped schema declares EMAIL VARCHAR(30) with no NOT NULL and no UNIQUE constraint. All four students on file happen to have an address and no two of them match, and LEASE rows point at students using STUDENT_ID. Layla Ibrahim then replaces her personal address with a new university one. Which column should be STUDENT's primary key, and what is EMAIL's real status?

                          • ✘a. Four tidy sample rows are a coincidence, not a guarantee - the same sample fallacy as LAST_NAME -> STUDENT_ID, and here the schema itself would accept a duplicate address or none at all.
                          • ✘b. A candidate key must be unique and never null for every possible row; because EMAIL is declared without NOT NULL or UNIQUE, the DBMS would happily store a second student with Layla's old address, so EMAIL is not a candidate key and cannot be an alternate key here.
                          • ✘c. Composite keys are for tables where no single column identifies a row; STUDENT_ID already does, and pairing them would make the key change every time an email does and let a NULL into the key.
                          • ✔d. Correct - STUDENT_ID is stable, always present, unique, and already referenced by LEASE, while EMAIL carries no uniqueness or not-null guarantee at all.

                          Remember: A column is only a candidate key when the schema guarantees it is unique and never missing; and among real candidates, choose the one that never changes.

                          Q3Two payments on the same day

                          A StayWell design intern sketches a redesign of PAYMENT and proposes that the pair (LEASE_ID, PAYMENT_DATE) serve as the primary key instead of PAYMENT_ID, reasoning that a lease normally receives one payment a month. Bruce Feldman confirms that most of his tenants do pay once a month, and the four payment rows on file do happen to have distinct lease-and-date pairs. Apply the same repeat-across-different-things test the lesson uses when deciding whether a column needs a partner. What is wrong with her plan?

                          • ✘a. More columns does not mean more unique; a composite key is only correct when no single column identifies a row, and PAYMENT_ID already does that on its own.
                          • ✔b. Correct - the test asks whether the value could repeat across rows that are genuinely different things, and two payments posted to one lease on one date do exactly that, no matter how tidy today's four rows look.
                          • ✘c. Dates are legal inside keys - the trouble is repetition, not the data type, and the same pair would be just as unsafe built from any other repeatable column.
                          • ✘d. ROOM's primary key is (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM), and PROPERTY_ID is also a foreign key to PROPERTY, so a foreign key can absolutely sit inside a primary key.

                          Remember: Add a column to the key only when no single column identifies a row, then run the repeat test on the combination itself.

                          🧩 Sort the columns: could this be a primary key?

                          Click a column card, then click the zone that fits it. Exactly one zone is defensible per card: ask whether the value repeats, whether the business can change it after it is assigned, and whether pairing it with one specific partner column is what makes this table's declared key.
