                                  2-4 Database DesignObjective 3

                                  Good database design rarely starts with SQL. It starts with understanding what the organization actually needs to track, then moving through a deliberate sequence of design phases:

                                  1

                                  Requirements gathering

                                  Find out what questions the database has to answer and what data already exists. The answers are usually sitting in what the organization already produces — its spreadsheets, order forms, invoices, receipts, and schedules. KimTay's paper invoices and StayWell's lease sheets are the requirements documents for those two databases, and for your own project the records you already have are yours.

                                  2

                                  Conceptual design

                                  Identify entities (CUSTOMER, ROOM, LEASE...), their attributes, and how they relate to one another. This is usually sketched as an ER diagram before a single table is created — see Lesson 2-6.

                                  3

                                  Logical design & normalization

                                  Turn the ER diagram into a set of relational tables, choosing primary/foreign keys and applying the normalization rules from Lesson 2-5 to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

                                  4

                                  Physical design

                                  Decide concrete data types, constraints, indexes, and which DBMS to implement it in (MySQL, Oracle, Access — Module 3 covers how these differ).

                                  5

                                  Implementation & maintenance

                                  Create the tables, load data, build the queries and applications that use it, then monitor and evolve the design as requirements change.

                                  📝
                                  Where KimTay and StayWell came from

                                  Both schemas you've been using since Module 1 went through exactly this process: a conceptual ER diagram (Lesson 2-6), a check for functional dependencies and normal form violations (Lessons 2-2 and 2-5), and finally a physical CREATE TABLE implementation (Module 3). Skipping straight to "physical" — just picking columns that seem convenient — is how most of the redundancy and anomaly problems from Lesson 1-1 creep back in.

                                  🔍 Knowledge check: the five design phases

                                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                  Q1The requirements nobody gathered

                                  KimTay's owner emails a developer a list of column names and says "just build this table by Friday." Nobody has looked at the invoices, stock sheets, or reports the bookkeeper and the warehouse staff actually work from today. According to this course's five design phases, what should happen before anything else?

                                  • ✘a. Data types and DBMS choice are physical design, phase four, and cannot be decided sensibly before anyone knows what the system must do.
                                  • ✔b. Requirements gathering is phase one -- you work out what questions the database must answer and what data the business already keeps, before designing anything.
                                  • ✘c. Building first skips phases one through three entirely, and there is nothing to normalize until requirements and a conceptual design exist.
                                  • ✘d. A list of column names is one person's guess; conceptual design needs the real business questions behind it, which the existing paperwork reveals.

                                  Remember: Design starts with people, not columns: gather requirements before anything is drawn or built.

                                  Q2Picking VARCHAR and an index

                                  StayWell's ER diagram is finished and the tables have been normalized on paper. The developer now decides ROOM_TYPE will be VARCHAR(10), adds an index on STUDENT.LAST_NAME, and chooses MySQL as the DBMS. Which design phase is the developer working in?

                                  • ✘a. Requirements gathering collects business questions, not column types, and it happens long before any DBMS is chosen.
                                  • ✘b. Conceptual design ends once the entities, attributes, and relationships are settled, and the ER diagram here is already done.
                                  • ✘c. Logical design turns the diagram into tables with primary and foreign keys; the type stored in a column is a separate, later decision.
                                  • ✔d. Concrete data types, constraints, indexes, and which DBMS to implement in are exactly what phase four, physical design, covers.

                                  Remember: Data types, indexes, constraints, and DBMS choice all belong to physical design, phase four.

                                  Q3Normalizing after go-live

                                  A developer drafting KimTay's database built a flat INVOICE table that repeats the customer's city on every invoice row, then loaded 4,000 rows into it. Noticing the repetition only now, the developer says it can be "normalized later, since the DBMS will sort it out." What is wrong with that plan?

                                  • ✘a. Physical design covers data types, constraints, and indexes; normalization is a logical-design step that comes before any of that.
                                  • ✘b. An index speeds up lookups, but it never removes redundant repeated values or the update anomalies they cause.
                                  • ✔c. Normalization is phase three, logical design, so doing it after 4,000 rows are loaded turns a paper decision into a risky data migration.
                                  • ✘d. Requirements gathering is phase one and produces business questions, not tables, so there is nothing to normalize until logical design creates them.

                                  Remember: Normalize during logical design, on paper -- after go-live it becomes a data migration.

                                  2-5 NormalizationObjective 3

                                  The idea, before any database words

                                  Say you run payroll for a small company, and you keep the whole thing on one spreadsheet. You add a row every time someone files a week of hours, and you write down everything you might need:

                                  The timesheet — one row per employee, per week
                                  EmployeeWeekDepartmentManagerManager's phoneCertificationsHours
                                  R. AlvarezMar 4ShippingD. Okafor555-0134forklift, first aid38
                                  R. AlvarezMar 11ShippingD. Okafor555-0134forklift, first aid41
                                  T. BoydMar 4BillingS. Marsh555-0199notary35
                                  T. BoydMar 11BillingS. Marsh555-0199notary40

                                  It works in week one. Then four things go wrong — and every one of them has happened to a real company that stored its data this way.

                                  You write the same thing over and over

                                  Okafor's phone number lands on every row Alvarez files. That is fifty-two copies of one phone number in a year, for one employee, and fifty-two chances to mistype it.

                                  Changing one fact means fixing it everywhere

                                  Okafor gets a new number. Now every row in Shipping has to change. Miss one and the sheet shows two different numbers — with nothing marking which is the wrong one.

                                  Erasing one thing erases another by accident

                                  Boyd leaves the company, so you delete their rows. You just erased the only record that Billing exists and that Marsh's number is 555-0199.

                                  You cannot write down a fact on its own

                                  A new department opens on Monday, before anyone has logged an hour against it. There is nowhere to put it. The sheet can only describe a department while somebody is filing hours.

                                  Normalization is the fix your common sense already suggests: stop writing everything on one sheet. Keep a sheet for employees, a sheet for departments, a sheet for managers, and a sheet for hours. Write each fact in exactly one place. When you need the whole picture back, you look things up across the sheets — which is what a join does, and what Module 5 is about.

                                  So how do you decide which sheet a fact belongs on? Ask one question about it: what does this fact actually describe?

                                  • The phone number describes the manager. It goes on the manager sheet.
                                  • The department describes the employee. It goes on the employee sheet.
                                  • The hours describe the employee in that week — you need both to know the number. They go on the timesheet.
                                  • The certifications describe the employee, but "forklift, first aid" is two separate facts squashed into one box. Try counting how many people hold a forklift certification without reading every box by eye.

                                  The three normal forms are just that same question asked three times, in order:

                                  📖
                                  All three rules, in plain English

                                  1NF — one box, one independently queryable value. If a cell contains a list of separate facts, store those facts as separate rows. A comma inside one otherwise atomic value, such as a mailing address, does not by itself violate 1NF.
                                  2NF — if it takes two things to name a row, do not store facts that only need one of them. It takes an employee and a week to name a timesheet row, but the department only needs the employee, so the department does not belong here.
                                  3NF — every fact on a row should describe what the row is about. The manager's phone number describes the manager, not the week's hours, so it does not belong here either.

                                  That is the whole idea. You can stop there and still be right about most things.

                                  The rest of this lesson is the careful version. It gives each rule its proper name, shows you how to work out which facts depend on which, and shows you how to check that the current data still reconstructs after you split the page apart.

                                  The same four problems, with real data

                                  Now watch the timesheet's four problems happen to StayWell. Imagine they started with one wide spreadsheet-style report instead of six tables — something a manager might actually build first:

                                  An unnormalized StayWell lease report
                                  STUDENT_IDSTUDENT_NAMEPROPERTY_IDPROPERTY_NAMEMANAGER_NAMEROOM_NUMROOM_TYPEMONTHLY_RENTPAYMENT_DATES
                                  S001Trang NguyenP100Millbrook CommonsDiane Ortiz101Single595.002026-08-01, 2026-09-01
                                  S002Miles CarterP100Millbrook CommonsDiane Ortiz102Double450.002026-08-01
                                  S003Layla IbrahimP200Sycamore CourtBruce Feldman201Studio725.002026-08-01
                                  ⚠️
                                  Spot the repeating group

                                  PAYMENT_DATES crams multiple values into a single cell for S001 — that's a repeating group, and it's the first thing normalization removes.

                                  Those problems have proper names, which you will need for the exam and will meet in the textbook. They are the timesheet's problems wearing lab coats — the word anomaly just means "something that goes wrong that should not have to":

                                  • Update anomaly — one fact, many copies. Fixing Diane Ortiz's name means finding and changing it on every one of her properties' rows. This is Okafor's phone number all over again.
                                  • Deletion anomaly — erasing one thing quietly erases another. Remove StayWell's only student at Sycamore Court and you also delete the fact that Sycamore Court exists. This is Boyd leaving the company.
                                  • Insertion anomaly — you cannot record a fact by itself. You cannot add a new property until it has a student, because there is nowhere to put PROPERTY_NAME on its own. This is the new department with no hours logged against it yet.

                                  Normalization is the step-by-step process of splitting a table like this into smaller, better-behaved tables, so that none of the three can happen in the first place.

                                  All three point to misplaced dependencies, and Lesson 2-2 already gave you the language for them. A key determines every column in a valid relation; the question is whether another, smaller determinant reveals that the row is mixing different kinds of facts. In the flat StayWell report, the row identifier determines PROPERTY_ID, which determines MANAGER_ID and then MANAGER_NAME. The manager fact therefore belongs with its real determinant, not repeated on every lease row.

                                  Normalization is just taking that seriously. Write down the functional dependencies you can see in the data. Then split tables until each one states one kind of fact about one key, and nothing else. The normal forms are names for how far you have got.

                                  📖
                                  The version to memorise

                                  After a relation satisfies 1NF, a useful 2NF/3NF mnemonic is that every non-key attribute depends on the whole key and nothing but the key. "The whole key" points to 2NF — the department needed only the employee, not the employee and the week. "Nothing but the key" points to 3NF — the phone number described the manager, not the week's hours.

                                  Keep 1NF separate from that mnemonic: it requires relational rows and atomic values for the domain, with no repeating groups or independently queryable lists inside one cell.

                                  Simple 1NF example

                                  Two columns, two rows. One cell has a comma in it. That is all it takes to break 1NF:

                                  ❌ Breaks 1NF

                                  EMPLOYEECERTIFICATIONS
                                  R. Alvarezforklift, first aid
                                  T. Boydnotary

                                  Two facts are squashed into one box. To the database that highlighted cell is a single lump of text, not two certifications.

                                  ✅ Satisfies 1NF

                                  EMPLOYEECERTIFICATION
                                  R. Alvarezforklift
                                  R. Alvarezfirst aid
                                  T. Boydnotary

                                  The list became rows. Two rows turned into three, the employee name repeats, and that is fine — repeating a value down a column is normal.

                                  Nothing was lost and nothing was invented. The same three facts now sit in three boxes instead of two. That is the whole rule. The payoff is immediate: "how many people hold a forklift certification?" is now something you count, where before it meant reading every box by eye and hoping nobody typed it differently.

                                  In plain English: one box, one independently queryable value. A list such as "forklift, first aid" needs separate rows; ordinary punctuation inside a single atomic value does not.

                                  Rule: every column must hold a single, atomic value — no lists inside a cell. Fix: give each payment its own row, in its own table, linked back by a key:

                                  PAYMENT (1NF-compliant)
                                  STUDENT_IDPAYMENT_DATE
                                  S0012026-08-01
                                  S0012026-09-01
                                  S0022026-08-01
                                  S0032026-08-01

                                  In plain English: if it takes two things to name a row, do not store facts that only need one of them. It took an employee and a week to name a timesheet row, so the employee's department — which only needs the employee — did not belong on that sheet.

                                  Rule: once the repeating groups are gone and a key has been chosen, every non-key column must depend on the whole key. A column determined by only part of a composite key is a partial dependency, and removing partial dependencies is the entire job of 2NF.

                                  Once a relation is in 1NF, it has no partial dependency when every candidate key is a single column: there is no proper subset of a one-column key. A single-column chosen primary key alone is not enough if another candidate key is composite. The unnormalized StayWell report above cannot be called 2NF until its repeating payment list has first been brought into 1NF.

                                  Second: the rule bites as soon as a key has two columns. That is what a table of order lines, enrolments or lease-months looks like. KimTay's flat shipping report is the textbook case:

                                  INVOICE_FLAT — one row per item on an invoice, key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID)
                                  INVOICE_NUMITEM_IDINVOICE_DATECUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEITEM_DESCRIPTIONCATEGORYNUM_ORDEREDQUOTED_PRICE
                                  50710CF212026-06-141120Access Pet CenterGrain-Free Dry Food 30lbFood342.50
                                  50710DG042026-06-141120Access Pet CenterNylon Dog Leash 6ftAccessory211.99
                                  50711CF212026-06-141420Whiskers & Wags BoutiqueGrain-Free Dry Food 30lbFood242.50
                                  50711GR152026-06-141420Whiskers & Wags BoutiqueSmall Animal Grooming KitGrooming115.25
                                  50712AV072026-06-151225Downtown Aquarium & PetsAviary Starter CageHabitat164.99
                                  50712FT882026-06-151225Downtown Aquarium & PetsFish Tank Filter KitHabitat227.75

                                  It takes both columns to identify one line, so the key is (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID). Now interrogate every other column in turn — what is the smallest thing that fixes its value?

                                  PARTIAL   INVOICE_NUM            →  INVOICE_DATE, CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
PARTIAL   ITEM_ID                →  ITEM_DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY
FULL      INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID   →  NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE

                                  The label on the left is the verdict: PARTIAL where the determinant is only part of the key, FULL where it is the whole key. Only the FULL row is allowed to stay in a table keyed by (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID).

                                  Fix: give each determinant a table of its own, and leave behind only the columns that genuinely need both halves of the key. Three tables come out: INVOICE (INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE, CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME), ITEM (ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY), and INVOICE_LINE (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE). Notice that CF21's description, written down twice in the flat report, is now written down once.

                                  StayWell's room sheet follows the same test. ROOM_TYPE and MONTHLY_RENT require the whole room key (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM), so they stay in ROOM. If those room facts were copied into a LEASE table keyed by LEASE_ID, they would instead be reached through the room reference and would not belong there.

                                  In plain English: every fact on a row should describe what the row is about. The manager's phone number describes the manager, not the week's hours, so it belongs on the manager's own sheet — not on every timesheet row they will ever sign off.

                                  Rule: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column instead of on the primary key. When it does, the dependency reaches the key only by passing through something else, which is why it is called a transitive dependency.

                                  In the StayWell report, MANAGER_NAME is determined by MANAGER_ID, and each property row carries that manager reference. The dependency chain is therefore row key → PROPERTY_ID → MANAGER_ID → MANAGER_NAME. The manager fact is reached through non-key attributes rather than describing the lease row directly.

                                  The cost is easy to see. Diane Ortiz's name gets stored once per student living in one of her buildings, instead of once per manager. Change it and you have to find every copy.

                                  The same fault survives into KimTay's 2NF result. Look at the INVOICE table that came out of step 2:

                                  INVOICE after 2NF — in second normal form, still not in third
                                  INVOICE_NUM (key)INVOICE_DATECUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMECUSTOMER_CITY
                                  507102026-06-141120Access Pet CenterMaple Grove
                                  507112026-06-141420Whiskers & Wags BoutiqueBrookville
                                  507122026-06-151225Downtown Aquarium & PetsNorthfield

                                  CUSTOMER_NAME and CUSTOMER_CITY are fixed by CUSTOMER_NUM, and CUSTOMER_NUM is not this table's key: INVOICE_NUM → CUSTOMER_NUM → CUSTOMER_NAME. A customer who places fifty invoices has their name and city recorded fifty times, and a customer who has never ordered cannot be recorded at all.

                                  Fix: move the dependent columns into a table keyed by their real determinant, and leave a foreign key behind. CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_CITY) splits off, INVOICE keeps (INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE, CUSTOMER_NUM), and StayWell's MANAGER splits off from PROPERTY in exactly the same motion.

                                  💡
                                  The tell

                                  2NF and 3NF violations look identical in the data — a value repeated down a column. What separates them is what the repeated value depends on. Depends on part of the key: 2NF. Depends on a column that is not in the key at all: 3NF. When you are unsure, name the determinant out loud and then check whether it is the key, part of the key, or neither.

                                  💡
                                  Where you end up

                                  Apply all three steps to the flat report and you arrive at… exactly the six StayWell tables from Lesson 1-3: MANAGER, PROPERTY, ROOM, STUDENT, LEASE, and PAYMENT. Normalization isn't a separate academic exercise — it's how that schema was derived in the first place.

                                  Try it yourself: KimTay's shipping department keeps a flat table keyed by (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID): INVOICE_NUM, CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_CITY, ITEM_ID, ITEM_DESCRIPTION, QUANTITY. Which dependencies violate 2NF, which violate 3NF, and how would you fix them?

                                  INVOICE_NUM → CUSTOMER_NUM is a dependency on only part of the composite key, so invoice facts first move to INVOICE during 2NF. Inside that result, INVOICE_NUM → CUSTOMER_NUM → CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_CITY is transitive, so the customer facts move to CUSTOMER during 3NF. ITEM_ID → ITEM_DESCRIPTION is a 2NF partial dependency, not a transitive dependency, because ITEM_ID is the other part of the original composite key.

                                  The fix is the KimTay schema you already know: CUSTOMER stores customer facts, ITEM stores item facts, INVOICE stores invoice facts and CUSTOMER_NUM, and INVOICE_LINE keeps the composite key plus line-specific facts such as QUANTITY.

                                  🎛️ Try it: walk one bad table up to 3NF

                                  Drag through the stages

                                  This is StayWell's lease data as one wide spreadsheet. Slide from left to right to apply first, second, and third normal form one step at a time, and watch which tables appear.

                                  2-5a A procedure you can follow on your own data

                                  Normalization reads like theory until you have to do it to a table somebody handed you. It is actually a mechanical routine, and it is the same routine every time. The three labs below walk this list twice with an instructor and once alone, so read it now and keep it beside you.

                                  1

                                  Say what one row means

                                  Out loud, in one sentence: "one row is one payment", "one row is one item on one invoice". If the sentence needs an and, the table is probably doing two jobs and will split before you are done.

                                  2

                                  Choose the key

                                  What is the smallest set of columns that identifies one row? Write it down. Everything that follows is measured against this, so a wrong key gives you a wrong answer with no warning.

                                  3

                                  Write down the dependencies

                                  For every non-key column ask "what is the smallest thing that fixes this value?" and write determinant → column. This list is the whole analysis; the normal forms are just three ways of reading it.

                                  4

                                  1NF — remove the lists

                                  Any cell holding a list of independently queryable values becomes its own table, one row per value, carrying the key of the row it came from.

                                  5

                                  2NF — remove the part-of-key dependencies

                                  Any determinant that is a proper subset of a candidate key gets its own table, taking its dependent columns with it. There is nothing to remove when every candidate key has only one column.

                                  6

                                  3NF — remove the non-key determinants

                                  Any determinant that is not in the key at all gets its own table too, and a foreign key stays behind where it used to sit.

                                  7

                                  Check the reconstruction

                                  Join your new tables back together and compare the result with the current source rows. A mismatch disproves the split immediately; an exact match is strong regression evidence for this sample. A general lossless-join guarantee comes from the keys and join dependencies, not from testing one finite dataset.

                                  💡
                                  Use data to falsify a proposed dependency

                                  If INVOICE_NUM determines INVOICE_DATE, then no invoice number in the data can carry two different dates. Run SELECT INVOICE_NUM, COUNT(DISTINCT INVOICE_DATE) FROM INVOICE_FLAT GROUP BY INVOICE_NUM;: any count above 1 disproves the dependency. Counts of 1 only show that it holds in this sample; the business rule or declared constraint is what establishes it generally.

                                  Before the labs: you have not learned SQL yet

                                  That is not a problem, and it is worth saying out loud. SQL is taught from Module 3 onwards — making tables in Module 3, asking questions in Module 4, joining tables in Module 5. These labs come earlier because normalization is easier to believe when you watch it happen than when you read about it.

                                  So you are not expected to write any of this yet, or even to read it fluently. Every box below has a plain-English translation underneath it, and the ones using material well ahead of you say so. Press Run, read the answer, and let the SQL wash over you. It will be second nature by Module 5.

                                  💡
                                  What you just validated

                                  You joined the pieces back together and compared the current sample in both directions. Both differences came back empty, so these four small tables reproduce every row in the six-row sample without adding one.

                                  That is strong implementation evidence, but it is not a proof for every possible future row. The keys and functional dependencies are what justify calling the decomposition lossless. The information did not change; what changed is how many places each fact is written down — and so how many ways it can go wrong.

                                  StayWell's front office keeps a spreadsheet of what they own. One row per room, and every row drags the building and its manager along with it. Take it to 3NF. This one has all three faults in it, so you will use all three rules.

                                  • MY_PROPERTY — PROPERTY_ID primary key, PROPERTY_NAME, PROPERTY_CITY, MANAGER_ID foreign key

The COUNT(DISTINCT ...) test tells you whether a dependency you suspect is really there. The amenities are the one part you type by hand.

                                  Unlike every other box in this lesson, this one is yours to write in. Run it before you write anything and it fails, because the tables it checks do not exist yet. Your job is to make all seven checks say PASS.

                                  SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                  In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                  One table, PROPERTY_SHEET. Write your CREATE and INSERT statements in the marked area, then press Run: the single check table at the bottom grades your work. ⬇ .db saves your finished schema as a real SQLite file you can hand in.

                                  ⚠️
                                  A word on the COUNT(DISTINCT) test

                                  The test tells you whether a dependency holds in the rows you happen to have. That is not the same as whether it holds in the business. Five rows of StayWell data fit "a property has one manager". They fit "a property has one manager so far" just as well.

                                  So the query can disprove a dependency instantly, and can never quite prove one. Use it to catch yourself being wrong. Then ask a human.

                                  2-5e How far should you go?

                                  Third normal form is where this course stops, and where most working designs stop too. Higher forms do exist. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) tightens 3NF by insisting that every determinant is a candidate key; it catches a rare problem with overlapping composite keys. 4NF and 5NF go further still, into multi-valued dependencies. Know that the names exist.

                                  In practice, a 3NF schema has already removed the anomalies that do real damage. The cases left over are rare enough that you will notice them by the trouble they cause.

                                  The opposite question comes up more often at work. Storing a fact twice on purpose, to make a common query faster, is called denormalization. It is a real technique, not a polite word for sloppiness.

                                  The rule is that it comes second. Normalize first. Measure a query that is genuinely too slow. Then denormalize that one thing deliberately, write down why, and put something in place to keep the copies in step. A design that was never normalized is not denormalized. It is just wrong, and nobody wrote down why.

                                  🤝
                                  The exception you have already met

                                  LEASE.MONTHLY_RENT and INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE look like violations. The rent is already in ROOM; the price is already in ITEM. But they are not redundancy, and they are not denormalization either. They record the amount agreed at the time.

                                  That is a different fact from today's list price, and once the list price changes it is gone for good. Before you delete a column that looks duplicated, check that it is not quietly recording history.

                                  🔍 Knowledge check: 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF

                                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                  Q1Three rooms in one cell

                                  A flat StayWell property report gives Sycamore Court (P200) one row whose ROOM_NUMS cell reads "101, 201, 202", while Millbrook Commons' row reads "101, 102". Which normalization rule does this break, and what is the fix?

                                  • ✘a. A partial dependency is a 2NF problem about composite keys, and it never explains three values crammed into one cell -- 1NF has to be satisfied first.
                                  • ✘b. A transitive dependency is a 3NF problem where one non-key column drives another, and room numbers are not determined by the manager's name.
                                  • ✔c. 1NF requires every column to hold a single atomic value, so the repeating group becomes one ROOM row per room: P200/101, P200/201, and P200/202.
                                  • ✘d. It fits in the column, but a list is not one value: you cannot count rooms, join to LEASE, or price one room, which is precisely why 1NF exists.

                                  Remember: 1NF first: no cell may hold a list, so every repeating group becomes its own rows.

                                  Q2The description that rides along

                                  A KimTay table has the composite key (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) and also stores DESCRIPTION. Every row that contains CF21 repeats "Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb" -- once for invoice 50710 and again for invoice 50711. What is the precise problem?

                                  • ✔a. 2NF demands that every non-key column depend on the whole key, and DESCRIPTION needs only ITEM_ID, so it belongs in ITEM.
                                  • ✘b. Transitive means a non-key column drives another non-key column; here the determinant, ITEM_ID, is part of the primary key, which makes it partial instead.
                                  • ✘c. A repeating group is several values inside one cell, which is a different symptom from a value legitimately repeating down a column.
                                  • ✘d. Sitting outside the key is not permission to sit anywhere: a non-key column must depend on the entire key or move to another table.

                                  Remember: If a non-key column needs only part of a composite key, that is a partial dependency and 2NF moves it out.

                                  Q3Valerie Kaiser changes her name

                                  KimTay keeps one table keyed by CUSTOMER_NUM that also stores CUSTOMER_NAME, REP_NUM, and REP_LAST_NAME. Rep 20, Valerie Kaiser, serves both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, so when she changes her last name a clerk has to edit it on every one of her customer rows -- and one row gets missed. What is the underlying design flaw?

                                  • ✘a. 1NF is about lists inside a single cell; a value repeating down a column is what 2NF and 3NF address.
                                  • ✘b. CUSTOMER_NUM is a single-column key, so there is no part of it for anything to depend on: a table whose primary key is one column cannot have a partial dependency and is automatically in 2NF.
                                  • ✘c. The normal form is right but the fix is backwards -- dropping REP_NUM destroys the link to the rep, while 3NF removes the descriptive column and keeps the foreign key.
                                  • ✔d. That is a transitive dependency, CUSTOMER_NUM to REP_NUM to REP_LAST_NAME, and moving rep details into REP stores the name in one place.

                                  Remember: When a non-key column determines another non-key column, split the determinant into its own table and keep the foreign key.

                                  Q4The building with no tenants yet

                                  StayWell is taking over a third building, Cedar Ridge, and no student has signed a lease there yet. In the old flat lease report, where every row has to start with a student, there is nowhere to record that Cedar Ridge exists at all. Which anomaly is this?

                                  • ✘a. A deletion anomaly is losing a fact when you remove a row, but nothing is being removed here -- the fact cannot get in at all.
                                  • ✔b. That is the insertion anomaly exactly, and a separate PROPERTY table lets Cedar Ridge exist with zero leases attached.
                                  • ✘c. An update anomaly is one fact stored in many rows drifting out of sync; the problem here is that the fact cannot be stored even once.
                                  • ✘d. A partial dependency is a structural 2NF defect, not an anomaly; anomalies are the symptoms users actually feel.

                                  Remember: Insertion anomaly means a fact you cannot record, deletion means a fact you lose, update means a fact stored in too many places.

                                          2-6 Diagrams for Database DesignObjective 2 Objective 3

                                          An entity-relationship diagram (ERD) is the blueprint that comes out of conceptual design (Lesson 2-4) and drives everything after it. Every ERD in this course uses the same visual language you first saw in Lessons 1-2 and 1-3:

                                          • Rectangle = entity (becomes a table)
                                          • Bold, underlined text = primary key attribute(s)
                                          • Italic text = foreign key attribute
                                          • Line between entities = a relationship, with symbols on each end describing cardinality

                                          Click through the cardinality symbols — these are what turn a plain line into precise business rules:

                                          Two short tick marks: this side of the relationship must have one and only one related row. Every LEASE belongs to exactly one STUDENT.

                                          A circle plus one tick mark: optional, at most one. A PROPERTY might not have a MANAGER assigned yet.

                                          The "crow's foot": many related rows are allowed on this side. One REP has many CUSTOMERs.

                                          Crow's foot plus a circle: optional, many. An ITEM might appear on zero invoices (brand new stock) or many.

                                          Now those symbols make the KimTay diagram from Lesson 1-2 fully readable at a glance:

                                          Primary key (underlined, bold)Foreign key (italic)One recordMany records (crow's foot)

                                          REP–CUSTOMER reads as "one rep serves many customers, and each customer has exactly one rep" — the whole business rule, encoded in two symbols.

                                          🔍 Knowledge check: reading an ER diagram

                                          Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                          Q1A line read from the bottom up

                                          On StayWell's diagram the STUDENT box is drawn below LEASE, and the vertical line between them carries two short tick marks -- this course's "exactly one" marking -- at the STUDENT end and a crow's foot at the LEASE end. What business rule does that line state?

                                          • ✘a. That reads the line backwards: the crow's foot sits at the LEASE end, so the many-ness belongs to leases, not students.
                                          • ✘b. That would require the two-tick marking at both ends; a crow's foot at the LEASE end deliberately allows a student more than one lease.
                                          • ✘c. A relationship line constrains how rows match up, not how many rows each table holds; today's four students and four leases are a coincidence, not a rule.
                                          • ✔d. Read each end on its own: two ticks at the STUDENT end mean exactly one student per lease, and the crow's foot at the LEASE end lets that student hold many leases.

                                          Remember: A vertical line is read exactly like a horizontal one: the marking touching a box tells you how many of that box's rows take part.

                                          Q2Reading one line out loud

                                          On the KimTay diagram, the line joining REP and CUSTOMER carries two short tick marks -- this course's "exactly one" marking -- at the REP end and a crow's foot at the CUSTOMER end. KimTay's bookkeeper asks what business rule that encodes. What do you tell her?

                                          • ✘a. This reverses the symbols -- the crow's foot sits at the CUSTOMER end, so the many-ness belongs to customers, not reps.
                                          • ✘b. The two ticks sit at the REP end and fix how many reps a customer gets; the crow's foot still lets rep 20 serve both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic.
                                          • ✔c. Read each end separately: the two ticks mean exactly one on the REP side, and the crow's foot means many on the CUSTOMER side.
                                          • ✘d. A relationship line means a foreign key match, not identical key values, and CUSTOMER_NUM and REP_NUM are different things entirely.

                                          Remember: Read each end of the line on its own: the symbol nearest a box describes how many of that box's rows take part.

                                          Q3The lamp nobody has ordered yet

                                          KimTay's buyer wants to stock a turtle basking lamp that may sit unsold for months before it starts selling steadily, so KimTay asks for a diagram that plainly permits an item with no invoice lines at all. On the ITEM-INVOICE_LINE line, the INVOICE_LINE end is the end that counts how many invoice lines one item can appear on. Which marking states that relaxed rule?

                                          • ✔a. The circle allows zero and the crow's foot allows many, which is exactly the rule for brand-new stock that may later sell often.
                                          • ✘b. Two ticks mean exactly one, which would forbid unsold stock and would also forbid CF21, which already sells on invoices 50710 and 50711.
                                          • ✘c. That is the stricter marking, and it is the very requirement the buyer is asking to relax: it demands that every item appear on at least one invoice line.
                                          • ✘d. A circle with one tick allows zero but caps the item at a single line, and CF21 already appears on two invoice lines.

                                          Remember: A circle allows zero and a crow's foot allows many, so together they mean optional and unlimited.

                                          Q4The same column name in two boxes

                                          A new KimTay intern spots REP_NUM twice on the ER diagram: bold and underlined at the top of the REP box, and in orange italics on the last line of the CUSTOMER box. What does the italic copy tell her?

                                          • ✘a. Optionality is shown by a circle on the relationship line, never by how an attribute name is styled.
                                          • ✔b. In every diagram this course uses, orange italic text means foreign key -- a column that references another table's primary key.
                                          • ✘c. A table has exactly one primary key, and this diagram shows CUSTOMER's in bold underline as CUSTOMER_NUM at the top of the box.
                                          • ✘d. Nothing is computed here; REP_NUM is a stored value that must match an existing row in REP.

                                          Remember: Bold underline means primary key and italics mean foreign key, so one column name can be both in different boxes.

                                                  Summary Module Summary

                                                  This module moved from concepts to concrete design skill. You compared four ways of organizing data (hierarchical, network, relational, object-oriented) and saw why the relational model won out for general business use. You learned that functional dependence is the underlying rule that makes a column a good primary key, walked the five phases of the database design process, and used normalization (1NF → 2NF → 3NF) to turn one messy flat report into StayWell's clean six-table schema. Finally, ER diagrams gave you a precise visual language — keys, foreign keys, and crow's-foot cardinality — for describing all of it.

                                                  Module 3 puts all of this to work: you'll write the actual SQL that creates these tables and starts filling them with data.

                                                  Continue to Module 3 →

                                                  Terms Key Terms

                                                  Functional Dependence

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  Column B is functionally dependent on column A if every value of A is associated with exactly one value of B (A is the determinant).

                                                  Determinant

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  The column (or columns) on the left side of a functional dependency — the one that determines the other.

                                                  Candidate Key

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  Any column or column set that is unique and non-null for every row, and so could serve as the primary key.

                                                  Primary Key

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  The candidate key chosen to uniquely identify each row and be referenced by foreign keys.

                                                  Composite Key

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  A primary key made up of two or more columns together, e.g. (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM).

                                                  Foreign Key

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  A column in one table that references the primary key of another table, creating a relationship.

                                                  Normalization

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  The step-by-step process of organizing tables to eliminate redundancy and update/insertion/deletion anomalies.

                                                  1NF

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  First Normal Form: every column holds a single, atomic value — no repeating groups.

                                                  2NF

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  Second Normal Form: 1NF, plus every non-key column depends on the entire primary key, not just part of it.

                                                  3NF

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  Third Normal Form: 2NF, plus no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency).

                                                  Entity

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  A person, place, thing, or event the database tracks — becomes a table.

                                                  Cardinality

                                                  Click / press Enter to flip
                                                  The ERD notation (one, many, optional) describing how many rows on one side of a relationship connect to rows on the other.

                                                  🔍 Knowledge check: key terms in practice

                                                  Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                  Q1The email that looks like a key

                                                  In StayWell's STUDENT table, Layla Ibrahim's row holds STUDENT_ID S003 and an EMAIL value, and the four students on file today all have different emails. EMAIL is declared VARCHAR(30) with no NOT NULL rule, and StayWell does not require an applicant to supply an email or forbid two students from sharing one. Using this course's vocabulary, what is EMAIL?

                                                  • ✔a. A candidate key must be guaranteed unique and never blank for every possible row, and EMAIL is guaranteed neither, so today's tidy values are a coincidence rather than a key.
                                                  • ✘b. Four rows that happen not to collide prove nothing about the fifth student, who may leave the column blank or share a family address.
                                                  • ✘c. A foreign key stores a value belonging to another table's primary key, but EMAIL belongs to STUDENT itself and points at nothing.
                                                  • ✘d. Composite means two or more columns acting together as one key, not two parts inside a single text value.

                                                  Remember: A candidate key is a guarantee that a value is unique and never blank for every possible row, not a pattern you happen to notice in today's data.

                                                  Q2The room 101 that would be rejected

                                                  Sycamore Court (P200) has a room 101, and Millbrook Commons (P100) already had one. Suppose StayWell had built ROOM with ROOM_NUM alone as the primary key instead of (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM). On a DBMS that enforces primary keys, what happens when the leasing office inserts the Sycamore Court row?

                                                  • ✘a. That is exactly what the real key (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) buys you, but with ROOM_NUM alone the DBMS has no way to tell the two rooms apart.
                                                  • ✘b. A primary key never silently overwrites an existing row; a colliding insert is refused and the older row is left untouched.
                                                  • ✔c. A primary key is a uniqueness rule the DBMS enforces, so a second row numbered 101 cannot be stored until PROPERTY_ID joins the key.
                                                  • ✘d. Rejecting the new row is right, but a refused insert changes nothing that is already stored -- Millbrook Commons' room 101 survives untouched.

                                                  Remember: A primary key is a uniqueness promise the DBMS enforces, so when one column's values can repeat across genuinely different rows, the key needs a second column.

                                                  Q3Why the lease carries two columns

                                                  StayWell's LEASE rows record the rented room as a pair of values -- L001 stores P100 and 101, while L003 stores P200 and 201. A developer asks why LEASE cannot just store ROOM_NUM and be done with it. What is the reason?

                                                  • ✘a. No line is drawn between LEASE and PROPERTY at all -- a lease reaches its property through ROOM, which is why both room columns travel together.
                                                  • ✘b. How a value is stored is beside the point: room 101 is ambiguous in any data type, because both buildings number a room 101.
                                                  • ✘c. A foreign key repeats only the referenced table's primary key columns; ROOM_TYPE, MONTHLY_RENT, and MAX_OCCUPANTS stay in ROOM.
                                                  • ✔d. Room 101 exists at both P100 and P200, so only the pair identifies one room, and the referencing table has to carry the pair.

                                                  Remember: When the table you point at has a composite primary key, the foreign key must carry every one of that key's columns.

                                                          Review Review Questions

                                                          🔍 Module 2 cumulative review: design, keys, and normal forms

                                                          Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                          Q1The cell with two dates in it

                                                          StayWell's office assistant keeps a lease spreadsheet in which the row for student Trang Nguyen lists PAYMENT_DATES as "2026-08-01, 2026-09-01" inside a single cell. The assistant asks whether that is acceptable before the sheet is loaded into the real database. Which answer is correct?

                                                          • ✘a. A partial dependency is a 2NF problem and requires a composite key; here the problem is a list crammed into one cell, which is 1NF's job.
                                                          • ✘b. Readable is not the same as atomic - a comma-separated list forces you to pick text apart instead of querying rows, which is what 1NF forbids.
                                                          • ✔c. First Normal Form requires one atomic value per cell, and giving each payment its own row in PAYMENT is exactly the 1NF fix this module walks through - which is why lease L001 shows up as two PAYMENT rows, not one cell with two dates.
                                                          • ✘d. A transitive dependency is a 3NF problem about one non-key column determining another, and nothing here depends on another non-key column.

                                                          Remember: Multiple values stuffed into one cell is a repeating group, and repeating groups are always a 1NF violation.

                                                          Q2The item description that rode along on every line

                                                          KimTay's bookkeeper builds a reporting table whose primary key is (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID) and which also stores NUM_ORDERED and DESCRIPTION. DESCRIPTION depends only on ITEM_ID, so "Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb" is retyped on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711, the two invoices that both sell CF21. Which statement names the violation and its fix?

                                                          • ✔a. DESCRIPTION depends on part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency, and pulling it into ITEM turns ITEM_ID into a foreign key pointing at ITEM.
                                                          • ✘b. Normal forms are entirely about how the non-key columns depend on the key, so the non-key columns are exactly what you examine.
                                                          • ✘c. A composite key is perfectly legal in 1NF; 1NF only cares that every cell holds a single atomic value.
                                                          • ✘d. ITEM_ID is half of the primary key, not a non-key column, so this is a partial dependency (2NF), not a transitive one.

                                                          Remember: Depends on part of a composite key means 2NF; depends on a non-key column means 3NF.

                                                          Q3The rep name copied onto forty rows

                                                          Suppose KimTay grows well past its four sample customers to several hundred, with rep Juan Perez working with forty of them. A new sales analyst builds a wide mailing-list table with one row per customer, keyed on CUSTOMER_NUM alone, that also stores REP_NUM and REP_LAST_NAME. Correcting the spelling of Perez's last name now means editing forty separate rows. What is wrong, and what does fixing it create?

                                                          • ✘a. CUSTOMER_NUM is a single-column key, and a single-column key has no parts, so a partial dependency is impossible here.
                                                          • ✔b. A non-key column determining another non-key column is a transitive dependency, and moving rep facts into REP leaves the mailing-list table holding only the REP_NUM foreign key.
                                                          • ✘c. Those forty copies of one name are precisely the update anomaly normalization exists to remove - one real-world change should require one edit.
                                                          • ✘d. Adding columns to the key does not remove the duplication; it only makes the key bigger while the name still repeats on every row.

                                                          Remember: A non-key column that depends on another non-key column is a 3NF violation, and the fix always leaves a new foreign key behind.

                                                          Q4The description that wanted to be the key

                                                          KimTay's ITEM table uses ITEM_ID as its primary key, and a catalog rule guarantees that no two items ever share a DESCRIPTION and that a description is never left blank. The developer drafting next year's schema proposes identifying items by DESCRIPTION instead of ITEM_ID. Which response is correct?

                                                          • ✘a. Nothing about a key requires a short or numeric value; a key only has to be unique and never null for every row.
                                                          • ✘b. A foreign key references the primary key of another table inside this database, not a document from outside it.
                                                          • ✘c. Any number of columns may be unique, and every column that is unique and non-null counts as a candidate key.
                                                          • ✔d. Both columns qualify as candidate keys, but the primary key is the one foreign keys elsewhere point at, so swapping it means rewriting INVOICE_LINE too.

                                                          Remember: A table can have several candidate keys, but the primary key is the one the rest of the schema references.

                                                          Q5The duplicate room number

                                                          StayWell's ROOM table holds Room 101 at Millbrook Commons (P100) and Room 101 at Sycamore Court (P200) - the same room number in two different buildings. Suppose the designer had made ROOM_NUM alone the primary key of ROOM. What would happen when the second of those rooms was inserted, and why is (PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM) the right key?

                                                          • ✘a. A primary key conflict never overwrites an existing row; the database refuses the new row and reports an error instead.
                                                          • ✔b. Entity integrity means every primary key value is unique and non-null, and pairing the room number with the property makes (P100,101) and (P200,101) two distinct keys.
                                                          • ✘c. Entity integrity has two halves - never NULL and never duplicated - and this insert breaks the second half.
                                                          • ✘d. ROOM_NUM is part of ROOM's own primary key, not a foreign key; only PROPERTY_ID references PROPERTY.

                                                          Remember: Use a composite key whenever one column's values legitimately repeat across rows that are genuinely different things.

                                                          Q6The city that looked like a determinant

                                                          Looking at KimTay's four sample customers, a classmate notices that the two Maple Grove rows both show STATE 'OH' and that the Northfield and Brookville rows do too. He writes down CITY -> STATE as a functional dependency. Why is that a mistake?

                                                          • ✘a. A small sample can make an accident look like a rule, which is the exact warning this module gives about the Maple Grove rows.
                                                          • ✘b. Any column can be a determinant - ZIP determines CITY and STATE without being anybody's primary key.
                                                          • ✔c. Functional dependence is a business rule about all possible data, and Springfield, OH plus Springfield, IL breaks CITY -> STATE immediately.
                                                          • ✘d. Data type has nothing to do with dependency; a two-character column can be determined by another column perfectly well.

                                                          Remember: A functional dependency is a rule about every row the business could ever store, not a pattern you spotted in the sample.

                                                          Q7We can normalize it later

                                                          KimTay's sales manager asks for one wide table holding customer name, rep name, item description, and quantity, saying the team can clean it up after go-live. Measured against the four design phases in this module - requirements, conceptual design, logical design with normalization, and physical design - what actually went wrong?

                                                          • ✘a. Physical design is the last phase, where data types and storage details get chosen, and it is not what this shortcut skipped.
                                                          • ✘b. The manager did state a requirement; what he skipped was turning it into entities, relationships, and normalized tables.
                                                          • ✘c. Physical design implements an already normalized logical design - it does not invent a flat spreadsheet.
                                                          • ✔d. Jumping straight to a table skips the ER diagram and the 1NF to 2NF to 3NF pass, which is how the anomalies from Lesson 1-1 get back in.

                                                          Remember: The four phases are requirements, conceptual design, logical design with normalization, and physical design, and skipping the two middle phases is what reintroduces anomalies.

                                                          Q8Reading the KimTay diagram out loud

                                                          On KimTay's ER diagram the CUSTOMER box lists CUSTOMER_NUM in bold underline on its first line and REP_NUM in italics on its last line. The line joining CUSTOMER to REP carries the exactly-one symbol (two short tick marks, no circle) at the REP end and a crow's foot at the CUSTOMER end. What business rule is drawn there?

                                                          • ✘a. That reads the symbols backwards: the two tick marks sit on the REP end, so it is the rep side that is limited to exactly one.
                                                          • ✔b. Two tick marks with no circle mean exactly one, a crow's foot means many, and the italic REP_NUM on CUSTOMER's last line is the foreign key that physically carries the relationship.
                                                          • ✘c. Bold underline marks the primary key and italics mark a foreign key, so REP_NUM is a reference rather than part of CUSTOMER's key.
                                                          • ✘d. Italics mean foreign key in this course's diagrams; optionality is shown with a circle on the relationship line, not with italics.

                                                          Remember: Bold underline is the primary key, italics is the foreign key, and the symbols on each line end tell you how many rows sit on that side.

                                                          Q9Nesting the lines inside the invoices

                                                          A study partner suggests KimTay could skip the relational model and store everything as a strict hierarchy, with each invoice owning its lines the way a folder owns its files. You point at item CF21: the Grain-Free Dry Food appears on invoice 50710 and again on invoice 50711, and each of those invoices also lists a second item. Why does that sink the hierarchy?

                                                          • ✔a. A strict tree gives every child exactly one parent, and a many-to-many relationship has no single parent, which is why INVOICE_LINE exists in the relational design with ITEM on one side and INVOICE on the other.
                                                          • ✘b. Hierarchies handle many levels perfectly well; the real limit is one parent per child.
                                                          • ✘c. Storing numbers is not the issue - the issue is the shape of the relationship between the records.
                                                          • ✘d. The relational model connects tables by matching key values, so a connecting table like INVOICE_LINE resolves many-to-many cleanly.

                                                          Remember: Many-to-many relationships break a strict hierarchy, and a connecting table with a composite key is the relational answer.

                                                          Q10The property that disappeared

                                                          StayWell's old flat report kept one row per lease, and every row also carried the property's name, address, and manager. Riverbend Hall appears on exactly one of those rows. That student's lease ends, the row is deleted, and now nothing in the database records that Riverbend Hall exists at all. Name the problem and the fix.

                                                          • ✘a. An insertion anomaly is the opposite problem: not being able to add a new property until some student lives there.
                                                          • ✘b. An update anomaly is having to repeat the same edit across many rows, but here the fact vanished entirely instead.
                                                          • ✔c. Losing an unrelated fact as a side effect of deleting a row is the deletion anomaly, and a separate PROPERTY table stores that fact on its own row.
                                                          • ✘d. StayWell absolutely needs to know about a vacant property so it can advertise and lease those rooms.

                                                          Remember: Insertion, update, and deletion anomalies are three different symptoms, and each one disappears once every fact lives in its own table.

                                                                    Exercises Case Exercises

                                                                    Two original design exercises — think it through, then reveal the sample reasoning.

                                                                    1. KimTay wants to add a REGION to each rep (Northeast, Midwest, etc.), along with a REGION_MANAGER name. If you just add REGION and REGION_MANAGER as columns directly on REP, what normalization problem are you creating, and how would you fix it?

                                                                    REGION_MANAGER would depend on REGION, not directly on REP_NUM — a transitive dependency (a 3NF violation), and it also duplicates the manager's name on every rep row in that region. The fix is a separate REGION table (REGION_ID primary key, REGION_NAME, REGION_MANAGER), with REP storing only a REGION_ID foreign key.

                                                                    2. Using the cardinality notation from Lesson 2-6, describe the STUDENT–LEASE relationship in StayWell in one sentence, the way you would read it off a diagram.

                                                                    One STUDENT can have zero, one, or many LEASE rows over time (a student might not have signed a lease yet, or might have leased in multiple semesters), while each LEASE belongs to exactly one STUDENT — so the STUDENT side gets a single tick mark ("one and only one") and the LEASE side gets a crow's foot with a circle ("zero or many").

                                                                    3-1 Creating and Running SQL CommandsObjective 4

                                                                    Most SQL commands in this module fall into two families you'll use constantly:

                                                                    DDL — Data Definition Language

                                                                    CREATE, ALTER, DROP — commands that define or change the structure of the database (tables, columns, constraints).

                                                                    DML — Data Manipulation Language

                                                                    SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — commands that work with the data inside those tables. These four map directly to Objective 4: Create, Read, Update, Delete.

                                                                    Terminology note: This course follows the common classroom convention of grouping SELECT with DML. Some references call read-only queries DQL and reserve DML for statements that change rows. The SQL itself is the same either way; later modules also introduce transaction-control commands such as COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

                                                                    In a real class you might run SQL in MySQL Workbench, Oracle SQL Developer, or the Access query designer. This site includes a live SQL sandbox — a real SQLite database engine compiled to run directly in your browser (via a library called sql.js), no server or install required. Every sandbox in this module keeps its own tables in memory, seeded to wherever that lesson picks up. Try the one below right now:

                                                                    SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                    In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                    The strip above lists every table in this database right now — click one to see its rows. Use the menu to load KimTay or StayWell data, ⬇ .db to save your database as a real SQLite file, and Reset to start over.
