                                                                    🔍 Knowledge check: running SQL commands

                                                                    Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                    Q1KimTay's two Monday commands

                                                                    A developer at KimTay is rebuilding the company's database from scratch, and she warms up on a cut-down two-column practice table. First she runs CREATE TABLE REP_PRACTICE (REP_NUM CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY, LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL); and then she runs INSERT INTO REP_PRACTICE VALUES ('20', 'Kaiser');. A teammate asks which SQL family each command belongs to. What is the correct answer?

                                                                    • ✘a. DDL is the family that defines structure, and INSERT defines nothing; it puts one row of data inside a structure that already exists.
                                                                    • ✔b. Right: CREATE TABLE defines the shape of the practice table, and INSERT moves data into that shape.
                                                                    • ✘c. DML is SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and CREATE TABLE never touches a single row of data.
                                                                    • ✘d. The two labels are swapped, because the 'define' in DDL means defining structure, not filling in one row.

                                                                    Remember: DDL defines structure, as CREATE TABLE does; DML works with data through SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

                                                                    Q2KimTay's week in four tasks

                                                                    KimTay's bookkeeper lists everything she did with the database this week: she looked up Access Pet Center's balance, added a brand-new customer, fixed a typo in a customer's street, and removed an account that closed. Her manager asks which SQL commands those four tasks correspond to, in that same order. What is the right list?

                                                                    • ✘a. CRUD is a nickname for the four operations, not SQL syntax, so typing READ where SELECT belongs is an error.
                                                                    • ✘b. These are the right four commands in the wrong order, because looking up a balance came first and that task is SELECT.
                                                                    • ✘c. Removing a closed account takes the whole row out of the table, which is DELETE rather than a second UPDATE.
                                                                    • ✔d. Correct: read is SELECT, create is INSERT, update is UPDATE and delete is DELETE, the four DML commands.

                                                                    Remember: CRUD names the four jobs; SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are the SQL commands that carry them out.

                                                                    Q3The table that disappeared overnight

                                                                    A classmate types a short table-creating statement of her own into the sandbox on this page, runs it, and gets a success message. The next morning she opens the same page and runs SELECT * FROM PRACTICE;, and the sandbox reports that no such table exists. Why is her table gone?

                                                                    • ✘a. SQLite has no CREATE DATABASE statement at all, and every page load already hands you a working database.
                                                                    • ✘b. Nothing you type into a sandbox is stored on a server, so signing in would not bring the table back.
                                                                    • ✔c. Correct: the sandbox is a SQLite database that lives only in memory, so it starts empty again on each page load.
                                                                    • ✘d. SELECT only reads data and never removes a table; running it a hundred times would change nothing.

                                                                    Remember: Each sandbox is an in-memory SQLite database that resets on page load, so keep your SQL in a saved script.

                                                                    3-2 Creating a DatabaseObjective 6

                                                                    Before you can create tables, most database engines expect you to first create (or select) a database to hold them — except Access, which handles this differently, and our in-browser sandbox, which skips the step entirely since each page load already starts you with a fresh database. This is a good first look at Objective 6: the same idea, four different implementations.

                                                                    -- CREATE DATABASE: makes a new, empty database on the server. Nothing is inside
--   it yet - no tables and no rows - and this name is what you connect to.
CREATE DATABASE kimtay_pet_supplies;

-- USE: points the rest of this session at that database, so every CREATE TABLE
--   and INSERT you type afterwards lands inside it rather than somewhere else.
USE kimtay_pet_supplies;
                                                                    -- Oracle treats a "database" as an entire instance (a DBA-level
-- operation using DBCA). Day to day, you instead work inside your
-- own schema/user. A DBA can create a minimally privileged account:
-- CREATE USER: makes the account, which in Oracle doubles as the schema that
--   owns your tables. IDENTIFIED BY sets its password.
CREATE USER kimtay IDENTIFIED BY "replace-with-a-secure-secret"

-- DEFAULT TABLESPACE: which storage area new tables go into unless told
--   otherwise. USERS is the ordinary place for application data.
  DEFAULT TABLESPACE users

-- QUOTA: the ceiling on how much of that tablespace this account may fill.
--   With no quota the account can create tables but never store a row in them.
  QUOTA 100M ON users;

-- GRANT: privileges are separate from the account itself. CREATE SESSION allows
--   logging in at all, CREATE TABLE allows building tables, and nothing else is
--   granted - which is what makes the account minimally privileged.
GRANT CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE TO kimtay;

                                                                    Access has no SQL "CREATE DATABASE" statement at all. A database is a single .accdb file, so you create one through the interface instead:

                                                                    1. Open Access → File → New → Blank Database
                                                                    2. Choose a file name and location, e.g. KimTayPetSupplies.accdb
                                                                    3. Click Create — tables, queries, and everything else live inside that one file

                                                                    Q1Hunting for CREATE DATABASE in Access

                                                                    KimTay's office manager has been told to build the company's database in Microsoft Access. He has spent twenty minutes hunting for somewhere to type CREATE DATABASE kimtay_pet_supplies; and cannot find it anywhere in the program. What should you tell him?

                                                                    • ✔a. Correct: in Access the database is one .accdb file, created through File, New, Blank Database.
                                                                    • ✘b. There is no CREATE DB command in Access or in any other engine, so a shorter spelling will not help.
                                                                    • ✘c. MySQL and Access are separate programs with separate storage, so a MySQL database is invisible to Access.
                                                                    • ✘d. USE is a MySQL statement for switching between databases on a server, and Access has no such server.

                                                                    Remember: Access has no CREATE DATABASE statement; the database is a single .accdb file created through the interface.

                                                                    Q2MySQL says no database selected

                                                                    The developer setting up KimTay's MySQL server opens MySQL Workbench on a brand-new server and immediately runs the CREATE TABLE REP (...); statement. MySQL refuses it with the message 'No database selected'. Which fix matches the two-step pattern this lesson shows for MySQL?

                                                                    • ✘a. Column definitions never carry a database name; the database is chosen once with USE, not repeated on every column.
                                                                    • ✘b. A table and a database are different things, so renaming the table tells MySQL nothing about where to store it.
                                                                    • ✔c. Correct: MySQL wants the database created and then selected with USE before any table is built inside it.
                                                                    • ✘d. MySQL never invents a database for you, which is exactly why it answered 'No database selected'.

                                                                    Remember: In MySQL, CREATE DATABASE and then USE come before any CREATE TABLE statement.

                                                                    Q3The Oracle login with no database name

                                                                    KimTay's contractor sets up an Oracle version of the database and hands the company's new analyst a username and password instead of a database name. The analyst wants to know why nobody ran a CREATE DATABASE statement the way they would in MySQL. What is the best explanation?

                                                                    • ✘a. Creating an Oracle database means building an entire instance with a DBA tool, not something an ordinary user runs.
                                                                    • ✔b. Correct: Oracle hands you a schema or user account that behaves like your own personal database.
                                                                    • ✘c. The single-file design belongs to Microsoft Access; Oracle stores everything inside a server instance.
                                                                    • ✘d. Oracle definitely has databases, and it separates each user's tables into that user's own schema.

                                                                    Remember: In Oracle, everyday work happens inside your own schema or user account, not a database you create yourself.

                                                                    3-3 Creating a TableObjective 4

                                                                    The CREATE TABLE statement defines a table's structure: its column names, data types, and constraints like PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL. Here's the KimTay REP table — the same structure you designed a primary key for back in Lesson 2-3:

                                                                    -- CREATE TABLE: names the new table and opens the list of columns. Everything
--   inside the parentheses describes one column - its name, the kind of data it
--   holds, and any rule attached to it.
CREATE TABLE REP (

    -- CHAR(2): exactly two characters, always. PRIMARY KEY makes this the column
    --   that identifies a row: unique across the table, and never left empty.
    REP_NUM      CHAR(2)      PRIMARY KEY,

    -- VARCHAR(15): up to fifteen characters, storing only what is actually used.
    --   NOT NULL refuses any row that leaves this blank.
    LAST_NAME    VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,

    -- Same rule again: a rep must have a first name on file.
    FIRST_NAME   VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,

    -- No NOT NULL on the address columns, so a rep may be added before the
    --   address is known.
    STREET       VARCHAR(20),
    CITY         VARCHAR(15),

    -- CHAR rather than VARCHAR, because a state code is always exactly two.
    STATE        CHAR(2),

    -- CHAR(5), not a number: a ZIP is an identifier rather than a quantity, and
    --   storing it as a number would swallow the leading zero in 04101.
    ZIP          CHAR(5),

    -- DECIMAL(8,2): eight digits in total, two of them after the point. Exact
    --   money, without the rounding drift a floating-point type would bring.
    COMMISSION   DECIMAL(8,2),

    -- DECIMAL(4,2) holds values like 0.05. The last column takes no comma.
    RATE         DECIMAL(4,2)

-- The closing parenthesis ends the column list, and the semicolon ends the
-- statement.
);

                                                                    Q1The STUDENT table that will not build

                                                                    The developer building StayWell's STUDENT table runs CREATE TABLE STUDENT (STUDENT_ID CHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY, LAST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL, FIRST_NAME VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,); and the engine reports a syntax error near the closing parenthesis. Every column name and type is spelled correctly. Which correction fixes it?

                                                                    • ✘a. The size in CHAR(4) always sits in parentheses, so removing them would create a brand-new error.
                                                                    • ✘b. VALUES belongs to INSERT, which adds rows; CREATE TABLE lists column names, types and constraints instead.
                                                                    • ✔c. Correct: commas separate columns, so a comma with no column after it leaves the list unfinished.
                                                                    • ✘d. In standard SQL single quotes mark text values, and an identifier is quoted with double quotes or backticks when it is quoted at all; either spelling still leaves a comma with no column after it.

                                                                    Remember: Inside CREATE TABLE, commas separate columns, so the last column must not be followed by one.

                                                                    Q2The email that cannot be the key

                                                                    The developer building StayWell's STUDENT table has to choose a primary key. A teammate notices that all four students already on file have an email address and that no two addresses match, and suggests using EMAIL as the primary key instead of STUDENT_ID. What should the developer say?

                                                                    • ✘a. Four rows that happen to differ today guarantee nothing about tomorrow's rows, and the schema puts no uniqueness rule on EMAIL.
                                                                    • ✔b. Correct: EMAIL is declared VARCHAR(30) with no NOT NULL, so a student row may carry no address at all, while STUDENT_ID is always there.
                                                                    • ✘c. Column order carries no meaning in SQL, and STUDENT_ID would still be the right key if it were listed last.
                                                                    • ✘d. Primary keys hold text all through this course, including CHAR(4) keys such as STUDENT_ID and CHAR(2) keys such as REP_NUM.

                                                                    Remember: A primary key has to be present and unique on every row by the schema's own rules, which is why STUDENT_ID is the key and EMAIL is not.

                                                                    Q3Two guarantees built into the table

                                                                    KimTay wants two guarantees built into the REP table itself: no rep row can ever be saved without a last name, and no two reps can ever share the same REP_NUM. The owner asks how to enforce both without trusting whoever types the data. Which approach delivers it inside the CREATE TABLE statement?

                                                                    • ✘a. Constraints like PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL are exactly what CREATE TABLE is for, so the database enforces them itself.
                                                                    • ✘b. VARCHAR(15) only sets a maximum length, and the column still accepts NULL until you write NOT NULL.
                                                                    • ✘c. Column order means nothing to SQL, and columns allow NULL by default until you declare otherwise.
                                                                    • ✔d. Correct: PRIMARY KEY blocks duplicate rep numbers and NOT NULL blocks a missing last name.

                                                                    Remember: PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL are declared with the columns in CREATE TABLE, and the engine enforces them for you.

                                                                          Every column needs a data type. The same concept goes by different names across engines — another piece of Objective 6:

                                                                          Data type equivalents
                                                                          ConceptMySQLOracleMicrosoft Access
                                                                          Short textVARCHAR(n)VARCHAR2(n)Short Text
                                                                          Long textTEXTCLOBLong Text (Memo)
                                                                          Whole numberINT, SMALLINTNUMBER(p,0)Number (Integer / Long Integer)
                                                                          Decimal / moneyDECIMAL(p,s)NUMBER(p,s)Currency, or Number (Decimal)
                                                                          Date / timeDATE, DATETIMEDATE, TIMESTAMPDate/Time
                                                                          Auto-generated IDAUTO_INCREMENTIdentity column / sequenceAutoNumber
                                                                          Yes/NoBOOLEAN (a synonym for TINYINT(1))BOOLEAN in Oracle 23ai+; NUMBER(1) or CHAR(1) on older releasesYes/No
                                                                          ⚠️
                                                                          "DECIMAL(7,2)" isn't just decoration

                                                                          The two numbers matter: DECIMAL(7,2) means up to 7 total digits, 2 of them after the decimal point — enough for a price up to 99,999.99. Undersize it and a real MySQL or Oracle server will reject or truncate values that don't fit.

                                                                          This sandbox uses an ordinary SQLite table, which is intentionally relaxed about types (it uses "type affinity" rather than rigid enforcement) — that makes it a forgiving place to practice the standard CHAR, VARCHAR(n), DECIMAL(p,s), and DATE syntax you'd use in MySQL or Oracle, even though SQLite itself won't reject an out-of-range value the way a production MySQL server in strict mode would. SQLite also supports opt-in STRICT tables, but their smaller set of type names makes them a separate lesson. Experiment:

                                                                          Q1The 1,250 dollar aviary

                                                                          An early draft of KimTay's ITEM table declares PRICE DECIMAL(4,2). Before the table is ever built, a reviewer points out that KimTay is about to stock a large walk-in aviary that sells for 1250.00, and that a real MySQL server would reject that price. What is wrong with the draft, and what fixes it?

                                                                          • ✘a. The first number is the total digit count and the second is how many of those follow the point, not an extra allowance.
                                                                          • ✘b. DECIMAL(4,4) would put all four digits after the decimal point, leaving no room for dollars at all.
                                                                          • ✘c. SMALLINT stores whole numbers only, so it would throw away the cents and still not solve the size problem.
                                                                          • ✔d. Correct: DECIMAL(4,2) tops out at 99.99, while DECIMAL(7,2) reaches 99,999.99, which is the width the shipped ITEM table uses.

                                                                          Remember: In DECIMAL(p,s), p is the total number of digits and s is how many of them sit after the decimal point.

                                                                          Q2The same email column, three engines

                                                                          StayWell's STUDENT table stores EMAIL as VARCHAR(30) in MySQL, holding values like tnguyen@example.edu. One classmate is rebuilding that table in Oracle and another is rebuilding it in Microsoft Access. What should EMAIL become in each of those two engines?

                                                                          • ✘a. CLOB and Long Text are for very long text such as paragraphs, far more than a 30-character email needs.
                                                                          • ✔b. Correct: short text is VARCHAR(n) in MySQL, VARCHAR2(n) in Oracle and Short Text in Access.
                                                                          • ✘c. Type names are one of the biggest differences between engines, which is why the lesson includes an equivalents table.
                                                                          • ✘d. NUMBER holds numbers and AutoNumber generates counting ids, so neither one can store an email address.

                                                                          Remember: The same concept has different names per engine: VARCHAR(n), VARCHAR2(n) and Short Text all mean short text.

                                                                          Q3The two-letter state that held four

                                                                          This page's sandbox is SQLite, which uses type affinity rather than strict checking. A classmate builds a practice table with STATE CHAR(2) in that sandbox, inserts the value 'Ohio', and the row is stored and displayed in full with no complaint at all. She concludes that the widths written into a CREATE TABLE statement never really matter. Why is that conclusion unsafe?

                                                                          • ✔a. Correct: type affinity makes the sandbox forgiving, so a declared width is a promise you keep for the engines that do enforce it.
                                                                          • ✘b. Nothing was trimmed; the sandbox stored all four characters, which is exactly why the row looked fine.
                                                                          • ✘c. The lesson's own warning says an undersized column is rejected or truncated on a production MySQL or Oracle server.
                                                                          • ✘d. A width in CHAR(n) counts characters and never words, in every engine this course covers.

                                                                          Remember: The SQLite sandbox is deliberately relaxed about declared widths, so size every column for the engine that will really enforce it.

                                                                                    3-5 Using NullsObjective 4

                                                                                    NULL means unknown or not applicable — it is not zero, not an empty string, and not the same as another NULL. This trips up more students than any other SQL topic, so it earns its own lesson.

                                                                                    📖
                                                                                    Three-valued logic

                                                                                    Most comparisons in SQL return TRUE or FALSE — but any comparison involving NULL returns a third value: UNKNOWN. WHERE STREET = NULL never matches anything, even rows where STREET really is NULL, because NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. You must use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead.

                                                                                    Try it — this sandbox has an empty REP table ready:

                                                                                    In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                    Run it as-is first, then compare the two SELECT statements' results.

                                                                                    🔍 Knowledge check: nulls

                                                                                    Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                    Q1The rep the query cannot find

                                                                                    KimTay adds rep 88 to the REP table but leaves STREET out, because HR has not collected that rep's address yet. The bookkeeper runs SELECT * FROM REP WHERE STREET = NULL; to list reps with missing addresses and gets zero rows back. Which correction returns the new rep's row?

                                                                                    • ✘a. An empty string is a real value stored in the column, and it is not the same thing as an unknown value.
                                                                                    • ✔b. Correct: IS NULL is the only test that matches a row whose value is unknown.
                                                                                    • ✘c. Quoting NULL turns it into the four-letter word NULL, so the query hunts for a street literally named NULL.
                                                                                    • ✘d. There is no == operator in standard SQL, and swapping one operator for another does not make a missing value something you can match by comparing it.

                                                                                    Remember: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to test for missing values, because = NULL never matches anything.

                                                                                    Q2The commission report that skips a rep

                                                                                    KimTay runs SELECT * FROM REP WHERE COMMISSION < 30000; to list its lower-earning reps. Rep 88 was hired this month and that row's COMMISSION is still NULL, but the row does not appear anywhere in the results. Why was it left out?

                                                                                    • ✘a. NULL is not zero; it means the value is unknown, so SQL will not treat it as the number 0.
                                                                                    • ✘b. A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, and UNKNOWN is not TRUE.
                                                                                    • ✔c. Correct: NULL < 30000 evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows that evaluate to TRUE.
                                                                                    • ✘d. NULL has no data type of its own and is allowed in a DECIMAL column, so the column type is not the issue.

                                                                                    Remember: Any comparison involving NULL returns UNKNOWN, so those rows quietly drop out of a WHERE clause.

                                                                                    Q3Zero dollars versus no answer

                                                                                    Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) has paid every invoice, so KimTay knows its balance is exactly 0.00. A different customer signed up this morning and nobody has worked out that account's balance yet. KimTay's bookkeeper asks how those two BALANCE values should be stored. What do you tell her?

                                                                                    • ✔a. Correct: 0.00 records a known balance of nothing owed, while NULL records that the balance is still unknown.
                                                                                    • ✘b. Zero is a measured amount and NULL means nobody knows yet, so storing both as 0.00 hides a real difference.
                                                                                    • ✘c. The clinic's balance is not unknown at all, since KimTay knows it is exactly zero, and NULL would lose that fact.
                                                                                    • ✘d. An empty string is text rather than a number, and it is still a stored value, not a statement that the value is unknown.

                                                                                    Remember: 0.00 means a known amount of nothing, while NULL means unknown or not applicable.

                                                                                    3-6 Adding Rows to a TableObjective 4

                                                                                    INSERT INTO adds new rows — the "Create" in CRUD. You can list columns explicitly (recommended) or rely on the table's column order:

                                                                                    -- INSERT INTO: names the table that will receive the row, then lists the columns
--   you are about to supply. Listing them is optional but worth doing - it keeps
--   the statement correct if the table later gains a column.
INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME, STREET, CITY, STATE, ZIP, COMMISSION, RATE)

-- VALUES: the data itself, in exactly the same order as the column list above.
--   Text goes in single quotes and numbers do not. REP_NUM is quoted even though
--   it looks numeric, because the column was declared CHAR(2).
VALUES ('20', 'Kaiser', 'Valerie', '624 Randall Dr.', 'Maple Grove', 'OH', '44601', 21560.00, 0.05);

                                                                                    Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                    Q1The rep who landed in the wrong column

                                                                                    KimTay's rep 35 is Richard Hull. Re-typing the REP rows, a student enters INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('Hull', '35', 'Richard');. This page's SQLite sandbox does not enforce declared lengths, so the row is stored exactly as typed, and SELECT * FROM REP; shows a new row whose REP_NUM is Hull and whose LAST_NAME is 35. Why did the values land there?

                                                                                    • ✔a. Right - VALUES is positional: the first value goes into the first column you listed, the second into the second, and so on.
                                                                                    • ✘b. SQL never guesses from a value's contents or its type; position in your list is the only thing that decides where a value lands.
                                                                                    • ✘c. The column list is a real part of the statement and the engine follows the exact order you wrote - alphabetical order plays no part.
                                                                                    • ✘d. The engine never inspects a value and slides the rest sideways; nothing was shifted, because nothing was matched by meaning in the first place.

                                                                                    Remember: VALUES is positional - the nth value always goes into the nth column you listed.

                                                                                    Q2Sam's missing street address

                                                                                    Sam Alvarez is joining KimTay as rep 88, but his street address has not been confirmed yet. His rep number, last name and first name are all that has been entered so far, and REP declares STREET without NOT NULL. Which statement adds his row correctly and leaves STREET unknown?

                                                                                    • ✘a. Skipping the column list means you must supply a value for every one of REP's nine columns, in order, so this fails with a wrong-number-of-values error.
                                                                                    • ✘b. Typing the word unknown stores real text that later queries treat as an address, and WHERE STREET IS NULL will never find it.
                                                                                    • ✔c. Right - naming only the columns you have values for leaves STREET as NULL, the marker for an unknown value, and STREET is a column that allows NULL.
                                                                                    • ✘d. An empty string is a value the column really holds, and '' is not the same thing as NULL.

                                                                                    Remember: List only the columns you have values for; any column you leave out is set to NULL - which works only for columns that allow NULL.

                                                                                    Q3Two lines on the same invoice

                                                                                    KimTay is loading a fresh, empty copy of INVOICE_LINE one row at a time. The line for item CF21 on invoice 50710 is already stored, and the leash line is next: INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE) VALUES ('50710', 'DG04', 2, 11.99);. Item DG04 already exists in ITEM. On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity, what happens?

                                                                                    • ✘a. INVOICE_NUM alone is not the primary key here; only the combination of invoice number and item has to be unique.
                                                                                    • ✔b. Right - a composite primary key only forbids repeating the whole pair, which is exactly what lets one invoice list several items.
                                                                                    • ✘c. INSERT never overwrites an existing row; it either adds a new row or fails with an error.
                                                                                    • ✘d. On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity the foreign key would require DG04 to already exist in ITEM - and it does, so nothing needs to be re-inserted.

                                                                                    Remember: A composite primary key only forbids repeating the whole combination, not either column alone.

                                                                                    3-7 Viewing Table DataObjective 4

                                                                                    SELECT is the "Read" in CRUD, and the command you'll type more than any other. This sandbox is preloaded with REP and CUSTOMER, fully populated:

                                                                                    SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                    In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                    Try: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY FROM CUSTOMER WHERE STATE = 'OH';

                                                                                    Pulling two tables back together: your first JOIN

                                                                                    Back in Lesson 1-2 you walked through why KimTay's data lives in five separate tables instead of one, and followed the shared key values from one table to the next by hand. That operation has a name, and a single command that performs it: a JOIN. CUSTOMER only stores a rep's REP_NUM, not their name, so showing a customer's rep by name means matching CUSTOMER.REP_NUM back to REP.REP_NUM:

                                                                                    -- SELECT: one column from each table. AS renames the second so the heading reads
--   REP_LAST_NAME rather than the bare LAST_NAME.
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, r.LAST_NAME AS REP_LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the first table, given the short alias c. From here on c means CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER c

-- JOIN ... ON: brings in the second table as r, and ON states how the two line
--   up - keep a pairing only where the rep numbers match. One row per customer
--   comes back, each carrying the name of the rep who serves it.
JOIN REP r ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUM;

                                                                                    Read it in three parts: FROM CUSTOMER c picks a starting table and gives it a short alias (c), JOIN REP r adds a second table with its own alias, and ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUM tells SQL exactly which rows to match up — each customer row is paired with the one REP row that shares the same REP_NUM. Once they're joined, every column from both tables is fair game in the SELECT list.

                                                                                    SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                    In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                    Add r.RATE to the SELECT list (it's already available since REP is joined in), then add ORDER BY c.CUSTOMER_NAME at the end.

                                                                                    Now try writing one yourself:

                                                                                    💡
                                                                                    One output row per match

                                                                                    A JOIN produces one row for every matching pair. Since each customer has exactly one rep here, you get one joined row per customer. If you joined INVOICE to INVOICE_LINE, a single invoice with three lines would produce three joined rows. That is the one-to-many side of the INVOICE relationship; INVOICE_LINE as a whole is also the bridge that implements the many-to-many relationship between invoices and items.

                                                                                    What a JOIN is really doing

                                                                                    The statement above is short, but a lot happens inside it. Step through the match one customer at a time and watch the rule in ON being applied.

                                                                                    🎛️ Try it: watch the match happen, row by row

                                                                                    Drag to step through

                                                                                    Joining CUSTOMER to REP, one customer row at a time.

                                                                                    not startedrow 2done

                                                                                    Reading the statement, piece by piece

                                                                                    Every part of FROM CUSTOMER c JOIN REP r ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUM
                                                                                    PieceWhat it does
                                                                                    FROM CUSTOMERNames the first table. SQL starts with its rows.
                                                                                    cAn alias — a nickname for that table, so you can write c.REP_NUM instead of CUSTOMER.REP_NUM. Optional, but once two tables are in play it saves a lot of typing.
                                                                                    JOIN REPBrings a second table into the query. Nothing is matched yet.
                                                                                    rThe alias for REP.
                                                                                    ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUMThe matching rule. This is the part that does the real work: keep a pair of rows only when the customer's REP_NUM equals the rep's REP_NUM.

                                                                                    Once the two tables are joined, every column from both is available to the SELECT list, to WHERE, and to ORDER BY. The join comes first; the filtering and sorting happen on the joined result.

                                                                                    💡
                                                                                    Relationship joins usually follow a foreign key to a key

                                                                                    Look at what the ON clause pairs: CUSTOMER.REP_NUM, which is a foreign key, against REP.REP_NUM, which is REP's primary key. That is the pattern most relationship joins in this course follow, and it comes straight out of Module 2. If you drew the relationship on your ER diagram, you already know what to put after ON — the line on the diagram is the join.

                                                                                    How many rows come back

                                                                                    The row count is not arbitrary; it falls out of the relationship between the two tables.

                                                                                    Row counts against KimTay's real data
                                                                                    JoinRows backWhy
                                                                                    CUSTOMER to REP4Each of the 4 customer rows matches at most one REP row because REP_NUM is unique, so this join cannot multiply the customer rows.
                                                                                    INVOICE to INVOICE_LINE6One-to-many: invoice 50710 has 2 lines, 50711 has 2, 50712 has 2. The invoice columns repeat once per line.
                                                                                    CUSTOMER to INVOICE3Only 3 invoices exist, so only 3 rows — and Companion Care Clinic vanishes entirely, because it has never been invoiced.
                                                                                    ⚠️
                                                                                    Rows with no match disappear

                                                                                    KimTay has four customers, but SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER c JOIN INVOICE i ON c.CUSTOMER_NUM = i.CUSTOMER_NUM returns only three names. Companion Care Clinic is dropped because no invoice row matches it. This surprises almost everyone the first time. A plain JOIN keeps a row only when the ON condition is satisfied on both sides, so "list every customer and their orders" is a different question from "list every order with its customer." The tool for keeping unmatched rows is an outer join; Module 5 teaches it. For now, just know why this inner join's count came out short.

                                                                                    Chaining a third table

                                                                                    Nothing changes when you need more tables — add another JOIN and another ON. To answer "what did each customer actually order, by product name," you have to walk CUSTOMER to INVOICE to INVOICE_LINE to ITEM, following the same foreign keys the ER diagram draws:

                                                                                    -- SELECT: three columns drawn from three different tables. Needing all three at
--   once is the reason the query has to travel across four tables.
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, it.DESCRIPTION, l.NUM_ORDERED

-- FROM: the starting table, aliased c.
  FROM CUSTOMER c

-- JOIN: hop 1 - each customer to its own invoices, matched on customer number.
  JOIN INVOICE i       ON c.CUSTOMER_NUM = i.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- JOIN: hop 2 - each invoice to its own line items, matched on invoice number.
  JOIN INVOICE_LINE l  ON i.INVOICE_NUM  = l.INVOICE_NUM

-- JOIN: hop 3 - each line item to the item it names, matched on item id. Four
--   tables need three hops; the chain always takes one fewer join than tables.
  JOIN ITEM it         ON l.ITEM_ID      = it.ITEM_ID;

                                                                                    That returns 6 rows — one per invoice line — and it is the query that finally answers the question Lesson 1-1 opened with, the one no pile of spreadsheets could answer. Try it in the sandbox at the end of this module, where all five KimTay tables are loaded.

                                                                                    Four mistakes worth making once, here

                                                                                    What actually happens — each of these was run against the seeded database
                                                                                    MistakeWhat you getFix
                                                                                    Leaving off ON entirelyNo error — 12 rows. Every customer is paired with every rep, 4 x 3. This is called a Cartesian product, and on real tables it produces millions of rows.Always give JOIN an ON.
                                                                                    Using a bare column both tables have: SELECT REP_NUM ...ambiguous column name: REP_NUMQualify it: c.REP_NUM or r.REP_NUM.
                                                                                    Matching the wrong pair: ON c.CUSTOMER_NUM = r.REP_NUMNo error — 0 rows. The values simply never match, so every pair is rejected. This is the dangerous one: it looks like there is no data.Check the ON clause against your ER diagram before you suspect the data.
                                                                                    Guessing a column name: r.NAMEno such column: r.NAMEREP stores LAST_NAME and FIRST_NAME. Click the table in the sandbox strip to see its real columns.

                                                                                    The first and third are worth dwelling on: a join can be wrong without being an error. Zero rows and far too many rows are both silent failures. When a result looks wrong, read the ON clause first.

                                                                                    Q1The balance report for the four customers

                                                                                    KimTay's four customers have balances of 3512.50 (Access Pet Center), 1200.00 (Downtown Aquarium & Pets), 0.00 (Companion Care Clinic) and 4820.75 (Whiskers & Wags Boutique). KimTay's bookkeeper runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000 ORDER BY BALANCE DESC;. What comes back?

                                                                                    • ✘a. WHERE runs first and removes Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 row; ORDER BY only arranges the rows that already survived.
                                                                                    • ✘b. The list after SELECT decides which columns appear - ask for two columns and you get exactly those two.
                                                                                    • ✘c. DESC means descending, largest first, so 1200.00 is the last row here rather than the first.
                                                                                    • ✔d. Right - WHERE keeps the three balances above 1000, the SELECT list limits output to two columns, and DESC puts the largest balance on top.

                                                                                    Remember: WHERE picks the rows, the SELECT list picks the columns, and ORDER BY DESC puts the largest value first.

                                                                                    Q2Rep 20's customer list, in alphabetical order

                                                                                    Valerie Kaiser is rep 20, and two KimTay customers are assigned to her. The bookkeeper needs just those two customer names, listed alphabetically. Which statement produces that?

                                                                                    • ✘a. The clauses have a fixed order - SELECT, FROM, WHERE, then ORDER BY - so this is a syntax error, not just odd style.
                                                                                    • ✔b. Right - FROM picks the table, WHERE keeps only rep 20's customers, and ORDER BY puts those names in alphabetical order.
                                                                                    • ✘c. REP stores the reps themselves and has no CUSTOMER_NAME column; customer names live in the CUSTOMER table.
                                                                                    • ✘d. Without ORDER BY the engine may return rows in any order; alphabetical output is never guaranteed by default.

                                                                                    Remember: Clause order is fixed - SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY - and without ORDER BY no order is guaranteed.

                                                                                    Q3The customer that never shows up

                                                                                    The developer building KimTay's invoice report runs SELECT i.INVOICE_NUM, c.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM INVOICE i JOIN CUSTOMER c ON i.CUSTOMER_NUM = c.CUSTOMER_NUM;. KimTay's three invoices belong to customers 1120, 1420 and 1225; customer 1310 (Companion Care Clinic) has never been invoiced. Which customer names appear in the result?

                                                                                    • ✔a. Right - the ON condition produces one row per match, and Companion Care Clinic has no invoice to match, so it produces no row at all.
                                                                                    • ✘b. Being joined in makes CUSTOMER's columns available, but a customer row still has to match an invoice row to appear.
                                                                                    • ✘c. It is the opposite: an unmatched row is the one row that does NOT survive the join.
                                                                                    • ✘d. Once CUSTOMER is joined in, all of its columns are usable in SELECT - the name comes from the matched CUSTOMER row.

                                                                                    Remember: A JOIN keeps only the rows the ON condition can match - a customer with no invoice simply does not appear.

                                                                                            3-8 Correcting Errors in a TableObjective 4

                                                                                            UPDATE and DELETE complete CRUD. Both are dangerous without a WHERE clause — leave it off and you'll update or delete every row in the table.

                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                            Always verify WHERE before you run

                                                                                            Get in the habit of checking the intended predicate with a SELECT first — run SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM='1120'; to confirm it matches only what you expect, then reuse that same WHERE condition in the UPDATE or DELETE.

                                                                                            Same REP/CUSTOMER data as Lesson 3-7. Practice correcting a mistake:

                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                            The script prints a BEFORE and AFTER result. Press Reset before running it again so the $500 is not subtracted twice.

                                                                                            🔍 Knowledge check: fixing data safely

                                                                                            Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                            Q1The 500 dollars that came off every account

                                                                                            Access Pet Center paid down 500 dollars. Meaning to update only customer 1120, a clerk runs UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500;. The clerk then runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER; to check the work. What does that SELECT show?

                                                                                            • ✘a. An UPDATE with no WHERE has nothing to stop it, so it works through every row in the table - here, all four.
                                                                                            • ✔b. Right - no WHERE means no filter, so all four rows were changed, and 0.00 minus 500 leaves Companion Care Clinic negative.
                                                                                            • ✘c. No engine protects you here; WHERE is optional to SQL, and leaving it off is a perfectly legal statement.
                                                                                            • ✘d. SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500 reads each row's own balance first and subtracts from it, so values dropped rather than being replaced.

                                                                                            Remember: An UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE clause applies to every row in the table.

                                                                                            Q2Before deleting Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                            Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) has closed permanently, it has never been invoiced, and KimTay's bookkeeper has been asked to remove its row. Lesson 3-8's safety habit says to do one thing before running the DELETE. What is it?

                                                                                            • ✘a. Emptying a table to remove one row risks the other three customers plus any typing mistake you make re-entering them.
                                                                                            • ✘b. No rule requires a zero balance before a delete, and this statement changes a value without removing anything - Companion Care Clinic's balance is already 0.00 anyway.
                                                                                            • ✘c. This sandbox has no per-statement undo button. Reset can rebuild the entire lesson database, while production recovery requires a transaction, backup, or another deliberate recovery plan.
                                                                                            • ✔d. Right - testing your WHERE clause as a SELECT first shows you exactly which rows the DELETE will hit.

                                                                                            Remember: Test the WHERE clause as a SELECT first. This sandbox commits the statement immediately; Reset rebuilds the whole lesson database rather than undoing one change.

                                                                                            Q3The customer that would not delete

                                                                                            Access Pet Center is customer 1120, and invoice 50710 belongs to that customer. INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM is a foreign key pointing at CUSTOMER. A clerk runs DELETE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120'; on a DBMS that enforces referential integrity - this page's SQLite sandbox does not. What does that DBMS do?

                                                                                            • ✘a. Removing the child rows automatically happens only when the table was built to cascade; a plain foreign key blocks the delete instead of quietly deleting invoices.
                                                                                            • ✘b. An invoice pointing at a missing customer is exactly the broken state referential integrity exists to prevent, so the DBMS refuses rather than allowing it.
                                                                                            • ✔c. Right - the foreign key requires every INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM to match a real CUSTOMER row, so the parent row cannot go while invoice 50710 still refers to it.
                                                                                            • ✘d. A DELETE names one table; what stops this statement is the foreign key rule, not a requirement to list other tables.

                                                                                            Remember: With referential integrity enforced, a row that other rows still point to cannot be deleted - deal with the dependent rows first.

                                                                                                    3-9 Saving SQL CommandsObjective 4

                                                                                                    Retyping SQL from scratch every session doesn't scale. Every real engine lets you save your commands as a script file (a plain text file, conventionally named with a .sql extension) that you can re-run, hand to a teammate, or check into version control:

                                                                                                    -- kimtay_setup.sql
-- Run with: mysql -u root -p kimtay_pet_supplies < kimtay_setup.sql

-- 1. Table structures
-- The CREATE TABLE statements come first, parents before children: REP has to
-- exist before CUSTOMER can point a foreign key at it.
CREATE TABLE REP ( ... );
CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER ( ... );

-- 2. Starting data
-- The INSERTs come only once every table exists, in the same parent-before-child
-- order, so no row ever references a row that has not been created yet.
INSERT INTO REP VALUES ( ... );
                                                                                                    💡
                                                                                                    This is exactly what the capstone project uses

                                                                                                    Keeping every CREATE TABLE and INSERT statement in saved, ordered .sql files (rather than typed once and forgotten) is how real teams rebuild a database from nothing, share it with teammates, and track changes in git over time. The real-world project asks you to do exactly this.

                                                                                                    💾
                                                                                                    The sandbox's .db buttons save something different

                                                                                                    The ↓ .db button saves a snapshot of the database as it exists now: tables, rows, and current values. A .sql script saves the ordered recipe that can rebuild that state and can be reviewed in version control. A snapshot is a useful checkpoint; the script is the reproducible source.

                                                                                                    🔍 Knowledge check: saving SQL as a script

                                                                                                    Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                    Q1The work that vanished on reload

                                                                                                    A student spends an hour typing KimTay's CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements into the sandbox, then reloads the page and finds everything gone. Lesson 3-9's answer is to keep the work in a script file. What does that file actually give her?

                                                                                                    • ✔a. Right - a script is saved text: the ordered commands that recreate the structure and the data whenever you run them.
                                                                                                    • ✘b. A script stores commands, not rows; the data only comes back because re-running the INSERT statements puts it back.
                                                                                                    • ✘c. Query results are output, not commands - a script holds the statements you would run to produce those results again.
                                                                                                    • ✘d. Saving a file has nothing to do with who may change a table; that is a permissions question, not a script.

                                                                                                    Remember: A script is saved commands, not saved data - re-running it rebuilds the database from nothing.

                                                                                                    Q2The setup script that ran in the wrong order

                                                                                                    A classmate's kimtay_setup.sql lists all of the INSERT statements first and all of the CREATE TABLE statements at the bottom. He runs the whole file against a brand new, empty database. What happens?

                                                                                                    • ✘a. An engine executes a script one statement at a time, in the order written, with no advance reading or rearranging.
                                                                                                    • ✘b. There is no holding area - an INSERT that names a table which does not exist simply fails on the spot.
                                                                                                    • ✘c. Scripts run top to bottom, which is exactly why structure has to be defined before data is loaded.
                                                                                                    • ✔d. Right - CREATE TABLE has to come before the INSERT statements that fill it, which is why script order matters.

                                                                                                    Remember: Scripts run top to bottom, so every CREATE TABLE must come before the INSERTs that fill it.

                                                                                                              3-10 Creating the Remaining Database TablesObjective 4

                                                                                                              Time to finish the KimTay schema. REP and CUSTOMER already exist in the sandbox below (built in earlier lessons) — add ITEM, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE yourself, then populate all three.

                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                              The catalog query lists user tables in a stable order and hides SQLite's internal tables. Press Reset before rerunning a complete CREATE-and-INSERT solution.

                                                                                                              Reference — the full KimTay schema, for when you want to check your column names:

                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: the product catalogue - one row per item KimTay sells.
CREATE TABLE ITEM (

    -- CHAR(4): item ids are always four characters, such as CF21. PRIMARY KEY
    --   makes each one unique and never empty.
    ITEM_ID        CHAR(4)      PRIMARY KEY,

    -- NOT NULL: an item with no description would be useless on any report.
    DESCRIPTION    VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,

    -- Left nullable, so an item can be added before it has been categorised.
    CATEGORY       VARCHAR(15),

    -- SMALLINT: a whole number in a small range, which is plenty for a count of
    --   units in stock.
    ON_HAND        SMALLINT,

    -- DECIMAL(7,2): exact money to two decimal places.
    PRICE          DECIMAL(7,2),

    -- The stock level at which reordering starts. Last column, so no comma.
    REORDER_LEVEL  SMALLINT
);

                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: the invoice header - one row per invoice.
CREATE TABLE INVOICE (

    -- CHAR(5) because invoice numbers are always five characters, and PRIMARY
    --   KEY makes each one unique and never empty.
    INVOICE_NUM    CHAR(5)   PRIMARY KEY,

    -- The link back to the customer. It is declared with the same type and width
    --   as CUSTOMER's own key, which is what allows the two to be compared.
    CUSTOMER_NUM   CHAR(4),

    -- DATE stores a real date, so the engine can sort and compare it properly
    --   instead of treating it as text.
    INVOICE_DATE   DATE,

    -- FOREIGN KEY: a table-level rule rather than a column one. It refuses any
    --   invoice whose CUSTOMER_NUM does not already exist in CUSTOMER, which is
    --   what stops orphan rows from appearing.
    FOREIGN KEY (CUSTOMER_NUM) REFERENCES CUSTOMER(CUSTOMER_NUM)
);

                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: the line items - one row per item ordered on an invoice.
CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE (

    -- Which invoice this line belongs to.
    INVOICE_NUM    CHAR(5),

    -- Which item was ordered on it.
    ITEM_ID        CHAR(4),

    -- How many were ordered.
    NUM_ORDERED    SMALLINT,

    -- The price actually charged at the time. It is stored here rather than read
    --   from ITEM because the price on the day of the sale must not change when
    --   the catalogue price changes later.
    QUOTED_PRICE   DECIMAL(7,2),

    -- PRIMARY KEY over TWO columns - a composite key. Neither column identifies
    --   a row on its own; the pair does. It also stops the same item being
    --   listed twice on one invoice.
    PRIMARY KEY (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID),

    -- Two foreign keys, one per parent table. Each value must already exist on
    --   the side it points at.
    FOREIGN KEY (INVOICE_NUM) REFERENCES INVOICE(INVOICE_NUM),
    FOREIGN KEY (ITEM_ID) REFERENCES ITEM(ITEM_ID)
);

                                                                                                              🔍 Knowledge check: finishing the KimTay schema

                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                              Q1One key made of two columns

                                                                                                              The developer building KimTay's INVOICE_LINE table has typed the four columns INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED and QUOTED_PRICE, and now has to add the key line. KimTay's rule is that one invoice can list several different items, and one item can be sold on several different invoices. Which line inside CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE states the primary key correctly?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. An invoice that lists several items has several lines, so INVOICE_NUM repeats and cannot identify a line on its own.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. An item sold on several invoices appears on several lines, so ITEM_ID repeats too and cannot identify a line by itself.
                                                                                                              • ✔c. Right - a composite primary key names both columns in one declaration, and only the combination has to be unique.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. A table gets exactly one primary key; when it needs two columns, they go inside a single PRIMARY KEY declaration.

                                                                                                              Remember: When neither column is unique on its own, name both inside one PRIMARY KEY declaration.

                                                                                                              Q2Where the price really lives

                                                                                                              ITEM lists CF21 Grain-Free Dry Food at a PRICE of 42.50. On invoice 50710, the INVOICE_LINE row for CF21 shows NUM_ORDERED 3 and QUOTED_PRICE 42.50. Which statement about those two columns is correct?

                                                                                                              • ✔a. Right - storing the quoted price on the line means a later price change in ITEM does not rewrite what an old invoice charged.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Nothing keeps the two in step; they are equal here only because this customer paid list price that day.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. The line total is QUOTED_PRICE times NUM_ORDERED, worked out when needed - the column itself holds a per-item price.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. Each column sits where it belongs: a list price describes the item, and a quoted price describes one line on one invoice.

                                                                                                              Remember: ITEM.PRICE is today's list price; INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE is what one invoice actually charged.

                                                                                                              Q3The CREATE TABLE that returned nothing

                                                                                                              Working in a brand new, empty database that holds no KimTay tables yet, the developer runs the CREATE TABLE ITEM statement and the output area comes back empty, with no error message. Running SELECT * FROM ITEM; next returns the column headings with no rows underneath them. What does that tell the developer?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. CREATE TABLE reports success without returning rows, so an empty output area with no error is not a failure message.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Nothing is hidden - in a brand new database, rows exist only after INSERT statements put them there, which is the next step in the lesson.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. These statements finish before the output appears; there is no partial result waiting to fill itself in.
                                                                                                              • ✔d. Right - CREATE TABLE creates structure only, and headings with no rows underneath is exactly what a brand new empty table looks like.

                                                                                                              Remember: CREATE TABLE builds an empty structure - column headings with no rows means the table exists and is waiting for INSERTs.

                                                                                                              3-11 Describing a TableObjective 4 Objective 6

                                                                                                              Once a table exists, how do you check its structure without opening a diagram? Objective 6 shows up here too — every engine has its own command:

                                                                                                              "Describe a table" across engines
                                                                                                              EngineCommand
                                                                                                              MySQLDESCRIBE tablename; or SHOW COLUMNS FROM tablename;
                                                                                                              Oracle SQL*Plus / SQLclDESCRIBE tablename; (or DESC for short)
                                                                                                              SQL ServerEXEC sys.sp_help 'tablename';
                                                                                                              Microsoft AccessNo SQL command — open the table in Design View
                                                                                                              This sandbox (SQLite)PRAGMA table_info(tablename);
