                                                                                                              🔍 Knowledge check: describing a table

                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                              Q1The DESCRIBE that did not work here

                                                                                                              Lesson 3-11 lists the inspection command engine by engine: DESCRIBE tablename; in MySQL and Oracle clients, EXEC sys.sp_help 'tablename'; in SQL Server, and PRAGMA table_info(tablename); in SQLite. A student who learned MySQL types DESCRIBE CUSTOMER; into this course's sandbox and gets an error, because the sandbox on this page is SQLite. She wants CUSTOMER's column names, their declared types, and which column is the primary key. What should she run instead?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. SHOW COLUMNS is another MySQL wording, and it is not in the lesson's table at all - the whole point is that each engine words this differently.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. SELECT * shows column names and data, but not the declared types and not which column is the primary key.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. sys.sp_help is the SQL Server row only, and it is not what a SQLite sandbox accepts.
                                                                                                              • ✔d. Right - this page's sandbox is SQLite, and PRAGMA table_info(CUSTOMER); is the SQLite row of the lesson's table.

                                                                                                              Remember: Every engine words table inspection differently - DESCRIBE in MySQL and Oracle clients, sys.sp_help in SQL Server, and PRAGMA table_info in SQLite - so match the command to the engine you are on.

                                                                                                              Q2Reading the output for INVOICE_LINE

                                                                                                              In the SQLite sandbox, PRAGMA table_info(INVOICE_LINE); returns one row per column, with fields for position, name, declared type, whether the column is NOT NULL, its default value, and a pk field. Which part of that output shows the primary key is made of two columns?

                                                                                                              • ✔a. Right - the pk field is the one that reports key membership, and a non-zero value on two rows means a two-column key.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Position only reflects the order the columns were declared; a key column can sit anywhere in the list.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. Data type has nothing to do with keys - over in StayWell, PAYMENT's key is a plain number rather than text.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. NOT NULL only says a value is required, and CUSTOMER_NAME is NOT NULL without being a key; in SQLite a key column can even show 0 in that field unless NOT NULL was declared explicitly.

                                                                                                              Remember: In PRAGMA table_info output, the pk field - not position, data type, or NOT NULL - tells you which columns form the key.

                                                                                                              Summary Module Summary

                                                                                                              You now have hands-on reps with this module's core SQL commands: CREATE DATABASE/ CREATE TABLE to establish a database and define table structure, data types and constraints to declare what columns accept, NULL to mark unknown or inapplicable values, and the full CRUD cycle — INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE — to manage data (Objective 4). Along the way you saw exactly how MySQL, Oracle, and Access diverge on the same tasks (Objective 6), and you rebuilt the entire KimTay schema yourself from Lesson 3-3 through 3-10.

                                                                                                              The real-world project is where these skills leave the sandbox: designing and deploying a database of your own for a scenario you choose.

                                                                                                              See the capstone project →

                                                                                                              Terms Key Terms

                                                                                                              DDL

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              Data Definition Language — CREATE, ALTER, DROP: commands that define or change database structure.

                                                                                                              DML

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              Data Manipulation Language — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE: commands that work with data.

                                                                                                              NULL

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              A marker representing an unknown or not-applicable value — never equal to anything, including another NULL.

                                                                                                              Constraint

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              A rule enforced on a column or table, such as PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, or FOREIGN KEY.

                                                                                                              Script

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              A saved, reusable text file of SQL commands, typically with a .sql extension.

                                                                                                              CRUD

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four fundamental operations on stored data (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE in SQL).

                                                                                                              JOIN

                                                                                                              Click / press Enter to flip
                                                                                                              A SQL operation that combines rows from two or more tables by matching values in a shared column — typically a foreign key matching the primary key it references, e.g. CUSTOMER JOIN REP ON CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM.

                                                                                                              🔍 Knowledge check: Module 3 key terms

                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                              Q1Sorting the morning's commands

                                                                                                              The developer setting up KimTay's database ran four statements this morning: CREATE TABLE ITEM (...), INSERT INTO ITEM (...), UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = 44.00 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'; and SELECT * FROM ITEM;. Using this course's definitions, how do those four sort into DDL and DML?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. INSERT adds a row of data, not a piece of structure - what a command touches, not whether it adds something, decides the category.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Changing things is not the test; an UPDATE edits values inside a table, which makes it DML no matter how much it changes.
                                                                                                              • ✔c. Right - DDL is Data Definition Language and defines structure (CREATE TABLE), while DML is Data Manipulation Language and works with the data (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
                                                                                                              • ✘d. Reading is only part of DML - INSERT and UPDATE are DML as well, even though they change data rather than read it.

                                                                                                              Remember: DDL defines structure (CREATE TABLE); DML works with the data inside it (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

                                                                                                              Q2The blank street address

                                                                                                              CUSTOMER declares CUSTOMER_NAME as NOT NULL, and a new customer is entered whose STREET is not yet known, so STREET is left NULL. Which sentence uses this course's key terms correctly?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. NULL is not a rule and not zero - it is the marker for an unknown or not-applicable value, while NOT NULL is the constraint.
                                                                                                              • ✔b. Right - a constraint is a rule enforced on a column, and NULL is the marker for a value that is unknown or does not apply.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. NOT NULL only requires that a value be present; an empty string counts as a value and would be accepted.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. NULL is never equal to anything, including another NULL - comparing them gives UNKNOWN, which is why IS NULL exists.

                                                                                                              Remember: A constraint is a rule on a column; NULL is a marker for unknown and never equals anything.

                                                                                                              Review Review Questions

                                                                                                              🔍 Module 3 cumulative review: writing and reading SQL

                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                              Q1The query that came back empty

                                                                                                              KimTay's four sample customers carry balances of 3512.50, 1200.00, 0.00, and 4820.75. A clerk runs SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 5000; and stares at a blank result. What actually happened?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. WHERE filters rows by testing the condition against each one; it does not pass everything through.
                                                                                                              • ✔b. The largest balance in the sample is 4820.75, so nothing satisfies BALANCE > 5000 and an empty result is the right answer; the statement ran perfectly well.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. SQL compares the stored value exactly as it is and never rounds it to make a comparison succeed.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. Numeric literals are written without quotes; quoting turns 5000 into text, which is a different kind of comparison.

                                                                                                              Remember: An empty result usually means your condition worked correctly and nothing matched, not that the query is broken.

                                                                                                              Q2The rep with no street address

                                                                                                              A new rep is added with INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME) VALUES ('88', 'Alvarez', 'Sam');, so STREET and COMMISSION are both left out of the statement and land in the row as NULL. Afterward SELECT * FROM REP WHERE STREET = NULL; returns no rows at all, while SELECT COMMISSION + 100 FROM REP WHERE REP_NUM = '88'; returns one row containing NULL. Which single explanation covers both results?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. The row does exist - the second statement found it and returned a row, which is why you got a NULL result rather than no rows at all.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. NULL means unknown and is not an empty string, a zero, or a blank; an empty string is a real value somebody actually typed.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. WHERE is always evaluated, but STREET = NULL produces UNKNOWN, and a WHERE clause treats UNKNOWN as not matching.
                                                                                                              • ✔d. Three-valued logic means NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN instead of TRUE, and an unknown commission plus 100 is still unknown, so WHERE STREET IS NULL is the only way to find the row.

                                                                                                              Remember: NULL is unknown, so it never equals anything and never survives arithmetic - use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

                                                                                                              Q3Who is the Whiskers and Wags rep?

                                                                                                              The sales manager wants one list showing every KimTay customer's name beside their rep's last name. CUSTOMER stores only REP_NUM, while the names live in REP. Which statement produces that list?

                                                                                                              • ✔a. The ON clause pairs each customer with the one REP row sharing its REP_NUM, which is exactly the foreign-key relationship a join follows.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Naming two tables with no matching condition pairs every customer with every rep, producing twelve nonsense rows instead of four.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. Joining CUSTOMER_NUM to REP_NUM compares unrelated values; ON must compare the foreign key to the key it actually references.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. CUSTOMER has no LAST_NAME column at all, so no WHERE clause can make a rep's name appear without joining REP.

                                                                                                              Remember: A JOIN needs an ON clause that equates the foreign key with the primary key it references.

                                                                                                              Q4How many rows should come back?

                                                                                                              KimTay has three invoices and six INVOICE_LINE rows, two lines on each invoice. A clerk runs SELECT i.INVOICE_NUM, l.ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE i JOIN INVOICE_LINE l ON i.INVOICE_NUM = l.INVOICE_NUM;. How many rows come back?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. An invoice with two lines appears twice in the output; the join repeats the INVOICE row once per matching line.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. A join does not stack two tables end to end, so you count matching pairs rather than adding the two row counts together.
                                                                                                              • ✔c. One output row per matching pair means all six INVOICE_LINE rows find their invoice, giving six rows.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. Pairing everything with everything is what happens when you leave the ON clause off, not when you supply one.

                                                                                                              Remember: A JOIN returns one row per matching pair, so the many side usually decides the row count.

                                                                                                              Q5The 500 dollars that came off every account

                                                                                                              A KimTay clerk meant to credit Access Pet Center for a 500 dollar payment, but typed UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 500; and pressed Run. What happened, and what habit prevents it next time?

                                                                                                              • ✔a. Running SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120'; first proves the filter matches only the intended row before you change anything.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. The statement is perfectly valid SQL, which is exactly why it is dangerous - the database runs it without complaint.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. UPDATE changes every row that satisfies the WHERE clause, and with no WHERE clause every row satisfies it.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. A DBMS keeps no memory of your previous SELECT; each statement stands entirely on its own.

                                                                                                              Remember: UPDATE and DELETE with no WHERE clause hit every row, so always test the filter with a SELECT first.

                                                                                                              Q6The cheap, well-stocked restock list

                                                                                                              KimTay's buyer wants a short restock list: every item priced under 30 dollars that also has at least 25 units on hand, most expensive first. ITEM holds Aviary Starter Cage (64.99, 15 on hand), Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb (42.50, 48), Nylon Dog Leash 6ft (11.99, 120), Fish Tank Filter Kit (27.75, 30), and Small Animal Grooming Kit (15.25, 22). Which statement produces the list?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. OR widens the result because a row only has to satisfy one condition, so the 42.50 dry food and the 22-unit grooming kit come back too.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. ORDER BY always follows the WHERE clause. Written this way the database cannot even parse the statement: it reports a syntax error at WHERE and never runs the query, which is different from a valid query that runs and simply matches no rows.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. SORT BY is not SQL - the keyword for arranging the rows you selected is ORDER BY - so the database rejects the statement with an error instead of running it and returning an empty grid.
                                                                                                              • ✔d. AND requires both conditions to be true on the same row, leaving the filter kit at 27.75 and the leash at 11.99, sorted from the higher price down.

                                                                                                              Remember: AND narrows a result while OR widens it, and the clause order is always SELECT, then FROM, then WHERE, then ORDER BY.

                                                                                                              Q7The price that would not fit

                                                                                                              KimTay's ITEM.PRICE column is declared DECIMAL(7,2). The buyer wants to add a custom aquarium priced at 129999.99. Can the current column hold it, and which MySQL and Oracle declarations would be wide enough?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. The first number is the total digit count, so DECIMAL(7,2) tops out at 99999.99.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. That reading double counts: the precision 7 covers all digits including the 2 after the point, not 7 plus 2.
                                                                                                              • ✔c. 129999.99 has eight digits, which overflows DECIMAL(7,2). Precision 8 leaves room for six digits before the point and two after it in both DECIMAL(8,2) and NUMBER(8,2).
                                                                                                              • ✘d. Oracle stores decimals in NUMBER(p,s); keeping money as text would break sorting and arithmetic.

                                                                                                              Remember: In DECIMAL(p,s) the p is total digits and the s is how many of those digits fall after the decimal point.

                                                                                                              Q8The rep whose first name became her last

                                                                                                              Intending to add rep Amelia Ross, a clerk runs INSERT INTO REP (REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME) VALUES ('72', 'Ross', 'Amelia');. Then SELECT * FROM REP; shows something odd. What went wrong?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. A DBMS has no idea which strings are first names; it simply lines the values up positionally against the column list.
                                                                                                              • ✔b. The first value goes to the first column named and the second to the second, so swapping the names in VALUES swaps them in the stored row.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. Both columns did receive a value, so the NOT NULL constraints were satisfied - the values were merely in the wrong places.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. You may list the columns in any order you like, as long as the VALUES appear in that same order.

                                                                                                              Remember: INSERT matches values to columns strictly by position, so the column list and the VALUES list must line up.

                                                                                                              Q9The invoice for a customer who is not there

                                                                                                              INVOICE was created with FOREIGN KEY (CUSTOMER_NUM) REFERENCES CUSTOMER(CUSTOMER_NUM). Someone runs INSERT INTO INVOICE VALUES ('50713', '9999', '2026-06-20'); and KimTay has no customer 9999. Assume a DBMS such as MySQL or Oracle, where referential integrity is enforced. What should the DBMS do, and why?

                                                                                                              • ✘a. A foreign key constraint refuses bad values; it never invents the missing parent row on your behalf.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. The constraint is checked on INSERT and UPDATE too, which is what stops orphaned invoices from ever being created.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. Uniqueness is a primary key or UNIQUE rule; CUSTOMER_NUM is meant to repeat in INVOICE, because one customer has many invoices - 1120, 1420, and 1225 each own an invoice here.
                                                                                                              • ✔d. A foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, so an invoice can never point at a customer who does not exist.

                                                                                                              Remember: On a DBMS that enforces referential integrity, a foreign key guarantees that every reference points at a row that really exists in the referenced table.

                                                                                                              Q10The setup script that failed halfway

                                                                                                              A student saves kimtay_setup.sql with CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE first, then ITEM and INVOICE, and runs it against MySQL with mysql -u root -p kimtay_pet_supplies < kimtay_setup.sql. MySQL rejects the very first statement. What is wrong, and what is the fix?

                                                                                                              • ✔a. FOREIGN KEY (ITEM_ID) REFERENCES ITEM(ITEM_ID) cannot be honored until ITEM exists, so parent tables always come first in a setup script.
                                                                                                              • ✘b. Alphabetical order is a coincidence at best; what matters is that a referenced table is created before the table that references it.
                                                                                                              • ✘c. A script is simply a list of statements run in order, and running many statements at once is the whole point of saving one.
                                                                                                              • ✘d. The database kimtay_pet_supplies already exists here - it is named on the command line - and not every engine even has CREATE DATABASE, since in SQLite the database is simply the file you open.

                                                                                                              Remember: In a setup script, create the tables a foreign key points at before the tables that point at them.

                                                                                                                        Exercises Case Exercises

                                                                                                                        An open sandbox with both full databases loaded — KimTay and StayWell together. Use it for the exercises below (and for anything else you want to try):

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        All 11 tables are available: REP, CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, MANAGER, PROPERTY, ROOM, STUDENT, LEASE, PAYMENT. Reset before rerunning the full solution.

                                                                                                                        1. Write a query that lists each KimTay customer's name alongside their assigned rep's last name.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: one column from each table. AS renames the second so the heading reads
--   REP_LAST_NAME rather than the bare LAST_NAME.
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, r.LAST_NAME AS REP_LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the first table, given the short alias c. From here on c means CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER c

-- JOIN ... ON: brings in the second table as r, and ON states how the two line
--   up - keep a pairing only where the rep numbers match. One row per customer
--   comes back, each carrying the name of the rep who serves it.
JOIN REP r ON c.REP_NUM = r.REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                        2. StayWell wants a list of every student whose lease has a monthly rent above $500, cheapest first.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns - two from STUDENT, one from LEASE.
SELECT s.FIRST_NAME, s.LAST_NAME, l.MONTHLY_RENT

-- FROM: the student table, aliased s.
FROM STUDENT s

-- JOIN ... ON: brings in LEASE as l and matches the two on student id, so each
--   student is lined up with their own lease row.
JOIN LEASE l ON s.STUDENT_ID = l.STUDENT_ID

-- WHERE: filters the joined rows. It tests a LEASE column, which only became
--   available to the query once the join brought that table in.
WHERE l.MONTHLY_RENT > 500

-- ORDER BY: sorts what survives by rent, ASC meaning smallest first. ASC is the
--   default and could be left out; writing it makes the intent unmistakable.
ORDER BY l.MONTHLY_RENT ASC;

                                                                                                                        3. Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) has no invoices. Delete that unreferenced customer, then confirm the row is gone without listing the whole CUSTOMER table.

                                                                                                                        -- DELETE FROM: removes rows from a table, and the WHERE clause is the only thing
--   deciding which ones. A DELETE with no WHERE empties the entire table, which
--   is why you read the WHERE clause before you press run.
DELETE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- SELECT COUNT(*): the check. Counting the rows that still match the same
--   condition is how you prove the delete did exactly what you meant.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS still_there

-- FROM ... WHERE: the same table and the same condition as the DELETE above.
FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- still_there should now be 0
