                                                                                                                        4-1 Constructing Simple Queries

                                                                                                                        Module 3 was about getting data into KimTay's tables and pulling it back out. Module 4 is about asking sharper questions. Every query in this lesson reads a single table, which keeps the moving parts small while you learn the clauses that do the real filtering work.

                                                                                                                        A query is a question you put to the database in a form it can answer. The shape you already know is SELECT (which columns you want), FROM (which table they live in), and optionally WHERE (which rows qualify). Everything in this lesson is a refinement of those three lines.

                                                                                                                        Start with the data: this is the complete ITEM table used by the first examples. Read its five rows before looking at the first query.

                                                                                                                        Source table: ITEM — all columns and all five rows
                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONCATEGORYON_HANDPRICEREORDER_LEVEL
                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter CageHabitat1564.995
                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lbFood4842.5015
                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ftAccessory12011.9925
                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter KitHabitat3027.7510
                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming KitGrooming2215.258
                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                        What you are building on

                                                                                                                        You already have SELECT, FROM, a WHERE with one comparison, and ORDER BY. This lesson adds compound conditions, ranges, arithmetic, pattern matching, and value lists. None of it replaces what you know; all of it plugs into the same statement.

                                                                                                                        4-1a Retrieving Certain Columns and All Rows

                                                                                                                        Start with the most common request a business makes: give me a few facts about everything. KimTay's bookkeeper wants an ID, a description, and a price for every item in stock, and nothing else. Name the columns you want, separated by commas, in the order you want to read them.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: names the three columns you want to see, in the order you want them.
--   Everything not listed here stays in the table and simply is not returned.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: which table to read them out of. With no WHERE clause, every row of ITEM
--   comes back - all five of them.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                        That returns all five ITEM rows and exactly three columns. Two separate decisions produced that result: naming three columns is what limited the width, and leaving out WHERE is what kept every row.

                                                                                                                        Result of the three-column query against ITEM (prices shown as they are stored)
                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONPRICE
                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage64.99
                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb42.50
                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft11.99
                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit27.75
                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming Kit15.25
                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                        Why the sandbox drops trailing zeros

                                                                                                                        MySQL prints a DECIMAL(7,2) column with both decimal places, so PRICE reads 42.50 and a zero balance reads 0.00. The browser engine on this page prints the shortest form of the same number, so you will see 42.5, and 0 instead of 0.00, and 7500 instead of 7500.00. The stored value is identical; only the printing differs. Tables in this lesson show the stored form.

                                                                                                                        The order of the names in the SELECT list is the order of the columns in the result. If the warehouse manager wants the description on the left, write SELECT DESCRIPTION, ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM; and you get the same five rows rearranged. Nothing about the stored table changes.

                                                                                                                        4-1b Retrieving All Columns and All Rows

                                                                                                                        When you want every column, you can list all six by name, or use the shorthand asterisk.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT *: the asterisk is shorthand for "every column, in the order the table
--   defines them". Handy while exploring, risky in saved code - the moment
--   somebody adds a column, your output silently changes shape.
SELECT *

-- FROM: the table being read. Five rows, six columns.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                        That returns the same five rows with all six columns, in the order they were defined in CREATE TABLE: ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY, ON_HAND, PRICE, REORDER_LEVEL. The asterisk is not a chooser and it is not a wildcard for rows; it means every column.

                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                        Fine for exploring, risky in a saved script

                                                                                                                        SELECT * is the fastest way to look around a table you do not know yet. In a script you plan to keep, name the columns. If the table is ever rebuilt with an extra column, SELECT * silently changes what your report returns, while a named list keeps returning what you asked for.

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        Five rows either way; only the number of columns should change, from three to six.

                                                                                                                        4-1c Using a WHERE Clause

                                                                                                                        Most business questions are about some rows, not all of them. A WHERE clause states a condition, and the engine keeps only the rows for which that condition is true. You have used WHERE with a single equality. Here is the full set of comparison operators.

                                                                                                                        Comparison operators you can use in a condition
                                                                                                                        OperatorMeansExample condition
                                                                                                                        =equal toPRICE = 42.50
                                                                                                                        >greater thanON_HAND > 25
                                                                                                                        <less thanON_HAND < 25
                                                                                                                        >=greater than or equal toCREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500
                                                                                                                        <=less than or equal toPRICE <= 15.25
                                                                                                                        <>not equal toCATEGORY <> 'Habitat'

                                                                                                                        KimTay's warehouse manager wants a short list of the items running thin. Anything under 25 on hand is worth a look.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the three columns to display.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the filter. It is tested once per row, and a row is returned only when
--   the condition comes back true. Two items are stocked below 25.
WHERE ON_HAND < 25;

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: AV07 with 15 on hand and GR15 with 22. The other three items hold 30, 48, and 120, so the condition is false for them and the engine drops them.

                                                                                                                        Conditions on text look the same, with one difference: the value goes inside single quotes.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: two columns from the customer table.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: an equality test against a text value, so the value goes in single
--   quotes. Numbers never take quotes; text and dates always do.
WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove';

                                                                                                                        That returns two rows: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic.

                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                        Quote text, leave numbers bare

                                                                                                                        Character values need single quotes: CITY = 'Maple Grove'. Numeric values do not: ON_HAND < 25. Leave the quotes off a word and the engine reads it as a name, not as text, and refuses to run the statement. Watch out too for columns that look numeric but are not -- CUSTOMER_NUM is declared CHAR(4), so it is text, and you write WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120' to get Access Pet Center.

                                                                                                                        <> is the not-equal operator. Both MySQL and SQLite also accept !=, but <> is the standard spelling and works everywhere, so prefer it.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the id and the category, so the filter can be checked by eye.
SELECT ITEM_ID, CATEGORY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: <> means "not equal to". Some engines also accept !=, but <> is the
--   standard spelling and works everywhere.
WHERE CATEGORY <> 'Habitat';

                                                                                                                        Three rows come back: CF21 in Food, DG04 in Accessory, and GR15 in Grooming. The two Habitat items, AV07 and FT88, are excluded.

                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                        Name the table

                                                                                                                        Decide which single table holds the fact you are filtering on, and put it after FROM.

                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                        Pick the column

                                                                                                                        Find the column that stores the value you care about. ON_HAND for stock levels, CITY for location, CATEGORY for kind of item.

                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                        Choose the operator

                                                                                                                        Equality for an exact match, < or > for a threshold, <> for everything except one value.

                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                        Write the value in the column's own form

                                                                                                                        Single quotes for character columns, bare digits for numeric columns.

                                                                                                                        5

                                                                                                                        Read the row count before you trust it

                                                                                                                        If a five-row table gives back five rows, your condition probably is not filtering anything. Check it against the data by hand.

                                                                                                                        The right side of a condition does not have to be a fixed value. It can be another column in the same row. SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND < REORDER_LEVEL; asks which items have fallen below their own reorder point. Against the current data it returns no rows at all, and that is the answer: nothing needs reordering today. An empty result is not an error.

                                                                                                                        4-1d Using Compound Conditions

                                                                                                                        Real questions usually carry more than one requirement. "Maple Grove customers who owe us money" is two conditions at once. You join simple conditions with AND and OR, and you flip one with NOT.

                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                        Compound condition

                                                                                                                        A condition built from two or more simple conditions joined by AND or OR, and optionally reversed by NOT. AND keeps a row only when every part is true. OR keeps a row when at least one part is true.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns, including BALANCE so the second condition is visible.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the first of two conditions.
WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove'

-- AND: a compound condition. BOTH sides must be true for the row to be kept, so
--   this is stricter than either condition alone. Companion Care Clinic is in
--   Maple Grove but owes nothing, so it fails here.
  AND BALANCE > 1000;

                                                                                                                        One row comes back: 1120 Access Pet Center, with a balance of 3512.50. Companion Care Clinic is also in Maple Grove, but its balance is 0.00, so it fails the second half and AND drops it.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the first of two conditions.
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Food'

-- OR: EITHER side being true is enough to keep the row, so this is looser than
--   either condition alone. A row satisfying both is still returned once.
   OR PRICE > 60;

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: AV07 at 64.99, which qualifies on price alone, and CF21 at 42.50, which qualifies on category alone. Neither row has to satisfy both halves, because OR asks for at least one.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the id and the category being tested.
SELECT ITEM_ID, CATEGORY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: NOT reverses the condition inside the parentheses - keep the row when
--   the test is false. The parentheses are optional here but worth writing, as
--   they make it unmistakable which condition NOT applies to.
WHERE NOT (CATEGORY = 'Habitat');

                                                                                                                        That returns CF21, DG04, and GR15 -- the same three rows as CATEGORY <> 'Habitat'. NOT earns its keep in front of a longer condition, where there is no single operator to reverse.

                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                        Parentheses change the answer

                                                                                                                        When you mix AND and OR in one clause, AND is evaluated first. That is the single most common source of a query that runs cleanly and returns the wrong rows. Put parentheses around the part you want grouped, every time, even when you think you do not need them.

                                                                                                                        Without parentheses: 2 rows

                                                                                                                        WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food' AND PRICE < 30 reads as Habitat OR (Food AND under 30). Both Habitat items pass untested on price, so AV07 at 64.99 and FT88 at 27.75 come back. CF21 is Food at 42.50, so it fails.

                                                                                                                        With parentheses: 1 row

                                                                                                                        WHERE (CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food') AND PRICE < 30 reads as (Habitat or Food) AND under 30. Now the price test applies to all three of those items, and only FT88 at 27.75 survives.

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        Two rows before the parentheses, one row after. If both runs match, the parentheses landed in the wrong place.

                                                                                                                        4-1e Using the BETWEEN Operator

                                                                                                                        Range questions come up constantly: prices in a window, dates in a month, balances in a band. You can always write a range as two conditions joined by AND, and BETWEEN is a shorter way to say the same thing. KimTay's buyer wants every item priced from 15.25 through 27.75.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns, PRICE included so the range is easy to verify.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: BETWEEN tests a range and is INCLUSIVE at both ends, so an item priced
--   at exactly 15.25 or exactly 27.75 is kept. The smaller value must be written
--   first; reverse them and the condition matches nothing at all.
WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75;

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: FT88 at 27.75 and GR15 at 15.25. Notice that both of those prices sit exactly on a boundary, and both matched.

                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                        BETWEEN includes both endpoints

                                                                                                                        PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75 means exactly PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75. It adds no power to SQL, only readability. Two rules follow: write the low value first, because BETWEEN 27.75 AND 15.25 can never be true and returns an empty result without complaining; and if you need an exclusive edge, write the comparisons out with > or < instead.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the same three columns as the BETWEEN version above.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the same table.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: exactly what BETWEEN means, spelled out. Two comparisons joined by AND,
--   each using >= or <= so both endpoints are included. Same rows, more typing -
--   which is the whole argument for BETWEEN.
WHERE PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75;

                                                                                                                        Same two rows, FT88 and GR15. Use whichever version reads more clearly to the next person who opens your script.

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        Four of the five rooms qualify; only the 725.00 studio in Sycamore Court falls outside the window. The rents print as 595 and 450 here, without the trailing zeros.

                                                                                                                        4-1f Using Computed Columns

                                                                                                                        Some numbers a business needs are not stored anywhere. KimTay stores ON_HAND and PRICE, but nobody stores the value of the stock on the shelf, because it would go stale the moment either number changed. You calculate it in the query instead.

                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                        Computed column

                                                                                                                        A column that appears in the result but does not exist in the table. The engine works it out for each row from values that do exist, using +, -, *, and /. Nothing is written back to the table.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: two stored columns, then a computed one. ON_HAND * PRICE is worked out
--   once for each row as the result is built; nothing is stored back in the
--   table. AS gives the computed column the heading ON_HAND_VALUE, which is
--   worth doing - without it the heading is the arithmetic itself.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS ON_HAND_VALUE

-- FROM: the table supplying both columns being multiplied.
FROM ITEM;
                                                                                                                        Value of the stock on hand, calculated per row, as each engine prints it
                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONON_HAND_VALUE on this pageON_HAND_VALUE in MySQL
                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage974.8499999999999974.85
                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb20402040.00
                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft1438.81438.80
                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit832.5832.50
                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming Kit335.5335.50

                                                                                                                        Read the AV07 row twice, because it is the interesting one. MySQL multiplies DECIMAL values exactly and reports 974.85. The browser engine on this page converts DECIMAL to binary floating point, where 64.99 has no exact representation, so 15 * 64.99 comes back as 974.8499999999999. Rounded to cents the two agree, and your query is correct in both.

                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                        Money and binary floating point

                                                                                                                        A long tail such as 974.8499999999999 in the sandbox is the storage format showing through, not a mistake in your arithmetic. It is also the reason production systems keep money in an exact type such as DECIMAL rather than a floating-point type, and the reason you round money for display rather than trusting the raw digits.

                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                        Always name a computed column

                                                                                                                        Without AS, the heading is whatever the engine decides to call the expression, and it differs between systems. AS ON_HAND_VALUE gives it a stable name you can rely on in a report. Keep alias names to one word with underscores: MySQL quotes identifiers with backticks while standard SQL uses double quotes, so a one-word alias saves you from having to choose.

                                                                                                                        Arithmetic works on any numeric columns, including two columns from the same row. KimTay's credit manager wants to know how much room each customer has left.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: two stored columns plus a subtraction. The calculation answers a
--   question the table never stored: how much of the credit limit is still free.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE AS AVAILABLE_CREDIT

-- FROM: the table holding both of the columns being subtracted.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                        All four customers come back: 1120 with 3987.50 available, 1225 with 3800.00, 1310 with the full 10000.00, and 1420 with 1179.25. These subtractions land on exact cents in both engines, so the only difference you will see on this page is the missing trailing zeros.

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: 1120 at 3987.50 and 1310 at 10000.00. Notice that the whole expression is repeated in the WHERE clause rather than the alias being reused. That is deliberate, and it is a real difference between engines: the browser engine on this page would accept WHERE AVAILABLE_CREDIT > 3900, while MySQL rejects an alias in WHERE. Repeating the expression runs everywhere.

                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                        Logical Execution Order of SQL Clauses

                                                                                                                        Why can't you use a SELECT alias in a WHERE clause on standard SQL engines? Because of the order SQL evaluates your query: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. WHERE runs before SELECT creates the alias, while ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so ORDER BY can use the alias safely.

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        Two customers qualify. Repeat the whole expression in the WHERE clause instead of using the alias, so the query also runs on MySQL.

                                                                                                                        4-1g Using the LIKE Operator

                                                                                                                        Equality is all-or-nothing: STREET = '77 Elm St.' finds one exact value and misses everything close to it. When you only know part of the value, use LIKE with a pattern.

                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                        Wildcard

                                                                                                                        A character in a pattern that stands for other characters. % stands for any run of characters, including none at all. _ stands for exactly one character. Everything else in the pattern has to match literally.

                                                                                                                        Patterns and what they find in the KimTay data
                                                                                                                        PatternWhat it matchesRows it finds
                                                                                                                        '%St.'any value ending in St.customers 1225 and 1420, on STREET
                                                                                                                        '%Kit'any value ending in Kititems FT88 and GR15, on DESCRIPTION
                                                                                                                        '_F__'four characters, F in second placeitem CF21, on ITEM_ID
                                                                                                                        '%Cat%'Cat anywhere in the valueno rows at all, on DESCRIPTION
                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns, STREET included so the pattern match is visible.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, STREET

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: LIKE matches a pattern instead of an exact value. % stands for any run
--   of characters, including none, so '%St.' means "anything, ending in St.".
--   LIKE is for text only, and it is slower than = because every row's value has
--   to be examined character by character.
WHERE STREET LIKE '%St.';

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: 1225 at 642 Chestnut St. and 1420 at 77 Elm St. The leading % absorbs the house number and the street name, and because the pattern ends right after St., the match is anchored to the end of the value.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the id and the description being matched.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the same trailing-% pattern applied to product names - anything that
--   ends in the word Kit. Two of the five items do.
WHERE DESCRIPTION LIKE '%Kit';

                                                                                                                        Two rows: FT88 Fish Tank Filter Kit and GR15 Small Animal Grooming Kit. Move that percent sign to the other end and you would be asking for descriptions that start with Kit, which no item does.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the id and the description.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the other wildcard. _ stands for EXACTLY ONE character, so '_F__' means
--   a four-character id whose second character is F, with any characters in the
--   other three positions. FT88 does not qualify - its F is in position one.
WHERE ITEM_ID LIKE '_F__';

                                                                                                                        One row: CF21. The pattern is four characters long, so it can only match a four-character ID, and the F is pinned to the second position. FT88 has its F first, so it does not qualify.

                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                        Two things to know before you rely on LIKE

                                                                                                                        First, letter case. As configured here, both MySQL and the browser engine ignore case for these ASCII values, so '%cat%' and '%Cat%' behave alike; other systems and other collations do not, so match the case you see in the data. Second, speed. A pattern that starts with % forces the engine to examine every row, which costs nothing on five items and a great deal on five million.

                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                        Database Portability: LIKE vs ILIKE

                                                                                                                        While SQLite and MySQL treat ASCII text in LIKE case-insensitively by default, standard ANSI SQL and PostgreSQL treat LIKE case-sensitively. In PostgreSQL, use ILIKE for case-insensitive pattern matching (e.g. WHERE STREET ILIKE '%st.').

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        One customer qualifies. A percent sign on both sides is what says anywhere in the value, rather than only at the end.

                                                                                                                        4-1h Using the IN Operator

                                                                                                                        The last shorthand in this lesson handles the question "is this column any one of these values?" KimTay's bookkeeper is preparing a mailing for the customers in Maple Grove and Brookville.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns, CITY included so the membership test can be checked.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: IN is a membership test - true when the row's CITY equals ANY value in
--   the parenthesised list. The list can be as long as you like, and each value
--   is separated by a comma.
WHERE CITY IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville');

                                                                                                                        Three rows come back: 1120 and 1310 in Maple Grove, and 1420 in Brookville. Only 1225, in Northfield, is left out.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the same three columns as the IN version above.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY

-- FROM: the same table.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: exactly what IN means, written out as separate equality tests joined by
--   OR. Identical rows come back. IN is simply shorter, and stays readable when
--   the list grows to ten values instead of two.
WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' OR CITY = 'Brookville';

                                                                                                                        Identical three rows. IN is shorthand for that OR chain, and it gets easier to read the longer the list grows. The values inside the parentheses follow the same quoting rules as anywhere else: quotes for character columns, bare digits for numeric ones.

                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                        IN is a list, so it pairs with OR and never with AND

                                                                                                                        A common wrong turn is WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' AND CITY = 'Brookville', which asks for rows whose one city value is two cities at once. It returns nothing, with no error to warn you. If you find yourself writing AND between two tests on the same column, you almost certainly want IN.

                                                                                                                        Put NOT in front of IN to exclude a list instead of including it.

                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the id and the category being tested.
SELECT ITEM_ID, CATEGORY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: NOT IN keeps a row whose value matches NONE of the listed values. It is
--   the reverse of IN, and the same as writing CATEGORY <> 'Habitat' AND
--   CATEGORY <> 'Food'.
WHERE CATEGORY NOT IN ('Habitat', 'Food');

                                                                                                                        Two rows come back: DG04 in Accessory and GR15 in Grooming. Later, in lesson 4-4, you will see that the list inside IN can be produced by another query instead of typed by hand. The operator behaves the same way; only the source of the values changes.

                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                        Two rows either way, CF21 and GR15. If you get five rows, check that the list is inside one pair of parentheses.
                                                                                                                        • Name the columns you want in the SELECT list; keep SELECT * for exploring, not for scripts you save
                                                                                                                        • Quote character values in single quotes and leave numeric values bare, even when a character column looks numeric
                                                                                                                        • Use parentheses whenever AND and OR appear in the same WHERE clause
                                                                                                                        • Write BETWEEN with the low value first, and remember that both endpoints are included
                                                                                                                        • Give every computed column an alias with AS, and repeat the expression rather than the alias in WHERE so the query runs on MySQL too
                                                                                                                        • Expect a computed money column to show a floating-point tail such as 974.8499999999999 in this page's sandbox; MySQL prints the exact 974.85
                                                                                                                        • Reach for LIKE when you know part of a text value, and remember % is any run of characters while _ is exactly one
                                                                                                                        • Reach for IN when one column has to match any value in a list, and never join those tests with AND
                                                                                                                        • Check the row count against the data by hand before you trust a new query; an empty result is an answer, not an error

                                                                                                                        🔍 Knowledge check: columns, rows, and a first WHERE

                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                        Q1The report with three columns too many

                                                                                                                        KimTay's bookkeeper asks for the ID, description, and price of every item in the ITEM table, and nothing else. A classmate hands back a result with all six columns in it. Which statement produces exactly what she asked for?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The asterisk is not a chooser; it means every column in the table, which is the six-column result she rejected.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. FROM is never optional in a query against a table, because without it the engine has no table to read.
                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Right - the SELECT list controls which columns appear, and the absence of WHERE leaves all five rows in.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The asterisk is not a wildcard inside a comparison, so this looks for an ITEM_ID stored as a literal asterisk and returns zero rows.

                                                                                                                        Remember: The SELECT list decides the columns; leaving out WHERE is what keeps every row.

                                                                                                                        Q2The warehouse manager wants the description first

                                                                                                                        KimTay's warehouse manager prints a pick list and wants DESCRIPTION on the left, then ITEM_ID, then PRICE. The ITEM table was created with ITEM_ID first. What is true about getting the order he wants?

                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right - SELECT DESCRIPTION, ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM; returns the same five rows with the description on the left.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Declaration order is only the default that SELECT * follows, and naming the columns yourself overrides it.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Nothing about the stored table changes; the SELECT list rearranges the result, not the table.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. ORDER BY sorts rows from top to bottom and has no effect on the left-to-right order of columns.

                                                                                                                        Remember: Column order in the result comes from your SELECT list, not from how the table was built.

                                                                                                                        Q3The missing quotation marks

                                                                                                                        Someone at KimTay wants the customers in Maple Grove and types WHERE CITY = Maple Grove with no quotation marks anywhere. What happens, and why?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Capital letters mean nothing to the parser, and anything left unquoted is read as a name rather than as text.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. There is no quiet empty result here, because the statement never runs; the engine rejects it before any row is examined.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. It is the other way around: numbers are written bare and character values are wrapped in single quotes.
                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right - write WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove', which returns customers 1120 and 1310. Two bare words break the syntax outright, and a single bare word such as Northfield is reported as an unknown column.

                                                                                                                        Remember: Character values go inside single quotes; leave them off and the engine reads your text as a name and refuses to run the statement.

                                                                                                                        🔍 Knowledge check: compound conditions and BETWEEN

                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                        Q1Two queries, two different answers

                                                                                                                        Against KimTay's ITEM table, WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food' AND PRICE < 30 returns AV07 and FT88, while WHERE (CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food') AND PRICE < 30 returns FT88 alone. Why do they differ?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The precedence runs the other way, which is exactly why the unparenthesized version behaved unexpectedly.
                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right - it reads as Habitat OR (Food AND PRICE < 30), so both Habitat rows came back untested on price.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The two results differ by a row, so they cannot be identical, and stored order never changes which rows match.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Parentheses group conditions inside the WHERE clause and have no effect on the SELECT list.

                                                                                                                        Remember: AND binds tighter than OR, so add parentheses whenever you mix the two.

                                                                                                                        Q2The buyer's price window

                                                                                                                        KimTay's buyer asks for every item priced from 15.25 through 27.75, endpoints included. A clerk runs WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75 and gets GR15 at 15.25 and FT88 at 27.75. Which statement describes what BETWEEN did?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. If both endpoints were excluded, neither GR15 nor FT88 would appear, since each sits exactly on a bound.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. No rounding happens; the stored prices are compared against the bounds as written.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. FT88 is not a surprise, because the high endpoint is included in the same way the low one is.
                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right - BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75 means PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75.

                                                                                                                        Remember: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, the same as >= paired with <=.

                                                                                                                        Q3The empty range

                                                                                                                        A student writes WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 27.75 AND 15.25 against KimTay's ITEM table, expecting the same two items as before. The result is empty and no error appears. What went wrong?

                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right - it expands to PRICE >= 27.75 AND PRICE <= 15.25, which no single price can satisfy.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. No engine reorders your endpoints, so the low bound has to be written first or nothing matches.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. BETWEEN works on any comparable type, decimals included, so the column type is not the problem.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The AND inside BETWEEN is part of the operator's syntax, not a joiner you are free to swap for OR.

                                                                                                                        Remember: Write BETWEEN low AND high; reversed endpoints return an empty result without complaining.

                                                                                                                        🔍 Knowledge check: LIKE patterns and IN lists

                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                        Q1The streets that end in St.

                                                                                                                        KimTay is mailing a flyer to customers whose STREET value ends in St. The four stored streets are 215 Foster Ave., 642 Chestnut St., 89 River Rd., and 77 Elm St. Which condition finds the right two?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. With no wildcard at all, LIKE behaves like equals, so this matches only a street stored as exactly St.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The underscore stands for exactly one character, so this matches four-character values such as 1St. and finds nothing here.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A trailing percent sign allows extra characters after St., which unanchors the end rather than anchoring it.
                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right - the percent sign stands for any run of characters, and ending the pattern at St. anchors the match.

                                                                                                                        Remember: Percent stands for any number of characters, so where you place it decides what gets anchored.

                                                                                                                        Q2The four-character item ID

                                                                                                                        KimTay's item IDs are always four characters: AV07, CF21, DG04, FT88, GR15. The warehouse manager wants the ones whose second character is F. Which condition does that?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Percent stands for any number of characters rather than one, so this finds F anywhere and returns CF21 and FT88.
                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right - one underscore, then F, then two underscores pins the F to the second position and matches CF21.
                                                                                                                        • ✘c. That pattern pins F to the first position, so it returns FT88, whose second character is actually T.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The underscore is the single-character wildcard in LIKE, working alongside the percent sign.

                                                                                                                        Remember: Underscore matches exactly one character, so it pins a value to a fixed position and length.

                                                                                                                        Q3The two-city mailing list

                                                                                                                        KimTay's bookkeeper wants every customer in Maple Grove or Brookville and writes WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' AND CITY = 'Brookville'. The result is empty. What is the fix?

                                                                                                                        • ✘a. AND demands that both conditions be true for the same row, and one stored city cannot be two cities at once.
                                                                                                                        • ✘b. IN tests the column against every value in the list, so Brookville counts exactly as much as Maple Grove does.
                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Right - IN is shorthand for the OR chain, and it returns customers 1120, 1310, and 1420.
                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The stored city names are spelled correctly; the logic is what makes the condition impossible to satisfy.

                                                                                                                        Remember: IN matches one column against several values at once, which is what OR does and AND cannot.
