                                                                                                                                      4-2 Sorting

                                                                                                                                      A query answers a question. The order the answer arrives in decides whether anyone can use it. A list of 200 customers is a wall of text; the same 200 customers alphabetized is a phone directory. That is what ORDER BY is for.

                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                      Rows have no built-in order

                                                                                                                                      A table is a set of rows, not a list, so there is no such thing as the natural order of a table -- the DBMS hands back rows in whatever order is cheapest for it that day, and that order can change without warning. If you care about the order, you have to ask for it.

                                                                                                                                      4-2a Using the ORDER BY Clause

                                                                                                                                      You have used ORDER BY already. Here is the rule behind it: ORDER BY is the last clause in a SELECT statement, and it names the column you want the output sorted on. That column is called the sort key.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- ORDER BY: sorts the finished result. Without it a database makes no promise at
--   all about row order, so any report anybody is going to read needs one. Text
--   sorts alphabetically, and ascending is the default.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NAME;

                                                                                                                                      That returns all four KimTay customers, alphabetized by name: Access Pet Center, Companion Care Clinic, Downtown Aquarium & Pets, then Whiskers & Wags Boutique.

                                                                                                                                      Result of the customer listing sorted by CUSTOMER_NAME
                                                                                                                                      CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEBALANCE
                                                                                                                                      1120Access Pet Center3512.50
                                                                                                                                      1310Companion Care Clinic0.00
                                                                                                                                      1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets1200.00
                                                                                                                                      1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique4820.75
                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                      Why the sandbox shows 3512.5

                                                                                                                                      MySQL stores BALANCE as DECIMAL(9,2) and prints every value with two decimal places, so you see 3512.50 and 0.00; the SQLite engine behind the sandbox on this page drops trailing zeros and prints the same numbers as 3512.5 and 0. Only the display differs -- the stored values, the comparisons, and the sort order are identical, so the tables in this lesson use the MySQL form throughout.

                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                      Sort key

                                                                                                                                      A sort key is the column (or expression) whose values decide the order of the rows in the result; sorting rearranges the answer only, and never touches the rows stored in the table.

                                                                                                                                      Sorting runs from low to high unless you say otherwise. That is ascending order, and its keyword is ASC. Because ascending is the default, you almost never type ASC -- you type DESC when you want the largest value on top.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- ORDER BY: DESC reverses the sort, putting the largest value first - the usual
--   choice for "most expensive", "biggest total", "newest". ASC is the default
--   and rarely needs writing.
ORDER BY PRICE DESC;

                                                                                                                                      All five items come back most expensive first: AV07 at 64.99, CF21 at 42.50, FT88 at 27.75, GR15 at 15.25, and DG04 at 11.99. Drop the word DESC and the same five rows come back in the opposite order, cheapest first.

                                                                                                                                      Text sorts the same way, low to high, which for letters means A to Z. ORDER BY DESCRIPTION DESC returns the KimTay items starting at Small Animal Grooming Kit and ending at Aviary Starter Cage.

                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                      Capital letters and text order

                                                                                                                                      MySQL's default collation ignores case, so apple and Apple sort together, while SQLite compares raw character codes, which places every uppercase letter ahead of every lowercase letter; every text value in both case databases begins with a capital letter, so the two engines return the same order for the queries in this lesson.

                                                                                                                                      Where ORDER BY sits

                                                                                                                                      A single-table SELECT has a fixed clause order: SELECT, then FROM, then WHERE, then ORDER BY. Reading it out loud is a good way to remember what the DBMS does -- it takes the table, throws away the rows that fail the WHERE test, and sorts whatever survived.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: filters first - only well-stocked items get through.
WHERE ON_HAND > 20

-- ORDER BY: sorts what survived the filter. Order of clauses matters: WHERE
--   always comes before ORDER BY, and ORDER BY is always last.
ORDER BY ON_HAND DESC;

                                                                                                                                      Four rows come back -- DG04 with 120, CF21 with 48, FT88 with 30, and GR15 with 22. AV07 has 15 on hand, so it never reaches the sort at all. Filtering happens first, sorting happens to what is left.

                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                      ORDER BY goes last

                                                                                                                                      The WHERE clause must come before the ORDER BY clause; write them the other way around and the DBMS rejects the whole statement with a syntax error instead of guessing what you meant.

                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                      Run it as written (1225, 1120, 1420), then add DESC so the largest balance is on top.

                                                                                                                                      4-2b Additional Sorting Options

                                                                                                                                      One sort key is often not enough. KimTay's route planner wants the customer list arranged by town, and inside each town arranged by name. That takes two sort keys, separated by a comma, listed in order of importance.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY, BALANCE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- ORDER BY: two sort keys. CITY is the major key and decides the overall order;
--   CUSTOMER_NAME is the minor key and only breaks ties inside one city. Swap
--   them and you get a different report.
ORDER BY CITY, CUSTOMER_NAME;

                                                                                                                                      Whiskers & Wags Boutique (Brookville) comes first, then the two Maple Grove customers in name order -- Access Pet Center ahead of Companion Care Clinic -- and Downtown Aquarium & Pets (Northfield) last.

                                                                                                                                      Customers sorted by CITY, then by CUSTOMER_NAME inside each city
                                                                                                                                      CUSTOMER_NAMECITYBALANCE
                                                                                                                                      Whiskers & Wags BoutiqueBrookville4820.75
                                                                                                                                      Access Pet CenterMaple Grove3512.50
                                                                                                                                      Companion Care ClinicMaple Grove0.00
                                                                                                                                      Downtown Aquarium & PetsNorthfield1200.00
                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                      Major and minor sort keys

                                                                                                                                      The first column listed is the major sort key and decides the overall order; the second is the minor sort key and is consulted only when two rows tie on the major key -- swap ORDER BY CITY, CUSTOMER_NAME for ORDER BY CITY, BALANCE and the two Maple Grove rows flip, because Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 now sorts ahead of Access Pet Center's 3512.50.

                                                                                                                                      DESC belongs to the one key it follows, not to the whole clause. If you want both keys reversed, you have to write DESC twice.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY, BALANCE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- ORDER BY: DESC attaches to one column, not to the whole clause, so it has to
--   be repeated. Here both keys descend: cities in reverse alphabetical order,
--   and inside each city the largest balance first.
ORDER BY CITY DESC, BALANCE DESC;

                                                                                                                                      Now the towns run Z to A -- Northfield, Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville -- and inside Maple Grove the larger balance leads, so Access Pet Center at 3512.50 sits above Companion Care Clinic at 0.00.

                                                                                                                                      ORDER BY CITY, BALANCE DESC

                                                                                                                                      Towns A to Z, and inside a town the largest balance first: Brookville, then Access Pet Center at 3512.50 above Companion Care Clinic at 0.00, then Northfield. Only BALANCE is reversed; CITY stays ascending because nothing was written after it.

                                                                                                                                      ORDER BY CITY DESC, BALANCE DESC

                                                                                                                                      Towns Z to A, and inside a town the largest balance first, so Northfield leads and Brookville trails. Each key needed its own DESC, which is the mistake people make most often with two sort keys.

                                                                                                                                      Mixed directions are common in real reports. StayWell's leasing office wants one property at a time, priciest room first inside each property.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: four columns from StayWell's room table.
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, ROOM_TYPE, MONTHLY_RENT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ROOM

-- ORDER BY: mixed directions. PROPERTY_ID ascends so the properties come out in
--   a predictable order, and within each property the rents descend - the usual
--   shape of a grouped listing.
ORDER BY PROPERTY_ID, MONTHLY_RENT DESC;
                                                                                                                                      Rooms by property, most expensive first within each property
                                                                                                                                      PROPERTY_IDROOM_NUMROOM_TYPEMONTHLY_RENT
                                                                                                                                      P100101Single595.00
                                                                                                                                      P100102Double450.00
                                                                                                                                      P200201Studio725.00
                                                                                                                                      P200101Single610.00
                                                                                                                                      P200202Double465.00
                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                      Where NULLs land

                                                                                                                                      Every row shipped with the KimTay and StayWell databases is fully populated, so no result in this lesson contains a NULL, but you will meet them eventually: MySQL and SQLite both place NULL ahead of every non-null value in an ascending sort, while some other systems put NULLs at the end, so check your DBMS before you promise anyone a NULL-safe report.

                                                                                                                                      Sorting on a computed column

                                                                                                                                      You can sort on a value the table does not store. KimTay's bookkeeper wants the items ranked by how much money is sitting on the shelf, which is ON_HAND times PRICE. Give the calculation a name with AS, then sort by that name.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: two stored columns and one computed column named with AS.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS ON_HAND_VALUE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- ORDER BY: you may sort by the alias you just created. ORDER BY runs after the
--   SELECT list has been worked out, which is why the name is available here -
--   and why the same alias would NOT work in a WHERE clause.
ORDER BY ON_HAND_VALUE DESC;

                                                                                                                                      The ranking is CF21 at 2040.00, DG04 at 1438.80, AV07 at 974.85, FT88 at 832.50, and GR15 at 335.50. Note that the cheapest item, the 11.99 leash, is the second most valuable line on the shelf because there are 120 of them -- a ranking you cannot get by sorting on PRICE or on ON_HAND alone.

                                                                                                                                      💡
                                                                                                                                      Alias or expression

                                                                                                                                      MySQL and SQLite both let ORDER BY use the alias you defined in the SELECT list, and both also accept the full expression ORDER BY ON_HAND * PRICE DESC; repeating the expression is the version that works on every DBMS you are likely to meet, and the same trailing-zero difference applies to the computed column, which MySQL prints as 2040.00 and the sandbox prints as 2040.0.

                                                                                                                                      Sorting by column position

                                                                                                                                      ORDER BY also accepts a number, which means the column in that position in the SELECT list. ORDER BY 2 sorts on the second column you selected.

                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns; their positions in this list are 1, 2 and 3.
SELECT DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- ORDER BY: sorting by column POSITION rather than name - 2 is CATEGORY and 3 is
--   PRICE. It is legal and compact, and it is also fragile: reorder the SELECT
--   list and the sort silently changes. Prefer names in anything you keep.
ORDER BY 2, 3 DESC;

                                                                                                                                      This returns the leash (Accessory), the dry food (Food), the grooming kit (Grooming), then the two Habitat rows with the 64.99 cage ahead of the 27.75 filter kit -- exactly what ORDER BY CATEGORY, PRICE DESC returns.

                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                      Handy, but brittle

                                                                                                                                      Position numbers break silently: add one column to the SELECT list and ORDER BY 2 quietly starts sorting on something else, so use column names in any script you plan to keep and save the numbers for throwaway queries.

                                                                                                                                      1

                                                                                                                                      Decide what the reader scans first

                                                                                                                                      The column someone's eye runs down is the major sort key -- town for a route sheet, category for a reorder sheet, name for a directory.

                                                                                                                                      2

                                                                                                                                      Decide how ties should break

                                                                                                                                      Add a minor sort key for the rows that share a value in the major key. Two Maple Grove customers need a second key or their order is unpredictable.

                                                                                                                                      3

                                                                                                                                      Mark the reversals

                                                                                                                                      Attach DESC to each key that should run high to low. A key with nothing after it stays ascending.

                                                                                                                                      4

                                                                                                                                      Put the clause last

                                                                                                                                      Write SELECT, FROM, WHERE, then ORDER BY, and run it. If the order looks wrong, check which key is doing the deciding before you change anything else.

                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                      A StayWell room is let for a nine-month academic year; re-sort by ACADEMIC_YEAR_RENT descending so P200 201 (6525) leads and P100 102 (4050) trails.
                                                                                                                                      • ORDER BY is the last clause in the statement, after WHERE
                                                                                                                                      • Ascending is the default; type DESC for high to low
                                                                                                                                      • The first key listed is the major key, later keys break ties
                                                                                                                                      • DESC applies to one key only, so repeat it if you need it twice
                                                                                                                                      • Sorting on ON_HAND * PRICE works through an alias or the expression itself
                                                                                                                                      • Column position numbers such as ORDER BY 2 work but break when the SELECT list changes

                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                      Q1KimTay's reorder printout

                                                                                                                                      KimTay's warehouse manager wants one printout of the ITEM table with all items of the same category together, and inside each category the most expensive item at the top. Which ORDER BY clause does that?

                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. Price becomes the major key, so categories are scattered -- the two Habitat rows land in positions 1 and 3, split apart by the Food row -- and CATEGORY is never even consulted, because no two items share a price.
                                                                                                                                      • ✔b. Correct: the major key gathers each category together and the descending minor key puts the priciest item of each category on top, so the Habitat block reads 64.99 then 27.75.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. The extra DESC on CATEGORY reverses the category order to Habitat, Grooming, Food, Accessory, which the manager did not ask for.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Sorting defaults to ascending, so this puts the cheapest item of each category first -- the Habitat block would read 27.75 then 64.99, and DESC is what flips it.

                                                                                                                                      Remember: List sort keys in order of importance and attach DESC to each key that must run high to low.

                                                                                                                                      Q2StayWell's rent report

                                                                                                                                      StayWell's leasing office needs the rooms that rent for 500.00 or more, cheapest first. Which statement produces exactly that?

                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. ORDER BY has to be the last clause, so putting WHERE after it is a syntax error and the statement returns nothing at all.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. The filter is right but DESC reverses the request: this leads with P200 201 at 725.00 instead of the cheapest qualifying room.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. With no WHERE clause this returns all five rooms, including P100 102 at 450.00 and P200 202 at 465.00, which do not belong on the report.
                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Correct: WHERE keeps the three rooms at 500.00 or more and the ascending sort returns P100 101 at 595.00, P200 101 at 610.00, then P200 201 at 725.00.

                                                                                                                                      Remember: The clause order is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, and that is also the order the work happens in.

                                                                                                                                      Q3KimTay's shelf value ranking

                                                                                                                                      KimTay's bookkeeper wants the items ranked by the value sitting on the shelf, which is ON_HAND multiplied by PRICE, largest total first. What should the query do?

                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. ON_HAND here is ascending, so this leads with AV07 at 15 on hand and ends with DG04 at 120 -- the reverse of what the bookkeeper wants, and nothing like the value ranking either way.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. No new column is needed, and adding one would store a value that goes stale the moment ON_HAND changes.
                                                                                                                                      • ✔c. Correct: this ranks CF21 at 2040.00, DG04 at 1438.80, AV07 at 974.85, FT88 at 832.50, and GR15 at 335.50.
                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Position 1 is whatever column you listed first, which here is ITEM_ID, so this sorts by item ID instead.

                                                                                                                                      Remember: You can sort on a value the table never stores by naming the calculation itself or the alias you gave it.

                                                                                                                                              4-3 Using Functions

                                                                                                                                              Every query you have written so far handed back rows: three reps, five items, the customers in Maple Grove. Business questions are often smaller than that. KimTay's owner does not want the five ITEM rows on screen. The answer wanted is one number -- how many items are there, what do they average, which one costs the most.

                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                              Aggregate function

                                                                                                                                              An aggregate function reads many rows and returns one value. SQL gives you five: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN. They are also called set functions, because they work on a whole set of rows instead of one row at a time.

                                                                                                                                              The shape of the statement does not change. You still write SELECT, FROM, and WHERE when you need it. What changes is that the SELECT list holds a function call instead of a column name, and the result is a single row no matter how many rows went in.

                                                                                                                                              4-3a Counting rows with COUNT

                                                                                                                                              COUNT(*) counts rows. The asterisk stands for the whole row, so nothing inside a row can keep that row from being counted.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: COUNT(*) is an aggregate - it collapses many rows into one number.
--   The * means "count rows", not "count values", so nothing can be skipped.
SELECT COUNT(*)

-- FROM: the table whose rows are being counted. One row of output comes back,
--   whatever the size of the table.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                                              One row comes back holding the value 5, because KimTay stocks five items. Notice that the column heading is the function call itself, which is awkward to read on a report.

                                                                                                                                              Name the result with AS, the same way you named a computed column in 4-1. A WHERE clause still works exactly as it did, because it runs before the counting starts.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: the same row count, given a readable heading with AS.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being counted.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the filter runs FIRST, and the count is taken over whatever survives.
--   That ordering is the whole trick to aggregates: filter, then aggregate.
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';

                                                                                                                                              That returns one row with ITEM_COUNT = 2. WHERE keeps the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit, and COUNT(*) counts what survived.

                                                                                                                                              You can also count a named column instead of the whole row, and that is where the two forms part company.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: two counts side by side, and they answer different questions.
--   COUNT(*) counts ROWS. COUNT(REP_NUM) counts VALUES in that column, skipping
--   any row where it is null. Equal numbers mean no nulls; a gap between them is
--   how you discover nulls you did not know about.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROWS, COUNT(REP_NUM) AS WITH_A_REP

-- FROM: the table being counted. Every shipped row is filled in, so both read 4.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                              Both columns come back as 4, because every one of the four KimTay customers shipped with the course has a rep number on file. The two forms are not the same thing, though -- they only happen to agree while the data is complete.

                                                                                                                                              COUNT(*)

                                                                                                                                              Counts rows. Every row that got past the WHERE clause adds one, whatever is or is not stored inside it. Use it when the question is "how many records".

                                                                                                                                              COUNT(column)

                                                                                                                                              Counts values in that one column. Rows where the column is null add nothing. Use it when the question is "how many records have this filled in".

                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                              Nulls change the answer

                                                                                                                                              A null is the absence of a value, so COUNT on a column steps over it. Nothing in the shipped KimTay data is null, so you have to create one to see it: if KimTay reassigned Companion Care Clinic and left its REP_NUM null for a week, COUNT(*) would still report 4 while COUNT(REP_NUM) reported 3. A staffing report built on the wrong one is off by a customer, and nothing in the output tells you so.

                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                              Both statements run together, and only the SELECT prints a result. Press Reset when you are done -- it reloads the original KimTay data with the rep number back in place.

                                                                                                                                              4-3b Adding a column up with SUM

                                                                                                                                              SUM adds up the values in one numeric column. Ask for the money KimTay is owed across every account.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: SUM adds up the values in one column across every row it is given.
--   It only makes sense on numbers - there is nothing to add in a city name.
SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED

-- FROM: the table supplying the rows. One number comes back.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                              One row comes back with TOTAL_OWED = 9533.25, which is 3512.50 plus 1200.00 plus 0.00 plus 4820.75. Add a WHERE clause and you total a slice of the table instead.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: the same total, over a smaller set of rows.
SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS OWED_TO_REP_20

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: applied before the SUM, so only rep 20's customers are added together.
--   Change the WHERE and the single number changes with it.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20';

                                                                                                                                              That returns 3512.5 -- Access Pet Center plus Companion Care Clinic, whose balance is zero. The sandbox drops the trailing zero because SQLite stores the number rather than the display format; MySQL prints 3512.50, since BALANCE is declared DECIMAL(9,2). The value is the same either way.

                                                                                                                                              1

                                                                                                                                              Start with the table in FROM

                                                                                                                                              SQL begins with all four rows of CUSTOMER. Nothing has been added up yet.

                                                                                                                                              2

                                                                                                                                              Drop the rows WHERE rejects

                                                                                                                                              WHERE REP_NUM = '20' leaves two rows standing. This always happens before the function runs.

                                                                                                                                              3

                                                                                                                                              Collapse what is left

                                                                                                                                              SUM walks the surviving rows and adds their BALANCE values into one number.

                                                                                                                                              4

                                                                                                                                              Hand back one row

                                                                                                                                              The result set has exactly one row and one column, named by your AS clause.

                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                              An empty result still answers

                                                                                                                                              SUM skips nulls the same way COUNT(column) does. And when the WHERE clause leaves nothing standing, the query still returns one row: SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROWS_FOUND, SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 10000; reports ROWS_FOUND = 0 and an empty TOTAL, because COUNT of nothing is 0 while SUM of nothing is null. SQLite and MySQL behave identically here.

                                                                                                                                              4-3c AVG, MAX, and MIN

                                                                                                                                              These three read a column the same way SUM does. AVG averages the values, MAX returns the largest, MIN returns the smallest. You can call several of them in one SELECT list.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: three aggregates in one statement, each over the same column.
--   AVG is the mean of the values.
SELECT AVG(PRICE) AS AVG_PRICE,

--   MAX is the largest value present - not a calculation, just a pick.
       MAX(PRICE) AS HIGHEST,

--   MIN is the smallest. All three collapse the whole table to one row, so the
--   output is one row with three columns.
       MIN(PRICE) AS LOWEST

-- FROM: the table all three are computed over.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                                              One row comes back: AVG_PRICE = 32.496, HIGHEST = 64.99 (the Aviary Starter Cage), LOWEST = 11.99 (the Nylon Dog Leash). The average carries more decimal places than any price in the table, which is normal -- an average is a calculated number, not a stored one. One display difference to expect: MySQL widens the scale when it averages a DECIMAL column and prints 32.496000, while the SQLite sandbox prints 32.496; the value is the same.

                                                                                                                                              AVG divides by the number of values it found, not by the number of rows in the table. On CUSTOMER, SELECT AVG(BALANCE) AS AVG_BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER; returns 2383.3125 (MySQL writes it as 2383.312500), which is 9533.25 divided by 4. Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 is a real value, so it is counted and it pulls the average down.

                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                              Null is not zero

                                                                                                                                              Try this in the 4-3a sandbox, then press Reset to restore the data: run UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = NULL WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310'; followed by SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL, AVG(BALANCE) AS AVG_BALANCE, COUNT(BALANCE) AS COUNTED FROM CUSTOMER;. The total stays 9533.25, but the average jumps from 2383.3125 to 3177.75 because COUNTED is now 3. A zero is a number you divide by; a null is a row the average never sees.

                                                                                                                                              MAX and MIN are not limited to money. On dates they give you earliest and latest, and on character columns they give you alphabetical order.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: MIN and MAX are not restricted to numbers. On a DATE column they give
--   the earliest date...
SELECT MIN(INVOICE_DATE) AS FIRST_INVOICE,

--   ...and the latest one. This works because the column is a real DATE type; on
--   dates stored as text it would only work by luck of the format.
       MAX(INVOICE_DATE) AS LAST_INVOICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM INVOICE;

                                                                                                                                              That returns 2026-06-14 and 2026-06-15, the two days KimTay billed. Run SELECT MIN(LAST_NAME) AS FIRST_ALPHABETICALLY, MAX(LAST_NAME) AS LAST_ALPHABETICALLY FROM REP; and you get Hull and Perez, the ends of the rep list by last name.

                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                              Do not mix an aggregate with a plain column yet

                                                                                                                                              SELECT DESCRIPTION, MAX(PRICE) FROM ITEM; looks like it should name the costliest item, but one aggregate value cannot line up with five descriptions. SQLite has a special rule for a query whose only aggregate is a lone MIN or MAX, so it answers Aviary Starter Cage with 64.99, while MySQL rejects the statement under its default ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY setting -- the same SQL behaves differently depending on where you run it, which is reason enough not to lean on it. Keep aggregates on their own for now; 4-4 shows the subquery that pairs a value with its row, and 4-5 shows the GROUP BY that gives one aggregate per group.

                                                                                                                                              4-3d The DISTINCT operator

                                                                                                                                              Some questions are about variety rather than volume. Ask for the cities KimTay's customers are in and you get one row per customer, not one row per city.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: one column, with no filtering and no de-duplication.
SELECT CITY

-- FROM: the table being read. One row comes back per CUSTOMER row, so a city
--   used by two customers is printed twice. That repetition is the problem the
--   next query solves.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                              Four rows come back, one per customer: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, and Brookville. There is no ORDER BY here, so the engine may hand them back in any order it likes; what matters is that Maple Grove appears twice, because two customers are there. That is correct as a list of customers and wrong as a list of cities.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: DISTINCT removes duplicate ROWS from the result - it is not a function
--   attached to the column, but a keyword applied to the whole SELECT list.
SELECT DISTINCT CITY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- ORDER BY: sorts what is left. De-duplication happens first, sorting afterwards.
ORDER BY CITY;

                                                                                                                                              Now three rows come back in the order Brookville, Maple Grove, Northfield. DISTINCT removed the duplicate before ORDER BY sorted what was left.

                                                                                                                                              DISTINCT applies to the whole SELECT list, not to the column next to it. Two rows have to match on every selected column before one of them is dropped.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: DISTINCT applies to the COMBINATION of every listed column, not to
--   each column separately. Two rows are duplicates only when the city and the
--   state both match, so this returns distinct city-and-state pairs.
SELECT DISTINCT CITY, STATE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- ORDER BY: sorts the surviving pairs by city.
ORDER BY CITY;

                                                                                                                                              That still returns three rows, because the two Maple Grove customers share a state as well as a city. All four KimTay customers are in OH, so SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT STATE) FROM CUSTOMER; returns 1.

                                                                                                                                              DISTINCT also goes inside COUNT, where it changes the question from "how many" to "how many different".

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: three counts that answer three different questions.
--   COUNT(*) counts rows, regardless of what is in them.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROWS,

--   COUNT(CITY) counts non-null values in that column - rows with no city are
--     skipped entirely.
       COUNT(CITY) AS CITY_VALUES,

--   COUNT(DISTINCT CITY) counts how many DIFFERENT cities appear. Reading the
--     three side by side tells you about nulls and about repetition at once.
       COUNT(DISTINCT CITY) AS DIFFERENT_CITIES

-- FROM: the table all three are computed over.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                              One row comes back: 4, 4, and 3. The first counts customers, the second counts customers whose city is filled in, the third counts cities. Three different business questions, three different numbers, one table.

                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: the same three shapes of count, pointed at the line-item table.
--   How many invoice lines exist in total.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS LINE_COUNT,

--   How many different invoices those lines belong to.
       COUNT(DISTINCT INVOICE_NUM) AS INVOICES,

--   How many different items were ordered. Six lines can cover three invoices and
--     five items at the same time, which is exactly what these numbers show.
       COUNT(DISTINCT ITEM_ID) AS ITEMS

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM INVOICE_LINE;

                                                                                                                                              That returns 6, 3, and 5. There are six invoice lines spread across three invoices, and they cover five different items because CF21 was ordered on invoice 50710 and again on 50711.

                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                              Where DISTINCT goes

                                                                                                                                              DISTINCT is an operator, not a function, so it takes no parentheses of its own. On its own it sits immediately after SELECT and covers the entire select list. Inside a count it sits inside the parentheses, as in COUNT(DISTINCT CITY). Counting two columns inside one COUNT is one of the few places the engines disagree: COUNT(DISTINCT CITY, STATE) is an error in the SQLite sandbox but legal in MySQL, where it counts distinct city-and-state pairs. Give one count one column and the statement runs the same way everywhere.

                                                                                                                                              The aggregate functions, and DISTINCT, on KimTay data
                                                                                                                                              FunctionThe question it answersExample result
                                                                                                                                              COUNT(*)How many rows are in this result?SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ITEM; returns 5
                                                                                                                                              COUNT(column)How many rows have a value here?SELECT COUNT(REP_NUM) FROM CUSTOMER; returns 4
                                                                                                                                              SUM(column)What do these numbers add up to?SELECT SUM(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER; returns 9533.25
                                                                                                                                              AVG(column)What is the average of these numbers?SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM; returns 32.496
                                                                                                                                              MAX(column)What is the largest value here?SELECT MAX(PRICE) FROM ITEM; returns 64.99
                                                                                                                                              MIN(column)What is the smallest value here?SELECT MIN(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER; returns 0 (MySQL shows 0.00)
                                                                                                                                              COUNT(DISTINCT column)How many different values are there?SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CITY) FROM CUSTOMER; returns 3
                                                                                                                                              • The question asks for one number, not a list of rows -- otherwise you do not need an aggregate at all.
                                                                                                                                              • COUNT(*) for rows, COUNT(column) for filled-in values, COUNT(DISTINCT column) for variety.
                                                                                                                                              • Any WHERE clause is written for the rows you want counted, because it runs before the function.
                                                                                                                                              • No plain column shares the SELECT list with an aggregate until you reach 4-4 and 4-5.
                                                                                                                                              • Every aggregate in a finished query is named with AS, so the report heading reads like English.
                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                              Question 2 needs a WHERE clause; question 3 needs three functions in one SELECT list.

                                                                                                                                              Aggregates answer questions about a whole table or a whole slice of one. The next two lessons loosen that. In 4-4 a subquery lets one query feed another, so you can ask which item costs the most and get its description back. In 4-5 GROUP BY runs these same five functions once per group -- a total per rep, an average per category -- instead of once for everything.

                                                                                                                                              🔍 Check yourself: aggregate functions

                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                              Q1A customer left without a rep

                                                                                                                                              KimTay reassigns the Companion Care Clinic account, so a clerk runs UPDATE CUSTOMER SET REP_NUM = NULL WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310'; and leaves it that way for the week. (The shipped data has a rep number on every customer; this query is what changes that.) The bookkeeper then runs SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROWS, COUNT(REP_NUM) AS WITH_A_REP FROM CUSTOMER; against the four customer rows. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Wrong: COUNT(*) counts every surviving row, null columns and all, so it stays at 4.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Wrong: COUNT(REP_NUM) counts values rather than rows, and a null is the absence of a value.
                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct: COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) counts the rows that have a value in that column.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Wrong: COUNT handles nulls without complaint; it counts around them instead of failing.

                                                                                                                                              Remember: COUNT(*) answers how many records exist; COUNT(column) answers how many have that field filled in.

                                                                                                                                              Q2A credit review that finds nobody

                                                                                                                                              A credit review at KimTay runs SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 10000;. No KimTay customer carries a balance that large. What does the query return?

                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct: COUNT of nothing is 0, but SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN of nothing are null. SQLite and MySQL agree here.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Wrong: that is COUNT behavior; SUM over an empty result returns null, so treat the two differently.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. Wrong: an aggregate query with no grouping returns exactly one row even when no rows survived the WHERE clause.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Wrong: WHERE always runs first and decides which rows the function ever sees.

                                                                                                                                              Remember: An aggregate over an empty result still returns one row, and for SUM and AVG that row holds null.

                                                                                                                                              Q3Counting what KimTay actually sold

                                                                                                                                              INVOICE_LINE holds six lines across three invoices, and item CF21 appears on two of them. The warehouse manager runs SELECT COUNT(*) AS LINE_COUNT, COUNT(DISTINCT ITEM_ID) AS ITEMS FROM INVOICE_LINE;. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Wrong: DISTINCT inside COUNT is what changes the question from how many to how many different.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Wrong: DISTINCT inside one COUNT affects that count only; COUNT(*) still reports all six lines.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. Wrong: that reverses the two; counting different values can never exceed counting rows.
                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct: six lines are counted as rows, while the five different item ids are counted once each.

                                                                                                                                              Remember: COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different values; COUNT(*) counts rows, duplicates included.

                                                                                                                                              Q4Naming the most expensive item

                                                                                                                                              The warehouse manager wants the description of KimTay's costliest item and writes SELECT DESCRIPTION, MAX(PRICE) FROM ITEM;. What should you tell them?

                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Wrong: an aggregate with no grouping collapses the whole table into one row, so it never produces a row per item.
                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct: SQLite has a special rule for a query whose only aggregate is a lone MIN or MAX and answers Aviary Starter Cage with 64.99, while MySQL rejects the mix under its default ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY setting, so a subquery is the dependable route.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. Wrong: MIN(PRICE) returns 11.99, the cheapest item, which is the opposite of what was asked.
                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Wrong: sorting does not change the fact that one aggregate value cannot line up with five descriptions.

                                                                                                                                              Remember: Keep aggregates alone in the SELECT list until 4-4 and 4-5 show you how to pair them with columns.

                                                                                                                                                        4-4 Nesting Queries

                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's warehouse manager wants a list of the items that cost more than the average item. Read that request again and you will notice it is two questions stacked on top of each other: what is the average price across the whole table, and then which rows beat that number? Everything you have written so far answers one question at a time, so this one does not fit into a flat WHERE clause.

                                                                                                                                                        Here is the statement most people try first.

                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: a deliberate error, and the most common one in this lesson.
-- SELECT: two ordinary columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: BROKEN. An aggregate cannot appear in a WHERE clause. WHERE is tested
--   one row at a time, while AVG(PRICE) needs the whole table before it can
--   produce a number, so the engine is being asked to use an answer that does
--   not exist yet. SQLite says "misuse of aggregate function AVG()". The fix is
--   to work the average out first, in a subquery.
WHERE PRICE > AVG(PRICE);

                                                                                                                                                        It does not run. SQLite answers misuse of aggregate function AVG() and MySQL answers Invalid use of group function. The reason is worth remembering: a WHERE clause is tested against one row at a time, and one row has no average. AVG(PRICE) is a fact about all five rows together, so it has to be worked out before the row-by-row filtering starts.

                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                        Subquery

                                                                                                                                                        A subquery is a complete SELECT statement written inside parentheses within another statement. The database runs the inner query first, keeps its result, and then runs the outer query using that result as though you had typed the value in yourself.

                                                                                                                                                        A subquery that returns one value

                                                                                                                                                        Build it in two moves. First write the inner query on its own so you can see what it produces.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: step 1 of the fix - work out the average on its own, and look at it.
--   Run any subquery by itself before nesting it, so you know what it returns.
SELECT AVG(PRICE)

-- FROM: the table being averaged. One row, one column, one number.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                                                        That returns a single row with a single column. The five prices add up to 162.48, so the answer is 32.496. This page (SQLite) prints 32.496; MySQL prints 32.496000, because averaging a DECIMAL column widens the number of decimal places it reports. The value is the same either way. One row, one column -- that is exactly what a comparison operator such as > or = needs on its right-hand side.

                                                                                                                                                        Now drop that query, parentheses and all, into the spot where the number would go.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns, PRICE included so the comparison can be checked by eye.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the subquery in parentheses runs FIRST and collapses to a single number,
--   the average price. The outer WHERE then compares each row against that one
--   value. Because the subquery is an aggregate over the whole table, it is
--   guaranteed to return exactly one row, which is what makes = or > safe here.
WHERE PRICE > (SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the survivors, dearest first.
ORDER BY PRICE DESC;
                                                                                                                                                        Result: the two items priced above the 32.496 average
                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONPRICE
                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage64.99
                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb42.50
                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                        Trailing zeros on screen

                                                                                                                                                        The tables in this lesson print prices the way the data was entered, so CF21 shows as 42.50. SQLite does not pad numbers to a fixed number of decimal places, so the sandbox on this page will show 42.5 for the same value; MySQL, which stores the column as DECIMAL(7,2), shows 42.50. Same number, different display -- do not treat it as a wrong answer.

                                                                                                                                                        Trace the order of events. The inner query runs once and produces 32.496. The outer query then behaves exactly as if you had written WHERE PRICE > 32.496. The difference is that nobody had to work the average out by hand, so the statement stays correct tomorrow when prices change.

                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                        Three habits that prevent errors

                                                                                                                                                        Wrap the subquery in parentheses, select exactly one column inside it, and put no semicolon inside the parentheses -- the semicolon belongs at the very end of the whole statement.

                                                                                                                                                        When = is safe

                                                                                                                                                        A comparison with = is safe whenever the subquery cannot possibly return more than one row. Suppose a buyer wants every item that shares a category with item FT88. You do not have to know that the category is Habitat; you can look it up.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: step 1 again - find the value you are going to compare against.
SELECT CATEGORY

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: filtering on the PRIMARY KEY, so at most one row can come back. That
--   guarantee is what will make it safe to use this query with = in a moment.
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88';

                                                                                                                                                        That returns one row holding Habitat. It can never return two, because ITEM_ID is the primary key of ITEM and a primary key value matches at most one row. That guarantee is what makes = legitimate in the outer query.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the subquery finds FT88's category, and the outer query keeps every item
--   in that same category - FT88 itself included. = is safe here only because the
--   subquery filters on a primary key and so cannot return two rows.
WHERE CATEGORY = (SELECT CATEGORY FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88')

-- ORDER BY: sorts the result by item id.
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
                                                                                                                                                        Result: both Habitat items, including FT88 itself
                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONPRICE
                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage64.99
                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit27.75
                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                        FT88 matches itself

                                                                                                                                                        FT88 appears in its own result because its category equals its own category; if the buyer wants the other Habitat items, add AND ITEM_ID <> 'FT88' to the outer WHERE clause.

                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
