                                                                                                                                                        Run it to see all four customers, then add a WHERE that compares BALANCE to a subquery over the whole table -- the four balances total 9533.25, so the average is 2383.3125 and two customers should survive.

                                                                                                                                                        A subquery that returns several values

                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's bookkeeper now wants the stock picture for every item that a customer ordered two or more of on any invoice line. The list of qualifying item IDs lives in INVOICE_LINE, and the stock figures live in ITEM. Start, as always, with the inner query.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: one column, which is a requirement - a subquery used with IN or = must
--   return exactly one column.
SELECT ITEM_ID

-- FROM: the line-item table, where quantities are recorded.
FROM INVOICE_LINE

-- WHERE: keeps the lines of two or more units. Run alone, this returns several
--   rows, and CF21 appears twice because it was ordered in bulk on two invoices.
WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2;

                                                                                                                                                        Four rows come back: CF21, DG04, CF21 and FT88. Without an ORDER BY the engine may list them in any order, so read the set rather than the sequence. Notice CF21 appears twice, because it was ordered in quantity on two different invoices. That duplication does not matter here -- asking whether a value is in a list gives the same answer whether the list mentions it once or twice.

                                                                                                                                                        A single value would fit next to =, but four values will not. IN is the operator that compares one value against a whole list, and it accepts a subquery in place of the parenthesised list you met in lesson 4-1h.

                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: three columns from the item table.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: IN handles a subquery returning MANY rows - read it as "keep this item
--   if its id is one of the ids the inner query found". Duplicates in that inner
--   list are harmless, because each item is tested once and either matches or
--   does not.
WHERE ITEM_ID IN (SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the result by item id.
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
                                                                                                                                                        Result: the three distinct items ordered two or more at a time
                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONON_HAND
                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb48
                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft120
                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit30

                                                                                                                                                        Read the condition out loud as a membership test: keep this ITEM row if its ITEM_ID is one of the IDs the inner query found. AV07 and GR15 were each ordered one at a time, so neither one is in the list and neither one appears.

                                                                                                                                                        The classic error: = against many rows

                                                                                                                                                        Sooner or later you will write the previous query with = instead of IN, because the shape of the statement looks identical.

                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the classic error - the previous query written with = instead of IN.
-- SELECT: two columns.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: BROKEN. = compares one value against ONE other value, and the subquery
--   here returns several rows. MySQL refuses the statement outright (error 1242,
--   "Subquery returns more than 1 row"). SQLite, the engine on this page, does
--   not complain at all - it keeps whichever value came back first and quietly
--   answers the wrong question, which is far more dangerous. Use = only when the
--   subquery is an aggregate or filters on a key; otherwise use IN.
WHERE ITEM_ID = (SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2);
                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                        This is where the two engines part ways

                                                                                                                                                        MySQL refuses the statement with error 1242, Subquery returns more than 1 row. SQLite, the engine running in this page, does not complain at all -- it keeps whichever value the inner query handed back first and returns that single row, which on this data is CF21. Nothing promises it will always be CF21, because the inner query has no ORDER BY; that is the point. A wrong answer delivered with no error message is worse than an error, so treat a silent one-row result from a = subquery as a bug to investigate, not as a pass.

                                                                                                                                                        Reach for =

                                                                                                                                                        The inner query is an aggregate over the whole table, such as SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM, or it filters on a primary key, such as WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88'. In both cases one row is guaranteed.

                                                                                                                                                        Reach for IN

                                                                                                                                                        The inner query filters on any non-key column, such as WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2 or WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove'. Today it might return one row by luck; next week's data can return five.

                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                        Write the inner query alone and run it

                                                                                                                                                        You need to see two things before going further: how many rows it returns and how many columns. A subquery used with = or IN must return exactly one column, or both engines reject the whole statement.

                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                        Count the rows, then pick the operator

                                                                                                                                                        One row that can never become two means = (or >, <, >=, <=). Any chance of more than one row means IN.

                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                        Paste it into the outer query inside parentheses

                                                                                                                                                        Drop the trailing semicolon from the inner query, wrap it in parentheses, and put it where a literal value would otherwise sit.

                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                        Sanity-check the row count

                                                                                                                                                        If the outer query returns exactly one row and you expected several, suspect that you used = where IN was needed.

                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                        The inner query returns two property IDs, P100 and P200, because each property has one Double room. Nest it inside a query on PROPERTY to name both buildings, then swap IN for = and watch this engine hand back Millbrook Commons on its own.
                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain why WHERE PRICE > AVG(PRICE) is rejected by both MySQL and SQLite
                                                                                                                                                        • I run the inner query on its own first and check how many rows and columns it returns
                                                                                                                                                        • I use = only when the inner query is an aggregate or filters on a primary key
                                                                                                                                                        • I use IN whenever the inner query could return more than one row
                                                                                                                                                        • I know that a = subquery returning many rows errors in MySQL but silently returns one row in SQLite
                                                                                                                                                        • I remember that the subquery goes inside parentheses, selects one column, and carries no semicolon of its own

                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: nesting queries

                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                        Q1KimTay's above-average price review

                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager wants every row of ITEM whose PRICE is higher than the average price of all five items, and wants the same saved statement to still be correct after prices change. Which approach meets both requirements?

                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. An aggregate cannot appear in WHERE, which is tested one row at a time, so SQLite reports misuse of aggregate function and MySQL reports invalid use of group function.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. This lists AV07 and CF21 correctly today, but 32.496 is frozen into the text of the statement, so the saved query reports the wrong rows the moment any price changes.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. The inner query returns the single value 32.496 first, and the outer query then keeps AV07 at 64.99 and CF21 at 42.50, recomputing the average every time it runs.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. IN tests for an exact match against the list, and no item is priced at exactly 32.496, so this returns zero rows.

                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Comparing a row to a summary of the whole table requires a subquery, because the summary has to be computed before row-by-row filtering begins -- and computing it inside the statement keeps the statement correct as data changes.

                                                                                                                                                        Q2StayWell's Double rooms

                                                                                                                                                        The leasing office runs SELECT PROPERTY_ID FROM ROOM WHERE ROOM_TYPE = 'Double'; and gets P100 and P200. Someone then nests it in a query on PROPERTY using WHERE PROPERTY_ID = (...) instead of IN. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. MySQL raises error 1242, subquery returns more than 1 row; SQLite keeps only the first value the inner query produced, here P100, and reports Millbrook Commons alone with no warning.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. = never expands into IN; a comparison operator demands a single value on its right-hand side and has no way to test membership in a list.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. = compares CHAR values without difficulty, which is why the SQLite result is a plausible-looking single row rather than an empty one.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. A subquery is never ignored; it is evaluated before the outer query and its result is always used.

                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A silent single-row answer from a = subquery is a warning sign, because the engine may be discarding values instead of reporting the mistake.

                                                                                                                                                        Q3Matching item FT88's category

                                                                                                                                                        A KimTay buyer writes WHERE CATEGORY = (SELECT CATEGORY FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88') and gets AV07 and FT88. Why is = the correct operator in this statement?

                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. CATEGORY is not unique at all -- AV07 and FT88 share the value Habitat, which is precisely why the outer query returns two rows.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. MySQL raises an error rather than taking the first row, so relying on that behaviour produces a statement that fails on the engine used in Module 3.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Plenty of subqueries without aggregates return many rows, such as the INVOICE_LINE lookup that returned four item IDs.
                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. A primary key value identifies at most one row, so the inner query is guaranteed to yield the single value Habitat.

                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Choose between = and IN by asking what guarantees the inner query's row count, not by looking at today's data.

                                                                                                                                                        🧩 Sort the queries: one value, many values, or no subquery at all

                                                                                                                                                        Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                        Each card is either a request someone made or a statement someone typed. Decide what each one needs before it can be used.

                                                                                                                                                                0 / 8 placed

                                                                                                                                                                4-5 Grouping

                                                                                                                                                                Lesson 4-3 handed you one number for a whole table: COUNT(*) over every item, AVG(PRICE) over every price. That is useful about once. What a business actually asks for is the same number broken out by something: the average price per category, the number of customers per rep, the total per invoice. You do not want one answer, you want one answer per pile.

                                                                                                                                                                GROUP BY builds the piles. It takes the rows that made it past WHERE, sorts them into groups that share the same value in the column you name, and runs your aggregate function once inside each group. Then HAVING throws away whole groups you do not want. Everything in this lesson still happens inside a single table.

                                                                                                                                                                📖
                                                                                                                                                                GROUP BY

                                                                                                                                                                GROUP BY column collapses the rows into one result row per distinct value of that column. Five ITEM rows spread across four categories come back as four rows. Any aggregate in the SELECT list is then computed separately for each group instead of once for the table.

                                                                                                                                                                One row per group

                                                                                                                                                                KimTay's warehouse manager wants to know how the catalog is spread across categories and what a typical item costs in each one. The ITEM table holds five rows and four category values, so the answer should be four lines long:

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column, then two aggregates. Each aggregate is now
--   computed once PER GROUP rather than once over the whole table.
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT, AVG(PRICE) AS AVG_PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- GROUP BY: sorts the rows into piles, one pile per distinct CATEGORY value, and
--   returns one output row per pile. Four distinct categories means four rows.
GROUP BY CATEGORY;
                                                                                                                                                                Four rows back, one per CATEGORY
                                                                                                                                                                CATEGORYITEM_COUNTAVG_PRICE
                                                                                                                                                                Accessory111.99
                                                                                                                                                                Food142.5
                                                                                                                                                                Grooming115.25
                                                                                                                                                                Habitat246.37

                                                                                                                                                                Read COUNT(*) differently than you did in Lesson 4-3. It is no longer counting rows in the table, it is counting rows in a group. Habitat is the only category holding more than one item, so it is the only row where the count is 2 and the only row where the average is doing real work: 64.99 for the Aviary Starter Cage and 27.75 for the Fish Tank Filter Kit average out to 46.37. The other three groups hold a single item each, so their average is that item's price.

                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                Two things the output will not do for you

                                                                                                                                                                The sandbox prints 42.5 where a MySQL server would print 42.50. That is an engine difference rather than a different number: the sandbox runs SQLite, which keeps a price as a plain number and drops a trailing zero, while MySQL's DECIMAL(7,2) column pads every value it returns out to two decimal places. Expect averages in particular to come back with a different number of decimal places on the two engines. Separately, although SQLite and MySQL both tend to hand grouped rows back in group order, neither one promises to, so if the order matters put an ORDER BY on the end exactly as you did in Lesson 4-2.

                                                                                                                                                                The grouping column does not have to be a category name. INVOICE_LINE stores one row per item on an invoice, so grouping it by INVOICE_NUM turns six line rows into a total per invoice:

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column, then an aggregate over a calculation. The
--   multiplication happens per line, and SUM adds those line values within the
--   group - so the arithmetic runs before the aggregation, as you would expect.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, SUM(NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE) AS INVOICE_TOTAL

-- FROM: the line-item table - six rows, before grouping.
FROM INVOICE_LINE

-- GROUP BY: one pile per invoice number, so six lines become three totals.
GROUP BY INVOICE_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the summary rows, largest total first. Sorting by the alias is
--   allowed because ORDER BY runs last of all.
ORDER BY INVOICE_TOTAL DESC;
                                                                                                                                                                Six line rows become three invoice totals
                                                                                                                                                                INVOICE_NUMINVOICE_TOTALWhere it comes from
                                                                                                                                                                50710151.483 x 42.50 plus 2 x 11.99
                                                                                                                                                                50712120.491 x 64.99 plus 2 x 27.75
                                                                                                                                                                50711100.252 x 42.50 plus 1 x 15.25
                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                MIN and MAX group the same way COUNT does. Expect Habitat first with 2, 27.75 and 64.99, then the three single-item categories, where the lowest and the highest are the same price.

                                                                                                                                                                The rule: grouped or aggregated, nothing else

                                                                                                                                                                Here is the one rule that catches everybody. Every column in the SELECT list of a grouped query must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or sit inside an aggregate function. There is no third option, and the reason is arithmetic rather than pedantry: the result has one row per group, so every column has to have exactly one value per group.

                                                                                                                                                                Watch it break. Someone wants the category counts and thinks adding the product name would be a nice touch:

                                                                                                                                                                -- GOAL: a deliberate error, and the rule that catches everybody.
-- SELECT: BROKEN. Every column here must either appear in GROUP BY or sit inside
--   an aggregate. CATEGORY is grouped and COUNT(*) is aggregated, but DESCRIPTION
--   is neither. The Habitat pile holds two rows with two different descriptions,
--   and the query has asked for one - there is no correct answer to give.
SELECT CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- GROUP BY: one pile per category. MySQL rejects the whole statement because of
--   its ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY setting; SQLite runs it and picks a description at
--   random from the pile, which is worse - a wrong answer with no warning.
GROUP BY CATEGORY;

                                                                                                                                                                The Habitat group holds two rows with two different descriptions, and the query has asked for one description. There is no correct answer to give.

                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                This is where the two engines part company

                                                                                                                                                                MySQL rejects the statement outright, because its default ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY setting refuses a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated. SQLite runs it and quietly picks one row's description out of each group. In this sandbox you get four rows, and the Habitat line carries just one of its two descriptions with no sign that the other item was ever there. Nothing in the SQL decides which one you get, so do not learn the answer this sandbox happens to give. Silent is worse than an error: learn the rule rather than trusting the engine to enforce it.

                                                                                                                                                                There are two honest fixes, and picking between them means deciding what question you are asking. Drop DESCRIPTION from the SELECT list if you want a summary. Add it to GROUP BY if you want a finer grain, which changes the question from "per category" to "per category and description" and gives you five rows instead of four:

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the same three columns, now legal, because of the line below.
SELECT CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- GROUP BY: adding DESCRIPTION makes a pile out of each distinct CATEGORY and
--   DESCRIPTION combination, so every column in SELECT is now either grouped or
--   aggregated. This is the "finer grouping" fix; the other fix is to drop
--   DESCRIPTION from the SELECT list and keep the coarse summary.
GROUP BY CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION

-- ORDER BY: sorts the groups for reading.
ORDER BY CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION;

                                                                                                                                                                Grouping on more than one column

                                                                                                                                                                Listing two columns after GROUP BY makes a group out of each distinct combination of the two, not two separate sets of groups. Grouping KimTay's customers by rep and city answers "which rep covers which town, and with how many accounts":

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: two grouping columns plus a count.
SELECT REP_NUM, CITY, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- GROUP BY: listing two columns makes one pile per distinct COMBINATION of the
--   two - not two separate sets of piles. This answers "which rep covers which
--   city, and how many customers there", a question neither column answers alone.
GROUP BY REP_NUM, CITY

-- ORDER BY: sorts the summary rows by rep, then by city.
ORDER BY REP_NUM, CITY;
                                                                                                                                                                Three combinations exist in the data, so three rows come back
                                                                                                                                                                REP_NUMCITYCUSTOMER_COUNT
                                                                                                                                                                20Maple Grove2
                                                                                                                                                                35Northfield1
                                                                                                                                                                65Brookville1

                                                                                                                                                                Rep 20 gets one row rather than two because both of that rep's customers, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, sit in Maple Grove. If one of them moved to Northfield, the same query would return four rows the next time it ran. The number of groups follows the data, never the number of columns you listed.

                                                                                                                                                                HAVING: a WHERE clause for groups

                                                                                                                                                                Grouping tends to raise a follow-up question, and the follow-up is almost always about the groups themselves. Which categories hold more than one item? Which reps are carrying more than 2,000 dollars of customer balance? Those are tests on a finished group, and the clause that runs them is HAVING.

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column and a count.
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- GROUP BY: one pile per category.
GROUP BY CATEGORY

-- HAVING: filters the GROUPS, after they have been formed and counted. This is
--   the one place an aggregate may appear in a condition, and it is exactly what
--   WHERE cannot do - WHERE runs before the piles exist. Only the category
--   holding more than one item survives.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
                                                                                                                                                                One row survives: only Habitat holds more than one item
                                                                                                                                                                CATEGORYITEM_COUNT
                                                                                                                                                                Habitat2

                                                                                                                                                                Without the HAVING line that query returns four rows. With it, the three single-item groups are formed, counted, tested and thrown out. They were built and then discarded, which is exactly what HAVING means: the groups all get made, and then some of them do not make the cut.

                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                An aggregate cannot go in WHERE

                                                                                                                                                                Moving the same test up to WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 fails on both engines, because when WHERE runs there are no groups yet and so no count to compare against. SQLite reports misuse of aggregate: COUNT() and MySQL reports Invalid use of group function. Different wording, same reason.

                                                                                                                                                                WHERE (Row Filter)

                                                                                                                                                                Runs before grouping. Filters individual rows using raw table columns (e.g., WHERE PRICE > 20). Cannot contain aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM().

                                                                                                                                                                HAVING (Group Filter)

                                                                                                                                                                Runs after grouping. Filters entire summary rows using aggregate calculations (e.g., HAVING COUNT(*) > 1). Designed specifically for aggregate function results.

                                                                                                                                                                WHERE first, then GROUP BY, then HAVING

                                                                                                                                                                You write a query in one order and the engine runs it in another. Committing the running order to memory is what makes the rest of this lesson obvious instead of fiddly.

                                                                                                                                                                1

                                                                                                                                                                1. FROM picks the table

                                                                                                                                                                All five ITEM rows, or all four CUSTOMER rows, are on the table to start with.

                                                                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                                                                2. WHERE filters rows

                                                                                                                                                                Each row is tested on its own values and either survives or is dropped. Nothing has been grouped or counted yet, which is why an aggregate is illegal here.

                                                                                                                                                                3

                                                                                                                                                                3. GROUP BY builds the groups

                                                                                                                                                                Only the surviving rows get sorted into piles. A row thrown out in step 2 cannot influence any group's count, sum or average.

                                                                                                                                                                4

                                                                                                                                                                4. HAVING filters groups

                                                                                                                                                                Every aggregate is now computed, so a test on COUNT(*), SUM(BALANCE) or AVG(PRICE) finally has something to compare. Whole groups are kept or discarded.

                                                                                                                                                                5

                                                                                                                                                                5. SELECT produces the output row

                                                                                                                                                                One row per surviving group, holding the grouping columns and the aggregate values.

                                                                                                                                                                6

                                                                                                                                                                6. ORDER BY sorts the result

                                                                                                                                                                Sorting happens last, on the summary rows, which is why you can order by an aggregate or by a column alias here.

                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                Say it out loud once

                                                                                                                                                                FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Filter rows, build groups, filter groups, report, sort. Almost every confusing result in this lesson is a step that ran earlier or later than you pictured.

                                                                                                                                                                When swapping WHERE and HAVING changes the answer

                                                                                                                                                                KimTay's bookkeeper has two questions that sound alike in English. Rep 20 has two customers: Access Pet Center with a balance of 3512.50, and Companion Care Clinic with a balance of 0.00.

                                                                                                                                                                Question A: per rep, how many customers owe more than 1,000?

                                                                                                                                                                This is a question about customers. Test each customer row for a balance over 1000.00, drop the ones that fail, and count what is left in each rep's pile. The test happens before the grouping, so it belongs in WHERE.

                                                                                                                                                                Question B: which reps' books total more than 1,000, and how many customers do they have?

                                                                                                                                                                This is a question about reps. Keep every customer row, add up each rep's balances, and drop the reps whose total falls short. The test needs a SUM that does not exist until the group is built, so it belongs in HAVING.

                                                                                                                                                                Same table, same grouping column, same threshold of 1000.00. Here is question A:

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column and a count.
SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: filters ROWS, before any grouping happens. Customers owing 1000.00 or
--   less are removed here and never reach a pile at all.
WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00

-- GROUP BY: piles up whatever rows survived the WHERE, one pile per rep.
GROUP BY REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the summary rows.
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                Question A: Companion Care Clinic is dropped before counting
                                                                                                                                                                REP_NUMCUSTOMER_COUNT
                                                                                                                                                                201
                                                                                                                                                                351
                                                                                                                                                                651

                                                                                                                                                                And here is question B, with the identical threshold moved into HAVING and applied to a sum:

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column and a count.
SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT

-- FROM: the table being read - every row this time, with no WHERE.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- GROUP BY: one pile per rep, containing all of that rep's customers.
GROUP BY REP_NUM

-- HAVING: filters the finished piles on a total computed from every row in the
--   pile. Note the difference from the previous query: there a customer owing
--   nothing was thrown out before counting, here it is still counted and simply
--   contributes 0.00 to its rep's total.
HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 1000.00

-- ORDER BY: sorts the summary rows.
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                Question B: nothing is dropped before counting, so rep 20 counts both customers
                                                                                                                                                                REP_NUMCUSTOMER_COUNT
                                                                                                                                                                202
                                                                                                                                                                351
                                                                                                                                                                651

                                                                                                                                                                Look at rep 20: 1 in the first result, 2 in the second. Nothing about the data changed. In query A, Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 balance failed the row test in step 2, so it was gone before COUNT(*) ever saw it. In query B no row was filtered at all; rep 20's group was built from both customers, its total came to 3512.50, that total cleared 1000.00, and both rows stayed counted. Neither answer is wrong. They answer different questions, and the clause you put the test in is what picks the question.

                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                A WHERE that empties a group deletes the group

                                                                                                                                                                SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE > 20.00 GROUP BY CATEGORY ORDER BY CATEGORY; returns two rows, Food with 1 and Habitat with 2. Accessory and Grooming do not come back with a count of 0; they do not come back at all, because both of their rows were removed in step 2 and a group is only built from rows that survive. GROUP BY can never report on rows that WHERE already threw away.

                                                                                                                                                                The two clauses are not rivals. Most real reporting queries use both, and reading one of these from top to bottom is reading the pipeline in order: filter the rows, group what is left, filter the groups, sort the survivors.

                                                                                                                                                                -- SELECT: the grouping column and two aggregates.
SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT, SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: step 1 - throw out individual rows. Only balances above 1000.00 go on.
WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00

-- GROUP BY: step 2 - pile up what is left, one pile per rep.
GROUP BY REP_NUM

-- HAVING: step 3 - throw out whole piles whose total is too small. WHERE and
--   HAVING are doing different jobs in the same statement, which is the point of
--   this example: rows first, groups second.
HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 2000.00

-- ORDER BY: step 4 - sort what survived, largest total first.
ORDER BY TOTAL_OWED DESC;
                                                                                                                                                                Rep 35 is built as a group, then dropped by HAVING because 1200.00 falls short of 2000.00
                                                                                                                                                                REP_NUMCUSTOMER_COUNTTOTAL_OWED
                                                                                                                                                                6514820.75
                                                                                                                                                                2013512.5
                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                A test on the grouping column can sit in either clause

                                                                                                                                                                When a query says GROUP BY CATEGORY, both WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' and HAVING CATEGORY = 'Habitat' are legal on either engine and both return the single row Habitat | 2, because the grouping column has exactly one value per group. Prefer WHERE: it discards the rows before any group is built, so the engine does less work and a reader can tell at a glance that the test is about rows.

                                                                                                                                                                Your turn, at StayWell

                                                                                                                                                                StayWell's rental office wants a report on the higher-end rooms. Build it one clause at a time and run it after each change, so you can see which step removed what.

                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                The rent test is about one room row, the count test is about a finished group. The starter gives P100 with 2 rooms at 522.5 and P200 with 3 at 600; the finished query gives one row, P200 with 2 rooms at 667.5.

                                                                                                                                                                Run it in stages and the pipeline is visible. Adding WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00 drops the 450.00 double at Millbrook Commons and the 465.00 double at Sycamore Court, which pulls P100 down to one room and P200 down to two, and pushes both averages up. Adding HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 then removes P100 entirely, because after the row filter it has only one qualifying room left.

                                                                                                                                                                Checklist for a grouped query

                                                                                                                                                                • Decide what one output row represents. That noun is your GROUP BY column list.
                                                                                                                                                                • Check every entry in the SELECT list: it is either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate, with no exceptions.
                                                                                                                                                                • Put a test that reads one row's own values in WHERE, where it will run before any group exists.
                                                                                                                                                                • Put a test that reads COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX in HAVING, where the aggregate is already computed.
                                                                                                                                                                • Remember that a group whose rows were all removed by WHERE does not show up as a zero; it does not show up at all.
                                                                                                                                                                • Add ORDER BY if the order of the summary rows matters, because grouping does not guarantee one.
                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                Naming the aggregate pays off twice

                                                                                                                                                                SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED gives the column a readable heading and gives ORDER BY TOTAL_OWED DESC something short to sort by. Strict standard SQL does not allow that alias back in HAVING, but SQLite and MySQL both accept HAVING TOTAL_OWED > 2000.00; repeating the full SUM(BALANCE) in HAVING works everywhere, so that is the safer habit while you are learning.

                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: grouping, HAVING, and the order things run

                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                Q1The warehouse manager's category sheet

                                                                                                                                                                KimTay's warehouse manager asks for a sheet showing how many items are stocked in each product category. The ITEM table holds five rows spread across four categories: Accessory, Food, Grooming and Habitat. Someone runs SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT FROM ITEM GROUP BY CATEGORY;. How many rows come back, and why?

                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. GROUP BY replaces the detail rows with one summary row per group, so the five item rows never appear individually.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. COUNT(*) collapses to a single number only when there is no GROUP BY; here it is computed once inside each group.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct -- four distinct category values means four groups, and the Habitat row shows 2 while the other three show 1.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Nothing is filtered here, and a group of one still produces a row; dropping those would take HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

                                                                                                                                                                Remember: GROUP BY gives you one result row per distinct group, not one row per underlying table row.

                                                                                                                                                                Q2The extra column that looked harmless

                                                                                                                                                                A student wants the category counts plus the product name, so they write SELECT CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION, COUNT(*) FROM ITEM GROUP BY CATEGORY;. The Habitat category holds two items, the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit. What is wrong with that statement?

                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct -- the Habitat group holds two different descriptions but the result has room for one, so MySQL rejects the statement outright while SQLite runs it and silently reports only one of them.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Counts and text columns mix freely; the real problem is that DESCRIPTION varies inside a group while COUNT(*) does not.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. One row per group is the whole point of GROUP BY, so a second Habitat line is exactly what you do not get.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Every description in ITEM has a value, and HAVING filters finished groups rather than repairing an ungrouped column.

                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Every column in the SELECT list must be named in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function.

                                                                                                                                                                Q3Two questions for KimTay's bookkeeper

                                                                                                                                                                Rep 20 has two customers: Access Pet Center with a balance of 3512.50 and Companion Care Clinic with a balance of 0.00. Query A is SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00 GROUP BY REP_NUM; and query B is SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY REP_NUM HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 1000.00;. What does each report for rep 20?

                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Query A tests each row before grouping, so Companion Care Clinic is already gone by the time COUNT(*) runs.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Query B filters no rows at all; it tests the finished group, whose total of 3512.50 clears 1000.00, so both customers stay counted.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. HAVING runs after the groups are built, not before, so it cannot remove one customer row from inside a group.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct -- WHERE filters rows first so A counts 1, while HAVING tests the group total 3512.50 and keeps both rows, so B counts 2.

                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Moving a threshold from WHERE to HAVING can change the numbers, because one filters rows and the other filters groups.

                                                                                                                                                                Q4StayWell's higher-end room report

                                                                                                                                                                StayWell's rental office wants each property's average rent counting only rooms that rent for more than 500.00, and wants to see only the properties left holding more than one such room. Which clause takes which test?

                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. No count exists yet while WHERE is running, and both engines reject an aggregate in that clause outright.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✔b. Correct -- the rent test reads one room row so it filters first, and the count test reads a finished group so it filters after.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. That is backwards: rent is a value on a single room row, while a count only exists once rows have been gathered into groups.
                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. COUNT(*) > 1 is fine in HAVING, but MONTHLY_RENT is not. MySQL rejects it there, and this sandbox's SQLite runs it and hands back P100 with 2 rooms at 522.5 and P200 with 3 at 600 -- the rent test removed nothing, so the cheap rooms are still counted and still pulling the averages down.

                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Row-level tests belong in WHERE; tests on an aggregate belong in HAVING.

                                                                                                                                                                🧩 Sort each test into the clause that can run it

                                                                                                                                                                Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                Each card is a condition from a single-table KimTay query that groups rows. Assume GROUP BY CATEGORY for the ITEM conditions and GROUP BY REP_NUM for the CUSTOMER conditions, then drop each card on the clause where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                      0 / 8 placed

                                                                                                                                                                      4-6 Nulls

                                                                                                                                                                      Module 3 introduced the null while you were building tables: a column declared without NOT NULL is allowed to hold no value at all, and the data-type lesson already warned you that WHERE STREET = NULL never matches anything. This lesson is where that warning stops being a footnote. You will create a null on purpose and watch it change the answers to ordinary queries -- filters, arithmetic, counts and averages -- without ever raising an error.

                                                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                                                      Null

                                                                                                                                                                      A null is the absence of a value. It is not zero, it is not an empty string, and it is not the word "unknown" typed into the column. It means the database has nothing recorded in that spot and cannot tell you what belongs there.

                                                                                                                                                                      StayWell has two columns where a null is the honest answer, and Module 3 declared both of them without NOT NULL: STUDENT.HOME_STATE and ROOM.MONTHLY_RENT. A housing application can arrive with the home state left blank, and a room that is being reconfigured can sit in the ROOM table before anyone has decided next year's rent. In both cases the row exists and the value does not.

                                                                                                                                                                      Every row that ships with this course is filled in -- there is not a single null anywhere in KimTay or StayWell -- so nothing you have queried so far has contained one. To study how nulls behave you will create one on purpose in your own copy of the data.

                                                                                                                                                                      Create a null to work with

                                                                                                                                                                      Suppose StayWell's housing office finds that the home state on one student record was entered from an unreadable form, and clears it until the student confirms it. That is an UPDATE, which you learned in Module 3. Run the update, then list the table.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- UPDATE: names the table whose rows are about to change.
UPDATE STUDENT

-- SET: which column gets a new value, and what that value is. NULL is a keyword,
--   not text - writing 'NULL' in quotes would store the four letters N-U-L-L.
SET HOME_STATE = NULL

-- WHERE: which rows are affected. Leave this line off and every student in the
--   table loses their home state, so read it before running the statement.
WHERE STUDENT_ID = 'S003';

-- SELECT: the check. Look at the table after any change you make.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE

-- FROM: the table just updated.
FROM STUDENT

-- ORDER BY: sorts the four rows so the cleared one is easy to find. S003 now
--   prints as NULL, which is this page's way of showing "no value recorded".
ORDER BY STUDENT_ID;

                                                                                                                                                                      Four rows come back: S001 Nguyen OH, S002 Carter PA, S003 Ibrahim, and S004 Park OH. In the S003 row the HOME_STATE cell reads NULL, which is how this page's result grid prints a missing value. Other tools pick other conventions -- some show an empty cell, some print (null) -- and all of them mean the same thing. None of them is a value you can compare against.

                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                      This only changes your copy

                                                                                                                                                                      The database on this page lives in your browser. The update above edits your session and nothing else, and reloading the page or pressing Reset restores the original StayWell rows.

                                                                                                                                                                      Why = NULL never works

                                                                                                                                                                      Your first instinct is to look for the missing value with WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL. It reads like English and it fails every time. Here is what the database actually does with it.

                                                                                                                                                                      1

                                                                                                                                                                      Take one row at a time

                                                                                                                                                                      The engine walks through STUDENT row by row and asks whether that row's HOME_STATE equals NULL.

                                                                                                                                                                      2

                                                                                                                                                                      Compare a value against an unknown

                                                                                                                                                                      NULL is not a value, it is the absence of one. Asking whether something equals an unknown does not give true or false, it gives a third answer: unknown.

                                                                                                                                                                      3

                                                                                                                                                                      Keep only what tests true

                                                                                                                                                                      WHERE keeps a row only when the condition comes back true. Unknown is not true, so the row is discarded. Every row is discarded, including the one you were hunting for.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- GOAL: a deliberate error, and the one every beginner writes.
-- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM STUDENT

-- WHERE: BROKEN, though it reads like plain English. NULL is not a value, it is
--   the absence of one, so "equals NULL" cannot be answered true or false - it
--   comes back unknown. WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE, and
--   unknown is not true, so every row is discarded, including the very row you
--   were hunting for. No error message appears; you simply get nothing.
WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL;

                                                                                                                                                                      That query matches nothing, even though S003 is sitting right there with no home state recorded. Watch what the sandbox prints when you run it underneath the UPDATE: instead of an empty grid you get the message Statement ran. 1 row affected. That 1 is the update's row, not a match -- the giveaway is that no result table appeared at all. Writing WHERE HOME_STATE <> NULL matches nothing for exactly the same reason.

                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                      A silent wrong answer

                                                                                                                                                                      = NULL is legal SQL. There is no error, no warning, and no red text -- only an empty result that looks like a truthful "nothing matched." This is one of the easiest ways to hand someone a report that is quietly wrong.

                                                                                                                                                                      IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

                                                                                                                                                                      SQL gives you a separate test for the question "is there a value here at all?" It is IS NULL, and its opposite is IS NOT NULL. Neither one is a comparison, so neither one falls into the unknown trap.
