                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM STUDENT

-- WHERE: IS NULL is the only test that works, because it asks about the presence
--   of a value rather than comparing values. It is a phrase in its own right -
--   there is no = anywhere in it.
WHERE HOME_STATE IS NULL;

                                                                                                                                                                      One row comes back -- S003 Ibrahim -- and this time you get a real result grid, with NULL printed in the HOME_STATE cell. Flip the test to find the rows that do have a value.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM STUDENT

-- WHERE: IS NOT NULL is the mirror image - keep the rows that DO have a value.
--   Together, IS NULL and IS NOT NULL account for every row in the table, which
--   ordinary comparisons like <> never do.
WHERE HOME_STATE IS NOT NULL

-- ORDER BY: sorts what comes back.
ORDER BY STUDENT_ID;

                                                                                                                                                                      Three rows come back: S001 Nguyen OH, S002 Carter PA, and S004 Park OH. One row plus three rows accounts for all four students, which is what you want from a pair of opposite tests.

                                                                                                                                                                      Four ways to write a null test, and what each one really does
                                                                                                                                                                      What you writeHow the database reads itWhat comes back
                                                                                                                                                                      HOME_STATE = NULLIs this value equal to an unknown? Answer: unknownNo rows, ever
                                                                                                                                                                      HOME_STATE <> NULLIs this value different from an unknown? Answer: unknownNo rows, ever
                                                                                                                                                                      HOME_STATE IS NULLIs this column empty? Answer: true or falseThe rows with nothing recorded
                                                                                                                                                                      HOME_STATE IS NOT NULLDoes this column hold a value? Answer: true or falseThe rows with something recorded
                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                      Both engines agree here

                                                                                                                                                                      IS NULL and IS NOT NULL work the same way in MySQL and in the SQLite engine running on this page. Each product also offers a shorthand of its own -- MySQL has <=> and SQLite has IS -- but IS NULL is the portable form, so write that one.

                                                                                                                                                                      Nulls in arithmetic

                                                                                                                                                                      Room 202 at Sycamore Court is being reconfigured, and next year's rent has not been set. Clear that rent, then price out a nine-month academic year for every room at that property.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- UPDATE: the table being changed.
UPDATE ROOM

-- SET: clear the rent, because next year's figure has not been decided yet. A
--   null is the honest record of "not known"; 0 would be a lie about the price.
SET MONTHLY_RENT = NULL

-- WHERE: two conditions, because ROOM's primary key is made of two columns.
--   Both are needed to identify exactly one room.
WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P200' AND ROOM_NUM = '202';

-- SELECT: the stored rent alongside a calculation that uses it. Any arithmetic
--   touching a null produces a null, so the cleared room shows NULL in the rent
--   column and NULL again in the total - the unknown spreads.
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT, MONTHLY_RENT * 9 AS NINE_MONTH_TOTAL

-- FROM: the table just updated.
FROM ROOM

-- WHERE: narrows the report to the one property.
WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P200'

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three rooms by number.
ORDER BY ROOM_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                      Three rows come back. Room 101 shows 610 and 5490, room 201 shows 725 and 6525, and room 202 shows NULL in the rent column and NULL again in the total. The rule is short: any arithmetic that touches a null produces a null. If you do not know the rent, you cannot know nine times the rent, and SQL refuses to invent a number. 595.00 + NULL returns null for the same reason.

                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                      About those trailing zeros

                                                                                                                                                                      The rents were stored as 610.00 and 725.00, but this page's SQLite engine prints them as 610 and 725, while MySQL prints 610.00 and 725.00. Only the display differs; the stored value is identical, and every comparison and total in this lesson is unaffected.

                                                                                                                                                                      Nulls in comparisons split your data

                                                                                                                                                                      The unknown answer bites hardest in ordinary comparisons that have nothing to do with nulls. Ask StayWell for the out-of-state students with the home state still cleared on S003.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: three columns.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM STUDENT

-- WHERE: an ordinary comparison with nothing to do with nulls - and it still
--   drops the null row. S003 is missing not because that student is known to
--   live in Ohio, but because "unknown is not equal to OH" cannot be answered,
--   and WHERE keeps only what is definitely true.
WHERE HOME_STATE <> 'OH';

                                                                                                                                                                      One row comes back: S002 Carter PA. S003 is missing from the list -- not because the student is known to live in Ohio, but because the comparison could not be answered. A row with no value is excluded by = 'OH' and excluded by <> 'OH' at the same time.

                                                                                                                                                                      The same thing happens with numbers. Count the rooms above and below a 500.00 rent line.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: count the rooms above the line.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROOMS_OVER_500

-- FROM: the table being counted.
FROM ROOM

-- WHERE: the first half of what looks like a complete split of the data.
WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00;

-- SELECT: count the rooms at or below the line.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROOMS_500_OR_LESS

-- FROM: the same table.
FROM ROOM

-- WHERE: the opposite condition. The two counts come to 3 and 1, but ROOM holds
--   5 rows - the unpriced room fell out of BOTH halves, because a comparison
--   against a null is unknown either way. Whenever two opposite filters fail to
--   add up to the row count, look for nulls.
WHERE MONTHLY_RENT <= 500.00;

                                                                                                                                                                      The first count is 3 and the second is 1. ROOM holds 5 rows, and 3 plus 1 is 4. The unpriced room fell out of both halves. Whenever two opposite filters fail to add up to the row count, look for nulls first.

                                                                                                                                                                      Nulls inside aggregate functions

                                                                                                                                                                      Aggregate functions do not fail on nulls, they skip them, and the skipping is where reports go wrong. Run all four numbers at once.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: four numbers that only agree with each other when there are no nulls.
--   COUNT(*) counts rows, so it reports all five rooms.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROOMS,

--   COUNT(column) counts values, so it reports the four rooms that have a rent.
       COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT) AS RENTS_RECORDED,

--   SUM skips the null and adds those same four values.
       SUM(MONTHLY_RENT) AS TOTAL_RENT,

--   AVG divides the total by 4, not by 5. That is the trap: the average is of the
--     rooms that have a rent, which is not the same as the average across all
--     rooms - and no error is raised to tell you which one you got.
       AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) AS AVERAGE_RENT

-- FROM: the table all four are computed over.
FROM ROOM;

                                                                                                                                                                      You get 5, 4, 2380 and 595. COUNT(*) counted all five rows because it counts rows, not values. COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT) counted the four rooms that have a rent. SUM added those same four. And AVG divided 2380 by 4, not by 5, so it reported 595. If you had assumed five rooms you would have expected 476, and been off by 119 dollars a month.

                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                      Say which count you mean

                                                                                                                                                                      "How many rooms are there?" and "how many rooms have a rent on file?" are different questions with different answers, and COUNT(*) and COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT) answer them separately. Before you put a number in front of anyone, decide which question you are answering and pick the matching form.

                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                      Run it unchanged first. The page answers "Statement ran. 1 row affected." -- that 1 belongs to the UPDATE, and the absence of any result table is the SELECT matching nothing. Now swap the comparison for the null-aware test and you get a real grid: one row, S003, with NULL in HOME_STATE.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Test for a missing value with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, because = NULL returns nothing at all.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Read a NULL in the result grid as "nothing recorded here" -- not as a zero, and not as an empty string.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Expect any arithmetic that touches a null to come back null, including multiplication and addition.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Remember that <> throws out the rows with no value, exactly as = does.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Decide between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) before you report a number to anyone.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Read AVG as the average of the values that exist, not as the average of every row.

                                                                                                                                                                      🔍 Knowledge check: what a missing value does to your query

                                                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                      Q1StayWell's blank home state

                                                                                                                                                                      StayWell's housing office clears the HOME_STATE on one STUDENT row until the student re-verifies it, then runs SELECT STUDENT_ID FROM STUDENT WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL; and gets no rows back at all. What went wrong?

                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. The row was cleared on purpose, so a missing home state does exist and the empty result is wrong.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. The statement is legal SQL and runs without complaint, which is exactly what makes the empty result dangerous.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔c. Right - a null is an unknown, an unknown compared with anything stays unknown, and WHERE discards everything that is not true.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. The equals sign compares text as readily as numbers, as in HOME_STATE = 'OH', so the data type is not the problem.

                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Write IS NULL, because = NULL evaluates to unknown on every row and therefore returns nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                      Q2Sycamore Court's unpriced room

                                                                                                                                                                      Room 202 at Sycamore Court is being reconfigured and its MONTHLY_RENT has been cleared. The housing office counts the rooms renting above 500.00 and gets 3, counts the rooms at 500.00 or less and gets 1, and expected the two to add up to the 5 rows in ROOM. What happened?

                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔a. Right - both > 500.00 and <= 500.00 evaluate to unknown against a missing rent, so that row survives neither filter.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. COUNT(*) counts rows whatever they contain; it was WHERE that removed the row before counting began.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. The two conditions are opposites, so no room can satisfy both and double counting is impossible.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Both queries compare against the same literal in the same engine, and rounding plays no part in the missing row.

                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: A row with a null sits outside both halves of a comparison, so opposite filters do not add up to the table's row count.

                                                                                                                                                                      Q3The average rent that looks too high

                                                                                                                                                                      With room 202's rent still cleared, a StayWell report runs SELECT SUM(MONTHLY_RENT), AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) FROM ROOM; The sum is 2380 and ROOM holds 5 rows, so the reader expects an average near 476, but AVG returns 595. Which explanation is correct?

                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. AVG did no rounding here; 2380 divided by 4 is exactly 595, with nothing left over.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. A null counted as zero would drag the average down toward 476 rather than up to 595.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. AVG reads every row the WHERE clause allows through, and this query has no WHERE clause at all.
                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Right - AVG skips nulls in the total and in the divisor, so it divided by 4 instead of by 5.

                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: AVG is the average of the values that exist, so report COUNT(column) next to it whenever the column can be empty.

                                                                                                                                                                      4-7 Summary of SQL Clauses, Functions, and Operators

                                                                                                                                                                      Everything in this module was one table at a time, and it all fits into six clauses, five aggregate functions and a short list of operators. This section is the reference page. You are not expected to memorize it in one sitting -- you are expected to come back to it while you write.

                                                                                                                                                                      The six clauses

                                                                                                                                                                      There are two orders that matter. The written order is the order you type the clauses in, and getting it wrong is a syntax error. The evaluated order is the order the database does the work in, and getting it wrong is a logic error.

                                                                                                                                                                      The clauses of a single-table query, in both orders
                                                                                                                                                                      ClauseWhat it doesWrittenEvaluated
                                                                                                                                                                      SELECTNames the columns and computed values you want to see1st5th
                                                                                                                                                                      FROMNames the table the rows come from2nd1st
                                                                                                                                                                      WHEREKeeps or discards one row at a time3rd2nd
                                                                                                                                                                      GROUP BYCollapses the surviving rows into one row per group4th3rd
                                                                                                                                                                      HAVINGKeeps or discards whole groups5th4th
                                                                                                                                                                      ORDER BYArranges the finished rows for display6th6th

                                                                                                                                                                      SELECT is the only clause a statement cannot do without -- SELECT 595.00 + NULL; is a complete statement in both engines -- but every query that reads a table needs FROM as well. The remaining four are optional, and when you use them they have to appear in the written order above.

                                                                                                                                                                      The gap between the two orders explains two rules that otherwise look arbitrary. An aggregate function cannot appear in WHERE, because WHERE runs before any group exists; both engines refuse it, and SQLite words the complaint "misuse of aggregate". And an alias you invent in SELECT is meant for ORDER BY rather than for WHERE, because ORDER BY runs after the SELECT list is built while WHERE runs before it.

                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                      Where the engines differ: an alias in WHERE

                                                                                                                                                                      MySQL rejects SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE * 2 AS DOUBLED FROM ITEM WHERE DOUBLED > 60; with "Unknown column 'DOUBLED' in 'where clause'". The SQLite engine on this page accepts it as an extension and returns AV07 and CF21, so a query that runs here can still fail on a MySQL server. Repeat the whole expression -- WHERE PRICE * 2 > 60 -- and it works in both.

                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT: the grouping column and two aggregates - every column here is either
--   grouped or aggregated, as the rule requires.
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT, AVG(PRICE) AS AVERAGE_PRICE

-- FROM: the table being read. This is the clause order the engine follows:
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: 1st - discard individual rows before anything is grouped.
WHERE ON_HAND > 10

-- GROUP BY: 2nd - pile up the survivors, one pile per category.
GROUP BY CATEGORY

-- HAVING: 3rd - discard whole piles, using a condition on an aggregate.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

-- ORDER BY: 4th and last - sort what is left for reading.
ORDER BY CATEGORY;

                                                                                                                                                                      Against KimTay's five items that query returns exactly one row: Habitat, 2, 46.37. All five items pass ON_HAND > 10, they fall into four categories, and Habitat is the only category holding more than one item, so HAVING discards the other three groups. Remove the HAVING line and four rows come back instead.

                                                                                                                                                                      The aggregate functions

                                                                                                                                                                      Each of these collapses many rows into a single number. There are five of them, in six forms, because COUNT comes in two: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column). Every form except COUNT(*) ignores nulls, which is the detail that turns an aggregate into a wrong report.

                                                                                                                                                                      Aggregate functions and how each one treats a missing value
                                                                                                                                                                      FunctionWhat it returnsNulls
                                                                                                                                                                      COUNT(*)The number of rows, whatever those rows containCounts every row, nulls included
                                                                                                                                                                      COUNT(column)The number of rows where that column holds a valueSkips nulls
                                                                                                                                                                      SUM(column)The total of the values present in that columnSkips nulls
                                                                                                                                                                      AVG(column)The total divided by the number of values presentSkips nulls in the total and in the divisor
                                                                                                                                                                      MAX(column)The largest value presentSkips nulls
                                                                                                                                                                      MIN(column)The smallest value presentSkips nulls

                                                                                                                                                                      Run SELECT MIN(PRICE), MAX(PRICE), SUM(ON_HAND), COUNT(*) FROM ITEM; against KimTay and you get 11.99, 64.99, 235 and 5. Every ITEM row is filled in, so nothing is skipped and the four numbers describe all five items.

                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                      Crucial Distinction: COUNT(*) vs. COUNT(column)

                                                                                                                                                                      COUNT(*) counts every row in the table or group, including rows with NULLs. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that specific column is NOT NULL. For example, if 2 out of 5 reps have a NULL commission, COUNT(*) returns 5 while COUNT(COMMISSION) returns 3.

                                                                                                                                                                      The operators

                                                                                                                                                                      Operators are what you build conditions out of. The comparison and logical operators came from Module 3 and lesson 4-1; BETWEEN, LIKE, IN, and IS NULL were added across this module. The examples below are written against KimTay's ITEM and CUSTOMER tables.

                                                                                                                                                                      Operators you can use in a condition
                                                                                                                                                                      OperatorGroupWhat it testsExample
                                                                                                                                                                      =ComparisonTwo values are the sameCATEGORY = 'Food'
                                                                                                                                                                      <>ComparisonTwo values differCATEGORY <> 'Food'
                                                                                                                                                                      < and <=ComparisonA value is smaller, or smaller or equalON_HAND < 20
                                                                                                                                                                      > and >=ComparisonA value is larger, or larger or equalPRICE >= 42.50
                                                                                                                                                                      ANDLogicalBoth conditions hold for the same rowCATEGORY = 'Habitat' AND PRICE < 50.00
                                                                                                                                                                      ORLogicalAt least one of the conditions holdsCATEGORY = 'Food' OR CATEGORY = 'Grooming'
                                                                                                                                                                      NOTLogicalThe condition does not holdNOT CATEGORY = 'Habitat'
                                                                                                                                                                      BETWEENRangeA value falls inside an inclusive rangePRICE BETWEEN 15.00 AND 45.00
                                                                                                                                                                      LIKEPatternText matches a pattern built with % and _CUSTOMER_NAME LIKE 'Comp%'
                                                                                                                                                                      INListA value appears somewhere in a listREP_NUM IN ('20', '65')
                                                                                                                                                                      IS NULLNull testNo value is recorded in the columnMONTHLY_RENT IS NULL
                                                                                                                                                                      IS NOT NULLNull testSome value is recorded in the columnMONTHLY_RENT IS NOT NULL

                                                                                                                                                                      Those ten examples match, in order: CF21; the other four items; AV07; AV07 and CF21; FT88; CF21 and GR15; CF21, DG04 and GR15; CF21, FT88 and GR15; customer 1310 Companion Care Clinic; and customers 1120, 1310 and 1420. None of the fragments carries an ORDER BY, so the order the rows actually appear in is the engine's choice -- the item IDs are simply listed alphabetically here. The two null tests are written against StayWell's ROOM table, where IS NULL finds nothing and IS NOT NULL finds all five rooms until you clear a rent yourself, because every seeded room has one.

                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                      Where the engines differ: text and decimals

                                                                                                                                                                      Case sensitivity in LIKE depends on the product and its collation. This page's SQLite ignores case for ordinary letters, so LIKE 'comp%' still finds Companion Care Clinic, while MySQL follows the column's collation -- decide the case yourself rather than relying on either default. Decimal display also varies: a rent stored as 610.00 prints as 610 in this page's engine and as 610.00 in MySQL, and the stored value is identical either way.

                                                                                                                                                                      Written order is not working order

                                                                                                                                                                      You write SELECT first, but the database reads FROM and WHERE first and builds your output columns near the end. When a clause complains about something that looks perfectly defined, ask whether that thing exists yet at the moment the clause runs.

                                                                                                                                                                      A missing value is not a small value

                                                                                                                                                                      A null does not compare as zero, and COUNT(column) never counts one. In both this page's SQLite and in MySQL an ascending ORDER BY puts nulls ahead of every real value rather than treating them as low numbers. Any column created without NOT NULL can hold one, so check it with IS NULL before you trust a total, an average or a percentage built on it.

                                                                                                                                                                      A checklist for any single-table query

                                                                                                                                                                      • Name the one table in FROM, then decide what a single row must satisfy in WHERE.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Add GROUP BY only when you want one row per group instead of one row per record.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Put conditions about individual rows in WHERE and conditions about group totals in HAVING.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Repeat the full expression in WHERE instead of the alias you gave it in SELECT, so the query runs on both engines.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Put ORDER BY last, and name a tie-breaker column when the first sort column repeats.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Test any column that is allowed to be empty with IS NULL before you trust an average or a count.
                                                                                                                                                                      • Run it, read the row count out loud, and ask whether that number is believable for this business.
                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                      As written you get one row, Habitat. Delete the HAVING line and run it again to see the three single-item groups it was holding back, for four rows in total.

                                                                                                                                                                              Summary Module Summary

                                                                                                                                                                              Module 4 stayed inside one table on purpose. Every question you asked -- which rows, which columns, in what order, summarized how -- was answered without a join, because most real reporting work starts exactly there. You added ten new tools to the SELECT you already had: compound conditions, BETWEEN, computed columns, LIKE, IN, multi-column sorting, aggregate functions, DISTINCT, subqueries, and GROUP BY with HAVING.

                                                                                                                                                                              • You can name the columns you want in the SELECT list, and use * only when you truly want all of them.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can filter rows with a simple condition and combine conditions with AND, OR, and NOT, knowing AND is evaluated first.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You know BETWEEN tests a range and counts both endpoints as matches.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can build a computed column such as ON_HAND * PRICE and give it a readable heading with AS.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can search text with LIKE using the % and _ wildcards.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can replace a long chain of OR tests with IN and a list of values.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can sort on more than one column, with a major sort key and a minor sort key, and reverse either one with DESC.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can count, total, average, and find extremes with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You know an aggregate function returns one row for the whole table unless you group.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can strip repeated values out of a result with DISTINCT.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can nest one query inside another and let the inner result feed the outer condition.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can group rows with GROUP BY and get one summary row per group.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You can filter groups with HAVING, and explain why that is not the same as WHERE.
                                                                                                                                                                              • You still have IS NULL from Module 3 for testing missing values, because NULL is never equal to anything.

                                                                                                                                                                              The clause order that never changes

                                                                                                                                                                              Whatever the query, the clauses are written in one fixed order. Leave any of them out, but never reorder them. This statement uses all six of them on the KimTay ITEM table:

                                                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: the grouping column and a count, given a readable heading.
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_ITEMS

-- FROM: the table being read.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: filters rows first - only items dearer than 12 reach a pile.
WHERE PRICE > 12

-- GROUP BY: one pile per category, built from the surviving rows.
GROUP BY CATEGORY

-- HAVING: filters the piles. >= 1 keeps every pile that exists, so it changes
--   nothing here - it is written to show where the clause goes.
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1

-- ORDER BY: two keys - biggest count first, then category name to break ties.
ORDER BY NUM_ITEMS DESC, CATEGORY;

                                                                                                                                                                              That returns three rows: Habitat with 2, then Food with 1, then Grooming with 1. The HAVING test here is deliberately generous -- every group that forms has at least one row, so nothing is thrown away after grouping. Accessory is missing for a different reason: the 11.99 leash was removed by WHERE before any grouping happened. The tie between Food and Grooming is broken alphabetically by the second sort key.

                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                              Written order is not run order

                                                                                                                                                                              You write SELECT first, but the database works through the clauses in this order: FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY. That single fact explains why WHERE cannot test a group total while HAVING can, and why ORDER BY -- the last clause to run -- can sort by a column alias, while WHERE runs long before that alias exists.

                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                              Two engines, two small surprises

                                                                                                                                                                              The sandbox on this page runs SQLite; Module 3 taught MySQL. Almost everything in this module behaves identically in both, but watch two things. First, money: MySQL's DECIMAL arithmetic is exact, while SQLite calculates in binary floating point, so SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM; shows 32.496 under MySQL and 32.495999999999995 here, and 15 * 64.99 shows 974.85 there and 974.8499999999999 here. The stored data is identical -- only the arithmetic display differs, and the extra digits are noise, not a wrong answer. Second, aliases: SQLite lets you use a SELECT alias inside WHERE, MySQL does not, so repeat the expression instead of the alias and the same query runs on both.

                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                              Run it as written -- one row, Habitat with 2 items averaging 46.37. Then change HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to >= 1 and the other three categories reappear, in the order Habitat, Food, Grooming, Accessory.

                                                                                                                                                                              The next module lifts the one-table restriction for good. You met a basic join back in Module 3; from here on you will pull columns from several tables in a single statement and see how the pieces fit together. Everything in this module carries over unchanged: the same WHERE, the same sorting, the same aggregates, applied to a wider set of rows.

                                                                                                                                                                              Terms Key Terms

                                                                                                                                                                              These are the words your instructor, the textbook, and the error messages will use. Read the definition, then say the term out loud against a query you have already run -- the vocabulary sticks faster when it is attached to something you typed.

                                                                                                                                                                              Choosing rows and columns

                                                                                                                                                                              Module 4 key terms: filtering and selecting
                                                                                                                                                                              TermWhat it means
                                                                                                                                                                              Simple conditionA single comparison of one column against a value or another column, such as BALANCE > 1000.
                                                                                                                                                                              Compound conditionTwo or more simple conditions joined with AND or OR, or reversed with NOT.
                                                                                                                                                                              BETWEENAn operator that tests whether a value falls inside a range, counting both endpoints as matches.
                                                                                                                                                                              Computed columnA column that is not stored in the table but calculated for each row, such as ON_HAND * PRICE.
                                                                                                                                                                              Alias (AS)A temporary name given to a column or expression so the result carries a readable heading.
                                                                                                                                                                              LIKEAn operator that compares text against a pattern instead of against an exact value. By default both SQLite and MySQL match ordinary ASCII letters without regard to case, so '%Pet%' and '%pet%' return the same rows here.
                                                                                                                                                                              WildcardA character inside a LIKE pattern that stands for other characters: % for any number of them, _ for exactly one.
                                                                                                                                                                              INAn operator that tests whether a value appears somewhere in a list, replacing a chain of OR tests.
                                                                                                                                                                              IS NULLThe only correct test for a missing value, because NULL is never equal to anything, including another NULL.

                                                                                                                                                                              Sorting, summarizing, and grouping

                                                                                                                                                                              Module 4 key terms: ordering and aggregating
                                                                                                                                                                              TermWhat it means
                                                                                                                                                                              Sort keyThe column named in ORDER BY that decides the order of the rows.
                                                                                                                                                                              Major and minor sort keyWhen you sort on two columns, the first is the major key and the second breaks ties inside it.
                                                                                                                                                                              ASC and DESCDirection keywords; ascending is the default, and DESC applies only to the column it follows.
                                                                                                                                                                              Aggregate functionA function that collapses many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN.
                                                                                                                                                                              DISTINCTA keyword that removes repeated values from a result so each one appears once.
                                                                                                                                                                              SubqueryA query written inside another query; the inner one runs first and the outer one uses its result.
                                                                                                                                                                              GroupingCollecting rows that share a value so an aggregate can be computed once per group.
                                                                                                                                                                              GROUP BYThe clause that names the column whose equal values define the groups.
                                                                                                                                                                              HAVINGThe clause that filters whole groups after grouping, the way WHERE filters individual rows before it.
                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                              The one pair students mix up

                                                                                                                                                                              WHERE tests one row at a time and runs before any grouping; HAVING tests a finished group and runs after. If your condition mentions COUNT, SUM, or AVG, it belongs in HAVING. If it mentions a plain column value, put it in WHERE, where it removes rows early and keeps the groups honest.

The worked answer groups instead of de-duplicating, so you also see that Habitat holds 2 items and the rest hold 1.

                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Knowledge check: Module 4 key terms

                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                              Q1Naming the parts of one WHERE clause

                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay's bookkeeper writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000 AND CITY = 'Maple Grove'; and gets back one row, Access Pet Center. Using this module's vocabulary, what is that WHERE clause?

                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A simple condition is a single comparison; this clause contains two of them joined together.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. A computed column produces a value in the result, such as ON_HAND * PRICE, not a true-or-false test.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. Grouping happens only when GROUP BY is present, and this statement has no GROUP BY at all.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Right -- BALANCE > 1000 and CITY = 'Maple Grove' are each simple conditions, and AND makes the pair compound.

                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: One comparison is a simple condition; two or more joined by AND, OR, or NOT make a compound condition.

                                                                                                                                                                              Q2One value per row, or one value in total

                                                                                                                                                                              The warehouse manager runs SELECT DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS VALUE_ON_HAND FROM ITEM; and gets five rows, then runs SELECT SUM(ON_HAND * PRICE) AS TOTAL_VALUE FROM ITEM; and gets 5621.65 in a single row. Which sentence names the difference correctly?

                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Both statements use AS; an alias renames a column and has no effect on how many rows return.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Right -- ON_HAND * PRICE is computed once per row, and SUM collapses those five values into one.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A subquery is a complete SELECT nested inside another statement, which is not what an expression inside SUM is.
                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. The first statement has no aggregate function, and neither statement contains a HAVING clause.

                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A computed column returns one value per row; an aggregate function returns one value for the whole group.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Review Review Questions

                                                                                                                                                                                        Ten questions covering the whole module. Several of them hand you a finished statement and ask what it returns against the KimTay and StayWell data you have been using all along -- reading SQL is half of writing it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                        How to read a statement you did not write

                                                                                                                                                                                        Work through it the way the database does. Start at FROM to see which table is in play, apply WHERE to see which rows survive, apply GROUP BY and HAVING if they are there, then build the SELECT list, and only then put the rows in ORDER BY order. Predict the row count before you predict the values.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Answer from the data first, then confirm. Guessing and checking teaches you far less than deciding on an answer, running the statement, and finding out exactly where your reasoning went sideways. If a total or an average comes back with a long tail of decimal digits, that is the SQLite floating-point display noted in the module summary, not a mistake in your query.
