                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Module 4 cumulative review: reading and writing single-table queries

                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1The customer list that came back three long

                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's bookkeeper runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' OR CITY = 'Brookville' AND BALANCE > 4000; against the four sample customers. Which result is correct?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. OR does not switch off the rest of the condition; Downtown Aquarium & Pets sits in Northfield and fails both branches.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right -- AND is evaluated first, so the test reads: in Maple Grove, or else in Brookville with a balance over 4000.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The balance test belongs only to the Brookville branch, so both Maple Grove customers return regardless of balance.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Mixing AND and OR is legal; what you control with parentheses is which one is evaluated first.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: AND binds tighter than OR, so add parentheses whenever you want the OR grouped first.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Counting the shelves inside a range

                                                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager runs SELECT ITEM_ID FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND BETWEEN 15 AND 30;. The five stored ON_HAND values are 15, 48, 120, 30, and 22. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. BETWEEN includes its endpoints, so the 15 on hand and the 30 on hand both qualify alongside 22.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. BETWEEN works on any ordered type: numbers, text, and dates all compare the same way.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Both boundaries are tested, not just the low one, so 48 and 120 are excluded for exceeding the high value of 30.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right -- 15, 30, and 22 all fall inside an inclusive range, while 48 and 120 sit above it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: BETWEEN 15 AND 30 means the same as ON_HAND >= 15 AND ON_HAND <= 30, endpoints included.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Pulling the pet-named accounts

                                                                                                                                                                                        Marketing asks which KimTay customers mention pets. The query is SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NAME LIKE '%Pet%';. What is the result against the four stored names?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right -- the pattern means any characters, then Pet, then any characters, so Pets matches as well.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The trailing percent sign already covers that s, so Downtown Aquarium & Pets matches too.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A wildcard is legal at either end or in the middle; its position changes the meaning, not the legality.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. LIKE still tests every row: Companion Care Clinic and Whiskers & Wags Boutique contain no Pet.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: In a LIKE pattern, % stands for any number of characters, including none, and _ stands for exactly one.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q4Two reps in Maple Grove

                                                                                                                                                                                        Rep 20 and rep 35 both carry Maple Grove addresses. A clerk writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove');. What is wrong with it?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The engines disagree about how to punish it: MySQL stops with a subquery-returns-more-than-one-row error, while SQLite runs it quietly and compares against just one of the two values.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Reading REP is exactly the point of the subquery; the trouble is how many values come back from it.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Right -- IN accepts a list, so it covers rep 20 and rep 35 and returns all three of their customers.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The inner query runs first, and its result is precisely what the outer condition tests.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Use = only when a subquery is guaranteed to return one value; use IN whenever it can return several.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q5Which shelves hold over a thousand dollars

                                                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager runs SELECT ITEM_ID, ON_HAND * PRICE AS INVENTORY_VALUE FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND * PRICE > 1000;. What does the result contain?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The expression is computed for each row and then tested, so the three rows under 1000 are removed.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Repeating the expression in WHERE is always allowed; it is the alias name that is not portable there.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Quantity alone does not decide it: 15 aviary cages at 64.99 come to 974.85 and fall short.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right -- 48 times 42.50 is 2040.00 and 120 times 11.99 is 1438.80, while the other three land below 1000. This sandbox prints them as 2040 and 1438.8.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Repeat the expression in WHERE rather than the alias -- SQLite accepts an alias there, MySQL does not.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q6City counts after the zero balance drops out

                                                                                                                                                                                        Companion Care Clinic in Maple Grove carries a balance of 0.00. The bookkeeper runs SELECT CITY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 0 GROUP BY CITY ORDER BY CITY;. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right -- the clinic is filtered out first, so Maple Grove has one surviving row to count.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so the zero-balance clinic never reaches the Maple Grove group.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. GROUP BY produces one row per city, not one row overall; leaving it out would give a single total.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. CITY is the only non-aggregated column and it appears in GROUP BY, so the statement is valid.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: WHERE thins the rows before grouping, which changes every count, total, and average that follows.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q7The rep carrying more than one account

                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's sales manager runs SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY REP_NUM HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; against the four sample customers. What is the result?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Removing groups is exactly what HAVING does; only the group meeting the condition survives.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. A condition on an aggregate must be in HAVING, because WHERE runs before the groups exist.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Right -- rep 20 holds Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic; reps 35 and 65 hold one each.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Rep 65 is on one account only, Whiskers & Wags Boutique, so that group is filtered out.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: HAVING filters finished groups; a condition mentioning COUNT, SUM, or AVG can live nowhere else.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q8Rent sheets for the leasing office

                                                                                                                                                                                        StayWell's leasing office runs SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM ORDER BY PROPERTY_ID, MONTHLY_RENT DESC;. How do the five rooms come out?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. PROPERTY_ID is the major sort key, so every P100 room is listed before any P200 room.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right -- PROPERTY_ID sorts ascending as the major key, and DESC reverses only the rent inside each property.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. DESC applies to the column it follows and to nothing else, so PROPERTY_ID stays ascending.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Two sort keys work together: the second one breaks the ties the first one leaves behind.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: In ORDER BY, the first column is the major sort key and DESC attaches only to the column right before it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q9Counting the catalog two ways

                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay stocks five items across four categories, with two of them in Habitat. What does SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_ROWS, COUNT(DISTINCT CATEGORY) AS NUM_CATEGORIES FROM ITEM; return?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. DISTINCT removes repeated values before counting, so the two Habitat rows contribute one category.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. COUNT(*) counts every row without exception, so it reports 5 whatever the categories look like.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A SELECT list may hold as many aggregate functions as you need, each summarizing the same rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right -- five rows exist, and Accessory, Food, Grooming, and Habitat make four distinct categories.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts how many different values that column holds.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q10Above the average price

                                                                                                                                                                                        The buyer runs SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE > (SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM);. The five prices are 64.99, 42.50, 11.99, 27.75, and 15.25, which average 32.496 -- printed in this sandbox as 32.495999999999995. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right -- the subquery produces the average once, and only the cage and the food price exceed it.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The subquery is evaluated once here and yields a single number the outer condition tests.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. An aggregate inside a subquery is one of its most common uses, since it returns exactly one value.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. FT88 is a Habitat item priced at 27.75, which sits below the average, so only two rows qualify.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A subquery lets the database compute a value such as an average and compare every row against it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        • Computed and aggregated columns carry a readable heading supplied with AS.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-1 Querying Multiple Tables

                                                                                                                                                                                        Every query you have written so far has looked at one table. That was never the real limit of SQL - it was the limit of the questions. Ask the KimTay bookkeeper what she needs on a Monday morning and it sounds like this: "Give me each customer with the name of the rep who handles them." Nothing in CUSTOMER stores a rep's name, and nothing in REP stores a customer's name. The answer lives in two tables at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                        That split is on purpose. Back in the design modules you saw why a rep's name is stored once in REP instead of being repeated on every customer row: one place to store it, one place to correct it. The price of that clean design is that answering a business question often means putting two tables back together for the length of one query. That is what a join does.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Start with the data: the first join uses CUSTOMER and REP. Read both complete source tables before seeing how SQL matches their REP_NUM values.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Source table: CUSTOMER — all columns and all four rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMESTREETCITYSTATEZIPBALANCECREDIT_LIMITREP_NUM
                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center215 Foster Ave.Maple GroveOH446013512.507500.0020
                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets642 Chestnut St.NorthfieldOH440671200.005000.0035
                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care Clinic89 River Rd.Maple GroveOH446010.0010000.0020
                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique77 Elm St.BrookvilleOH444034820.756000.0065
                                                                                                                                                                                        Source table: REP — all columns and all three rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        REP_NUMLAST_NAMEFIRST_NAMESTREETCITYSTATEZIPCOMMISSIONRATE
                                                                                                                                                                                        20KaiserValerie624 Randall Dr.Maple GroveOH4460121560.000.05
                                                                                                                                                                                        35HullRichard313 Palma Dr.Maple GroveOH4460139355.000.07
                                                                                                                                                                                        65PerezJuan2632 Marshall Ave.BrookvilleOH4440323764.000.05
                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                        Join

                                                                                                                                                                                        A join combines rows from two tables by matching values in a column they share. CUSTOMER.REP_NUM and REP.REP_NUM hold the same kind of value, so a row in CUSTOMER and a row in REP belong together whenever those two values are equal.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-1a Joining two tables

                                                                                                                                                                                        A join needs three things, and every one of them lives in a clause you already know. Nothing new is being added to the language here - you are widening the FROM clause and adding one more condition to WHERE.

                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                        1. Name the columns you want, table and all

                                                                                                                                                                                        Write CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME rather than CUSTOMER_NAME. Qualifying a column with its table name is optional when the name appears in only one table, and required when it appears in both.

                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                        2. List both tables in FROM

                                                                                                                                                                                        FROM CUSTOMER, REP tells the engine which two tables are in play. On its own this pairs every customer with every rep, which is not what you want yet.

                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                        3. Write the matching condition in WHERE

                                                                                                                                                                                        WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM is the sentence that does the real work: keep a pairing only when the customer's rep number equals the rep's rep number.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: list every customer next to the name of the rep who serves that account.
-- SELECT: the four columns the answer will contain. Each one is written as
--   TABLE.COLUMN, so it is plain that two values are read out of CUSTOMER and
--   two out of REP.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME, REP.FIRST_NAME

-- FROM: puts both tables in play. On its own this line pairs every customer with
--   every rep - 4 customers x 3 reps = 12 pairings, most of them nonsense.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: the matching condition, and the line that turns those 12 pairings into
--   a join. A pairing survives only when the rep number stored on the customer
--   row equals the rep number on the rep row, which leaves 4 real rows.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the surviving rows by customer number. It decides the order
--   rows are printed in, never which rows match.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                        The ORDER BY on the end is not part of the join - the three parts above are the whole of it. It is there because a query without ORDER BY makes no promise about the sequence rows come back in, and every result printed in this module is easier to check against your own screen when the order is pinned down.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Result: four customers, each carrying its rep's name
                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMELAST_NAMEFIRST_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet CenterKaiserValerie
                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & PetsHullRichard
                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care ClinicKaiserValerie
                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags BoutiquePerezJuan

                                                                                                                                                                                        Read one row and the mechanism stops being mysterious. Customer 1120 stores REP_NUM 20. The engine looks for the row in REP whose REP_NUM is also 20, finds Valerie Kaiser, and glues the two rows together for output. Customer 1310 stores 20 as well, so Kaiser appears twice. Four customers in, four rows out - because every customer stores a rep number that matches exactly one rep, this join neither invents rows nor loses any.

                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                        Qualify anything that lives in both tables

                                                                                                                                                                                        REP_NUM exists in CUSTOMER and in REP, so writing it bare makes the request impossible to interpret. SELECT REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM; fails with ambiguous column name: REP_NUM. That error message is telling you exactly what to fix: put a table name in front of it. CUSTOMER_NAME and LAST_NAME appear in only one table each, so those may be written bare - but qualifying every column in a join keeps the statement readable for whoever inherits it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        The starter already joins the two tables correctly - it is only selecting from one of them. Add REP.LAST_NAME and REP.FIRST_NAME to the column list. The row count does not change; the rows just get wider.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-1b Adding conditions to a join

                                                                                                                                                                                        The matching condition is a WHERE condition like any other, which means the compound conditions you learned in Module 4 still apply. Connect the matching condition to a business restriction with AND, and you get a filtered join. Here is every customer with a credit limit of 7500.00 or more, along with the rep who handles them.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the same join, narrowed to customers with a credit limit of 7500 or more.
-- SELECT: three output columns - two read from CUSTOMER, one read from REP.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the two tables being joined.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: the matching condition - which customer row belongs with which rep row.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- AND: an ordinary business restriction, exactly like the ones in Module 4.
--   Nothing about it is join-specific. Both conditions have to be true, so the
--   4 joined rows become the 2 whose credit limit clears 7500.
  AND CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500

-- ORDER BY: sorts those two rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                        Result: two high-limit customers, both handled by Kaiser
                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMELAST_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet CenterKaiser
                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care ClinicKaiser
                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                        One condition per job

                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep the matching condition on its own line and the business restrictions underneath it. When a join returns something strange, the first line you check is the matching condition, and putting it first makes that a one-second check instead of a hunt.

                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        Add one more line with AND under the matching condition, restricting CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT. Four rows should become two.
                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                        Leave out the matching condition and the row count explodes

                                                                                                                                                                                        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER, REP; returns 12. With no condition tying the tables together, the engine pairs each of the four customers with each of the three reps, and every one of those twelve pairings is reported as a row. Eight of them are nonsense - Access Pet Center paired with a rep who does not handle it. The special-operations section later in this module (5-5) gives this behavior its formal name; for now, treat a suspiciously large row count as a missing matching condition.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: show what the row count does when the matching condition is left out.
-- SELECT: COUNT(*) counts the rows this query produces, and AS gives that single
--   number the heading COMBINATIONS.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS COMBINATIONS

-- FROM: two tables and no WHERE clause anywhere, so nothing restricts the
--   pairings. Each of the 4 customers is paired with each of the 3 reps, and the
--   answer comes back 12 - eight rows more than the real join returned.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP;

                                                                                                                                                                                        Sorting, grouping and the aggregate functions do not change at all once a join is in the picture. The join produces rows; everything downstream treats those rows exactly like rows from a single table. This counts customers and totals balances per rep.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: one summary line per rep - how many customers, and their total balance.
-- SELECT: the grouping column first, then two aggregates. COUNT(*) counts the
--   rows inside each group, SUM adds up the balances inside each group, and AS
--   gives each computed value a readable heading.
SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS, SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE) AS TOTAL_BALANCE

-- FROM: the two tables. Naming REP before CUSTOMER changes nothing - the order
--   of tables in FROM is cosmetic.
FROM REP, CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the matching condition. It is applied BEFORE the grouping, so the
--   aggregates are computed over joined rows and never over the raw tables.
WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM

-- GROUP BY: collapses the joined rows into one output row per rep last name.
--   Kaiser's two customers become a single line reading 2.
GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME

-- ORDER BY: sorts those summary lines alphabetically by last name.
ORDER BY REP.LAST_NAME;
                                                                                                                                                                                        Result: one row per rep
                                                                                                                                                                                        LAST_NAMENUM_CUSTOMERSTOTAL_BALANCE
                                                                                                                                                                                        Hull11200
                                                                                                                                                                                        Kaiser23512.5
                                                                                                                                                                                        Perez14820.75

                                                                                                                                                                                        Kaiser's total is 3512.5 because her two customers carry balances of 3512.50 and 0.00. A balance of zero is a real, recorded amount - Companion Care Clinic is counted in NUM_CUSTOMERS like any other customer, and contributes nothing to the sum.

                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        Start from the four detail rows, then collapse them: replace the customer columns with COUNT(*) and SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE), and add GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME. Four rows become three.

                                                                                                                                                                                        What goes wrong

                                                                                                                                                                                        Naming two tables in FROM and forgetting the matching condition. Writing a shared column name without its table. Assuming the order of the tables in FROM matters - it does not, FROM CUSTOMER, REP and FROM REP, CUSTOMER return the same rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                        What to do instead

                                                                                                                                                                                        Write FROM and the matching condition together as one habit, before you touch the column list. Qualify every column in a join. Run the join with no extra restrictions first, confirm the row count looks sane, and only then start filtering.

                                                                                                                                                                                        • Both tables appear in the FROM clause, separated by a comma
                                                                                                                                                                                        • A WHERE condition equates the matching columns from the two tables
                                                                                                                                                                                        • Any column name that exists in both tables is written as TABLE.COLUMN
                                                                                                                                                                                        • Extra business restrictions are joined to the matching condition with AND
                                                                                                                                                                                        • The row count is what you expected - a surprising jump means the matching condition is missing
                                                                                                                                                                                        • An ORDER BY is present whenever the order of the output matters to you

                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Knowledge check: joining two tables

                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1Putting a rep's name next to a customer

                                                                                                                                                                                        The KimTay bookkeeper needs a list showing each customer name with the last name of the rep who handles that customer. She has written SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER, REP and stopped. What has to come next for the names to line up correctly?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Naming two tables only makes both available; with no condition the engine pairs every customer with every rep, giving twelve rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right - the matching condition on the shared REP_NUM value is what turns twelve possible pairings into the four correct ones.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. ORDER BY changes the sequence rows are displayed in and never removes or corrects a wrong pairing.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, but the twelve pairings here are all different from one another, so none of them would be dropped.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A join is two tables in FROM plus a WHERE condition equating the columns they share - the condition, not the FROM clause, is what matches the rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2The twelve-row surprise at KimTay Pet Supplies

                                                                                                                                                                                        Someone runs SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER, REP; against the KimTay database and gets twelve rows, even though there are only four customers. What happened?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. CUSTOMER has four rows; nothing was hidden, and a SELECT with no WHERE clause never conceals rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Row counts come from how rows are combined, not from how many columns appear in the SELECT list.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. No padding takes place - each of the twelve rows holds a real customer and a real rep, they are merely paired wrongly.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Right - without a matching condition the engine reports every possible pairing, four customers times three reps.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A row count far larger than either table is the signature of a missing matching condition in the WHERE clause.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3The message that stopped the query

                                                                                                                                                                                        A student runs SELECT REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM; and the engine answers ambiguous column name: REP_NUM. What is the engine complaining about?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Right - a column name that appears in more than one table has to be qualified so the engine knows which table you mean.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The spelling is correct in all three places; the engine found the column in two tables, which is the actual problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. There is no such restriction - a join may select any column from any table listed in FROM.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. A column may appear in both the WHERE clause and the SELECT list as often as you need it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Ambiguous column name means the column lives in more than one table in your FROM clause - qualify it as TABLE.COLUMN.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Q4The rep with two customers

                                                                                                                                                                                        The grouped query SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS, SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE) AS TOTAL_BALANCE FROM REP, CUSTOMER WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME; reports Kaiser with NUM_CUSTOMERS of 2 and TOTAL_BALANCE of 3512.5, even though Kaiser handles Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. Why does the total match a single customer's balance?

                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. It was not dropped - it stores REP_NUM 20 and matches Kaiser, which is exactly why NUM_CUSTOMERS reports 2.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Right - a balance of 0.00 is a real recorded amount, so the row is counted by COUNT(*) and contributes zero to the SUM.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. SUM adds every value in the group; there is no rule that skips rows after the first.
                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Both are computed over the same group, which is why the count of 2 and the total of 3512.5 sit on one row together.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A zero is a value, not a missing row - it is counted like any other row and simply adds nothing to a total.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-2 Comparing Joins, IN, and EXISTS

                                                                                                                                                                                        Here is a question the KimTay bookkeeper actually asks: which customers have placed at least one order? SQL will answer it three different ways - with a join, with IN, and with EXISTS - and all three return the same three customers. That is not wasted effort on the language's part. Each shape says something different about what you meant, and one of them will read better than the others depending on what you need in the output.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep one row in mind for this whole section: Companion Care Clinic, customer 1310. It is a real customer with a 10000.00 credit limit and no invoice at all. It is the row that tells you whether a query is answering "has an order" or something subtly different.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-2a Using the IN operator

                                                                                                                                                                                        You already use IN with a list you type yourself. This asks for customers in either of two cities, and the engine checks the CITY value of each row against the two values in the parentheses.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the customers located in either of two named cities.
-- SELECT: three columns. Only one table is involved, so nothing has to be
--   qualified with a table name.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY

-- FROM: a single table - this query is not a join at all.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: IN is true when the row's CITY equals ANY value inside the parentheses.
--   It is shorthand for CITY = 'Maple Grove' OR CITY = 'Brookville', and the
--   longer the list, the more typing it saves.
WHERE CITY IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville')

-- ORDER BY: sorts the matching rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                        The step that makes IN powerful is realizing the list does not have to be typed. A subquery that returns a single column produces a list, and IN cannot tell the difference. Compare the two ways of answering the order question. First the join, using exactly the pattern from 5-1a.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: which customers have at least one invoice - answered with a join.
-- SELECT: DISTINCT throws away duplicate output rows. It is here because a join
--   returns one row per matching PAIR, so a customer holding three invoices
--   would otherwise be listed three times.
SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the customer table and the invoice table.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE

-- WHERE: the matching condition, written on the customer number the two tables
--   share. A customer with no invoice matches nothing here and disappears from
--   the result - which is exactly what "has at least one invoice" means.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the surviving customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                        Now the same question with IN. The inner query returns the customer numbers that appear in INVOICE; the outer query keeps the customers whose number is in that list.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the same question - customers with at least one invoice - written with a
-- subquery instead of a join.
-- SELECT: two columns, both from CUSTOMER. No DISTINCT is needed this time.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: one table only. INVOICE is reached by the subquery below, not by FROM.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the inner SELECT runs first, on its own, and returns a one-column list
--   of the customer numbers that appear in INVOICE. IN then tests each customer
--   once against that finished list, which is why no customer can come back
--   twice and why DISTINCT is unnecessary.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the kept customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                        Both statements return the same three customers
                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center
                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets
                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique
                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                        Why the join needed DISTINCT

                                                                                                                                                                                        A join returns one row per matching pair, so a customer with three invoices comes back three times. In the shipped data every customer that has an invoice at all happens to have exactly one - Companion Care Clinic has none - so this particular join returns three rows even without DISTINCT. That is an accident of this small data set, not a rule. Write DISTINCT whenever a join is being used to answer a "which rows have at least one match" question. IN needs no such defense: the outer query still looks at each customer exactly once.

                                                                                                                                                                                        The duplicate problem is visible in the shipped data if you join ITEM to INVOICE_LINE instead. Item CF21 was ordered on two different invoices, so the join reports it twice.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: show which invoices ordered each item, so the duplicate rows a join can
-- produce are visible in the shipped data.
-- SELECT: two columns from ITEM and one from INVOICE_LINE. There is deliberately
--   no DISTINCT here, because the repeats are the point of the example.
SELECT ITEM.ITEM_ID, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: the item table plus the line-item table that records what was ordered.
FROM ITEM, INVOICE_LINE

-- WHERE: the matching condition on the item id the two tables share. Item CF21
--   was ordered on two different invoices, so CF21 makes two matching pairs -
--   and a join reports one row per pair. Five items, six rows.
WHERE ITEM.ITEM_ID = INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: two sort columns - by item first, then by invoice within each item.
ORDER BY ITEM.ITEM_ID, INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                        Six rows for five items - CF21 appears on two invoices
                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONINVOICE_NUM
                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage50712
                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb50710
                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb50711
                                                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft50710
                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit50712
                                                                                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming Kit50711
                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                        The rule of thumb for IN

                                                                                                                                                                                        If the output shows columns from one table only, IN is usually the cleaner statement. If the output has to show columns from both tables - the invoice number next to the customer name, the description next to the quantity - a join is the only one of the three that can do it, because a subquery's columns never reach the output.

                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                        Your task: leave the starter alone and write a second statement below it that lists the ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION and PRICE of every item ordered on invoice 50710, using the same IN shape. Run the inner query by itself first - SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50710'; returns CF21 and DG04. Those two values are the list the outer query checks against, so expect two rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                        5-2b Using the EXISTS operator

                                                                                                                                                                                        EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question about the row currently being examined: is there at least one row over in that other table that matches me? It does not produce values, and nothing from inside it reaches the output. It returns true or false, and the outer WHERE keeps the row or drops it.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: customers with at least one invoice - the third way, using EXISTS.
-- SELECT: the two columns to print. Nothing from inside the subquery can ever
--   appear in this list.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the outer query walks CUSTOMER one row at a time.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: EXISTS is a yes-or-no test applied to the customer currently being
--   examined - did the inner query find at least one row? It answers true or
--   false and produces no values of its own.
WHERE EXISTS

    -- SELECT *: the column list is irrelevant, since no value from it is used.
    --   The * reads as "anything at all", which is the question EXISTS asks.
    (SELECT *

     -- FROM: the table being searched for a match.
     FROM INVOICE

     -- WHERE: this line names CUSTOMER, a table of the OUTER query, and that
     --   reference is what makes the subquery correlated: it cannot run on its
     --   own, and it is re-executed for each customer with that customer's
     --   number filled in. Customer 1310 finds no invoice, so EXISTS is false
     --   and that row is dropped.
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three kept customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                        Correlated subquery

                                                                                                                                                                                        Look at the inner WHERE: it mentions CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, a column of the outer query. That reference is what makes the subquery correlated - it cannot be run on its own, because it has no meaning until the outer query hands it a customer. An IN subquery is the opposite: SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE runs perfectly well by itself.

                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                        Customer 1120, Access Pet Center

                                                                                                                                                                                        The inner query becomes "is there an invoice whose CUSTOMER_NUM is 1120?" Invoice 50710 matches. The engine stops looking the moment it finds that first row - it never needs to know how many there are. True, so the row is kept.

                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                        Customer 1225, Downtown Aquarium & Pets

                                                                                                                                                                                        Invoice 50712 matches. True, kept.

                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                        Customer 1310, Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                        The inner query searches INVOICE for CUSTOMER_NUM 1310 and finds nothing. False, so the row is dropped. This is the one customer the query removes.

                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                        Customer 1420, Whiskers & Wags Boutique

                                                                                                                                                                                        Invoice 50711 matches. True, kept. Three rows come back, the same three the join and the IN version returned.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Writing SELECT * inside EXISTS is the convention, and it is not laziness. Since no value from the subquery is ever used, the column list is irrelevant - SELECT 1 returns the identical three customers. SELECT * reads as "anything at all," which is precisely the question being asked.

                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                        An EXISTS with no correlation is always true

                                                                                                                                                                                        Drop the inner WHERE and you get SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM INVOICE); - which returns all four customers, Companion Care Clinic included. The subquery no longer asks about a particular customer; it asks whether INVOICE has any rows at all, and it does. If an EXISTS query returns every row of the outer table, the correlation is missing.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Reverse the test and EXISTS earns its keep. NOT EXISTS finds the rows where the search comes back empty - the customers who have never been invoiced. There is exactly one, and by now you know which.

                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the opposite question - which customers have never been invoiced.
-- SELECT: the two columns to print.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the outer query walks CUSTOMER one row at a time, as before.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: NOT EXISTS flips the test. The customer is kept only when the inner
--   query finds NOTHING. This is the standard pattern for finding rows that have
--   no match at all on the other side.
WHERE NOT EXISTS

    -- SELECT *: again the column list does not matter; only whether a row exists.
    (SELECT *

     -- FROM: the table searched for a match.
     FROM INVOICE

     -- WHERE: the correlation back to the outer row. For each customer in turn
     --   the engine asks "is there an invoice carrying this customer number?"
     --   Only 1310 comes back empty, so only 1310 survives NOT EXISTS.
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the result, which here is a single row.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                        Result: the customer with no invoice
                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                        This is the shape a join cannot express with what you know so far. A join reports pairs that matched, so a customer with no invoice produces no row and disappears from the output entirely - you cannot see an absence in a list of matches. The special-operations section later in this module (5-5) introduces a kind of join built for exactly this, but NOT EXISTS answers it today.

                                                                                                                                                                                        Picking a shape
                                                                                                                                                                                        What the output needsBest shapeWhy
