                                                                                                                                                                                                5-2e to 5-2h Aliases, Self-Joins, and Joining Several Tables

                                                                                                                                                                                                Two things make multiple-table queries tiring. The first is typing CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM and INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM over and over. The second is harder: sometimes the question you are asked needs the same table twice in one query, and there is no way to tell the two copies apart. An alias solves both problems, and the second one cannot be solved any other way. Learn aliases first and the self-join stops being mysterious.

                                                                                                                                                                                                5-2e Using an alias

                                                                                                                                                                                                You create an alias in the FROM clause: write the table name, a space, and the short name you want to use. The word AS is optional and most people leave it out. From that point on, you qualify columns with the alias instead of the full table name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                Alias

                                                                                                                                                                                                An alias is a temporary name you give a table inside one statement. It exists only while that statement runs, it is not stored in the database, and it changes nothing about the table itself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                -- GOAL: show the smallest possible use of an alias - a short, temporary name for
-- a table that lives only as long as this one statement.
-- SELECT: C.CUSTOMER_NAME means exactly what CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME means. The
--   alias is already usable here even though it is defined on the next line.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: this is where the alias is created - table name, then the short name.
--   The word AS is optional and most people leave it out.
FROM CUSTOMER AS C

-- WHERE: an ordinary condition, written through the alias. One row comes back,
--   Whiskers & Wags Boutique, the only customer of rep 65.
WHERE C.REP_NUM = '65';

                                                                                                                                                                                                That returns one row, Whiskers & Wags Boutique. The AS is doing nothing the space would not do on its own, so the rest of this section drops it. Aliases pay off the most when two tables are in play, because every qualified column gets shorter and the matching condition becomes easy to read at a glance.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Give REP the alias R in the FROM clause, then use R on both sides of the matching condition.

                                                                                                                                                                                                You get four rows, one per customer, each carrying the last name and rate of the rep who handles the account. Kaiser appears twice because customers 1120 and 1310 are both hers. Hold on to that fact, because it is the whole reason the next lesson exists.

                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                An alias replaces the table name

                                                                                                                                                                                                Once you write FROM CUSTOMER C, the name CUSTOMER is no longer available in that statement. Writing CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM after aliasing produces an error, not a second way to say the same thing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                -- GOAL: a deliberate error. Once a table has an alias, the full table name is no
-- longer available anywhere in that statement.
-- SELECT: WRONG. C is defined below, so CUSTOMER is no longer a usable name and
--   the engine has no table by that name to look the column up in. SQLite says
--   "no such column: CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM"; MySQL and Oracle raise their own
--   version of the same unknown-table error. The fix is to write C.CUSTOMER_NUM.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- FROM: two aliases are defined here, C and R. From this point on they are the
--   only names by which the two tables can be reached.
FROM CUSTOMER C, REP R

-- WHERE: this line is correct - it uses the aliases on both sides. It is only
--   the SELECT list above that breaks the statement.
WHERE C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                5-2f Joining a table to itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                Here is a real request. The sales manager is routing a rep's travel and wants pairs of customers who share the same rep, so that rep can visit two accounts on one trip. Every piece of information needed sits in CUSTOMER, and yet no single-table WHERE clause can answer it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                The reason is that a WHERE clause looks at one row at a time. To decide whether Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic belong together, the database has to hold two different customer rows side by side and compare them. Getting two rows in play at once means listing the table twice, and listing the table twice means you need aliases to tell the copies apart.

                                                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                Nothing new is happening

                                                                                                                                                                                                A self-join is not a special command. It is an ordinary join in which both sides happen to be the same table. The aliases are the only thing that makes it possible, which is why 5-2e had to come first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Listing the table twice also makes every unqualified column name ambiguous. With two copies in play, CUSTOMER_NUM on its own could mean either one, and the database refuses to guess. In a self-join you must qualify every column, without exception.

                                                                                                                                                                                                -- GOAL: a second deliberate error, the one that makes aliases compulsory in a
-- self-join rather than merely convenient.
-- SELECT: WRONG. With two copies of CUSTOMER in play, a bare CUSTOMER_NUM could
--   mean the one from copy A or the one from copy B, and the engine refuses to
--   guess. SQLite says "ambiguous column name: CUSTOMER_NUM"; MySQL and Oracle
--   report the same ambiguity in their own wording. Write A.CUSTOMER_NUM.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM

-- FROM: the same table opened twice, under two different names. This is all a
--   self-join is - an ordinary join whose two sides happen to be one table.
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B

-- WHERE: the matching condition between the two copies, correctly qualified.
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                1

                                                                                                                                                                                                List the table twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                Write FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B. The database now has two independent copies to work with, named A and B.

                                                                                                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                                                                                                Match the copies

                                                                                                                                                                                                Add WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM so a row from A is only considered next to a row from B that shares its rep.

                                                                                                                                                                                                3

                                                                                                                                                                                                Restrict the pairs

                                                                                                                                                                                                Add a second condition on the primary key so each real pair appears exactly once. That step is 5-2g, and the next query shows why it is not optional.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Run it as written and count the rows before you read on. Six is more than you wanted.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Six rows come back and only one of them answers the question. Look at what the other five are.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Every row the unrestricted self-join produces
                                                                                                                                                                                                A.CUSTOMER_NUMB.CUSTOMER_NUMREP_NUMDo you want this row?
                                                                                                                                                                                                1120112020No, a row paired with itself
                                                                                                                                                                                                1120131020Yes, this is the pair you asked for
                                                                                                                                                                                                1225122535No, a row paired with itself
                                                                                                                                                                                                1310112020No, the same pair in reverse
                                                                                                                                                                                                1310131020No, a row paired with itself
                                                                                                                                                                                                1420142065No, a row paired with itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                The two problems have different causes. Every customer row matches itself because a rep number is always equal to itself, and every genuine pair shows up twice because the database has no idea which copy you consider first. One extra condition, chosen well, disposes of both.

                                                                                                                                                                                                5-2g Using a self-join on a primary key column

                                                                                                                                                                                                The fix is a second condition, and it goes on the primary key column: A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM. Two properties of a primary key are what make this work. It is unique, so no two different rows can tie, and it is never null, so the comparison always has a definite answer. Neither of those is guaranteed for CITY or CUSTOMER_NAME, which is why the restriction belongs on the key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Using <> gives two rows

                                                                                                                                                                                                A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM throws out the four self-paired rows, because a row can never differ from itself. It does nothing about ordering, so you still get 1120 with 1310 and 1310 with 1120. Half the result is redundant.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Using < gives one row

                                                                                                                                                                                                A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM is false when the numbers are equal, so self-pairs disappear, and it is true for exactly one of the two orderings, so mirrors disappear too. One condition, both problems solved.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Put a less-than sign between the two primary key columns, then try <> instead and compare the row counts.

                                                                                                                                                                                                One row: 1120 Access Pet Center with 1310 Companion Care Clinic. Swap < for > and you get one row again, 1310 with 1120, the same pair in the other order. Either direction is correct. What matters is choosing one so each pair is reported once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                The pattern generalizes. Match on the column that describes the relationship you care about, then restrict on the primary key. Here the shared attribute is the category instead of the rep.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                One row comes back, AV07 with FT88, because Habitat is the only category holding two items.

                                                                                                                                                                                                A self-join can also sit alongside other tables. If the sales manager wants the rep name printed next to each pair, bring REP into the same query and link it to either copy of CUSTOMER, since both copies carry the same rep number.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Three aliases, three conditions: match the copies, attach the rep, restrict the pair.

                                                                                                                                                                                                5-2h Joining several tables

                                                                                                                                                                                                Now a question that no two tables can answer: which items did each customer order, and how many? Customer names live in CUSTOMER. Item descriptions live in ITEM. Those two tables share no column at all, so there is nothing to match them on. INVOICE and INVOICE_LINE are the bridge between them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Think of it as a chain. CUSTOMER connects to INVOICE, INVOICE connects to INVOICE_LINE, INVOICE_LINE connects to ITEM. You list all four tables in the FROM clause and write one condition per link.

                                                                                                                                                                                                One condition for each link in the chain
                                                                                                                                                                                                LinkConditionWhat it means
                                                                                                                                                                                                CUSTOMER to INVOICEC.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUMThis invoice belongs to that customer
                                                                                                                                                                                                INVOICE to INVOICE_LINEI.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUMThis line appears on that invoice
                                                                                                                                                                                                INVOICE_LINE to ITEMIL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_IDThis line is for that item
                                                                                                                                                                                                1

                                                                                                                                                                                                Name every table you need

                                                                                                                                                                                                Work out which tables hold the columns you want to display and which tables are needed only to reach them. INVOICE and INVOICE_LINE are here mostly as connectors.

                                                                                                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                                                                                                Give each one an alias

                                                                                                                                                                                                With four tables, unqualified column names get ambiguous fast. Short aliases such as C, I, IL and IT keep the conditions readable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                3

                                                                                                                                                                                                Write one condition per link

                                                                                                                                                                                                A chain of four tables needs three conditions. Count them before you run the query; if you have fewer, a link is missing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                4

                                                                                                                                                                                                Add your filters last

                                                                                                                                                                                                Anything that narrows the result, such as a category or a customer name, goes in the same WHERE clause after the linking conditions.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                The last link joins INVOICE_LINE to ITEM, so the missing alias is IT.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Six rows, one for every invoice line in the database, each now readable in business terms: Access Pet Center ordered 3 bags of Grain-Free Dry Food and 2 nylon leashes, and so on. Companion Care Clinic does not appear at all, because it has no invoice. That is correct behavior for this kind of join, and 5-5 shows you how to include a customer with nothing to show.

                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                A missing condition does not raise an error

                                                                                                                                                                                                Delete I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM from that query and it still runs, returning 18 rows instead of 6. Each of the three invoices gets paired with all six line-and-item combinations. Nothing warns you. Counting your conditions is the defense.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Step 4 said filters go last, so try one. The three linking conditions stay exactly as they were, and a fourth condition narrows the result to a single category of merchandise.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Put the category in single quotes: 'Habitat'. Two rows come back, both on invoice 50712.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Two rows, the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit, both ordered by Downtown Aquarium & Pets on invoice 50712. Notice the filter did nothing structural. It sits in the same WHERE clause as the links and simply drops rows the manager did not ask for.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Chains can be longer. Adding REP in front of CUSTOMER makes five tables and four conditions, and the row count stays at 6 because each customer has exactly one rep. Notice you can also compute a column while you are at it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Five tables, four conditions. Kaiser's two lines extend to 127.50 and 23.98.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Because a joined result is an ordinary result, everything you learned in Module 4 still applies to it. Group the joined rows by invoice and you get a total for each invoice, with the customer name alongside it, without storing that total anywhere.

                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                Group by the invoice number, qualified with its alias. Totals are 151.48, 100.25 and 120.49.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Define an alias in the FROM clause and use it everywhere else in the statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Remember that the alias replaces the table name; the original name stops working
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Qualify every column once two copies of a table are in play, or the engine reports an ambiguous column name
                                                                                                                                                                                                • List a table twice with two aliases whenever a question compares two rows of one table
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Match the self-join copies on the shared column, such as REP_NUM or CATEGORY
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Restrict the pair with < on the primary key so self-pairs and mirrors both disappear
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Count your linking conditions: N tables in a chain need at least N minus 1
                                                                                                                                                                                                • Add business filters after the linking conditions, in the same WHERE clause
                                                                                                                                                                                                • If the row count looks too high, suspect a missing linking condition before anything else
                                                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                Another way to write these

                                                                                                                                                                                                Every join in this section is written by listing tables in FROM and matching them in WHERE. Section 5-5 introduces the INNER JOIN and OUTER JOIN keywords, which express the same idea with the matching condition moved into the FROM clause. Both styles run in the sandbox. Learn this one first, because it is the style this module uses for self-joins; you will meet both in practice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: aliases, self-joins, and multi-table chains

                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1Access Pet Center on the rep roster

                                                                                                                                                                                                A bookkeeper writes FROM CUSTOMER C, REP R and then asks for CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME in the SELECT list. What happens when the statement runs?

                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. An alias is a replacement rather than an addition; the original table name goes out of scope in that query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔b. Correct: after CUSTOMER C is written, the engine reports no such column: CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. How a column is named never duplicates rows; the row count comes from the join conditions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Aliases are legal in any query, including single-table ones; they are only required for a self-join.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: An alias renames a table for the length of the statement, so qualify every column with the alias once you define one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2Valerie Kaiser's two Maple Grove accounts

                                                                                                                                                                                                FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM returns six rows against the KimTay data. Why are five of them unwanted?

                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Balances play no part here; every customer row qualifies because a rep number always equals itself.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. REP is not needed at all, since both sides of this join are copies of CUSTOMER.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct: 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420 each pair with themselves, and 1310 with 1120 mirrors 1120 with 1310.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. An inequality on REP_NUM would return customers handled by different reps, which is the opposite question.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: An unrestricted self-join returns self-pairs and both orderings of every real pair, so it always needs a second condition.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3Companion Care Clinic paired twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                A student replaces the pair restriction with A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM and runs the self-join again. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. <> removes only the self-paired rows and keeps both orderings of every genuine pair, so it returns one row more than < does.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Customer numbers are unique, so <> is true for every combination of two different rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. <> does have an effect: it removes the four self-paired rows, bringing the result from six rows down to two.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct: only < keeps a single ordering per pair, which is what gets the answer down to one row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Use < rather than <> on the primary key so each pair of rows is reported exactly once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Q4Downtown Aquarium & Pets invoice detail

                                                                                                                                                                                                In the chain over CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE and ITEM, the condition I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM is deleted by accident. What does the warehouse manager see?

                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct: three invoices times the six matched line-and-item rows produces eighteen rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. SQL never requires a join condition, so a missing one is a logic error rather than a syntax error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Key columns connect tables only when you write the matching condition yourself in the WHERE clause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Tables left unmatched multiply rows instead of cancelling them, so you get more rows, never fewer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Count your linking conditions before running a multi-table query; a missing one inflates the result silently.

                                                                                                                                                                                                🧩 What job is this clause fragment doing?

                                                                                                                                                                                                Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                Every fragment below is copied verbatim from a KimTay query in this section. Drag each one to the job it performs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 / 6 placed

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-3 Set Operations

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every query you have written so far builds one result table from one SELECT. A set operation works differently. You write two complete SELECT statements, and a keyword between them tells SQL how to fold the two result tables into one. The reason to reach for one is that some business questions are really questions about two lists rather than one condition: which customers are on this list or that one, which are on both, which are on the first but missing from the second.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The four set operations
                                                                                                                                                                                                        OperationThe question it answersDuplicate rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        UNIONIn the first list, the second, or bothRemoved
                                                                                                                                                                                                        UNION ALLIn the first list, the second, or bothKept
                                                                                                                                                                                                        INTERSECTIn both listsRemoved
                                                                                                                                                                                                        EXCEPTIn the first list but not the secondRemoved
                                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Union compatibility

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two SELECT statements can be combined only if they are union compatible: each one returns the same number of columns, in the same order, and the columns that line up hold compatible kinds of data. The column names do not have to match. The combined result takes its headings from the first SELECT.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        That rule exists because the answer has to be a single table with a single set of headings. If the first SELECT returns two columns and the second returns one, there is no sensible way to line them up, and every SQL engine rejects the statement before running anything. Column types are a different story, and here the engines genuinely disagree. SQLite, the engine in the sandboxes below, enforces the column count but is relaxed about types, so it will cheerfully stack a BALANCE value underneath a CUSTOMER_NAME and hand the whole thing back as one column. MySQL is just as permissive and converts both sides to a common type. Oracle is the strict one: it rejects the mismatch with ORA-01790: expression must have same datatype as corresponding expression. Line your columns up on purpose rather than trusting the engine to catch you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        UNION: everything on either list

                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's office manager wants one mailing list that covers every customer served by rep 20 together with every customer that has an invoice on file. Some customers qualify on both counts, and each of those should still appear once. That is exactly what UNION does.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: one combined list - every customer served by rep 20, together with every
-- customer that has an invoice, each appearing only once.
-- SELECT: the first of two complete SELECT statements. Its two columns fix the
--   shape of the answer, and its headings are the headings of the whole result.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the first statement reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - the customers of rep 20. That is 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- UNION: folds the two results into one and removes duplicate rows. Both sides
--   must be union compatible: same number of columns, same order, compatible
--   types. The names do not have to match.
UNION

-- SELECT: the second complete statement begins here. Two columns again.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it happens to read the same table, but it does not have to.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the customers that appear in INVOICE. That is 1120, 1225
--   and 1420. Customer 1120 is on both lists, and UNION keeps one copy of it,
--   so the combined answer is four rows rather than five.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)

-- ORDER BY: a set operation is ONE statement, so it gets ONE ORDER BY, and it
--   belongs after the last SELECT. Sorting the first half on its own is an error.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The first SELECT returns 1120 and 1310. The second returns 1120, 1225 and 1420. Access Pet Center (1120) is on both lists, and UNION keeps one copy of it, so the combined answer is four rows rather than five.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Result of the UNION above
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care Clinic
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique
                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                        One ORDER BY, at the very end

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A set operation is a single statement, so it gets a single ORDER BY, and that ORDER BY belongs after the last SELECT. Sorting the first SELECT on its own is an error. SQLite answers ORDER BY clause should come after UNION not before.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        UNION ALL: keep the duplicates

                                                                                                                                                                                                        UNION ALL stacks the two results and stops there. Nothing is compared and nothing is thrown away. Ask for every city that appears in CUSTOMER or in REP and the difference shows up immediately.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: every city named in either table, with nothing removed.
-- SELECT / FROM: the first list - the four city values stored in CUSTOMER.
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION ALL: stacks the two lists and stops there. Nothing is compared and
--   nothing is discarded, so a city held by several rows is listed several times.
UNION ALL

-- SELECT / FROM: the second list - the three city values stored in REP. Seven
--   rows come back in all: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville,
--   then Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville.
SELECT CITY FROM REP;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        That returns seven rows: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville from CUSTOMER, then Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville from REP. Change the one keyword and the answer shrinks to the three distinct cities.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the same two lists, with the one keyword changed, to see what duplicate
-- removal costs and buys.
-- SELECT / FROM: the first list - the cities in CUSTOMER.
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION: same stacking as UNION ALL, plus a duplicate check. Seven rows shrink
--   to the three distinct cities. That check is real work, which is the reason
--   UNION ALL exists at all.
UNION

-- SELECT / FROM: the second list - the cities in REP.
SELECT CITY FROM REP

-- ORDER BY: sorts the combined three-row result. It sits at the very end of the
--   whole statement, never inside either half.
ORDER BY CITY;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Result of the UNION: three rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CITY
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Brookville
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Maple Grove
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Northfield

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Use UNION

                                                                                                                                                                                                        When the same real-world thing could be described by both queries and you want it counted once. Mailing lists, combined rosters, any "who qualifies under either rule" question.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Use UNION ALL

                                                                                                                                                                                                        When you know the two lists cannot overlap, or when the repeats are the point and you are about to count them. It skips the duplicate-removal work, so it is also the faster of the two.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        INTERSECT: only the overlap

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Swap in INTERSECT and the same two lists answer a different question: which customers are served by rep 20 and also have an invoice on file?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the overlap - customers who are served by rep 20 AND have an invoice.
-- SELECT: the first statement, two columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - rep 20's customers, 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- INTERSECT: keeps only rows produced by BOTH sides, and removes duplicates.
--   Order does not matter here: swapping the two halves asks the same question.
INTERSECT

-- SELECT: the second statement, the same two columns in the same order.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER too.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the invoiced customers, 1120, 1225 and 1420. Only 1120 is
--   on both lists, so one row comes back. 1310 belongs to rep 20 but has never
--   been billed, and 1225 and 1420 have invoices but belong to other reps.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE);

                                                                                                                                                                                                        One row comes back: 1120, Access Pet Center. Companion Care Clinic (1310) is served by rep 20 but has never been invoiced, so it drops out. Downtown Aquarium & Pets and Whiskers & Wags have invoices but belong to other reps, so they drop out too.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        EXCEPT: on the first list, missing from the second

                                                                                                                                                                                                        EXCEPT subtracts. It returns the rows produced by the first SELECT that the second SELECT did not also produce. That is how the bookkeeper finds rep 20's customers who have never been billed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the subtraction - rep 20's customers who have never been billed.
-- SELECT: the first statement, two columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - rep 20's customers, 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- EXCEPT: keeps the rows the first statement produced that the second did not
--   also produce. Order matters here in a way it never does for UNION or
--   INTERSECT: reverse the halves and you are asking which invoiced customers do
--   not belong to rep 20, which answers 1225 and 1420 instead. Oracle spells
--   this operation MINUS.
EXCEPT

-- SELECT: the second statement, matching shape.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER as well.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the invoiced customers. Removing them from the first set
--   leaves one row, 1310 Companion Care Clinic.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE);

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The answer is one row: 1310, Companion Care Clinic. Order matters here in a way it never does for UNION or INTERSECT. Put the two SELECT statements the other way round and you are asking a different question, "which invoiced customers do not belong to rep 20", and you get 1225 and 1420 instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Oracle spells it MINUS

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Oracle's traditional keyword for this operation is MINUS rather than EXCEPT, with the same meaning and the same sensitivity to order. Oracle 21c added EXCEPT as well, but MINUS is what you will meet in most Oracle code and in most Oracle-based textbooks. MySQL added EXCEPT and INTERSECT in 8.0.31. SQLite understands EXCEPT and rejects MINUS with near "SELECT": syntax error, so write EXCEPT in the sandbox.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        When the two SELECT statements do not line up

                                                                                                                                                                                                        This is the mistake you are most likely to make, so learn to recognise the error message rather than guessing at it:

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: a deliberate error - the mistake you are most likely to make with a set
-- operation, so that you recognise the message instead of guessing at it.
-- SELECT: the first statement returns TWO columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION: the two halves are not union compatible, and the engine rejects the
--   statement here without executing anything. SQLite says "SELECTs to the left
--   and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns".
UNION

-- SELECT: the second statement returns ONE column, and that is the whole problem.
--   The fix is always the same - add or remove a column until the counts agree.
SELECT REP_NUM

-- FROM: it reads REP.
FROM REP;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two columns above the line, one below it. SQLite refuses before executing anything and says SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns. MySQL and Oracle say the same thing in their own words. The fix is always the same: add or remove a column so the two counts agree.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The two SELECT statements can read different tables

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Nothing requires both halves to come from the same table. As long as the shapes match, you can stack results from anywhere. Here is a single Brookville contact list drawn from both CUSTOMER and REP.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: a single Brookville contact list, drawn from two different tables. The
-- halves of a union do not have to read the same table - only to match in shape.
-- SELECT: two columns, each renamed with AS. Headings always come from the FIRST
--   SELECT, which is why it is worth putting the aliases here.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM AS ID_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME AS NAME

-- FROM: the first half reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: restricts the first half to Brookville - customer 1420.
WHERE CITY = 'Brookville'

-- UNION: stacks the two lists and drops duplicates. Two columns on each side,
--   and a number lines up with a number, text with text, so the two are
--   union compatible.
UNION

-- SELECT: the second half returns a rep number and a last name. It never mentions
--   ID_NUM or NAME, and does not need to - only the count, order and types matter.
SELECT REP_NUM, LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the second half reads REP.
FROM REP

-- WHERE: restricts the second half to Brookville - rep 65, Perez.
WHERE CITY = 'Brookville'

-- ORDER BY: sorts the combined result, and must use the heading the first SELECT
--   established. ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM would be an error here.
ORDER BY ID_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two rows come back, 1420 Whiskers & Wags Boutique and 65 Perez, under the headings ID_NUM and NAME. Notice that the second SELECT never mentions those names. Headings always come from the first SELECT, which is why it is worth putting your AS aliases there. The 1420 row sorts ahead of the 65 row because both id columns hold characters, not numbers, and '1' comes before '6'.

Four rows becomes three: CF21, DG04, GR15.

Swap in EXCEPT and you get Companion Care Clinic (1310) on its own, because 1310 belongs to rep 20 and has no invoice.
