                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can state the union compatibility rule in one sentence
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know UNION removes duplicate rows and UNION ALL keeps them
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can predict which rows INTERSECT returns for two given lists
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know that reversing the two SELECT statements changes the answer for EXCEPT but not for UNION or INTERSECT
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know Oracle code normally writes MINUS where the standard writes EXCEPT
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I put the single ORDER BY after the last SELECT, never inside the first one

                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: set operations

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1KimTay builds one mailing list

                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's office manager needs a single mailing list. The first SELECT returns the two customers served by rep 20, which are 1120 and 1310. The second SELECT returns the three customers that have an invoice, which are 1120, 1225 and 1420. She combines them with UNION. How many rows come back, and why?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. That is the UNION ALL count. Plain UNION removes duplicate rows before returning the result.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. That describes INTERSECT, which would return 1120 alone. UNION keeps rows from either list.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Correct. 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420 each appear once, because UNION collapses the duplicate 1120.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Neither SELECT overwrites the other. A set operation combines both results into one table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: UNION returns everything on either list with duplicate rows removed, so overlapping rows appear once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Counting items across two KimTay invoices

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager lists the ITEM_ID values on invoice 50710 (CF21 and DG04) and on invoice 50711 (CF21 and GR15), combining them with UNION ALL. She then reruns the identical statement with UNION. What does she see?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Correct. UNION ALL keeps the repeated CF21; UNION removes it and leaves CF21, DG04 and GR15.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. UNION ALL stacks unchanged, but plain UNION removes the duplicate row, so the counts differ.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Duplicate removal is what UNION does and what UNION ALL deliberately skips, so the counts differ.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. That is the behaviour of INTERSECT. UNION ALL keeps everything from both queries.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: UNION ALL is the raw stack of both results; UNION is that stack with duplicate rows removed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Companion Care Clinic has never been billed

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A KimTay bookkeeper wants rep 20's customers that have no invoice on file. She puts the rep 20 query first and the has-an-invoice query second, joined by EXCEPT, and gets Companion Care Clinic. A colleague swaps the two SELECT statements and reruns it. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. UNION and INTERSECT ignore order, but EXCEPT subtracts the second list from the first.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Neither operand has to be larger. The statement runs; it answers a different question.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Reversal changes the question but does not empty it. Two invoiced customers belong to other reps.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Correct. EXCEPT subtracts, so putting the invoiced list first asks the opposite question.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: EXCEPT is directional: the first SELECT supplies the candidates and the second removes from them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-4 All and Any

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A subquery in a WHERE clause usually returns a list of values, and until now you have tested membership in that list with IN. ALL and ANY let you do something different: compare one value against every value in the list at once, using >, <, >= or <= instead of membership. BALANCE > ALL (...) means larger than every value the subquery produced. BALANCE > ANY (...) means larger than at least one of them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                        These do not run in the sandbox

                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQLite does not implement ALL or ANY as subquery comparisons, and the two fail in slightly different places. > ALL (SELECT ...) stops at near "ALL": syntax error, because ALL is a SQLite keyword in the wrong position. > ANY (SELECT ...) and > SOME (SELECT ...) stop one word later at near "SELECT": syntax error, because ANY and SOME are not SQLite keywords at all and the parser reads them as a column name. Either way nothing executes. MySQL and Oracle support all three. Every ALL or ANY statement in this lesson is shown in a plain code block for that reason, and each one is followed by a rewrite that does run, so you can see the answer for yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ALL: bigger than every one of them

                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's credit manager wants the customers whose balance is larger than the balance of every single customer rep 20 handles. Rep 20's customers are Access Pet Center at 3512.50 and Companion Care Clinic at 0.00. In MySQL or Oracle you would write this:

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the customers whose balance beats the balance of EVERY customer rep 20
-- handles. Written the MySQL or Oracle way; this is a syntax error in SQLite.
-- SELECT: three columns, including the balance being tested, so you can check the
--   comparison by eye.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: one table - the subquery reads the same table again, separately.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the subquery returns rep 20's balances, 3512.50 and 0.00. "Greater than
--   ALL" means the row's balance must beat every value in that list, which is
--   the same as beating the largest one. Read it out loud as "balance greater
--   than all of these".
WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Read it out loud as "balance greater than all of these". A row survives only if its balance beats 3512.50 and also beats 0.00. Beating the largest of the two is therefore the whole test, and that is the key to rewriting it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                        The rewrite that always works

                                                                                                                                                                                                        > ALL (subquery) asks the value to beat the largest thing in the list, so it is the same as > (SELECT MAX(...)). > ANY (subquery) asks the value to beat the smallest thing in the list, so it is the same as > (SELECT MIN(...)). Those rewrites run everywhere, including SQLite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the same question, rewritten so it runs everywhere, SQLite included.
-- SELECT: the same three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: because "greater than ALL" only ever tests the top of the list, MAX
--   collapses the subquery to the single number 3512.50, and an ordinary
--   comparison does the rest. One row clears it - 1420, at 4820.75.
WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')

-- ORDER BY: sorts whatever survives by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        One row beats every balance rep 20 handles
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEBALANCE
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique4820.75

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ANY: bigger than at least one of them

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Change the one keyword and the bar drops a long way. Now a row needs to beat only the weakest value in the list.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: change one keyword and the bar drops a long way - now a balance need only
-- beat the WEAKEST value in the list. MySQL or Oracle; a syntax error in SQLite.
-- SELECT: the same three columns as the ALL version.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the subquery returns the same two balances, 3512.50 and 0.00. "Greater
--   than ANY" means greater than at least one of them, which is the same as
--   greater than the smallest. SOME is an exact synonym for ANY.
WHERE BALANCE > ANY (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The smallest balance among rep 20's customers is Companion Care Clinic's 0.00, so the test collapses to "balance greater than 0.00". Three customers clear it. Companion Care Clinic itself does not, because 0.00 is not greater than 0.00.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the ANY version rewritten to run everywhere.
-- SELECT: the same three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: "greater than ANY" only ever tests the bottom of the list, so MIN
--   collapses the subquery to 0.00 and the test becomes "balance greater than
--   0.00". Three customers clear it. Companion Care Clinic does not, because
--   0.00 is not greater than 0.00.
WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three surviving rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Three rows beat at least one balance rep 20 handles
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEBALANCE
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center3512.50
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets1200.00
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique4820.75
                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SOME means ANY

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The SQL standard defines SOME as an exact synonym for ANY, and MySQL and Oracle accept both. > SOME (...) and > ANY (...) behave identically. Textbooks sometimes prefer SOME because "greater than any" reads in English as though it should mean "greater than all of them", which is the single most common misreading of this operator.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every combination, and what to write instead

                                                                                                                                                                                                        There are only six shapes to learn, and each one has a rewrite that runs in the sandbox. Work out which end of the list the comparison is really testing, and the rewrite follows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Translating ALL and ANY
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Written with ALL or ANYWhat it really testsRewrite that runs everywhere
                                                                                                                                                                                                        > ALL (subquery)Beats the largest value> (SELECT MAX(...))
                                                                                                                                                                                                        < ALL (subquery)Below the smallest value< (SELECT MIN(...))
                                                                                                                                                                                                        > ANY (subquery)Beats the smallest value> (SELECT MIN(...))
                                                                                                                                                                                                        < ANY (subquery)Below the largest value< (SELECT MAX(...))
                                                                                                                                                                                                        = ANY (subquery)Matches something in the listIN (subquery)
                                                                                                                                                                                                        <> ALL (subquery)Matches nothing in the listNOT IN (subquery)

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The last two rows are worth pausing on. = ANY is the operator IN you have been using since 5-2a, written a longer way, and <> ALL is NOT IN. When you meet them in someone else's code, translate them on sight.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                        One place the rewrite differs

                                                                                                                                                                                                        If the subquery returns no rows at all, > ALL is true for every row, because there is nothing to fail against, while > ANY is false for every row. An aggregate over zero rows returns NULL, so both rewrites make the comparison unknown and return nothing. That means the MIN rewrite still agrees with > ANY, since both hand back an empty result, but the MAX rewrite disagrees with > ALL, which would have handed back every row. The seed data always gives these subqueries something to chew on, so it will not bite you here, but know which of the two rewrites is the inexact one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        There is one Accessory item, the Nylon Dog Leash at 11.99, so MAX is 11.99 and the other four items all clear it: AV07, CF21, FT88 and GR15.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        = ANY is IN and returns the three invoiced customers 1120, 1225 and 1420. <> ALL is NOT IN and returns Companion Care Clinic (1310) on its own.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Part (a) clears the bar at 595.00 and returns two rooms, P200 101 and P200 201. Part (b) drops the bar to 450.00 and returns four rooms: P100 101, P200 101, P200 201 and P200 202.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can read > ALL as "greater than the largest" and > ANY as "greater than the smallest"
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know ALL and ANY are a syntax error in SQLite and need MySQL or Oracle
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can rewrite any ALL or ANY comparison using MAX, MIN, IN or NOT IN
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know SOME is another word for ANY
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain why > ANY does not mean "greater than all of them"

                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: ALL and ANY

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1Rewriting a credit report for the sandbox

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A KimTay analyst has an Oracle report containing WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20') and needs it to run in the course sandbox, where the statement is a syntax error. Rep 20's customers hold balances of 3512.50 and 0.00. Which rewrite returns the same rows?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. IN tests for an exact match on a value in the list, not for being larger than the whole list.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. Beating every value in the list is the same as beating the largest one, so MAX is the rewrite.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. MIN is the rewrite for > ANY. It would return three customers instead of the one that ALL returns.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The average is neither the largest nor the smallest value, so it answers a question nobody asked.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: > ALL (subquery) means "beats the largest value in the list", which rewrites to > (SELECT MAX(...)).

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Reading ANY out loud at StayWell

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A StayWell manager writes WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > ANY (SELECT MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P100') in MySQL. Property P100 has rooms renting at 595.00 and 450.00. She expects only rooms above 595.00. What does the query actually return?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. That is what > ALL would return, and it is only two rooms. > ANY sets the bar at the smallest value, not the largest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. ANY is built for multi-row subqueries; a single-value subquery needs no ANY at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Correct. Beating at least one value means beating 450.00, so P100 101, P200 101, P200 201 and P200 202 qualify.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The subquery only supplies comparison values; it does not limit which rows the outer query may return.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: > ANY sets a low bar: a row qualifies by beating the smallest value in the list, not the largest.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Inherited code at KimTay

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A developer inherits a query containing WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM <> ALL (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE) and must port it to the SQLite sandbox, which rejects ALL. What does that condition mean, and what replaces it?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. <> ANY is a much weaker test that almost any row passes; it is not equivalent and does not fix the engine problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. <> ALL asserts the value differs from every entry, which is the opposite of matching them all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Correct. Differing from every value in the list is the definition of NOT IN, and it returns customer 1310.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Nothing here counts anything. <> ALL is a value comparison against a list, not an aggregate test.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: = ANY is IN written the long way and <> ALL is NOT IN; translate them on sight.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-5 Special Operations

                                                                                                                                                                                                        This lesson names three things. The first you have already been doing since Module 3 without a formal name for it. The second fixes a gap the first one leaves. The third is what SQL hands you when you forget to say how two tables connect, and knowing it on sight will save you an afternoon one day.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-5a Inner join: the one you already know

                                                                                                                                                                                                        When you match rows in two tables on a shared value and keep only the pairs that match, you are performing an inner join. SQL has explicit words for it, INNER JOIN and ON, and they say out loud what the older comma-and-WHERE style leaves implied.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the very first join of this module, rewritten in the modern INNER JOIN
-- ... ON form. Same four rows, different words.
-- SELECT: the three output columns, qualified as always.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the two tables and the matching condition now sit on one line. INNER JOIN
--   names the second table and ON carries the condition, so the WHERE clause is
--   left free for real business filters. Forgetting ON is a syntax error you
--   cannot miss, which is why this form is worth preferring.
FROM CUSTOMER INNER JOIN REP ON CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Four customers, each with the rep that serves it
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMELAST_NAME
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet CenterKaiser
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & PetsHull
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care ClinicKaiser
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags BoutiquePerez

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The ON clause holds the matching condition. The WHERE clause is now free for actual filtering, which is the main practical reason to prefer this form: with three or four tables in a query, keeping the plumbing in ON and the business rules in WHERE is the difference between a query you can read and one you cannot. The word INNER is optional, so FROM CUSTOMER JOIN REP ON ... means the same thing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Inner joins chain. To put a description on every invoice line you walk from INVOICE through INVOICE_LINE to ITEM, one JOIN ... ON per hop.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: put a description on every invoice line by walking INVOICE to
-- INVOICE_LINE to ITEM. Inner joins chain - one JOIN ... ON per hop.
-- SELECT: one column from each of the three tables.
SELECT INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED

-- FROM: link 1 - each invoice is joined to its own line items. Everything to the
--   left of the next INNER JOIN behaves as a single combined table.
FROM INVOICE INNER JOIN INVOICE_LINE ON INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- Link 2 - that combined result is then joined to ITEM. Three tables need two
-- JOIN ... ON clauses, the same count as the two matching conditions the older
-- comma-and-WHERE form would have needed. Six rows come back.
INNER JOIN ITEM ON INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description within each invoice.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Six rows come back, one per invoice line, from Grain-Free Dry Food on 50710 through Fish Tank Filter Kit on 50712.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Inner join

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A join that returns only the rows that have a match on both sides. A row with no partner in the other table is dropped from the result, silently, with no warning of any kind. That silence is the whole reason the next lesson exists.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-5b Outer join: keep the rows that did not match

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Watch what the silence costs. Ask an inner join for every customer and its invoices.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: ask an inner join for every customer and its invoices, and watch what
-- silently goes missing.
-- SELECT: two customer columns and the invoice number.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that match on both sides. Customer 1310
--   has no row in INVOICE, so it has no partner and is dropped - with no warning
--   of any kind. Four customers go in, three rows come out.
FROM CUSTOMER INNER JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three surviving rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Three rows. KimTay has four customers.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEINVOICE_NUM
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center50710
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets50712
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique50711

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Companion Care Clinic (1310) is gone. It is a real customer with a 10000.00 credit limit, but it has never been invoiced, so it has no partner row in INVOICE and the inner join discards it. If the office manager reads that result as "our customer list", the one account with nothing billed against it is invisible. An outer join is the fix.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: the same question, with the unmatched customer kept in the answer.
-- SELECT: the same three columns as the inner join above.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table written on the LEFT of the
--   keyword, matched or not. CUSTOMER is on the left, so CUSTOMER is the table
--   being protected. Where a customer has no invoice, SQL invents one row's
--   worth of NULLs for the columns that came from the right-hand table, so 1310
--   comes back with a null invoice number. Four rows this time.
FROM CUSTOMER LEFT JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts all four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Four rows. The unmatched customer comes back with a NULL.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEINVOICE_NUM
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center50710
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1225Downtown Aquarium & Pets50712
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care Clinic(null)
                                                                                                                                                                                                        1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique50711

                                                                                                                                                                                                        LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table on the left of the keyword, matched or not. Where there was no match, SQL invents one row's worth of NULLs for the columns that came from the right-hand table. This is the first time in this course you will see a NULL in a result, and it is worth being clear about where it came from: nothing in KimTay's data is missing, and every column of every shipped row holds a real value. The NULL is manufactured by the join to fill a hole.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A LEFT JOIN B keeps everything in A. A RIGHT JOIN B keeps everything in B. They are mirror images, so FROM INVOICE RIGHT JOIN CUSTOMER ON ... returns the exact same four rows as the LEFT JOIN above. Most people write LEFT JOIN and put the table they care about first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        FULL OUTER JOIN

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Keeps unmatched rows from both sides at once. SQLite supports it from version 3.39 and so does Oracle. MySQL does not have it at all: there you emulate it with a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN combined by UNION, which is the set operation from 5-3 earning its keep.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Against the shipped data a FULL OUTER JOIN of CUSTOMER and INVOICE returns the same four rows as the LEFT JOIN, because every invoice does point at a real customer, so there is nothing unmatched on the right. The sandbox below adds an orphan invoice on purpose so you can see the difference the third join makes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        There is one more move to learn, and it is the reason outer joins pay for themselves. Keep the unmatched rows, then filter down to only those, and you have a query that finds gaps.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: find the gaps - the rows that have no match at all - in two steps.
-- SELECT: only the customer columns. The invoice column is used for testing and
--   would be null on every row that survives anyway.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: step 1 - LEFT JOIN keeps all four customers, filling the INVOICE columns
--   with NULL wherever no invoice matched.
FROM CUSTOMER LEFT JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- WHERE: step 2 - keep only the rows the join had to fill in. IS NULL is the only
--   way to test for a null; = NULL never matches anything, not even another null.
--   Here the test can be true only for a customer the join failed to match, so
--   the whole query reads as "customers with no invoice". One row: 1310.
WHERE INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        One row: Companion Care Clinic. IS NULL is the only way to test for a NULL, because = NULL never matches anything, not even another NULL. Here the test can only be true for a row the join failed to match, so the whole query reads as "customers with no invoice". Point the same pattern at StayWell and it finds rooms nobody has leased, or leases nobody has paid on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                        An outer join does not always add NULLs

                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM LEFT JOIN INVOICE_LINE returns six rows with no NULL anywhere, because every one of KimTay's five items has been ordered at least once, and CF21 has been ordered on two invoices so it appears twice. An outer join promises to keep unmatched rows. It does not promise there are any, and it will happily return more rows than the left table has.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        5-5c The product: what you get with no join condition

                                                                                                                                                                                                        List two tables and give SQL no instruction about how they relate, and it does the only thing it can: it pairs every row on the left with every row on the right.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: see the product - what SQL does when you never say how two tables relate.
-- SELECT: one identifying column from each table, so the pattern is easy to read.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM

-- FROM: two tables listed with a comma and nothing else. There is no WHERE clause
--   anywhere, so nothing restricts the pairings and every customer is paired with
--   every rep: 4 x 3 = 12 rows, eight of them nonsense. This is the accident you
--   cause by adding a table to FROM and forgetting its matching condition.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- ORDER BY: sorting by both columns makes the regular repeating pattern - the
--   symptom of an accidental product - obvious on sight.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay has four customers and three reps, so the result is 4 times 3, which is twelve rows: 1120 with 20, 1120 with 35, 1120 with 65, then 1225 with all three, and so on. Every customer appears matched to every rep, including the reps who do not serve it, so eight of the twelve rows are nonsense.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Product (Cartesian product, cross join)

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The product of two tables is every possible pairing of a row from the first with a row from the second. If one table has m rows and the other has n, the product has m times n rows. FROM A, B with no matching condition produces it, and so does the explicit FROM A CROSS JOIN B, which returns the same twelve rows and has the advantage of looking deliberate.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        You will almost never want a product on purpose. You will produce one by accident, usually by adding a table to the FROM list and forgetting to add its matching condition. The symptom is unmistakable once you know it: the row count explodes and the same value repeats down a column in a regular pattern. If a query over four customers hands you twelve rows, count your join conditions before you debug anything else.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Supply the missing condition and the product collapses back into an inner join. This is the older syntax, and it is exactly the first query in this lesson wearing different clothes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: supply the missing condition and watch the product collapse back into an
-- inner join. This is the first query of the lesson wearing different clothes.
-- SELECT: two customer columns and the rep's last name.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the same comma-separated pair of tables that produced the 12-row product.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: this single line is the entire difference. It throws away the eight
--   pairings where the customer's rep number does not equal the rep's, leaving
--   the same four rows the INNER JOIN ... ON version returned.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Four rows, identical to the INNER JOIN ... ON version. Both forms are legal everywhere and you will meet both in real code. Prefer INNER JOIN ... ON, because forgetting the ON clause is a syntax error you cannot miss, whereas forgetting a line of the WHERE clause is a silent product.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Ask what must appear in the answer

                                                                                                                                                                                                        If every customer has to be listed whether or not it has been billed, you need an outer join. If only billed customers belong in the answer, an inner join is correct and the missing rows are not a bug.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Put the table you must keep on the left

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Then write LEFT JOIN. Reaching for RIGHT JOIN usually means you listed the tables in the wrong order.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Write one ON clause per join

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two tables need one condition, three tables need two, four tables need three. Count them before you run anything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Check the row count against what you expected

                                                                                                                                                                                                        More rows than the left table has means the right table matched several times, which may be correct. A row count equal to m times n means you lost a join condition.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        The inner join returns three rows and hides Companion Care Clinic. The LEFT JOIN returns four, with an empty INVOICE_NUM on row 1310. Adding WHERE INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL narrows it to that one row. WHERE always goes before ORDER BY.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Five rows. One has an empty customer and invoice 50713, the orphan invoice. One has Companion Care Clinic and an empty invoice. Both unmatched sides survive, which is what makes the join full. Without the DELETE on the first line, a second run would fail on the primary key.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        The product is twelve rows, 4 times 3. Adding the WHERE condition cuts it to the four rows that are true, one per customer. FROM CUSTOMER CROSS JOIN REP also returns twelve and states the intent openly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Part (a) gives five rows and P200 room 101 has an empty LEASE_ID, so it is the vacant one. Part (b) also gives five rows, but for the opposite reason: L001 appears twice because it has two payments, and L004 appears once with an empty payment.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can write the same two-table query as INNER JOIN ... ON and as FROM A, B WHERE ...
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain why Companion Care Clinic disappears from an inner join of CUSTOMER and INVOICE
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know a LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right-hand columns with NULLs when nothing matched
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can add WHERE <right column> IS NULL to turn an outer join into a gap-finding query, and I know = NULL would never work
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN and can be given a LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN instead
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can predict the size of a product as m times n and recognise an accidental one by its row count

                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: joins and products

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1The customer report that lost a customer

                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's office manager runs an inner join of CUSTOMER and INVOICE on CUSTOMER_NUM and gets three rows, although the company has four customers. Companion Care Clinic (1310) is missing. What explains it?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. A zero balance is an ordinary value. Joins match on the ON condition and ignore every other column.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. 1310 has never been invoiced, so the inner join drops it silently; LEFT JOIN brings it back.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. CUSTOMER_NUM is the correct shared column. The row is missing because no invoice references it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Row counts on either side do not cap a join. A left outer join of the same two tables returns four rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: An inner join silently drops any row with no partner, so a short result is a signal to check for unmatched rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2StayWell hunts for a vacant room

                                                                                                                                                                                                        StayWell wants every room listed together with its lease, including rooms nobody has leased. The manager writes FROM ROOM LEFT JOIN LEASE ON ROOM.PROPERTY_ID = LEASE.PROPERTY_ID AND ROOM.ROOM_NUM = LEASE.ROOM_NUM. There are five rooms and four leases. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. That is the inner join count. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table whether or not it matched.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. All five rooms survive, and the one room with no lease gets NULLs in the LEASE columns.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A product needs no join condition. This query supplies one, so it matches instead of pairing everything.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. SQL fills unmatched columns with NULL, never with a substitute word. If you want a label there, you have to put it there yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right-hand columns with NULLs when nothing matched.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Twelve rows from four customers

                                                                                                                                                                                                        A KimTay developer writes SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP; and gets twelve rows, with each of the four customer numbers appearing three times. What has happened?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. CUSTOMER holds four distinct rows. The repetition is created by the query, not present in the table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. No join type is applied by default, and an outer join never invents pairings that the data does not support.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Nothing here stacks results. All twelve rows come from a single SELECT over two tables.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Correct. With nothing in ON or WHERE to connect them, every customer is paired with every rep.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Two tables in FROM with no matching condition produce the product, m times n rows, and it is nearly always a bug.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q4Finding KimTay's never-billed customers

                                                                                                                                                                                                        The bookkeeper needs a list of customers that have never been invoiced, and she wants it as a single query over CUSTOMER and INVOICE. Which approach returns exactly Companion Care Clinic?

                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. An inner join has already discarded the unmatched rows, so the IS NULL test can never be true and returns nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. The outer join keeps the unmatched customer, and IS NULL narrows the result to exactly those rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A cross join pairs all twelve combinations, and filtering on balance answers a question about money, not billing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. FROM CUSTOMER RIGHT JOIN INVOICE keeps every invoice, and testing the customer side finds orphan invoices instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Outer join first to keep the unmatched rows, then test the other table's column with IS NULL to keep only the gaps.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        🧩 Sort the result into the operation that produced it

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                        Each card describes what came back from a query over two or three tables. Decide whether that result was produced by an inner join, a left outer join, or a product with no join condition.
