                                                                                                                                                                                                              Summary Module Summary

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Module 5 rested on one idea: the answer you need is almost never sitting in a single table. KimTay keeps the customer in CUSTOMER, the sale in INVOICE, the line items in INVOICE_LINE, and the product in ITEM, so a question as ordinary as "what did Access Pet Center buy?" has to travel across four tables. You now have several ways to make that trip, and a good part of the skill is knowing which one a question calls for.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Reaching sideways

                                                                                                                                                                                                              A join, IN, EXISTS, or a nested subquery all answer questions of the form "rows from here, filtered or described by data over there." A join widens a row, because the result can carry columns from both tables; IN and EXISTS do not, because the second table only decides which rows qualify.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Stacking results

                                                                                                                                                                                                              UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT answer questions of the form "these rows together, or only the shared ones, or only the ones missing from the other list." They lengthen a result rather than widening it, and both sides have to be union compatible.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Here is the whole module in one list. If a line reads as unfamiliar, the lesson it came from is worth a second pass before you go on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Join two tables by matching a foreign key to a primary key, either in the WHERE clause or with INNER JOIN ... ON.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Qualify a column as table.column whenever that name exists in both tables, or the DBMS rejects the query as ambiguous.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Give a table an alias in the FROM clause, then use that alias everywhere else in the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Use IN or EXISTS when the second table only decides which rows qualify and contributes no columns to the output.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Nest a subquery inside another subquery when the answer takes two hops, and read it from the inside out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Join a table to itself, using two aliases, when you need to compare one row of a table with another row of the same table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Stack two union-compatible results with UNION, keep only the shared rows with INTERSECT, or subtract one from the other with EXCEPT.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Compare one value against a whole column of values with ALL and ANY on MySQL or Oracle, and rewrite both with MAX or MIN on SQLite.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Keep unmatched rows with an outer join, and expect NULL in every column that came from the side with no match.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Spot an accidental product: when the linking condition is missing, rows multiply instead of matching.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Predict how many rows a multi-table query should return before you run it, then check.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Engine note

                                                                                                                                                                                                              The sandbox on this page runs SQLite, and SQLite does not accept > ALL (subquery) or > ANY (subquery) at all: it stops with a syntax error at the keyword. MySQL and Oracle do accept them. The runnable equivalents return exactly the same rows: > ALL (SELECT BALANCE ...) is > (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) ...), and > ANY (SELECT BALANCE ...) is > (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) ...). Write whichever form your engine accepts, and know why the two agree.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              One last query pulls several of these together. It has to keep a customer that has no invoice, which rules out an inner join, and it has to count something that can be missing, which rules out COUNT(*). Try it before you reveal the answer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so an inner join drops it and a LEFT JOIN keeps it. Count I.INVOICE_NUM rather than *: the padded row is still a row, so COUNT(*) would report 1 for the clinic instead of 0.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything that follows in this course assumes you can reach across tables without thinking twice about it. Reading a multi-table statement and saying out loud how many rows it returns, and why, is the single best way to keep that skill sharp.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Terms Key Terms

                                                                                                                                                                                                              These are the words this module added to your vocabulary. Only one of them names something you were already writing before this module: the nested subquery from lesson 4-4. The rest are new here, and several of them name distinctions that get lost if you only ever say "joining tables."

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Terms for reaching across tables
                                                                                                                                                                                                              TermWhat it means
                                                                                                                                                                                                              JoinA query that combines rows from two or more tables by matching values in a column the tables share.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Inner joinA join that keeps only rows with a match on both sides; FROM A, B WHERE A.k = B.k and A INNER JOIN B ON A.k = B.k are two spellings of the same thing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Outer joinA join that also keeps unmatched rows, from the left table, the right table, or both, filling the missing columns with NULL.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Self-joinA join of a table to itself, written with two different aliases so one table can play two roles in a single query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              AliasA short alternate name you give a table in the FROM clause and then use everywhere else in the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Product (Cartesian product)Every row of one table paired with every row of another, which is what you get when the linking condition is missing: 3 reps and 4 customers produce 12 rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Terms for subqueries and set operations
                                                                                                                                                                                                              TermWhat it means
                                                                                                                                                                                                              UnionAll rows appearing in either of two union-compatible results, with duplicates kept only once.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              IntersectionOnly the rows that appear in both of two union-compatible results.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              DifferenceThe rows of the first result that do not appear in the second; EXCEPT in SQLite and SQL Server, MINUS in Oracle.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Union compatibleTwo results are union compatible when they have the same number of columns and matching columns hold the same kind of data; the column names need not match.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              EXISTSAn operator that is true when its subquery returns at least one row, used when another table decides which rows qualify but supplies no columns.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Correlated subqueryA subquery that refers to a column of the outer query, so the DBMS has to evaluate it once for every row the outer query considers.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              ALLCompares a value against every value a subquery returns; > ALL is true only when the value beats the largest of them. MySQL and Oracle only: SQLite rejects > ALL (subquery) with a syntax error, so in the sandbox below write > (SELECT MAX(...) ...) instead.
                                                                                                                                                                                                              ANYCompares a value against the values a subquery returns and is true if at least one comparison holds; > ANY is true when the value beats the smallest of them. MySQL and Oracle only, exactly like ALL: the sandbox equivalent is > (SELECT MIN(...) ...).
                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Union compatible is about shape, not names

                                                                                                                                                                                                              SELECT CITY FROM REP and SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER are union compatible because each returns one column of city text. SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER and SELECT PROPERTY_NAME FROM PROPERTY would be union compatible too, even though the columns carry different names, because both return one column of names. What breaks compatibility is a different number of columns, or columns that do not line up in kind: SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION SELECT CITY, STATE FROM CUSTOMER fails with "SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns."

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three of these terms are easier to recognize running than defined. The sandbox starts with the self-join; use Show solution to add the union and the correlated subquery underneath it, then run all three at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                              The self-join returns one row, Access Pet Center paired with Companion Care Clinic in Maple Grove. The union returns three cities. The correlated EXISTS returns the three customers that have an invoice, leaving out Companion Care Clinic.

                                                                                                                                                                                                              Notice what the aliases buy you in that first statement. CUSTOMER F and CUSTOMER S are the same table twice, and without two names there would be no way to say "this customer's city equals that customer's city." Notice also that once a table has an alias, the alias replaces the table name: after FROM CUSTOMER F, writing CUSTOMER.CITY is an error, and SQLite reports it as no such column: CUSTOMER.CITY.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Review Review Questions

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Ten questions covering the whole module. They are harder than the checks inside the lessons: several of them hand you a finished statement and ask what it returns against the real KimTay and StayWell data, which is exactly what an exam question looks like.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How to read a statement you did not write

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Read the FROM clause first and count the tables. Then look for a condition that links them. If there is no linking condition you are looking at a product, and the row count is one table's rows times the other's. If there is one, ask which rows have no match, because that is where inner and outer joins part company.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The scratch pad below is loaded with both databases. Use it after you commit to an answer, not before: predicting a result and being wrong teaches you more than watching the engine do it first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay: 3 reps, 4 customers, 3 invoices, 6 invoice lines, 5 items. StayWell: 2 managers, 2 properties, 5 rooms, 4 students, 4 leases, 4 payments. Those eleven numbers let you predict most row counts in your head.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Work through the questions below. Each explanation names the specific misconception behind every wrong option, so read all four notes even when you answered correctly.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Module 5 cumulative review: joins, subqueries, and set operations

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1The rep list that came back too long

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's billing clerk wants each rep next to the customers that rep handles, and writes SELECT R.LAST_NAME, C.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM REP R, CUSTOMER C; with no other clause. There are 3 reps and 4 customers on file. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. With nothing linking the tables the DBMS forms the product, 3 times 4, and the clerk has to hunt for the 4 real pairs inside 12 rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. No engine guesses a join for you; matching REP_NUM values is something you have to state in a WHERE or ON clause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Table order in the FROM clause changes nothing about the row count; this is not a loop with an outer table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The comma form is legal SQL and runs happily, which is exactly the danger: a missing condition is a silent bug, not an error.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A multi-table FROM clause with no linking condition is not an error, it is a product, and the rows multiply instead of matching.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Companion Care Clinic's invoice count

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Companion Care Clinic (1310) has no invoice. A clerk runs SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER C LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME; and checks the clinic's row. What number does it show?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. COUNT(*) counts rows, not values, so it has no way to notice that the invoice half of the row is empty.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Keeping that row is the whole point of the LEFT JOIN; the clinic is present, and only the count misleads.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. The outer join produced one row for the clinic, so COUNT(*) reports 1, while COUNT(I.INVOICE_NUM) reports the honest 0.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The combination is perfectly legal, which is why this mistake survives long enough to reach a report.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: After an outer join, count a column from the optional side rather than COUNT(*), or every unmatched row reports one instead of none.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3The unsold item at KimTay's warehouse

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager hunts for dead stock with SELECT DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM I WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM INVOICE_LINE L WHERE L.ITEM_ID = I.ITEM_ID); and the grid comes back empty. What does that empty result mean?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. NOT EXISTS is false for an item that does appear on a line, and all five do, so nothing survives the filter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. AV07, CF21, DG04, FT88 and GR15 all appear in INVOICE_LINE, so there is no dead stock and zero rows is the right answer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Being ordered once still counts as being ordered; NOT EXISTS asks whether any matching line exists, not how many.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. SELECT 1 is idiomatic inside EXISTS, because EXISTS only asks whether a row came back, never what was in it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: An empty result is an answer, not a failure: NOT EXISTS returning nothing means every row on the outer side had a match.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q4Downtown Aquarium and the mailing list

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A mailing list needs every city KimTay touches. A clerk compares SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER; with the same statement written UNION ALL. REP holds Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville; CUSTOMER holds Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville. What do the two return?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. UNION deduplicates the combined result, so the four Maple Grove values collapse into one across both sides.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. A plain SELECT keeps duplicates; only UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and DISTINCT remove them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. ALL is the opposite of narrowing: it means keep everything, repeats included. Narrowing to shared rows is INTERSECT.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Three distinct cities remain, Brookville, Maple Grove and Northfield, while UNION ALL stacks 3 plus 4 rows untouched.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: UNION removes duplicates and pays for the sort that finds them; UNION ALL keeps every row, so use it when duplicates cannot occur or do not matter.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q5The join that lost Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Asked for every customer alongside any invoice they have, including customers with none, a developer writes SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE I LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM;. What actually comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. LEFT preserves one side only, the table named before the keyword, which here is INVOICE rather than CUSTOMER.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Every invoice has a customer, so nothing gets padded, and the customer with no invoice never enters the result at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The clinic contributes no row whatsoever, so there is no null row to notice; the mistake is invisible in the output.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The statement is valid SQL and runs; it simply answers a different question than the one that was asked.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: In a LEFT JOIN the preserved table is the one written first, so keeping the rows you care about depends on the order you list the tables.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q6Access Pet Center against rep 20's other account

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Rep 20's two accounts have balances 3512.50 and 0.00. On MySQL a manager runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');. What comes back, and how would you ask the same question in this page's SQLite sandbox?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Beating one value is ANY. Access Pet Center's 3512.50 does not beat its own balance, so ALL rules it out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. That describes greater than ANY, which effectively uses the smallest value; ALL uses the largest, here 3512.50.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Only 4820.75 is greater than both balances, and beating every value is the same test as beating the maximum. SQLite will not parse the ALL form at all, so the MAX rewrite is the only version that runs on this page.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. ALL exists precisely for multi-row subqueries; a subquery returning one value would have no need of it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Greater than ALL means greater than the maximum and greater than ANY means greater than the minimum, which is also how you rewrite both for SQLite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q7The two Maple Grove accounts, listed twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A self-join finds KimTay customers that share a city: SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B WHERE A.CITY = B.CITY AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM;. Access Pet Center (1120) and Companion Care Clinic (1310) are both in Maple Grove, and no other city holds two customers. What comes back, and what would changing <> to < do?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. 1120 with 1310 and 1310 with 1120 both satisfy the inequality, and requiring A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM keeps just the first.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. One row is what less-than produces; the inequality shown produces two, and less-than certainly does not produce none.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The condition A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM is what removes the self-pairings, and it removes them before you see them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Less-than is a filter, not a sort, and it cuts the mirrored duplicate out of the result entirely.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A self-join on equality produces each pair twice plus the self-pairings, so a strict inequality between the keys keeps exactly one row per pair.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q8The query KimTay's DBMS refused

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Trying to match reps with customers, someone writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, LAST_NAME FROM REP, CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM; and presses Run. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The DBMS cannot tell which REP_NUM you mean on either side of the equals sign, so it refuses instead of guessing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. That would be the outcome if the reference were unambiguous, such as REP.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM, but the query never gets that far.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Both columns are CHAR(2) holding the same kind of value; the problem is the name, not the data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Qualifying both sides as REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM fixes it and turns the product into the four-row join that was intended.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: When a column name exists in more than one table in the FROM clause, every use of it must be qualified, and the DBMS refuses rather than choosing for you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q9The Sycamore Court room nobody has leased

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        StayWell runs SELECT R.PROPERTY_ID, R.ROOM_NUM FROM ROOM R WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM LEASE L WHERE L.PROPERTY_ID = R.PROPERTY_ID AND L.ROOM_NUM = R.ROOM_NUM); over 5 rooms and 4 leases. What comes back, and what makes that subquery correlated?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The subquery is re-run for each room and finds nothing for P200 room 101, which is precisely the room being hunted.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. A correlated subquery cannot be evaluated once and reused, because its result changes with every outer row handed to it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Leases cover P100 rooms 101 and 102 and P200 rooms 201 and 202, leaving P200 room 101 as the only room never leased.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. P100 room 101 sits on lease L001, so it is excluded; both halves of the composite key are compared, exactly as they should be.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A subquery that names a column of the outer query is correlated: it runs once per outer row, which is what lets NOT EXISTS test each row on its own.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q10Tracing the grain-free dry food back to a customer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        To find who bought item CF21, a clerk writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN (SELECT INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'));. CF21 appears on invoices 50710 and 50711, which belong to customers 1120 and 1420. What comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Read it inside out: two invoice numbers, then the two customer numbers on those invoices, then the two customer names.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Downtown Aquarium's invoice 50712 holds AV07 and FT88, so its customer number never reaches the outer condition.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. IN is built for multi-row subqueries at every level; only a subquery compared with = has to return a single value.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The outermost SELECT reports CUSTOMER_NAME from CUSTOMER, and nothing from ITEM appears in the result at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Read nested subqueries from the inside out, and remember that IN accepts many values at every level of the nesting.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Exercises Case Exercises

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Five exercises over KimTay and StayWell. Work each one out first, and write down the number of rows you expect before you run anything. The count is part of the answer: a query that returns 12 rows when you predicted 3 is telling you a linking condition went missing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1. The invoice list the office actually wants

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        KimTay's billing clerk wants one line per invoice showing the invoice number, the invoice date, the customer's name, and the last name of the rep who handles that customer. Three tables have to appear in the FROM clause, and the customer sits between the other two. How many rows should come back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2. What one rep's accounts are buying

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        List the description of every item that appears on an invoice belonging to a customer of rep 20. Four tables this time. Before you run it, work out which of rep 20's two customers can contribute anything at all, and how many invoices that leaves you with; that number tells you whether DISTINCT can change the answer on this data. Write it with DISTINCT anyway, because the query has to stay correct the day rep 20 picks up a second invoice that repeats an item.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3. Every student, paid or not

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        StayWell wants each student's last name, first name, and the total of their payments so far, and every student has to appear even if they have paid nothing yet. Every student does have a lease, so the requirement bites on the payment side, and exactly one student qualifies. What does the total column hold for that student, and why is it not 0?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4. The room nobody has rented

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        List every StayWell room that has never appeared on a lease, and write it twice. The NOT EXISTS version can report the property, room number and room type, because it selects from ROOM and only tests LEASE. The EXCEPT version cannot: LEASE has no ROOM_TYPE column, so the two sides are union compatible only on PROPERTY_ID and ROOM_NUM, and putting a third column on the left makes the statement fail outright. Both versions find the same room, one with three columns and one with two.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        5. Where KimTay sells but does not staff

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        List every city that has a KimTay customer but no KimTay rep. This is a difference between two single-column results, so check first that the two SELECT statements are union compatible. Exactly one city qualifies, and it is worth asking who covers that account.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You wrote down an expected row count for each exercise before running it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Every column name that exists in two of the tables you referenced is qualified with a table name or an alias.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Each pair of joined tables has a condition linking them, so a four-table query carries three linking conditions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Exercise 3 uses an outer join to PAYMENT, because an inner one would silently drop the student you were told to keep.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You can say in one sentence why exercise 4's two versions find the same room, and why only one of them can show that room's type.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Both databases are loaded in the sandbox below. The starter holds the five prompts as comments; Show solution replaces them with worked answers, including both versions of exercise 4.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Expected counts: 3 rows, 2 rows, 4 rows, 1 row, 1 row. Rep 20 has one invoiced customer and therefore one invoice, so exercise 2 returns two descriptions with or without DISTINCT; more than two means the rep 20 filter is missing or a linking condition is. In exercise 3 every student already has a lease, so the join that can drop Jason Park is the one to PAYMENT: if you get three rows, make that join LEFT.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If you want one more pass, redo exercise 1 in explicit INNER JOIN ... ON form and confirm you get the same three rows. Being fluent in both spellings matters, because the code you inherit will use whichever one its author preferred.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-1 Creating a New Table from an Existing Table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every statement you have written so far has pointed at KimTay's real tables, and every one of them has been a SELECT. A SELECT only reads. Module 6 is about statements that change what is stored, and a change you get wrong is not something you can undo by looking away from the screen. So the first skill in this module is not changing data at all. It is making yourself a working copy to change instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL can build a brand-new table out of the rows a query returns. You write CREATE TABLE, the name you want for the new table, the word AS, and then an ordinary SELECT. Whatever that SELECT returns becomes the contents of the new table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Start with the data: this is the complete ITEM table that the first statement copies. Inspect the original five rows before ITEM_COPY is created.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Source table: ITEM — the original table before any changes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONCATEGORYON_HANDPRICEREORDER_LEVEL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter CageHabitat1564.995
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lbFood4842.5015
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ftAccessory12011.9925
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter KitHabitat3027.7510
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming KitGrooming2215.258
                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: builds a brand new table and fills it in one statement.
--   The column names and types are taken from whatever the SELECT below returns,
--   so you never write a column list yourself.
CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS

-- SELECT *: every column, so the copy has the same shape as the original.
SELECT *

-- FROM: the table being copied. The copy is a snapshot of the rows as they are
--   right now - it is a separate table, and later changes to ITEM do not reach it.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_COPY now exists and holds all five item rows. It has the same six column names in the same order, because SELECT * handed over all six. From this point on you can do anything you like to ITEM_COPY and ITEM never notices.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_COPY immediately after it is created: all six columns, all five rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONCATEGORYON_HANDPRICEREORDER_LEVEL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter CageHabitat1564.995
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lbFood4842.515
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ftAccessory12011.9925
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter KitHabitat3027.7510
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming KitGrooming2215.258
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why the price reads 42.5 and not 42.50

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The database stores a number, not a piece of formatting. The value 42.50 and the value 42.5 are the same number, so the trailing zero is not printed back to you. That is a display detail, not a change to your data. Formatting money for a report is a separate job from storing it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Copying only part of a table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The query does not have to be SELECT *. Name the columns you want and add a WHERE clause, and the new table gets only that slice of the original.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: the new table's structure is decided entirely by the query.
CREATE TABLE HABITAT_ITEM AS

-- SELECT: naming four columns instead of * means the new table has four columns.
--   The ones left out simply do not exist in it.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND, PRICE

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE: the filter decides which ROWS are copied, just as the SELECT list decided
--   which columns. Only the habitat items end up in the new table.
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        HABITAT_ITEM ends up with four columns instead of six and two rows instead of five. The CATEGORY column is not in the new table at all, because you did not ask for it, even though the WHERE clause used it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        HABITAT_ITEM after the copy: four columns, two rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONON_HANDPRICE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage1564.99
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit3027.75
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Where the new column names come from

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The new table's column names come from the SELECT list. If you alias a column with AS, the alias becomes the column name in the new table. A computed column always needs an alias, because an expression like ON_HAND * PRICE is not a legal column name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: build and fill in one go.
CREATE TABLE ITEM_VALUE AS

-- SELECT: whatever a column is called in the result is what it is called in the
--   new table, so the AS aliases here are doing double duty - they name the
--   output columns AND the stored columns. A calculated column becomes a real,
--   stored column in the new table, frozen at the value it had when this ran.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION AS ITEM_NAME, ON_HAND * PRICE AS STOCK_VALUE

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM ITEM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_VALUE has three columns: ITEM_ID, ITEM_NAME, and STOCK_VALUE. Its STOCK_VALUE numbers were computed once, when the table was built. They are a snapshot. Change a price in ITEM tomorrow and ITEM_VALUE will still show yesterday's arithmetic.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What does not come along

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        This is the part that gets missed, on exams and in real jobs. CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies the column names and the rows. It does not copy the rules that were protecting the original table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • The primary key. ITEM_COPY has an ITEM_ID column, but nothing stops two of its rows from both saying AV07.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Foreign keys. A copy of CUSTOMER will cheerfully hold a REP_NUM that matches no rep in REP.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • NOT NULL and DEFAULT settings that were declared on the original columns.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Any index that was built on the original table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The column types come across as families, not as exact declarations

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Ask this sandbox for the copy's structure and you will see ITEM_ID TEXT, PRICE NUM, and ON_HAND INT, not the CHAR(4), DECIMAL(7,2), and SMALLINT that ITEM actually declares. SQLite rebuilds each column with a general type big enough to hold the values it copied. That is fine for a scratch table and one more reason never to promote one into the real database. MySQL and Oracle do keep the original declared types.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        You can prove the primary key is gone with one statement. Run this against the copy and it succeeds.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- INSERT INTO: with no column list after the table name, you are promising to
--   supply a value for EVERY column, in the table's own order. It is shorter to
--   type and easy to get wrong; naming the columns is the safer habit.
INSERT INTO ITEM_COPY

-- VALUES: six values for six columns, in the order ITEM_COPY defines them. Note
--   that ITEM_COPY was created by CREATE TABLE ... AS, which copies the columns
--   but NOT the primary key, so a duplicate ITEM_ID is accepted here without
--   complaint - a real difference between a copy and the original.
VALUES ('AV07', 'Second Aviary Starter Cage', 'Habitat', 9, 64.99, 5);

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_COPY now has six rows, two of which claim to be item AV07. Run the identical statement against ITEM instead and the database refuses it with a message about a unique constraint failing on ITEM.ITEM_ID. Same statement, same data, different answer, because only one of those two tables still has a primary key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A copy is a place to make mistakes, not a place to keep data

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Because none of the constraints came along, a working copy will accept duplicates, orphans, and blanks that the real table would have caught. That is exactly what makes it a safe scratch pad and exactly what makes it unfit to be promoted into the real database later. Test on the copy, then run your verified statement against the original.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An empty copy of the structure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Sometimes you want the shape of a table without any of its rows, so you have somewhere to collect rows later. Give the query a condition that can never be true and you get exactly that.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: the trick for cloning a table's structure without its data.
CREATE TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE AS

-- SELECT *: take the full set of columns, so the new table matches the original.
SELECT *

-- FROM: the table whose shape you want.
FROM ITEM

-- WHERE 1 = 0: a condition that is false for every row, so no row is copied. The
--   column names and types still come across, which leaves you with an empty
--   table of exactly the right shape - ready to receive archived rows later.
WHERE 1 = 0;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1 = 0 is false for every row, so no row qualifies and nothing is copied. The column list is still built from SELECT *, so ITEM_ARCHIVE comes out with six correctly named columns and zero rows. This is a common trick and you will use it again in 6-3, where you need a target table whose columns line up perfectly with the query that fills it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Cleaning up after yourself

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A working table is trash once you are done with it. DROP TABLE removes the table and everything in it in one step, and there is no undo.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- DROP TABLE: removes the table itself - its rows, its columns and its
--   definition. This is not a DELETE; there is nothing left to select from
--   afterwards, and outside a transaction there is no undo.
DROP TABLE ITEM_COPY;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Adding IF EXISTS makes the statement safe to run even when the table is not there, which is why the exercises in this module open with it. Without IF EXISTS, dropping a table that does not exist is an error, and creating a table that already exists is an error too.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- IF EXISTS: run the drop only if the table is there, and say nothing if it is
--   not. Without it, dropping a table that has already gone is an error that
--   stops a script part-way through - which is why setup scripts start with this.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_COPY;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Name throwaway tables like throwaways

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Use names that announce what they are: ITEM_COPY, CUSTOMER_TEST, ITEM_ARCHIVE. A table named ITEM2 found in a database six months from now is a mystery nobody wants to solve. A table named ITEM_COPY is obviously somebody's scratch paper and can be dropped without a meeting.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Other engines

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        MySQL and Oracle both support CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT, and on all three engines the rows come across while the primary key, the foreign keys, and the indexes do not. The engines part company on the smaller details.
