MySQL and Oracle keep each column's declared data type and carry a NOT NULL constraint over to the copy; SQLite keeps neither. So the headline lesson travels everywhere, but do not assume a copy made in Oracle is constrained the same way as a copy made here.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Copy

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM; so the original is out of the line of fire.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Confirm

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ITEM_COPY; before you touch anything. You should see 5. Knowing the starting count is what lets you notice later that something changed too many rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Work

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Point your UPDATE, INSERT, and DELETE statements at ITEM_COPY. Get the statement right there, where being wrong costs nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Discard

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run DROP TABLE ITEM_COPY; and then run the statement you verified against the real ITEM table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SELECT * copies all six columns, so the INSERT needs six values in that same order: id, description, category, on hand, price, reorder level. Finish by selecting from ITEM_COPY, not from ITEM. You should get six rows back, with AV07 appearing twice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can write CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT to copy a whole table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can copy only some columns and only some rows by editing the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain that the column names and rows are copied but the primary key, foreign keys, NOT NULL, defaults, and indexes are not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know the copy's column types are rebuilt as general types in this engine, not carried over exactly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can build an empty table with the right columns using WHERE 1 = 0.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can drop a working table when I am finished with it, and I know what IF EXISTS adds.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: copying a table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1A second AV07 at KimTay

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A clerk runs CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM; and then tries to insert a row into ITEM_COPY using the item id AV07, which the Aviary Starter Cage already uses. What does the database do?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. This is the central misconception of the section. The column names and the rows come across; keys, foreign keys, defaults, and indexes do not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Duplicate values are perfectly normal in most columns. It is the primary key constraint, not SQL itself, that forbids them in ITEM.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Correct. ITEM_COPY has an ITEM_ID column but no constraint on it, so a second AV07 row goes right in.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. There is no key on the copy to drop, so this step would fail and is not needed in the first place.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies data and column names, never the constraints that were protecting the original.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2An empty shell for the item archive

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The warehouse manager wants a table with ITEM's exact column layout but no data in it yet, and runs CREATE TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE AS SELECT * FROM ITEM WHERE 1 = 0;. What is created?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Correct. The condition is false for every row so nothing is copied, but the column list still comes from SELECT *.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The WHERE clause filters rows as the query runs, before anything is written to the new table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A query returning zero rows is a legitimate query, and the engine builds the table from its column list regardless.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The condition 1 = 0 is a test the database evaluates, not a template for a row of data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: A condition that is never true gives you a table's structure with none of its rows, which is exactly what you want as a target for a later load.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-2 Changing Existing Data in a Table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Prices go up. A customer pays down a balance. A rep retires and someone else takes over the account. The rows in a table are not carved in stone, and UPDATE is the statement that changes what is already there. It does not add rows and it does not remove them. It reaches into rows that already exist and replaces values in them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An UPDATE has three parts. You name the table you are changing. You write a SET clause giving each column its new value. You write a WHERE clause saying which rows. That third part is optional as far as the database is concerned and mandatory as far as you are concerned, for reasons that will be uncomfortably clear by the end of this section.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Work on a copy. Build one first, then change the price of the nylon leash on the copy.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: make a scratch copy first, so the practice UPDATE cannot
--   damage the real ITEM table.
CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS

-- SELECT *: same columns as the original.
SELECT *

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM ITEM;

-- UPDATE: names the table whose existing rows are about to be changed. Nothing is
--   added and nothing is removed - values inside rows are rewritten.
UPDATE ITEM_COPY

-- SET: which column gets a new value, and what that value is.
SET PRICE = 12.49

-- WHERE: which rows. Filtering on the id restricts this to a single row. Leave
--   this line off and every row in the table gets the new price.
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Exactly one row matched, so exactly one row changed. In ITEM_COPY the leash now costs 12.49. In ITEM it still costs 11.99, because you never touched ITEM.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Changing several columns at once

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Separate the assignments with commas. One UPDATE statement, one pass over the table, as many columns as you need.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- UPDATE: the table being changed.
UPDATE ITEM_COPY

-- SET: one SET clause can change several columns at once - separate the
--   assignments with commas, and write SET only once.
SET PRICE = 12.49,

--   The second assignment. Both are applied to the same row in one pass, which is
--   faster and safer than running two separate UPDATE statements.
    REORDER_LEVEL = 40

-- WHERE: which rows are affected.
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Notice there is only one SET. The word appears once, no matter how many columns follow it. Do not write two separate UPDATE statements for two columns of the same row. One statement is less work for the database, and more importantly it cannot leave the row half-changed if something goes wrong between the two.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_COPY after the two-column UPDATE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONPRICEREORDER_LEVEL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage64.995
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb42.515
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft12.4940
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit27.7510
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming Kit15.258

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        New values can be computed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The right side of an = in a SET clause is an expression, not only a typed-in constant. It can even refer to the column's own current value, and when it does, the database uses the value the row had before this statement started running. That is how you raise a whole category of prices without knowing any of them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- UPDATE: the table being changed.
UPDATE ITEM_COPY

-- SET: the new value is calculated FROM THE OLD ONE. PRICE * 1.05 is a five per
--   cent rise, and ROUND(..., 2) trims the result to two decimal places so the
--   stored price stays sensible money. The right-hand PRICE is the value before
--   the update; the left-hand one is where the answer goes.
SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.05, 2)

-- WHERE: this time the filter is not on a key, so SEVERAL rows change at once -
--   every habitat item gets the rise in a single statement.
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two rows are in the Habitat category, so two rows change. ROUND(value, 2) rounds the result to two decimal places. It rounds, it does not chop: the raw arithmetic for the aviary cage is 68.2395, so ROUND stores 68.24, not the 68.23 you would get by simply cutting the extra digits off. Leave ROUND out entirely and the cage is stored as 68.2395, which is not a price anybody can charge.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The Habitat rows before and after a five percent increase
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONPRICE BEFORERAW ARITHMETICPRICE AFTER ROUND
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage64.9968.239568.24
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit27.7529.137529.14

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The WHERE clause can hold a subquery

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Anything that is legal in a SELECT statement's WHERE clause is legal in an UPDATE statement's WHERE clause, including the subqueries from Module 5. The database works out which rows match, then changes those rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS: another scratch copy, so the real CUSTOMER table is safe.
CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER_COPY AS
SELECT *
FROM CUSTOMER;

-- UPDATE: the copy is what changes.
UPDATE CUSTOMER_COPY

-- SET: raise the limit by a fixed amount, computed from the existing value.
SET CREDIT_LIMIT = CREDIT_LIMIT + 1000.00

-- WHERE: the rows to change are chosen by a SUBQUERY, exactly as in Module 5.
--   Everything legal in a SELECT's WHERE clause is legal here too.
WHERE REP_NUM IN

--   The inner query runs first and returns the numbers of the Brookville reps.
      (SELECT REP_NUM
       FROM REP

--   Note whose city is being tested: the REP's, not the customer's.
       WHERE CITY = 'Brookville');

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The subquery returns rep 65, the only rep in Brookville. Whiskers & Wags Boutique is the only customer assigned to that rep, so one row changes and its credit limit goes from 6000 to 7000. The other three customers are untouched. You never had to know which rep number Brookville corresponded to; the subquery worked that out.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The forgotten WHERE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Leave the WHERE clause off entirely and the statement is still perfectly valid SQL. It means every row in the table. The database does not ask whether you are sure. There is no confirmation prompt, no warning, and no undo.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- UPDATE with NO WHERE clause: perfectly legal, and it changes EVERY row in the
--   table. Sometimes that is exactly what you want; far more often it is the
--   accident that ruins an afternoon. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE clause
--   first, so you know how many rows you are about to touch.
UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET ON_HAND = 0;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        All five items now read zero on hand: the cage, the food, the leash, the filter kit, and the grooming kit. Nothing was misspelled. No error appeared. The inventory counts are simply gone, and the old values are not saved anywhere for you to get back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_COPY after an UPDATE with no WHERE clause
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ITEM_IDDESCRIPTIONON_HAND
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AV07Aviary Starter Cage0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CF21Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DG04Nylon Dog Leash 6ft0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        FT88Fish Tank Filter Kit0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GR15Small Animal Grooming Kit0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Read the WHERE clause twice before you run it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An UPDATE with no WHERE changes every row in the table. An UPDATE whose WHERE names the wrong column changes the wrong rows just as quietly. This is the single most common way working databases get damaged, and it is almost never caused by a hard query. It is caused by a fast one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The habit that prevents this costs about five seconds. Before you run the UPDATE, run the same FROM and WHERE as a SELECT and look at what comes back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- SELECT: the check that should follow every change. Reading the row back is the
--   only way to know an UPDATE did what you intended.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE, REORDER_LEVEL

-- FROM: the table that was just updated.
FROM ITEM_COPY

-- WHERE: the same condition the UPDATE used, so you are looking at the same row.
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        One row comes back: the nylon leash, priced 11.99 with a reorder level of 25. That is what you meant to change, so the UPDATE built on the same WHERE clause is safe to run. If that SELECT had returned five rows when you expected one, you would have found the problem while it was still free to fix.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Rehearse, then commit

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Write the SELECT first. When it returns exactly the rows you want, turn it into the UPDATE by replacing the SELECT ... FROM part with UPDATE ... SET. The WHERE clause is never retyped, and retyping is where typos come from.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Matching nothing is not an error either

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If you mean to update DG04 and you type DG40, the statement succeeds and changes zero rows. No message, no complaint. That is safer than the alternative, but it also means that seeing no error is not proof that anything happened. Always look at the table afterward.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Copy

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Build a working table with CREATE TABLE ITEM_COPY AS SELECT * FROM ITEM; so a mistake costs you nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Rehearse

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run your WHERE clause as a SELECT against the copy and count the rows it returns. Is that the number you expected?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Update the copy

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Change SELECT ... FROM to UPDATE ... SET, leaving the WHERE clause exactly as it was.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Verify

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Select the changed rows back out and read the new values with your own eyes. Also check that a row you did not intend to change still looks right.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        5

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run it for real

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Only now, point the verified statement at the real table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The word SET appears once. Put a comma between the two assignments, not the word AND. If your result shows all five items with a price of 12.49, you left off the WHERE clause: run the whole script again from the top, because the DROP TABLE IF EXISTS line rebuilds the copy from the untouched ITEM table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can write an UPDATE with SET and WHERE that changes one specific row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can change several columns in one statement by separating the assignments with commas.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can compute a new value from the column's current value, and round it to two decimal places.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know ROUND rounds rather than truncates, so 68.2395 becomes 68.24 and not 68.23.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can use a subquery inside an UPDATE statement's WHERE clause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain exactly what an UPDATE with no WHERE clause does, and why no error appears.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I rehearse the WHERE clause as a SELECT before I run the UPDATE.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: changing data

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1Monday morning at the KimTay warehouse

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Meaning to zero the on-hand count for the grooming kit only, someone runs UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET ON_HAND = 0; against a copy holding all five items. What is the result?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The WHERE clause is optional to the parser. Omitting it is valid SQL that means every row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. No WHERE means every row, and a successful statement produces no warning of any kind.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The database has no memory of your previous queries. Each statement stands entirely on its own.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. There is no confirmation step. This is exactly why the damage is usually discovered hours later.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: An UPDATE with no WHERE clause changes every row in the table and tells you nothing about it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Whiskers & Wags Boutique gets adjusted

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The bookkeeper needs to set customer 1420's balance to 0.00 and its credit limit to 8000.00 in a single UPDATE on CUSTOMER_COPY. Which SET clause is written correctly?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. AND is a logical operator for conditions in a WHERE clause, not a separator for assignments in a SET clause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. A semicolon ends a whole statement, so this would chop one UPDATE into fragments the database cannot parse.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. The word SET appears exactly once in an UPDATE statement no matter how many columns are being changed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Correct. One SET, then a comma-separated list of column-equals-value assignments.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Write SET once and separate multiple column assignments with commas, so the whole row changes in one pass.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Rounding the five percent increase

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        On a copy of ITEM, someone runs UPDATE ITEM_COPY SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.05, 2) WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';. The Aviary Starter Cage starts at 64.99 and the raw arithmetic gives 68.2395. What is stored?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. That is what truncating would give. ROUND looks at the digits it is dropping and adjusts the last kept digit accordingly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. The dropped digits are 95, so the second decimal place rounds up from 3 to 4 and 68.24 is stored.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. ROUND produces a new value, and the UPDATE stores that value. Display formatting is a separate concern entirely.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Referring to a column's own current value is normal and is exactly how percentage increases are written.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: ROUND rounds rather than truncates, so verify which one your prices actually need before you commit the change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q4A transposed item id

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A clerk means to reprice item DG04 but types WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG40' instead. What does the database report back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Correct. Zero matching rows is a normal outcome, so the statement succeeds and quietly does nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Not finding rows is not an error condition. Only a SELECT would show you that nothing matched.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A WHERE clause matching nothing and no WHERE clause at all are opposites, not equivalents.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. The database compares values exactly. It has no notion of a near miss or a likely intended value.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Seeing no error message is not proof that your UPDATE changed anything, so always read the rows back afterward.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-3 Adding New Rows to an Existing Table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Module 3 taught you INSERT INTO ... VALUES, which adds one row that you type out yourself. That is the right tool when a shipment arrives and somebody hands you the details of a new item on a piece of paper. Nothing in the database knows about that item yet, so somebody has to key it in.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It is the wrong tool when the rows you need are already sitting in the database and there are two hundred of them. Retyping data that the database already has is slow, and every retyped character is a chance to introduce an error that was not there before.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        So INSERT has a second form. Replace the VALUES clause with a SELECT, and every row that query returns becomes a row in the target table. One statement, however many rows the query finds.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Building the target first

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The table you are inserting into has to exist already. INSERT never creates a table. Build it with a plain CREATE TABLE and a column list, exactly the way Module 3 showed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE: the ordinary form, where you declare the columns yourself instead
--   of letting a query decide them. The table is created empty.
CREATE TABLE PREMIUM_CUSTOMER

--   Each line is one column: a name, then the type that column will hold. The
--   types are chosen to match the CUSTOMER columns these values will come from -
--   if they did not match, the copy would fail or lose precision.
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME CHAR(35),
     BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2),

--   The last column takes no comma, and the closing parenthesis ends the list.
     CREDIT_LIMIT DECIMAL(9,2));

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Now load it. KimTay wants every customer whose credit limit is 7500 or more.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- INSERT INTO ... SELECT: an INSERT whose values come from a query rather than
--   from a typed VALUES list. The table must already exist; this only adds rows.
INSERT INTO PREMIUM_CUSTOMER

-- SELECT: the four columns being copied. Their number, order and types have to
--   line up with the target table's columns - the NAMES do not have to match.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: decides which rows get copied. One statement can move many rows, which
--   is what makes this the standard way to load a summary or archive table.
WHERE CREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500.00;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two customers qualify, so two rows are added. Look closely at what is not in that statement: no VALUES, no parentheses wrapped around the query, and no semicolon between the INSERT line and the SELECT line. It is one single statement that happens to occupy four lines.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        PREMIUM_CUSTOMER after the load
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEBALANCECREDIT_LIMIT
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1120Access Pet Center3512.57500
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1310Companion Care Clinic010000

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Making the columns line up

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The SELECT list has to match the target table's columns by count and by position. Names have nothing to do with it. The first value goes into the first column, the second into the second, and so on, no matter what anything is called.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If the counts disagree, the statement fails and nothing at all is inserted. That is the good outcome.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- GOAL: a deliberate error - the mismatch you will hit sooner or later.
-- INSERT INTO: the target table has FOUR columns.
INSERT INTO PREMIUM_CUSTOMER

-- SELECT: BROKEN. It supplies only TWO. The engine has no way to decide which two
--   of the four columns you meant, so it refuses the statement before inserting
--   anything. Count the columns on both sides whenever this error appears.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The database rejects that. In this sandbox the message is "table PREMIUM_CUSTOMER has 4 columns but 2 values were supplied". The exact wording differs between engines; the refusal does not. All three of SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle stop you here.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The dangerous case is when the counts agree

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If you supply the right number of values in the wrong order, nothing errors. Balances land in the credit limit column and credit limits land in the balance column, and the statement reports success. Naming the target columns explicitly, right after the table name, is what protects you from this.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE: two columns declared by hand.
CREATE TABLE REP_NAME
    (REP_NUM CHAR(2),

--   FULL_NAME is wide enough to hold a first and last name joined together.
     FULL_NAME CHAR(32));

-- INSERT INTO ... SELECT: naming the target columns explicitly is the safer form -
--   it keeps working even if the table later gains a column.
INSERT INTO REP_NAME (REP_NUM, FULL_NAME)

-- SELECT: the second value is CALCULATED, not stored anywhere. || is the standard
--   SQL concatenation operator, used here to glue first name, a space, and last
--   name into one string. SQLite and Oracle both accept ||; MySQL does not.
SELECT REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME || ' ' || LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM REP

-- WHERE: only the reps on the higher commission rate are copied.
WHERE RATE > 0.05;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        (REP_NUM, FULL_NAME) after the table name says which columns you are filling and in what order. Richard Hull's rate of 0.07 is the only one above 0.05, so REP_NAME gets one row: 35 and Richard Hull. The || operator glued the first name, a space, and the last name into one value, which shows that the query feeding an INSERT can compute values that exist in no column anywhere.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        || is not portable, CONCAT() is closer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        || means concatenate in this sandbox and in Oracle. MySQL reads || as a logical OR unless the server has been specially configured, so the same statement there would produce a number, not a name. Write CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME) if you want one spelling that works in all three. CONCAT() runs here too, and returns the identical Richard Hull.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- INSERT INTO ... SELECT: the same load, written for MySQL.
INSERT INTO REP_NAME (REP_NUM, FULL_NAME)

-- SELECT: CONCAT() is MySQL's way of joining strings, taking the pieces as
--   arguments rather than between || operators. Same result, different spelling -
--   string handling is one of the least portable corners of SQL.
SELECT REP_NUM, CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME)

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM REP

-- WHERE: the same filter as the previous version.
WHERE RATE > 0.05;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The query can be as complicated as you like

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Whatever a SELECT can produce, an INSERT can store. That includes grouped and aggregated results, which is how summary tables get built.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE: three columns declared by hand, sized for what will go in them.
CREATE TABLE REP_TOTAL
    (REP_NUM CHAR(2),

--   A count is a whole number, so SMALLINT is plenty.
     CUST_COUNT SMALLINT,

--   A total of money keeps the same exact DECIMAL type as the column it sums.
     TOTAL_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2));

-- INSERT INTO ... SELECT: load the table from a query.
INSERT INTO REP_TOTAL

-- SELECT: the query being loaded is a GROUPED one, so the rows going in are
--   summary rows rather than copies. This is how a reporting table gets built.
SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*), SUM(BALANCE)

-- FROM: the source table.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- GROUP BY: one row per rep, which is one row inserted per rep.
GROUP BY REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GROUP BY REP_NUM produces one row per rep, so three rows are inserted. Rep 20 carries two customers whose balances add up to 3512.5, because Companion Care Clinic's balance is 0.00 and Access Pet Center's is 3512.50. The other two reps have one customer each.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        REP_TOTAL after the aggregate load
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        REP_NUMCUST_COUNTTOTAL_BALANCE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2023512.5
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3511200
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6514820.75
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A summary table is a photograph, not a window

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        REP_TOTAL holds the numbers as they stood the instant the INSERT ran. Change a balance in CUSTOMER afterward and REP_TOTAL does not follow along. If you need numbers that are always current you want a view, which is coming later. If you need a record of what the numbers were on a particular day, a table like this is exactly right.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Combining what you learned in 6-1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Writing out a CREATE TABLE column list by hand only to match a table you already have is tedious and easy to get wrong. The WHERE 1 = 0 trick from 6-1 builds the target for you with columns that already line up perfectly with the source.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- CREATE TABLE ... AS with a false condition: the empty-clone trick again, this
--   time to make a staging table you will fill yourself.
CREATE TABLE BUDGET_ITEM AS
SELECT *
FROM ITEM

-- 1 = 0 is never true, so the structure is copied and none of the rows are.
WHERE 1 = 0;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        BUDGET_ITEM has ITEM's six columns and no rows. Now both forms of INSERT work on it. Use INSERT ... SELECT to bulk-load the rows that already exist, and INSERT ... VALUES for a brand-new item that is in no table yet. They are not competing techniques; most real loading jobs use both.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Running the same load twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        INSERT adds. That is all it does. It does not check whether a matching row is already sitting there, and it does not synchronize the target with the source.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A second run doubles your rows

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run the PREMIUM_CUSTOMER load once and you have two rows. Run the identical statement again and you have four, two of which are exact duplicates. Nothing complains, because that table has no primary key to complain with. Before you re-run a load, either check what is already in the target or empty it first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        INSERT ... VALUES

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        One row per statement, typed out by hand. Use it when the data is new to the database and has to come in from outside: a shipment, a phone call, a paper form. The row count is small and known.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        INSERT ... SELECT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        As many rows as the query returns, in one statement. Use it when the data is already in the database and you are copying, filtering, or summarizing it. The row count depends on the data, and can be zero.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        BUDGET_ITEM has all six of ITEM's columns, so both inserts have to supply six values. The bulk load uses SELECT and no VALUES keyword; the single new item uses VALUES and no SELECT. You should finish with three rows: DG04, GR15, and TY01.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can write INSERT INTO ... SELECT to load many rows from a query in one statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can say when INSERT ... VALUES is the better choice and when INSERT ... SELECT is.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know the target table must already exist, and I can build it with CREATE TABLE or with WHERE 1 = 0.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I can explain why the column count and order matter more than the column names.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I name the target columns explicitly to keep values from landing in the wrong place.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know || joins strings here and in Oracle, and that MySQL needs CONCAT().
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • I know that re-running an INSERT ... SELECT adds the rows a second time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: adding rows

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1Loading KimTay's premium customer list

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An empty PREMIUM_CUSTOMER table already exists, and the bookkeeper needs it filled with every customer whose credit limit is 7500 or more. Which approach does the entire load in one statement, with no values retyped?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. This eventually gets the rows in, but it is one statement per customer and every retyped value is a fresh chance for an error. The question asks for the single-statement load.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. The table already exists, and CREATE TABLE would fail on the duplicate name rather than adding rows to it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. UPDATE changes values in rows that are already in the target table. It cannot add rows that are not there.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Correct. INSERT ... SELECT loads however many rows the query returns, in one statement, with no retyping.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: When the rows you need are already in the database, let a SELECT feed the INSERT instead of typing them again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2Four columns, two values

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        PREMIUM_CUSTOMER has four columns. Someone runs INSERT INTO PREMIUM_CUSTOMER SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER;. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The database has no way to guess which unnamed columns you meant or where their values should come from.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct. The engine refuses the statement outright, so the target table is left exactly as it was.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Nothing is inserted at all. The count mismatch is caught before any row reaches the table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. Shifting is the danger when the counts match but the order is wrong, which is a different mistake entirely.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: The SELECT list must match the target's columns in count and position, and a mismatch stops the whole statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3Re-running the premium load

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The load has already put two rows into PREMIUM_CUSTOMER, a table created with a plain CREATE TABLE and no primary key. Someone runs the identical INSERT ... SELECT a second time. What is in the table now?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The database keeps no history of statements you have run and makes no attempt to detect a repeat.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. INSERT never removes or replaces existing rows. That would be the job of DELETE or UPDATE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔c. Correct. Two more copies of the same two rows go in, and nothing in the table is set up to object.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. No primary key was declared on this table, so nothing stops the duplicate customer numbers.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: INSERT ... SELECT adds rows every time it runs, so check or clear the target before repeating a load.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                6-4 Autocommit, Commit, and Rollback

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE you have written so far took effect the moment you pressed Run. You never told the database to save the change, and you never had a way to take it back. That behavior has a name, it is a setting rather than a law of nature, and this lesson is about turning it off on purpose.
