                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Autocommit: every statement saves itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Autocommit means the database wraps each statement you send in an invisible save. The statement runs, the change is written to disk, and the database is finished with it. There is no pending state and no undo. Most tools you will meet start this way, because for one quick correction that is exactly what you want.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Autocommit

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A session setting. When it is on, the database commits (permanently saves) each statement by itself the instant that statement succeeds. When it is off, your changes pile up unsaved until you say COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Watch it happen. Whiskers & Wags Boutique (customer 1420) owes KimTay 4820.75. Write the UPDATE that takes 200.00 off that balance, then run the whole block. There is no COMMIT anywhere in it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Until you write the UPDATE, both result sets read 4820.75. With the UPDATE in, BALANCE_BEFORE comes back 4820.75 and BALANCE_AFTER comes back 4620.75. There is no ROLLBACK here to protect you, so each Run subtracts another 200.00 — press Reset before you run it a second time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The balance is now 4620.75, and that number is on disk. If the 200.00 belonged on a different account, no keyword you know so far will bring the old value back. Try the obvious one. Clear the box, type this by itself, and press Run.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- ROLLBACK: undoes everything done since the transaction began, returning the
--   database to the state it was in at BEGIN. Nothing is written; it is as though
--   the statements in between never ran.
ROLLBACK;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The error is the answer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQLite replies cannot rollback - no transaction is active. It is not being difficult. Autocommit ended the transaction the moment your UPDATE finished, so there is nothing open left to undo. MySQL is quieter about the same situation, accepting the ROLLBACK and changing nothing, but the outcome is identical: the money stays moved.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                COMMIT and ROLLBACK

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Suspend autocommit and you get two new powers. Your changes become provisional, visible to you and to nobody else, and you decide at the end whether they are real. COMMIT says keep everything. ROLLBACK says forget everything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The three keywords that decide when a change becomes permanent
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KeywordWhat it doesWhen the data is written
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                BEGIN;Opens a transaction and suspends autocommit for the statements that followNothing is written yet
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                COMMIT;Ends the transaction and keeps every change made inside itEverything is written at once
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ROLLBACK;Ends the transaction and discards every change made inside itNothing is written, and the rows go back to what they were

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Here is the same UPDATE as before with BEGIN; in front of it and ROLLBACK; after it, plus a SELECT on each side so you can watch the value move and then move back. Press Reset on the sandbox above, paste this in, and run it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: opens a transaction. From here on, changes are provisional - visible to
--   you, but not yet permanent, and undoable in a single word.
BEGIN;

-- UPDATE: a change inside the transaction. It happens immediately as far as this
--   session can tell.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- SELECT: proof that the change IS in effect inside the transaction - the new
--   balance is what comes back.
SELECT BALANCE AS INSIDE_TRANSACTION
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- ROLLBACK: throw the change away. The transaction ends here.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: the same query again, now returning the ORIGINAL balance. That contrast
--   between the two SELECTs is the whole idea of a transaction.
SELECT BALANCE AS AFTER_ROLLBACK
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                INSIDE_TRANSACTION comes back 4620.75 and AFTER_ROLLBACK comes back 4820.75. Between the BEGIN and the ROLLBACK your session saw the new number and behaved as though it were true. The stored data never moved. That gap between what you can see and what has been saved is the whole idea.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The default is not the same on every engine

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Autocommit by engine, and how you take control of it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                EngineAutocommit by defaultHow you take control
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQLite (this sandbox)OnBEGIN; then COMMIT; or ROLLBACK;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                MySQLOnSET autocommit = 0; or START TRANSACTION;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                OracleOff in SQL*Plus, where the first DML opens a transaction that stays openCOMMIT; or ROLLBACK; before you disconnect
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL ServerOnBEGIN TRANSACTION; then COMMIT; or ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                This next block is MySQL only, so it is printed as plain text rather than in a sandbox. It switches autocommit off for the session, so the UPDATE stays provisional and the ROLLBACK really does put the balance back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- SET autocommit = 0: MySQL's way in. By default MySQL commits every statement
--   the moment it finishes, which leaves nothing to roll back; turning autocommit
--   off makes each statement provisional until you say COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
SET autocommit = 0;

-- UPDATE: a provisional change, now that autocommit is off.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- ROLLBACK: discard it.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: the balance is back to what it was. Had autocommit still been on, the
--   UPDATE would already be permanent and this would show the reduced figure.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Oracle runs the opposite way round, and this line is an Oracle SQL*Plus client command rather than SQL. It asks SQL*Plus to commit after each statement, which is how you make Oracle behave like the others.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- SET AUTOCOMMIT ON: the Oracle spelling, and the opposite default. Oracle does
--   NOT commit automatically, so a transaction is already open the moment you
--   change anything; this command switches that behaviour off. Same idea as
--   MySQL's autocommit setting, different name and different starting point.
SET AUTOCOMMIT ON;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What this sandbox supports

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK all run here. SET autocommit = 0; and SET AUTOCOMMIT ON; do not exist in SQLite, so the sandbox rejects both — that is why they appear as plain code blocks above. In SQLite the only way to suspend autocommit is to open a transaction with BEGIN, which is why every runnable example on this page that needs a transaction starts with that word. The very first sandbox on this page has no BEGIN on purpose: it is showing you what autocommit does when you leave it alone.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Do not disconnect with work pending

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                An open transaction that never reaches COMMIT is rolled back when the session ends. On Oracle in particular, closing the window after an afternoon of edits can throw away the whole afternoon. Type COMMIT; before you walk away.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can say in one sentence what autocommit does to a single UPDATE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know why a bare ROLLBACK; fails when autocommit is on.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can open a transaction with BEGIN; and end it with COMMIT; or ROLLBACK;.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know that MySQL and SQLite default to autocommit on, and Oracle SQL*Plus does not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know that leaving a session with work uncommitted discards that work.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: autocommit, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1Whiskers & Wags Boutique

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A clerk at KimTay opens a fresh session with autocommit on and runs UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';. A second later she realizes the 200.00 belonged on another account and immediately types ROLLBACK;. What is the balance for customer 1420 afterward?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. ROLLBACK acts on an open transaction, and autocommit closed this one the instant the UPDATE succeeded.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. COMMIT saves pending changes and never restores old ones, and there is no open transaction here for either keyword.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct: with autocommit on, the UPDATE was a complete transaction by itself and was written the moment it finished.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. No engine keeps a session-long snapshot to fall back on, since rollback reaches to the last COMMIT rather than to login.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: With autocommit on, every statement is its own committed transaction, so there is nothing left for ROLLBACK to undo.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2KimTay Pet Supplies

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The administrator turns autocommit off, runs three UPDATE statements against CUSTOMER, then leaves for lunch without typing anything else. A coworker in a different session runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER;. What does the coworker see?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct: isolation means pending work belongs to its own session, and everyone else keeps reading the last committed values.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Succeeding and committing are different events, and only the second one makes a change visible to other sessions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Row locks can make another writer wait, but a plain SELECT reads the last committed values instead of failing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Rows inside one transaction commit together or not at all, so a partial mixture is never what another session reads.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Until COMMIT runs, your changes exist only in your own session, no matter how many statements have succeeded.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3Downtown Aquarium & Pets

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A student writes a correction script for customer 1225 that has to behave identically on this course sandbox (SQLite), on MySQL at work, and on Oracle in the campus lab. Which statement about autocommit defaults is accurate?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Oracle SQL*Plus does not commit for you, and disconnecting without a COMMIT discards the work.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. SQLite and MySQL both write each standalone statement immediately unless you open a transaction first.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. This reverses the real defaults, since SQLite behaves like MySQL here rather than the other way around.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct: writing an explicit BEGIN and COMMIT is what makes one script behave the same on all three engines.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Never rely on an engine's autocommit default; state your transaction boundaries and the script travels safely.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                6-5 Transactions

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A 200.00 delivery charge that belongs to Access Pet Center was posted to Whiskers & Wags Boutique by mistake. Nobody was charged the wrong amount and nobody paid anything. The 200.00 is simply sitting on the wrong account, and moving it takes two statements: take 200.00 off customer 1420 and put 200.00 onto customer 1120.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run only the first of those two and KimTay's books are wrong in a way no error message will report. Whiskers & Wags stops owing 200.00 that was never theirs, which is correct, but Access Pet Center is never charged the 200.00 that is theirs, so the money has left the ledger entirely. The two statements are not two jobs. They are one job typed on two lines.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Transaction

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A group of statements the database treats as a single unit of work. Either every statement in the group takes effect, or none of them does. Nothing in between is ever stored.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The correction, and the total that must not move
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEBALANCE beforeBALANCE after
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                1120Access Pet Center3512.503712.50
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                1420Whiskers & Wags Boutique4820.754620.75
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                --Total owed to KimTay9533.259533.25

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                That last row is the test. A correction that moves a charge between two accounts must leave the total untouched. If the total changes, the correction is broken, and checking it is something you can do in SQL before you save anything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Two statements, autocommit on

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The first UPDATE is saved the instant it succeeds. For however long it takes you to type the second one, the total owed reads 9333.25 and KimTay's books are short 200.00. If your session dies in that gap, nothing brings that 200.00 back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Two statements, one transaction

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Nothing is saved until you type COMMIT. Other sessions keep reading 9533.25 the entire time. When the commit lands, both balances change together, and there is no instant at which the books are wrong.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The shape of every transaction you will ever write

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Open it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                BEGIN; suspends autocommit. From here on your changes are provisional and belong to you alone.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Do all of the work

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run every statement the job needs. Two, ten, it does not matter. What matters is that they all sit inside the same transaction.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Check before you save

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run a SELECT that proves the job is right. A total, a count, a look at the rows you touched. This is the step most people skip and the reason ROLLBACK exists.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Decide

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                COMMIT; if the check passed. ROLLBACK; if anything looks wrong. Either keyword closes the transaction and hands autocommit back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Write the two UPDATE statements that move the 200.00, and leave the totals and the COMMIT where they are. TOTAL_OWED_INSIDE should come back 9533.25, exactly matching TOTAL_OWED_BEFORE.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Both totals read 9533.25, and the final list shows 1120 at 3712.5 and 1420 at 4620.75. SQLite drops trailing zeros when it displays a number, so 3712.50 appears as 3712.5. This script ends in COMMIT, so press Reset before running it again or you will move another 200.00.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Half a transaction is worse than no transaction

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Here is the failure that catches people out. The second UPDATE names customer 9999, who does not exist. SQL matches no rows, changes nothing, and reports no error at all. Reset the sandbox, paste this in, and run it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: open a transaction around two changes that must both succeed or both
--   fail - the classic reason transactions exist.
BEGIN;

-- UPDATE: take 200 off one customer's balance.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- UPDATE: the matching half - except customer 9999 does not exist, so this
--   statement changes ZERO rows. It is not an error; SQL simply reports that
--   nothing matched, and the money has now vanished from the books.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '9999';

-- SELECT: the evidence. The total across all customers is 200 short of what it
--   was, which is the inconsistency the transaction is protecting you from.
SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED FROM CUSTOMER;

-- ROLLBACK: undo BOTH statements together. Half-finished work never reaches disk.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: the total is back where it started.
SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED FROM CUSTOMER;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                No error does not mean no problem

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The first total reads 9333.25. Two hundred dollars have vanished from KimTay's books and nothing on your screen said so. The check SELECT caught it, the ROLLBACK undid it, and the second total reads 9533.25 again. A statement that matches zero rows is a successful statement, which is why step 3 of a transaction is never optional.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why the rules have a name

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Database people describe a well-behaved transaction with four words, usually shortened to ACID. You do not need to memorize the theory to pass this course, but you have already seen all four at work.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Atomicity: all of the statements take effect or none of them do, which is why the half-finished correction above could never reach disk.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another valid state, so the total owed is 9533.25 before and 9533.25 after.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Isolation: your uncommitted changes are yours alone, and other sessions keep reading the old values until you commit.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a power cut, a crash, or someone tripping over the cable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Opening a transaction on other engines

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The idea is identical everywhere. Only the opening word changes. This version is MySQL, where START TRANSACTION is the usual spelling and works even when autocommit is on. SQLite does not accept START TRANSACTION, so this is a plain code block rather than a sandbox.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- START TRANSACTION: the standard spelling of BEGIN, and the one MySQL prefers.
--   Both do the same job.
START TRANSACTION;

-- UPDATE: the first half of the transfer.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- UPDATE: the second half, this time aimed at a customer that really exists, so
--   both statements change exactly one row each.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 200.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- COMMIT: make both changes permanent, together and at the same instant. After
--   this the transaction is closed and there is nothing left to roll back.
COMMIT;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                DDL can commit behind your back

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                On MySQL and Oracle, a data definition statement such as CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE forces an implicit commit before and after itself. Slip an ALTER TABLE into the middle of a transaction on those engines and every pending change is saved whether you meant it or not, and a later ROLLBACK has nothing left to undo.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQLite, and therefore this sandbox, does not behave that way. Data definition is transactional here, so you can create a table and then take it back. The check below reads sqlite_master, the internal catalog where SQLite keeps one row for every table, index, and view in the database; MySQL answers the same question from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES, which SQLite does not have. Paste this into the sandbox above and watch the count go from 1 to 0.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: open a transaction - this time around a structure change rather than a
--   data change.
BEGIN;

-- CREATE TABLE: a DDL statement. In SQLite and PostgreSQL it is transactional
--   like any other statement, which is what the rest of this example proves.
CREATE TABLE BALANCE_AUDIT (
    CUSTOMER_NUM  CHAR(4),
    OLD_BALANCE   DECIMAL(9,2)
);

-- SELECT: sqlite_master is SQLite's internal catalogue - the table that lists the
--   tables. Counting rows in it is how you ask "does this table exist?". It
--   answers 1: the new table is there.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS AUDIT_TABLE_COUNT
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE name = 'BALANCE_AUDIT';

-- ROLLBACK: undo the transaction, and with it the CREATE TABLE.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: the same catalogue question now answers 0 - the table is gone. In MySQL
--   and Oracle this would NOT happen: a DDL statement there commits the
--   transaction automatically and cannot be rolled back.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS AUDIT_TABLE_COUNT
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE name = 'BALANCE_AUDIT';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can explain why moving a charge between two accounts is one job, not two.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I open with BEGIN;, do all the work, prove it with a SELECT, then decide.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know a statement that matches zero rows reports success, not an error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can name a check that would catch a half-finished correction, such as SUM(BALANCE).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know that ALTER TABLE commits implicitly on MySQL and Oracle but not in this sandbox.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: transactions as one unit of work

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1Access Pet Center

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Inside an open transaction the bookkeeper runs UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE - 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420'; and then UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 200.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '9999';. No error appears, but SELECT SUM(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER; now returns 9333.25 instead of 9533.25. What should happen next?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. A statement matching no rows is not an error, so a clean run is no proof that the work is correct.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔b. Correct: the transaction is half finished, and ROLLBACK is the one command that returns the books to a consistent state.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Repeating a statement whose WHERE matches nothing changes nothing, because the customer number itself is wrong.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Committing writes the broken total to disk first, and the follow-up fix can fail just as easily as the original did.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: When the check SELECT shows the job is half done, roll the whole thing back rather than committing and patching.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2KimTay Pet Supplies

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Power fails in the middle of a transaction that had already run two UPDATE statements against CUSTOMER but had not yet reached COMMIT. When the server comes back up, what is in the table?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Executing is not committing, so until COMMIT the changes live in a workspace the crash recovery throws away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Atomicity means all or nothing, and the engine will never keep one half of a transaction over the other half.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Recovery restores all committed data, so rows the transaction never touched are still exactly where they were.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct: durability protects committed transactions, and anything still open at the crash is undone on restart.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A crash cannot leave you with half a transaction, because recovery finishes the job by rolling the whole thing back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Working in MySQL, an analyst types START TRANSACTION;, then UPDATE CUSTOMER SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';, then ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER ADD COLUMN LAST_REVIEW DATE;, then ROLLBACK;. What is the state of the table?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct: MySQL and Oracle force an implicit commit around DDL, so the pending 12000.00 was saved before ROLLBACK ran.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. That is how the SQLite sandbox behaves, but MySQL and Oracle commit around a data definition statement instead.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Data definition is as permanent as any committed change, and in MySQL it is harder to undo than a plain UPDATE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. The statement is accepted and runs normally; the surprise is what it quietly does to the transaction around it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: On MySQL and Oracle, keep data definition statements out of a transaction, because they commit whatever is pending.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                6-6 Changing and Deleting Existing Rows

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                UPDATE and DELETE are the two statements that can destroy work you cannot get back. INSERT adds something new, and if it is wrong you delete it. UPDATE overwrites a value that is now gone, and DELETE removes a row that is now gone. Inside a transaction both become reversible, and this lesson is about building that habit before you need it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Count the rows before you change them

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Both statements act on whatever the WHERE clause matches. So find out what it matches first, with a SELECT that carries the identical WHERE. Companion Care Clinic (customer 1310) is having its credit limit raised from 10000.00 to 12000.00, and exactly one row should move. Every statement below runs as written in this course's sandbox.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- Step 1: how many rows will this touch? Ask before you change anything.
-- SELECT COUNT(*): the same WHERE clause the UPDATE is about to use. If this
--   answers 400 when you expected 1, you have found the mistake for free.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROWS_I_AM_ABOUT_TO_CHANGE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- Step 2: BEGIN opens the safety net before the change is made.
BEGIN;

-- Step 3: the change itself, now provisional.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- Step 4: read the row back and confirm it looks right. This is the moment to
--   decide - ROLLBACK if anything is wrong, COMMIT if it is not.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- Step 5: COMMIT makes it permanent. The safety net is gone from here on.
COMMIT;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ROWS_I_AM_ABOUT_TO_CHANGE comes back 1. That is the number you expected, so the UPDATE is safe to run and the COMMIT is safe to type. Had it come back 4, you would have known the WHERE was wrong before a single value changed. This script does commit, so press Reset afterwards to put the credit limit back to 10000.00.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The WHERE you forgot to type

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A missing WHERE is not a syntax error. UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.10, 2); is a perfectly legal statement that raises the price of every product KimTay sells. The engine will not ask whether you meant it. It will report five rows affected and move on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                So make the mistake here, where it costs nothing. The ten percent increase was meant for the two Habitat items, AV07 and FT88, and nothing else. Run the block below top to bottom: it makes the mistake, shows you the damage, and takes it back. Then it leaves you a second transaction to write the version that has the WHERE clause on it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Four result sets come back every time. Before you write anything they read: the real prices; then 71.49, 46.75, 13.19, 30.53 and 16.78; then the real prices again, because your UPDATE is still missing; then the real prices once more. With WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' in place, the third set reads AV07 71.49 and FT88 30.53 while CF21 42.5, DG04 11.99 and GR15 15.25 stay exactly where they were. SQLite drops trailing zeros when it displays a number, so 42.50 appears as 42.5. Both transactions end in ROLLBACK, so you can run this as many times as you like without changing anything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Four result sets come back. The first and the last are identical, and the second one is the damage. Both UPDATE statements really did run against the rows: what the BEGIN held back was the saving, not the running, and each ROLLBACK threw the pending version away before it could reach disk.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The same drill works on DELETE, and this one is written out for you. Press Reset, paste it in, and run it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: open the transaction FIRST. The safety net has to exist before the
--   dangerous statement runs, not after.
BEGIN;

-- DELETE with no WHERE: removes every row in the table. The table itself survives
--   - this is emptying it, not dropping it.
DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE;

-- SELECT: confirms the damage. Zero rows left.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS LINES_LEFT FROM INVOICE_LINE;

-- ROLLBACK: puts all six rows back, exactly as they were.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: the count is back to six. Outside a transaction, that DELETE would have
--   been permanent and no amount of typing would have brought the rows back.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS LINES_BACK FROM INVOICE_LINE;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                LINES_LEFT reads 0 and LINES_BACK reads 6. One statement with no WHERE emptied the table, and one word put all six invoice lines back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                6-6a Executing a rollback

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ROLLBACK is one word with no options and no arguments. It ends the open transaction and returns every row that transaction touched to the value it held at BEGIN. It cannot roll back part of the work, and it cannot be aimed at one statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Stop typing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The transaction is still open, so nothing is on disk yet. Do not try to repair the damage with more UPDATE statements while you are still inside it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Look at what actually happened

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run a SELECT or a COUNT(*). Knowing whether five rows moved or one row moved decides everything that follows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Type ROLLBACK;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Every change since BEGIN disappears at once, and the transaction closes. Autocommit is back in force for the next statement you run.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Verify, then start over

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run the same SELECT again and confirm the old values are back. Now rewrite the statement with the WHERE clause it needed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ROLLBACK reaches back to the last COMMIT and no further

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                It is not an undo history. If you commit and then discover the mistake, ROLLBACK has nothing to work with. In this sandbox a ROLLBACK typed after a COMMIT fails with cannot rollback - no transaction is active, which is the same message you get from typing it under autocommit.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: open a transaction.
BEGIN;

-- UPDATE: a provisional change.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = 0
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

-- COMMIT: makes the change permanent AND ends the transaction. Those are two
--   separate consequences, and the second one is what people forget.
COMMIT;

-- This line fails. The transaction closed when COMMIT ran.
-- ROLLBACK: there is no open transaction left to undo, so this is an error rather
--   than a way back. Once you commit, the change is yours to keep.
ROLLBACK;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Run that one and the only thing on your screen is the error, but the COMMIT above it was real: customer 1420 is now sitting at a balance of 0 and no keyword will change that. Press Reset before you carry on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Which keyword ends the transaction, and when
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What the check told youWhat to typeWhat happens to your work
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The rows and totals are exactly what you expectedCOMMIT;Written to disk, visible to every session, permanent
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                More rows changed than you meant to changeROLLBACK;Discarded completely, and the rows return to their old values
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A statement matched zero rows and left the job half doneROLLBACK;Discarded, so no half-finished state is ever stored
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                You are not sure yetNothing, then run a SELECTStill pending, still private to you, still reversible

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The same protection covers deletes. Companion Care Clinic is the only KimTay customer with no invoice, so somebody might reasonably decide the record is dead and remove it. Inside a transaction that decision is reversible.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- BEGIN: open the transaction before the delete, as always.
BEGIN;

-- DELETE ... WHERE: a targeted delete - one customer, chosen by primary key.
DELETE FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

-- SELECT: three customers left, so the delete did what it said.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS_LEFT FROM CUSTOMER;

-- ROLLBACK: undo it.
ROLLBACK;

-- SELECT: four again. Run the same experiment without the BEGIN and the customer
--   is simply gone.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS_LEFT FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The count reads 3, then 4. Companion Care Clinic is back, with its address, its balance of 0.00, its credit limit of 10000.00, and its rep. A committed delete would have taken all of that with it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The habit worth carrying to your first job

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Type BEGIN; before any UPDATE or DELETE that touches production data. Run the SELECT that proves you were right. Then, and only then, type COMMIT;. It costs you two extra lines and it has saved a great many careers.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I run a SELECT with the same WHERE before I run an UPDATE or a DELETE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know a missing WHERE is legal SQL that quietly changes every row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can update a value, check it, roll back, and confirm the original is restored.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know ROLLBACK undoes the whole transaction and cannot undo one statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I know COMMIT is the point of no return, and recovery after it means a backup.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: changing rows, deleting rows, and undoing both

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1KimTay Pet Supplies

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A ten percent increase was meant to hit the two Habitat items only, but the warehouse manager runs UPDATE ITEM SET PRICE = ROUND(PRICE * 1.10, 2); inside an open transaction and sees five rows affected. What is the fastest correct recovery?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Dividing everything back also cancels the two Habitat increases that were correct, and rounding is not guaranteed to reverse itself cleanly, so the job still has to be redone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Deleting and reloading throws away any other work in the transaction and leaves every INVOICE_LINE pointing at rows that no longer exist.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Committing makes the mistake permanent and turns a one-word fix into three hand-typed corrections.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct: the transaction is still open, so ROLLBACK discards all five changes at once and puts the prices back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: While the transaction is open, ROLLBACK is always cheaper and safer than trying to compute your way back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2Sycamore Court

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A StayWell clerk opens a transaction, deletes a lease row, types COMMIT;, and only then learns from the property manager that the lease should have stayed. Can a ROLLBACK bring the row back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. ROLLBACK works on the open transaction, and COMMIT closed it, so a bare ROLLBACK now has nothing to undo.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔b. Correct: COMMIT is the point of no return, so recovery here means restoring a backup or reinserting the row by hand.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Other sessions are irrelevant, because the commit by itself put the change beyond the reach of ROLLBACK.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. DELETE is a data manipulation statement and is very much undoable, but only before the transaction commits.
