                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: COMMIT is the boundary: everything after it is a data recovery problem rather than a SQL problem.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3Whiskers & Wags Boutique

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                INVOICE_LINE holds six rows. A clerk runs BEGIN;, then DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50711';, then ROLLBACK;, then SELECT COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE;. What number comes back?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. ROLLBACK undoes every data change made in the transaction, deletes very much included, not only updates.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. ROLLBACK returns the table to its state at BEGIN, and it never empties a table that had rows in it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct: invoice 50711 has two lines, CF21 and GR15, both come back, and the table is whole again at six rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. COUNT(*) always reports what is in the table at the moment it runs, not what a rollback happened to touch.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A rolled-back DELETE leaves the table exactly as it was at BEGIN, so the count is the original six.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Each card is a short sequence run against KimTay in one session. Click a card, then click the state the data is in when the sequence finishes. Ask one question of each: has a COMMIT run, has a ROLLBACK run, or is the transaction still sitting there waiting for you to decide?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 / 8 placed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-7 Changing a Value in a Column to Null

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Sometimes the honest answer is that nobody knows. Suppose KimTay Pet Supplies takes a new account over the phone and whoever answered never wrote down the street address. The row still belongs in CUSTOMER, but one column has nothing trustworthy to put in it. Typing a placeholder like N/A or 0 turns a gap in your knowledge into a fact that is not true. SQL has a word for the gap itself: null.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every row that ships with this course is completely filled in, so there is not a single null anywhere in the seed data. That is deliberate. If you want to see how nulls behave, you have to create one, and creating one on purpose is exactly what this section teaches: taking a column that currently holds a value and deliberately emptying it, so the database stops claiming something it cannot back up. At the end of the section you will use IS NULL to find the row again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Null

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A null is the absence of a value. It is not a number, not a word, and not a blank space. It means the value is unknown, or that the column does not apply to this particular row. Two nulls are never treated as equal to each other, because you cannot say that two unknowns match.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The statement itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Setting a column to null is an ordinary UPDATE. The only difference is that you assign the keyword NULL rather than a literal, and you do not wrap it in quotation marks. 'NULL' in quotation marks is the four-letter word NULL stored as text, which is a real value and defeats the whole point.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- UPDATE: the table being changed.
UPDATE CUSTOMER

-- SET: storing a null is how you record "this value is not known", as opposed to
--   storing 0, which claims the customer owes nothing. The two are very different
--   statements about the world, and only one of them is honest here.
SET BALANCE = NULL

-- WHERE: the single row being cleared.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Bring a WHERE clause every time

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Leaving off WHERE sets the column to null in every row of the table, and there is no undo. Run the matching SELECT ... WHERE ... first and confirm you get back exactly the rows you meant to touch.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Look at what that statement changes in the shipped data. Companion Care Clinic, customer 1310, has a BALANCE of 0.00. That zero is a real, verified number: the clinic owes KimTay nothing. Now suppose the account was just migrated from an older system and nobody can confirm the figure. Zero would be a claim you cannot support. Null is the truth.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(BALANCE) counts only the rows where BALANCE holds a value. Watch which of the three numbers moves.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Before the update you get 4, 4, and 2383.3125. After it you get 4, 3, and 3177.75. The row count did not change, because the customer is still there. What changed is that one balance stopped counting. AVG divided by three instead of four, so the average jumped by almost eight hundred dollars. That is the whole reason null exists as a separate idea: an unknown balance should not be averaged in as if it were zero.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SUM(BALANCE) is the interesting control here. It reads 9533.25 both before and after, because the row you emptied held 0.00 and adding zero to a total changes nothing. The total stayed put while the average moved, and the only thing that moved it was the divisor.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Zero, an empty string, and null are three different things
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Stored valueWhat it tells the readerHow aggregates treat it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0.00The customer owes nothing. A real, verified amount.Counted by COUNT(BALANCE); pulls AVG down
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        '' (empty string)A text column holding zero characters. Still a value.Counted as present; LENGTH returns 0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        NULLNobody knows, or the column does not apply here.Skipped by COUNT(column), SUM, and AVG

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The empty string is the one that fools people. In a CHAR or VARCHAR column, '' looks blank on screen and looks identical to a null in most result grids, but the database considers it a stored value. Build your own two-row table and measure the difference with LENGTH.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        LENGTH('') is 0. LENGTH(NULL) is null, because the length of something unknown is also unknown. Dana Reyes and Owen Blake are invented contacts for this table, not people in the shipped data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Row 1120 comes back with a length of 0: there is a value, and it happens to be zero characters long. Row 1310 comes back with a null length, because a function given an unknown input can only produce an unknown answer. Nulls spread that way through almost every expression in SQL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The column has to allow nulls

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CONTACT_NAME in that table was declared NOT NULL. That is a rule stored in the table definition, and the engine enforces it on every write. Asking it to hold a null is not a warning; the statement is rejected and nothing changes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- This one fails on purpose. CONTACT_NAME was declared NOT NULL.
-- UPDATE: the table being changed.
UPDATE CONTACT_LOG

-- SET: BROKEN. NOT NULL is a promise made when the table was created, and the
--   engine enforces it on every statement afterwards - an UPDATE is checked just
--   as strictly as an INSERT. The change is refused and the row is left alone.
SET CONTACT_NAME = NULL

-- WHERE: which row would have been changed, had the constraint allowed it.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- SQLite reports: NOT NULL constraint failed: CONTACT_LOG.CONTACT_NAME
-- MySQL reports:  ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'CONTACT_NAME' cannot be null
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why forbid nulls at all

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Some columns are the reason the row exists. A contact with no name, an invoice with no number, a lease with no student: those rows cannot be used for anything. NOT NULL is how a designer says that out loud so no program can quietly break the rule later. Several columns in the course data are declared this way already, including CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, and STUDENT.LAST_NAME. If a SET column = NULL is refused, the fix is almost never to remove the constraint. It is to ask whether that row should exist.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Finding the nulls afterward

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Once a value is null, ordinary comparison stops working on it. BALANCE = NULL is not false, it is unknown, and a WHERE clause only keeps rows where the condition is definitely true. So the comparison matches nothing at all, including the very row you just emptied. IS NULL is the only test that works.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Read IS NULL as a single operator, like BETWEEN. It is not the = sign with a different word after it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The mirror image

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        IS NOT NULL keeps the rows that do have a value. WHERE BALANCE IS NOT NULL after the update above returns the other three customers, 1120, 1225, and 1420. Together the two tests cover every row in the table, which plain = and <> never do once nulls are present.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Assign the bare keyword NULL, never the quoted text 'NULL'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Include a WHERE clause, and test it as a SELECT first
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Confirm the column is not declared NOT NULL before you try
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Use null for unknown or not applicable, never as a stand-in for zero
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Search for the result with IS NULL, never with = NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Expect COUNT(column), SUM, and AVG to skip the nulled row

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-8 Changing a Table's Structure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A table's structure is not carved in stone. Businesses change, and the tables have to follow. KimTay decides to email invoices instead of mailing them, so CUSTOMER needs somewhere to keep an email address. A supplier's product names outgrow the thirty characters ITEM.DESCRIPTION was given. A column nobody ever filled in is only creating confusion. All three are structure changes, and the statement that makes them is ALTER TABLE.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ALTER TABLE names the table, then states one change to it. Unlike UPDATE, it is not about rows: it changes what columns exist and what they are allowed to hold, for every row at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Adding a column

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- ALTER TABLE: changes the STRUCTURE of an existing table rather than its data.
--   The table keeps its rows throughout.
ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER

-- ADD COLUMN: appends a new column at the end. Every existing row immediately has
--   this column, holding null, because no value was supplied for rows that were
--   already there. The word COLUMN is optional in MySQL and required in SQLite.
ADD COLUMN EMAIL VARCHAR(40);

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The word COLUMN is optional in SQLite, in MySQL, and in Oracle, so ADD EMAIL VARCHAR(40) does the same job; Oracle also accepts a parenthesized list, ADD (EMAIL VARCHAR2(40)). Spelling out ADD COLUMN is the safer habit because it reads unambiguously everywhere. The new column always lands at the end of the table. CUSTOMER ships with nine columns ending in REP_NUM, so EMAIL becomes the tenth. No engine lets you insert a column in the middle.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two statements: one ALTER TABLE to create the column, one UPDATE to put a value in a single row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every existing row starts out null

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The engine cannot invent email addresses for the four customers already stored, so it puts a null in each one. That is exactly the meaning you want here: the address is unknown, not blank. It also means the column you added in the morning will read as null all afternoon until somebody fills it in, and COUNT(EMAIL) will keep telling you how much of that work is left.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Because of that, you cannot add a NOT NULL column to a table that already has rows unless you also supply a DEFAULT. The engine would have to break the new rule the moment it created it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- Rejected: the engine would have to put null in five existing rows.
-- ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL: BROKEN on a table that already holds
--   rows. The new column has no value for them, so the only thing the engine
--   could store is null - which is exactly what NOT NULL forbids. The fix is to
--   add the column nullable, UPDATE every row with a real value, then tighten the
--   constraint; or to supply a DEFAULT the engine can use for the existing rows.
ALTER TABLE ITEM ADD COLUMN SUPPLIER VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL;

-- SQLite reports: Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL
-- Oracle reports ORA-01758: table must be empty to add mandatory (NOT NULL) column

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Give it a default and the same statement succeeds, because now the engine has something legal to write into the rows that are already there.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The clause order is type, then NOT NULL, then DEFAULT. All five items come back reading UNKNOWN.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Changing a column that is already there

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Widening CUSTOMER_NAME from VARCHAR(35) to VARCHAR(50), or changing ON_HAND from SMALLINT to INTEGER, is where the engines stop agreeing with each other. There is no portable statement. Learn the shape of the change, then look up the spelling for the engine in front of you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Changing an existing column, by engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        EngineStatementNotes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        MySQLALTER TABLE CUSTOMER MODIFY CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(50);MODIFY retypes; CHANGE renames and retypes at once
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        OracleALTER TABLE CUSTOMER MODIFY (CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR2(50));The parentheses around the column list are conventional
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL ServerALTER TABLE CUSTOMER ALTER COLUMN CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(50);One column per statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQLite (this page)Not supported at any versionRebuild the table with the copy pattern below
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- MySQL only. Neither of these runs in the sandbox on this page:
-- SQLite answers 'near "MODIFY": syntax error'.
-- MODIFY: changes an existing column's TYPE, leaving its name alone. You restate
--   the full new type, not just the part that is changing.
ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER MODIFY CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(50);

-- CHANGE takes the old name, the new name, and the full type.
-- CHANGE: renames a column and restates its type at the same time. Widening a
--   column is usually safe; narrowing one can truncate stored data, so check the
--   longest value in the column before you shrink it.
ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER CHANGE CUSTOMER_NAME CUSTOMER_TITLE VARCHAR(50);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Narrowing a column is a data change

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Widening is safe. Going the other way is not: shortening DESCRIPTION to VARCHAR(10) has to do something with Small Animal Grooming Kit. Oracle refuses outright if any stored value is too long. MySQL in strict mode refuses as well, and outside strict mode it truncates the text and keeps going. Measure the longest value first with SELECT MAX(LENGTH(DESCRIPTION)) FROM ITEM; which reports 25 on the shipped data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Renaming a column, without changing its type, is better supported: ALTER TABLE REP RENAME COLUMN RATE TO COMMISSION_RATE; works in MySQL 8.0, Oracle, and SQLite 3.25 and later, so it does run in the sandbox on this page. Every query, view, and report that spelled the old name breaks the instant you run it, so search your code for the old name first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Removing a column

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- ALTER TABLE: the table whose structure is changing.
ALTER TABLE CUSTOMER

-- DROP COLUMN: removes the column and every value stored in it, from every row.
--   There is no undo outside a transaction, and no warning about the data going
--   with it - so confirm nothing depends on the column first.
DROP COLUMN EMAIL;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The last SELECT * should come back with the original nine columns and no EMAIL.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Dropping a column takes its data with it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        There is no undo and no recycle bin. If EMAIL held four hundred addresses, they are gone the moment the statement succeeds. Engines also refuse the request in several cases. ALTER TABLE ITEM DROP COLUMN ITEM_ID; fails with cannot drop PRIMARY KEY column: "ITEM_ID", and dropping a column an index is built on fails too, with error in index ... no such column. Most engines block a column that is unique or pointed at by a foreign key until you remove that object first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-8a Making complex changes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Some changes have no single statement anywhere. Splitting one column into two. Reordering columns. Adding a primary key to a table that never had one. Turning a nullable column into NOT NULL after the fact. And, in SQLite, changing any column's type at all. For every one of these, the answer is the same four-step pattern, and it is worth learning even on engines that offer MODIFY, because it is the only approach that always works.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Create the replacement

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CREATE TABLE ITEM_NEW (...) with the structure you actually want, under a temporary name. Write out every column, including the new or retyped ones, and carry over the constraints you are not deliberately changing. ITEM.DESCRIPTION is VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, so the wider version stays NOT NULL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Copy the rows across

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        INSERT INTO ITEM_NEW (columns) SELECT columns FROM ITEM; Name the columns on both sides. Any column in the new table that you leave out of the list stays null, which is what you want for a column that did not exist yesterday.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Check, then drop the original

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Compare COUNT(*) on both tables and spot-check a row. Only then run DROP TABLE ITEM; This is the point of no return.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Rename the replacement

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ALTER TABLE ITEM_NEW RENAME TO ITEM; Every query, view, and program that already refers to ITEM keeps working, because the name it asks for now points at the rebuilt table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Here is the whole pattern on KimTay's ITEM table: DESCRIPTION gets wider, ON_HAND becomes a full INTEGER, and a SUPPLIER column appears. Everything else is copied over exactly as it was. Wrapping it in BEGIN and COMMIT matters, because step three destroys the original. If anything fails in between, the rollback leaves you with the table you started with instead of no table at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SUPPLIER is left out of the INSERT column list on purpose, so all five rows get a null there. Copying CATEGORY as VARCHAR(15) and PRICE as DECIMAL(7,2) keeps them unchanged; a rebuild is a chance to change things by accident as well as on purpose.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        All five items survive, SUPPLIER is null on every row, and a join from INVOICE_LINE to ITEM still returns the same six lines it did before. Nothing outside the table had to change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The copy carries rows, not rules

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE takes the indexes, triggers, and views built on the old table with it, and any foreign key in another table that pointed at it is now aimed at a name that was briefly gone. Write the CREATE INDEX and CREATE VIEW statements you will need to run afterward before you start, and keep them in the same script. On a production database, take a backup first and rehearse the whole script on a copy.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ADD COLUMN puts the column last and fills existing rows with null
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • A NOT NULL column can only be added with a DEFAULT
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Changing a column's type is MySQL MODIFY, Oracle MODIFY (...), SQL Server ALTER COLUMN
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • SQLite cannot retype a column at all, so use the copy pattern
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • DROP COLUMN destroys the data in it and is refused on key or indexed columns
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • For anything else: create, copy, drop, rename, inside one transaction

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6-9 Dropping a Table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE removes a table from the database. Not the rows in it, the table itself: the structure, the column definitions, the indexes, and every row inside. Afterward the name does not exist, and a query that mentions it fails the way a query for a misspelled table fails.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- DROP TABLE: removes the whole table - definition, columns and rows together.
--   Compare it with DELETE FROM ITEM_ARCHIVE;, which empties the table but leaves
--   it in place, ready to be filled again.
DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        That is the entire statement. Its brevity is the danger: there is no WHERE, no preview, and no confirmation prompt. Work through the whole life of a scratch table so you can see the before and the after.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two supporting pieces show up in that walkthrough. CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT builds a brand-new table whose columns and rows both come from a query, which is the quickest way to make something disposable. And to ask the database which tables currently exist, SQLite reads its own catalog table, sqlite_master; MySQL answers the same question with SHOW TABLES; or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES. Module 7 covers catalogs properly, so treat this as a peek.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The archive should hold two rows, AV07 and FT88. The first catalog list has six names; the second has five.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The rows go with the table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE; did not ask whether the two rows mattered. DELETE FROM ITEM_ARCHIVE; would have emptied the table and left the structure standing, ready to be refilled. DROP TABLE leaves nothing. On a real database, the only way back is a backup, so the question to answer before you press Enter is not whether you need the rows today but whether anyone needs them next quarter.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Dropping a table that might not be there

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A setup script that starts by dropping yesterday's scratch tables fails on the very first run, because the tables do not exist yet. IF EXISTS turns that error into a no-op, which is why nearly every rebuild script is written this way.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: the same removal, but silent when the table is already
--   gone. This is what makes a setup script safe to re-run from the top: the
--   drops succeed whether or not the tables happen to exist yet.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_ARCHIVE;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Engine support

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE IF EXISTS works in SQLite, MySQL, and SQL Server. Oracle had no IF EXISTS on DROP TABLE before 23ai; older Oracle scripts either accept the ORA-00942: table or view does not exist error or wrap the drop in a PL/SQL block that catches it. Note that IF EXISTS only suppresses the missing-table error. It does not suppress anything else, including a foreign key violation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The foreign-key ordering problem

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Tables are rarely alone. In KimTay's database INVOICE_LINE carries a foreign key to ITEM and another to INVOICE, and INVOICE carries one to CUSTOMER, which carries one to REP. Dropping ITEM while INVOICE_LINE still holds rows that name AV07 leaves those rows pointing at a table that is gone. The lines still exist, but nothing can tell you what was ordered.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An engine that is enforcing foreign keys stops you. MySQL and Oracle do this by default; SQLite only does it when the check has been switched on for the session, which is why the sandbox on this page lets the drop through.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- SQLite, with enforcement switched on for the session:
-- PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON: SQLite ships with foreign key checking OFF, and this
--   turns it on for the current connection. It has to be set before you rely on
--   any of the protection below.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- DROP TABLE: refused. INVOICE_LINE holds rows whose ITEM_ID points at this
--   table, and dropping it would leave those rows referring to nothing. The
--   database is protecting its own integrity - drop the child table first, or
--   remove the rows that depend on this one.
DROP TABLE ITEM;

-- Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

-- MySQL says the same thing at more length:
-- ERROR 3730 (HY000): Cannot drop table 'ITEM' referenced by a
-- foreign key constraint on table 'invoice_line'.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The rule is to drop children before parents: a table that points at another table has to go first. Read the relationships backwards, from the most dependent table to the least.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        List what points at what

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In KimTay: INVOICE_LINE points at INVOICE and ITEM. INVOICE points at CUSTOMER. CUSTOMER points at REP. ITEM and REP point at nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Drop the most dependent table first

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE INVOICE_LINE; Nothing points at it, so it comes off cleanly.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Work outward

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE INVOICE; then DROP TABLE ITEM; then DROP TABLE CUSTOMER; then DROP TABLE REP; Each one is safe because everything that referenced it is already gone. Only the dependencies are fixed, not the whole sequence: once INVOICE_LINE is gone, INVOICE and ITEM are independent of each other and may be dropped in either order.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Or remove the constraint instead

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        When you only want the one table gone, drop the foreign key from the child rather than the child itself: ALTER TABLE INVOICE_LINE DROP FOREIGN KEY ... in MySQL, ALTER TABLE INVOICE_LINE DROP CONSTRAINT ... in Oracle and SQL Server.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Now see the consequence for yourself. The sandbox on this page does not enforce foreign keys, so it will let you drop the parent, which makes it the perfect place to look at the wreckage.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every line survives with its ITEM_ID, but AV07 and FT88 are now codes with nothing to look them up in.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        All six invoice lines come back. 50712 still says it ordered one AV07 at 64.99, and there is no longer any way to learn that AV07 was an Aviary Starter Cage. Add INNER JOIN ITEM to that query and it does not return partial results, it fails outright with no such table: ITEM. Every report, view, and program that joined to ITEM broke at the same moment.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Four ways to remove something, and what survives
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        StatementWhat it removesWhat is left
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DELETE FROM ITEM WHERE ...Matching rows onlyThe table, its columns, indexes, and other rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DELETE FROM ITEM;Every rowAn empty table you can insert into again
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ALTER TABLE ITEM DROP COLUMN SUPPLIER;One column and its data (here, the column 6-8 added)The table and all its other columns
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DROP TABLE ITEM;The table, its rows, and its indexesNothing. Referencing queries now fail
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A habit worth keeping

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Before dropping anything on a database that matters, run CREATE TABLE ITEM_BACKUP AS SELECT * FROM ITEM; first. It costs one statement and a little disk, and it turns an unrecoverable mistake into an inconvenient one. Note that the copy carries the rows only, not the primary key, the indexes, or the foreign keys, so it is a rescue kit rather than a replacement. Drop the backup when you are sure, which is usually a week later, not the same afternoon.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • DROP TABLE removes the structure and every row, with no undo
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • DELETE empties a table; DROP TABLE erases it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Use IF EXISTS in scripts that may run more than once
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Drop child tables before the parent tables they point at
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Tables that do not reference each other may go in any order
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Take a copy first: CREATE TABLE X_BACKUP AS SELECT * FROM X;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Summary What You Learned in Module 6

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Module 6 moved you from asking a database questions to changing what it holds. The first half was about rows: creating a table, adding rows, correcting them, removing them, and doing that work inside a transaction so a half-finished change can be undone. The second half, sections 6-7 through 6-9, was about the shape of the tables themselves.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Working with nulls

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        UPDATE ... SET column = NULL empties a value on purpose, and it is the honest choice when a fact is unknown rather than zero. The column must not be declared NOT NULL. Find the result with IS NULL, never = NULL, and expect COUNT(column), SUM, and AVG to skip the row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Reshaping a table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN appends a column and nulls it on every existing row. DROP COLUMN destroys the column and its data. Changing a column's type is spelled differently in every engine and is not available in SQLite at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Underneath all four is one idea worth carrying into Module 7: statements that change data are not reversible by another query. A wrong SELECT wastes a minute. A wrong UPDATE without a WHERE, a wrong DROP COLUMN, or a wrong DROP TABLE costs whatever was in there. The professional habits are small and always the same: write the SELECT first, keep a backup or a transaction open, and change one thing at a time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The second UPDATE is the only one with a WHERE clause, and that is deliberate: the first is meant to touch all three rows.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        You should see Kaiser and Hull in the North territory and Perez with a null, then 3 reps of whom 2 have a known territory. The final ALTER TABLE puts REP back to its original nine columns, exactly the way the module found it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Looking ahead

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Everything in this module assumed you were allowed to make these changes. Module 7 is about who is allowed: views that show a user part of a table, GRANT and REVOKE for permissions, indexes for speed, and the system catalog that lists what exists. Several of those statements are MySQL and Oracle only. GRANT and REVOKE are not implemented in SQLite at all, and a view on this page can be created and queried but not updated through, so the text will name the engine each time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Data definition versus data manipulation

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE change the rows inside a table and are called data manipulation, or DML. CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, and DROP TABLE change what tables and columns exist and are called data definition, or DDL. The distinction matters on the job: in MySQL and Oracle, DDL commits your transaction the moment it runs, so a ROLLBACK after an ALTER TABLE will not put the column back. SQLite is the exception, which is why the rebuild pattern on this page can safely sit inside BEGIN and COMMIT.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        One small check to keep the most confused pair straight. IS NULL is a test, and it returns 1 for true and 0 for false in this engine. Run it against a null, a zero, and an empty string at the same time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        You should get 1, 0, 0. Only the null is null; zero and the empty string are values.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Review Module 6 Review

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The ten questions below are cumulative. Most of them are about sections 6-7 through 6-9, but several reach back to the WHERE clauses, joins, subqueries, and aggregate functions you have been using since Module 4, because that is how the material shows up in practice: a structure change is almost always followed by a query that has to still work. Read each scenario, decide before you look at the options, and read every note afterward, including the ones for the answers you did not pick.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How to use the notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Each wrong option has a note naming the specific mistake it represents. Those mistakes are the ones that cost people real data, so the note is more valuable than the checkmark. If a note describes something you would have done, go back to the section it came from before moving on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Before you start, warm up in the sandbox. This one combines a structure change from 6-8, a subquery from Module 5, and the null behavior from 6-7 in a single short script: KimTay wants to record, on each customer row, whether that customer was invoiced on June 14.

The other two customers keep the null the ADD COLUMN gave them, which is exactly the right answer for them.

Downtown Aquarium & Pets was invoiced on the fifteenth, and Companion Care Clinic has never been invoiced at all, so both stay null. The counts confirm it: 4 customers, 2 with a known invoice date.
