Three rows come back: AV07 at 64.99, CF21 at 42.5 and FT88 at 27.75.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can write CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ... and select from the result
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can explain that a view stores a query, not rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can say why a view is always current: the defining query runs on every use
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can rename a view's columns with a parenthesized list after the view name
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can build a view over a join and a view over GROUP BY
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can name the two reasons views exist: simplification, and showing a user only part of a table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: creating and using views

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1An overnight price change at KimTay

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KimTay defines HABITAT as a view selecting item id, description, on hand and price from ITEM where the category is Habitat. Overnight a buyer changes the price of AV07 in the ITEM table. The next morning a clerk runs SELECT * FROM HABITAT;. What price does the clerk see for AV07?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Treats a view as a snapshot of data. A view stores a query, never rows, so there is nothing to go out of date.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Assumes a view can become inconsistent with its base table. It cannot, since it reads that base table on every use.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct. The view has no rows of its own; the SELECT behind it executes fresh each time the view is named.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Confuses a plain view with an Oracle materialized view. Plain views in MySQL and SQLite have no refresh step.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A view is never stale because its defining query runs at the moment of use, not at the moment of creation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2The four-table join in three reports

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KimTay's sales, reorder and collections reports each retype the same four-table join across INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM and CUSTOMER. A DBA proposes storing that join as the view INVOICE_DETAIL. Which benefit of the proposal is genuine?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct. Simplification is the point: one definition to review, one place to fix when the join rules change.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. Describes caching. A plain view stores no results, so every use pays for the join again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. Views do not restrict what other queries may do; only granted permissions can do that.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Nothing about the base tables changes. The view leaves all four tables exactly as they were.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A view buys clarity and reuse, not stored results and not enforcement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3What the front counter may see

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KimTay wants counter staff to read customer numbers, names and balances from CUSTOMER, but never credit limits. Which approach uses a view the way views are meant to be used?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Destroys data the business needs elsewhere. A view restricts what one group sees without changing the table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. A view that exposes every column protects nothing. Relying on people not to look is not access control.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. A nightly copy is stale between refreshes and doubles the storage and the maintenance burden.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct. What the defining query omits cannot be read through the view, and the base table is untouched.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: Showing a user only part of a table is a design goal you meet by narrowing the view's column list, not by changing the table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                7-2 Using a View to Update Data

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Reading through a view is easy. Writing through one is where the rules start. The question the database has to answer is always the same: if you change a row of the view, can it work out exactly which row of exactly which base table to change, with no guessing? When the answer is yes, the view is updatable. When the answer involves a guess, the update is refused.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Updatable view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A view is updatable when every row it produces maps back to one identifiable row in one base table, so that UPDATE, INSERT and DELETE against the view can be rewritten into the same operation against that base table. A view that summarizes, combines or collapses rows breaks that mapping.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Engine note - read this before you run anything

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The sandbox on this page runs SQLite, which refuses every attempt to modify a view. UPDATE HABITAT SET PRICE = 69.99 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'AV07'; comes back as cannot modify HABITAT because it is a view. MySQL is different: it accepts updates through views it judges updatable. So on this page the update attempts are MySQL code blocks, marked as such and not runnable here. Every sandbox shows the route that does run everywhere: change the base table, then select from the view and watch it change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                7-2a Updating row-and-column subset views

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A row-and-column subset view draws from one base table, keeps a subset of its rows with a WHERE clause and a subset of its columns in the SELECT list, and does nothing else. No join, no GROUP BY, no aggregate, no DISTINCT. This is the one shape that is usually updatable, because each view row is one base row wearing fewer clothes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Consider a view over the customers assigned to rep 20.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- CREATE VIEW: define a named query called KAISER_CUST.
CREATE VIEW KAISER_CUST AS

-- SELECT: four of CUSTOMER's nine columns. The five left out are invisible to
--   anyone using this view - a simple and effective way to hide data.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

-- FROM: the base table the view reads from.
FROM   CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: restricts the view to one rep's customers. Someone querying KAISER_CUST
--   cannot see the others at all, no matter what they write.
WHERE  REP_NUM = '20';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                That view returns two customers from the shipped data: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic. In MySQL, raising the credit limit of Companion Care Clinic through the view works. MySQL rewrites the statement against CUSTOMER, adding the view's own condition to yours.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- UPDATE: a view can be updated when it is simple enough - one base table, no
--   grouping, no aggregates and the key present. This one qualifies.
UPDATE KAISER_CUST

-- SET: the new value. It is written through the view and lands in CUSTOMER, the
--   real table; the view stores nothing of its own.
SET    CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00

-- WHERE: the row being changed, which must be a row the view can see.
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                That is the happy case. Three things still go wrong often enough that you should expect them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Columns the view cannot see. KAISER_CUST has no REP_NUM column, so an INSERT through the view has no way to supply one. In MySQL the new customer lands in CUSTOMER with REP_NUM left null - a null produced by that insert, not one present in any shipped row - and it is immediately invisible through the very view that created it. Had REP_NUM been declared NOT NULL with no default, MySQL in strict mode would reject the insert outright with error 1364.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Rows that migrate out. If a view filters on a column it also exposes, an update to that column can push the row out of the view. The update succeeds, the base row is fine, and the row vanishes from the user's screen.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Required columns the view cannot reach. An INSERT through a view can only supply the view's own columns. Every other column of the base table must be able to take a default or a null. A NOT NULL column with no default that the view omits - very often the primary key itself, since keys like CUSTOMER_NUM are not auto-generated - makes the insert impossible, and MySQL reports error 1364.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- INSERT INTO a view: the new row is really added to CUSTOMER. The catch is that
--   the view only names four columns, so every other column of CUSTOMER - REP_NUM
--   included - is left null.
INSERT INTO KAISER_CUST (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT)

-- VALUES: the four values supplied. The new customer has no rep number, which
--   means the view's own WHERE clause excludes it: you insert a row through the
--   view and then cannot see it. That surprise is the reason for CHECK OPTION.
VALUES ('1550', 'Harbor Reef Supply', 0.00, 4000.00);

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                MySQL and Oracle both offer a guard against the migrating-row problem: add WITH CHECK OPTION to the view definition. Any change that would move a row out of the view is then rejected instead of quietly hiding it. SQLite has no WITH CHECK OPTION, so these two blocks are MySQL only.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- CREATE VIEW: another single-table view, this one restricted by city.
CREATE VIEW BROOKVILLE_CUST AS

-- SELECT: the four columns the view exposes.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY, BALANCE

-- FROM: the base table.
FROM   CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the rows the view can see.
WHERE  CITY = 'Brookville'

-- WITH CHECK OPTION: refuses any INSERT or UPDATE through this view that would
--   produce a row the view could not then see. It closes the trap in the previous
--   example - rows cannot be pushed out of sight through the view that made them.
WITH CHECK OPTION;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- UPDATE: an attempt to change a row through the protected view.
UPDATE BROOKVILLE_CUST

-- SET: BROKEN by the CHECK OPTION. Moving this customer to Northfield would put
--   it outside the view's WHERE clause, so the row would vanish from the very
--   view that changed it. The engine rejects the statement instead.
SET    CITY = 'Northfield'

-- WHERE: the row that would have been moved.
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Without WITH CHECK OPTION that update succeeds and the row disappears from the view. With it, MySQL raises error 1369, a CHECK OPTION failure, and nothing changes. The sandbox below shows the disappearing act for real, by changing the base table instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Whiskers & Wags Boutique is the only Brookville customer, so the view starts with one row and ends with none. The final query proves the row is still in CUSTOMER, alive and well, now showing Northfield. It stopped satisfying the defining query, that is all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Now the other half of the base-table route. Watch a subset view pick up exactly the rows that belong in it, and ignore the ones that do not.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Two customers were added to the base table and only one shows up in the view, which goes from two rows to three: 1550 belongs to rep 20, 1600 does not. Because the insert went to CUSTOMER, it could supply REP_NUM, which is precisely the column the view cannot reach.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                7-2b Updating views involving joins

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A view over a join is usually not updatable, and the reason is worth understanding rather than memorizing. A single row of a join view is assembled from two or more base rows. Change something in that view row and the database has to decide which base row you meant. Worse, one base row can feed several view rows, so a change that looks like it touches one line on your screen may quietly touch several.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- CREATE VIEW: a view over a JOIN, which is where views earn their keep - the
--   join is written once, and everybody else just selects from CUST_REP.
CREATE VIEW CUST_REP AS

-- SELECT: five columns drawn from two tables, using the aliases defined below.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, C.BALANCE, R.LAST_NAME, R.RATE

-- FROM: the first base table, aliased C.
FROM   CUSTOMER C

-- INNER JOIN ... ON: the second base table and the matching condition. Because
--   two tables feed the view, updating through it becomes much more delicate.
       INNER JOIN REP R ON C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                MySQL will accept an update through this view only when the statement changes columns belonging to exactly one base table. The statement below qualifies, since LAST_NAME comes from REP alone. It succeeds, and it changes more than the person typing it expected.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- UPDATE: a change through the join view.
UPDATE CUST_REP

-- SET: this looks like it edits one customer's row, but LAST_NAME belongs to REP.
--   Kaiser serves two customers, so the single change would alter the name shown
--   on both rows of the view - one statement, two rows affected, in a table the
--   user may not realise they touched.
SET    LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu'

-- WHERE: the customer being aimed at.
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The WHERE clause names one customer, so one view row looks targeted. But the update lands on rep 20's single row in REP, and rep 20 also serves Companion Care Clinic. Two rows of the view change. Run the base-table equivalent and see it for yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                One row of REP changed. Two rows of the view changed: Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, both served by rep 20, now show 0.06 while 1225 stays 0.07 and 1420 stays 0.05. That one-to-many fan-out is exactly the ambiguity that makes join views dangerous to write through.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Ask the join view to change columns from two base tables at once and MySQL stops cooperating altogether. The statement below touches BALANCE, which lives in CUSTOMER, and LAST_NAME, which lives in REP.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- UPDATE: a single statement touching both base tables at once.
UPDATE CUST_REP

-- SET: BALANCE lives in CUSTOMER...
SET    BALANCE   = 4000.00,

--   ...and LAST_NAME lives in REP. Most engines refuse to update two base tables
--   in one statement through a view, because there is no way to say which change
--   should happen first or what to do if only one succeeds.
       LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu'

-- WHERE: the row being aimed at.
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                MySQL rejects that with error 1393, Can not modify more than one base table through a join view. Oracle applies a related rule built on key-preserved tables: you may change columns of the one table whose primary key still uniquely identifies each row of the join, and nothing else. Different wording, same instinct.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What each engine does with a write against a view
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                StatementThis sandbox (SQLite)MySQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SELECT from any viewAllowedAllowed
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                UPDATE through a row-and-column subset viewRefused: cannot modify V because it is a viewAllowed, rewritten against the base table
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                INSERT or UPDATE through a join viewRefusedAllowed only when exactly one base table is touched
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                UPDATE through a GROUP BY viewRefusedRefused: target table is not updatable, error 1288

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                7-2c Updating views involving statistics

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A view built on aggregates is never updatable, in any engine, and there is no clever workaround. The reason is not a restriction someone chose to impose. It is that the number you want to change does not exist anywhere until the query computes it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- CREATE VIEW: a view built on a GROUPED query, so each of its rows summarises
--   several rows of the base table.
CREATE VIEW REP_BALANCE AS

-- SELECT: the grouping column...
SELECT REP_NUM,

--   ...and two aggregates. ROUND trims the total to two decimal places.
       COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS,
       ROUND(SUM(BALANCE), 2) AS TOTAL_BALANCE

-- FROM: the base table.
FROM   CUSTOMER

-- GROUP BY: one view row per rep. Every value in the view is computed, which is
--   what makes the next two statements impossible.
GROUP BY REP_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Rep 20's TOTAL_BALANCE is 3512.5, the sum of two customer balances: 3512.50 for Access Pet Center and 0.00 for Companion Care Clinic. Suppose someone tries to set it to 4000.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- UPDATE: BROKEN, and unavoidably so.
UPDATE REP_BALANCE

-- SET: TOTAL_BALANCE is a SUM of several customers' balances. Setting it to 4000
--   would mean the engine deciding how to split that figure back across the
--   individual rows, and there is no correct answer - so grouped views are simply
--   not updatable, in any engine.
SET    TOTAL_BALANCE = 4000.00

-- WHERE: picks the one row - rep 20's summary - the broken UPDATE targets.
WHERE  REP_NUM = '20';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Which balance should move? Access Pet Center's, Companion Care Clinic's, or some split between them? There is no answer in the statement and no answer in the data. MySQL reports error 1288, The target table REP_BALANCE of the UPDATE is not updatable. A DELETE fares no better: deleting a summary row would mean deleting an unspecified number of customers.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
-- DELETE FROM a grouped view: BROKEN for the same reason. One row of this view
--   stands for several real customer rows, and deleting it would have to mean
--   deleting all of them - which is certainly not what the statement says.
DELETE FROM REP_BALANCE

-- WHERE: rep 35's summary row - the one this broken DELETE would remove.
WHERE  REP_NUM = '35';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The correct move is the one the data supports: change a real balance on a real customer, and let the view recompute. Run this and watch the total follow.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Rep 20's total moves from 3512.5 to 4012.5 and the other two reps do not budge: 1200 for rep 35, 4820.75 for rep 65. You never wrote to the view. You wrote to one customer, and the aggregate recomputed on the next use, because that is what a view does.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The three questions

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Before writing through a view, ask in order. One table? If the defining query names more than one table, expect refusal or surprise. One row per row? If GROUP BY, DISTINCT or an aggregate collapses rows, the answer is no and the engine will say so. Every required column reachable? If a NOT NULL column with no default is missing from the view, an INSERT cannot succeed. Three yes answers and you probably have an updatable view. Any no, and the honest fix is to write to the base table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can define what makes a view updatable in one sentence about mapping to base rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can explain why a row-and-column subset view is usually updatable
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can describe the migrating-row problem and what WITH CHECK OPTION does about it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can explain why a join view update can change more rows than the WHERE clause names
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can state the MySQL rule that a join view update may touch only one base table
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can give the real reason an aggregate view is never updatable, not just assert that it is
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • I can always fall back to updating the base table and reselecting from the view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                🔍 Check yourself: updating through a view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q1Raising a credit limit at Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KAISER_CUST selects customer number, name, balance and credit limit from CUSTOMER where the rep number is 20. In MySQL a DBA runs UPDATE KAISER_CUST SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Overgeneralizes from SQLite, which refuses all view writes. MySQL accepts writes to views it judges updatable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔b. Correct. This is a row-and-column subset of one table, so each view row maps to exactly one CUSTOMER row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. There is no copy inside a view. Any change that succeeds lands in the base table or nowhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. The view's condition is added to your WHERE clause, not substituted for it, so only customer 1310 changes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A row-and-column subset view is updatable because every view row traces back to one unambiguous base row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q2Adding Harbor Reef Supply through a partial view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                KAISER_CUST exposes customer number, name, balance and credit limit, but not REP_NUM, which the CUSTOMER table permits to be null even though every shipped row has a rep. In MySQL a DBA inserts a new customer supplying values for the four view columns. What is the result?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. Columns you omit take their default or null. The insert is only rejected if an omitted column is NOT NULL with no default.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. It cannot appear: with REP_NUM null the new row fails the view's condition immediately.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. A WHERE clause filters rows; it never assigns values. WITH CHECK OPTION would reject the insert, not repair it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔d. Correct. The view cannot reach REP_NUM, so the new row misses the very condition that defines the view.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: A column missing from a view is a column an INSERT through that view cannot supply, and the new row may vanish on arrival.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q3Correcting a rep's name through CUST_REP

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                CUST_REP joins CUSTOMER to REP and shows the rep's last name beside each customer. In MySQL a DBA runs UPDATE CUST_REP SET LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu' WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';. MySQL allows it because only one base table is touched. What is the danger?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔a. Correct. Rep 20 also serves Companion Care Clinic, so a WHERE clause naming one customer alters two view rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. MySQL does not discard the update; it performs it against REP, which is exactly the problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘c. A view has no rows to change on its own. The write reaches REP or it does not happen.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. No engine duplicates base rows to resolve an update. The change lands on the single REP row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: One base row can feed many view rows, so an update through a join view can reach further than its WHERE clause suggests.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Q4Editing a rep's total balance

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                REP_BALANCE groups CUSTOMER by rep number and reports a customer count and the sum of balances. Rep 20's total is 3512.5. Why will no engine accept UPDATE REP_BALANCE SET TOTAL_BALANCE = 4000.00 WHERE REP_NUM = '20';?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘a. The data type is irrelevant. The same refusal applies to COUNT, MIN and every other aggregate.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘b. WITH CHECK OPTION guards migrating rows in a subset view; it has no bearing on aggregate views.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✔c. Correct. The total is computed from two customer balances, so the engine cannot tell which balance you meant.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ✘d. Recreating the view changes nothing. The obstacle is the aggregation itself, not the view's age.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Remember: An aggregate view is never updatable because the value you want to change is computed at query time and stored nowhere.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Each card describes one view over the KimTay tables. Drop it into the zone that says whether a change made through it could reach a single, unambiguous base-table row, and if not, what stands in the way.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-3 Dropping a View

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      When a view has outlived its usefulness, remove it with DROP VIEW. This is the least dramatic statement in the module, and the one students most often fear. Say the rule out loud once: DROP VIEW removes the stored query. It never removes data. It cannot remove data, because the view never held any.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DROP VIEW: removes the saved query and nothing else. The base tables and every
--   row in them are untouched - you are deleting a definition, not data. That is
--   the key difference between DROP VIEW and DROP TABLE.
DROP VIEW view_name;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Prove it rather than trusting it. The sandbox below builds a view of the cheaper items, confirms the view exists in the system catalog, drops it, and then goes looking for the data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The catalog lists SMALL_ITEM, then after the drop it lists nothing. The last two queries return the same three items the view was showing, DG04, FT88 and GR15, and confirm all five rows of ITEM are still there. The only thing that disappeared was the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      One word apart, worlds apart

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DROP VIEW SMALL_ITEM; costs you a definition you can retype in thirty seconds. DROP TABLE ITEM; costs you the company's product catalog. The statements look alike at three in the afternoon on a Friday. Read the second word before pressing Enter, and never test a DROP against production.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What each statement takes away
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      StatementRemovesLeaves behind
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DROP VIEW HABITAT;The stored HABITAT query onlyEvery row in ITEM, untouched
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DELETE FROM ITEM WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';The habitat rows in ITEMThe HABITAT definition, now returning nothing
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DROP TABLE ITEM;The ITEM table and all five rowsThe HABITAT definition, now broken

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two footnotes on that table. The middle row assumes foreign keys are not being enforced; with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON those two items are still quoted on invoice 50712, so the DELETE fails with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. And the third row deserves a moment of its own. Dropping a base table does not drop the views built on it. The definition survives as an orphan and fails the next time somebody uses it, with no such table: main.ITEM. Cleaning up a table means cleaning up its views too.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DROP VIEW and IF EXISTS

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Dropping a view that is not there is an error. In this engine the message is no such view: NOPE; MySQL reports error 1051, Unknown table. Both engines accept IF EXISTS, which turns the error into a shrug. That is why every sandbox in this module opens with DROP VIEW IF EXISTS: it lets you press Run twice without the second run failing on a name that is already gone.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DROP VIEW on something that is not there: an error that stops a script.
DROP VIEW NOPE;            -- error: the view does not exist

-- IF EXISTS: the same statement made safe to re-run. Nothing happens and no error
--   is raised, which is why teardown scripts are written this way.
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS NOPE;  -- no error, nothing to do

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Views built on views

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A view's defining query may name another view. That is convenient and it creates a dependency you have to remember when it is time to clean up. Drop the inner view and the outer one is left pointing at nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Only FT88 satisfies both filters, so CHEAP_HABITAT returns one row. Note that CHEAP_HABITAT filters on CATEGORY, a column it does not itself expose but which CHEAP_ITEM does. The drops run outermost first, VIEWS_LEFT is 0, and ITEM still has all five rows at the end.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Reverse the drop order and the database lets you do it. Neither this engine nor MySQL stops you from removing a view that another view depends on. The damage only shows up later, when somebody uses the survivor.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DROP VIEW: this one works, because CHEAP_ITEM exists.
DROP VIEW CHEAP_ITEM;        -- succeeds

-- SELECT from a view built ON that view: now broken. A view defined over another
--   view stores only the text of its query, so dropping the one underneath leaves
--   the survivor pointing at a name that no longer resolves. The failure appears
--   at query time, not at drop time - check what depends on a view before you
--   drop it.
SELECT * FROM CHEAP_HABITAT; -- fails: no such table: main.CHEAP_ITEM
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Before you drop anything

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      List what exists first. SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view'; shows every view in this engine. MySQL has no sqlite_master; there you would query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS instead. Reading the catalog costs one query and has saved a great many afternoons.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can drop a view with DROP VIEW name;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can state without hedging that DROP VIEW never deletes data
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can tell DROP VIEW, DELETE FROM and DROP TABLE apart by what each one destroys
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I know IF EXISTS prevents the no-such-view error and makes a script rerunnable
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I know dropping a base table leaves its views behind, broken
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can list the existing views from the system catalog before I drop anything

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      🔍 Check yourself: dropping a view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q1Retiring the HABITAT view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      KimTay no longer needs the HABITAT view, which showed AV07 and FT88 out of the five rows in ITEM. A DBA runs DROP VIEW HABITAT;. What is the state of ITEM afterwards?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. A view holds no rows, so dropping it cannot remove any. This is the fear the statement's name invites and it is unfounded.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔b. Correct. DROP VIEW removes a definition from the catalog and touches no data at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. No engine creates a backup on DROP VIEW. There is nothing to back up.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Dropping a view places no restriction of any kind on the base table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: DROP VIEW deletes a stored query and nothing else; the data was never inside the view to begin with.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q2Dropping the inner view first at KimTay

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CHEAP_HABITAT is defined over CHEAP_ITEM, which is defined over ITEM. A DBA runs DROP VIEW CHEAP_ITEM; without touching CHEAP_HABITAT first. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. Neither SQLite nor MySQL cascades the drop to dependent views; the orphan is left in the catalog.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. No dependency check happens at drop time, which is precisely why the problem is easy to create.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. Views never copy rows, so there is nothing stored to insulate CHEAP_HABITAT from the loss.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Correct. The drop succeeds quietly and the failure surfaces later as no such table: main.CHEAP_ITEM on the next use.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Dependencies are not enforced when you drop, so list your views first and remove the outermost one before the one it reads.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-4 Security

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Everything you have written so far assumes the person at the keyboard is allowed to see everything. Real databases do not work that way. KimTay's shipping desk needs a customer's street and city to print a label. It has no business seeing what that customer owes or how much credit the company has extended. Security in SQL is the work of matching each account's access to the job that account actually does.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The DBMS is the right place to do that work. If you enforce the rule inside the application, anyone who reaches the data another way walks straight past it - a reporting tool, a command line, a second app written next year. A privilege granted in the DBMS holds no matter how the account arrives.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Privilege

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A privilege is one action, on one database object, for one account: SELECT on CUSTOMER, UPDATE on ITEM. The DBA hands privileges out with GRANT and takes them back with REVOKE. Until some privilege is granted, an account can do nothing at all to that object.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Granting a privilege with GRANT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The shape of the statement reads like a sentence: GRANT the privilege ON the object TO the account. The account has to exist on the server already - GRANT hands out access, it does not create users.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- MySQL and Oracle only. GRANT is not implemented in SQLite,
-- so this statement cannot run in the sandboxes on this page.
-- GRANT: gives a privilege away. Read it in three parts - WHAT (SELECT), ON WHAT
--   (the CUSTOMER table), TO WHOM (the shipping_clerk account). Nothing else is
--   granted, so that account can read this one table and do nothing more to it.
GRANT SELECT ON CUSTOMER TO shipping_clerk;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      After that statement, shipping_clerk can read CUSTOMER and do nothing else to it - no INSERT, no UPDATE, no DELETE - and still has no access at all to ITEM, INVOICE, or anything else. Privileges are additive: the account holds exactly what has been granted, one grant at a time. In MySQL an account name normally carries a host, so you will more often write 'shipping_clerk'@'localhost'; Oracle uses the bare name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Engine note: this whole section is MySQL and Oracle

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQLite has no user accounts, so it implements neither GRANT nor REVOKE. Run the first in a sandbox and you get near "GRANT": syntax error; run the second and you get near "REVOKE": syntax error. That is why every security statement on this page sits in a plain code block, never in a sandbox. Read them as MySQL and Oracle code - with one split flagged further down, where PUBLIC is Oracle only. The view work at the end of the section does run in SQLite, and you can execute all of it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The privileges you will grant most often
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      PrivilegeWhat the account may doA plausible holder at KimTay
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SELECTRead rows from the table or viewA reporting account that reads INVOICE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      INSERTAdd new rowsThe account that loads new INVOICE_LINE rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      UPDATEChange values in existing rowsThe account that adjusts ON_HAND on ITEM
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DELETERemove rowsA cleanup account that clears cancelled invoices
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ALLEvery privilege the DBMS defines on that objectThe owner of the ITEM catalog, and nobody else
