                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You can list several privileges in one statement, and you can narrow UPDATE down to named columns. That last form is worth knowing: it lets one account change a customer's credit limit without touching the customer's balance.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- MySQL and Oracle only.
-- Several privileges at once: separate them with commas. This account may read,
--   add and change rows in ITEM - but not delete any, because DELETE is absent.
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON ITEM TO inventory_clerk;

-- A COLUMN-level grant: the parentheses narrow UPDATE to one column, so the
--   credit manager can change a credit limit and nothing else on the row.
GRANT UPDATE (CREDIT_LIMIT) ON CUSTOMER TO credit_manager;

-- ALL: every privilege the grantor holds on that table. Convenient, and the usual
--   way people accidentally hand out DELETE and DROP - name privileges instead.
GRANT ALL ON ITEM TO inventory_manager;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ALL is a decision, not a shortcut

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      GRANT ALL is quick to type and hard to undo mentally - once several accounts hold it, nobody remembers who needs what. Grant the specific privileges the job requires. If you find yourself reaching for ALL because listing them is tedious, that is a sign the account may not need direct table access at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Granting to everyone: PUBLIC in Oracle, a role in MySQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Some data really is for everyone. The ITEM catalog at KimTay is a fair example: every department needs to look up a description and a price, and nobody outside the buying team should change one. Oracle reserves an account name for exactly this case, PUBLIC, so you do not have to name account after account.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- Oracle. PUBLIC is a reserved name meaning every account in the database.
-- GRANT ... TO PUBLIC: hands the privilege to every existing account and every
--   account created afterwards. Reasonable for a reference table like a product
--   catalogue; a serious mistake on anything holding personal or financial data.
GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO PUBLIC;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      MySQL has no PUBLIC. Type that same statement there and MySQL reads PUBLIC as an ordinary account name; since MySQL 8 will not create an account as a side effect of GRANT, the server rejects the statement instead of quietly granting anything. The MySQL way to say "everyone" is a role you grant to each account - and because a role is not active until it is made a default, that second statement matters as much as the first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- MySQL. No PUBLIC exists, so build a role and hand it out.
-- CREATE ROLE: a named bundle of privileges. Granting to a role rather than to
--   people means one place to change when the rules change.
CREATE ROLE catalog_reader;

-- GRANT ... TO the role: the privilege attaches to the bundle, not to a person.
GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO catalog_reader;

-- GRANT the role to an account: MySQL identifies accounts as user@host, so the
--   host part is included. The clerk now holds everything the role holds.
GRANT catalog_reader TO 'shipping_clerk'@'localhost';

-- SET DEFAULT ROLE: MySQL roles are inactive until activated, so without this
--   line the clerk would log in with none of the privileges just granted.
SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO 'shipping_clerk'@'localhost';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      PUBLIC includes accounts that do not exist yet

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In Oracle, a grant to PUBLIC covers every account in the database, including the ones somebody creates next year. It also means REVOKE SELECT ON ITEM FROM temp_analyst; accomplishes nothing on its own - that account still reads ITEM through the PUBLIC grant, and the PUBLIC grant is the one that has to go. Reserve PUBLIC for data you would be comfortable showing any employee.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Taking it back with REVOKE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      REVOKE mirrors GRANT with one word changed: privileges are granted TO an account and revoked FROM one. The mismatch trips people up constantly, so read it out loud the first few times.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- MySQL and Oracle only.
-- REVOKE: takes a privilege back. It mirrors GRANT exactly - WHAT, ON WHAT, FROM
--   WHOM - and the account keeps everything you do not name here.
REVOKE SELECT ON CUSTOMER FROM shipping_clerk;

-- REVOKE ALL: strips every privilege that account holds on that table at once.
REVOKE ALL ON ITEM FROM inventory_manager;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Revoking removes one path, not every path

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      An account can hold the same privilege through more than one route: a direct grant, an Oracle grant to PUBLIC, and in either engine a role it belongs to. Revoking the direct grant leaves the others standing - that is exactly the trap in the PUBLIC note above. When access has to end, check every route before you call the job done.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Views as a security mechanism

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Here is the idea that ties this section to Module 7 as a whole. You do not have to choose between giving an account the whole table and giving it nothing. You can build a view that shows exactly the columns and rows the account should see, grant SELECT on the view, and grant nothing at all on the table underneath. The account cannot widen the view, because the WHERE clause and the column list live in the view definition rather than in the query the account writes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Start with the column case. The shipping desk needs the mailing address and nothing financial.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Add STREET, CITY, STATE and ZIP to the SELECT inside the view. All four customers come back, and there is no column in the result that could tell you what any of them owes. The DROP VIEW IF EXISTS line at the top is what lets you press Run as many times as you like.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      With that view in place, the grant is one line, and it is the only access the shipping desk gets.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- MySQL and Oracle only.
-- GRANT on a VIEW rather than a table: this is the pattern that makes views a
--   security tool. The account is given no privilege at all on the underlying
--   CUSTOMER table, so it can see exactly the rows and columns the view exposes
--   and has no way to reach around it.
GRANT SELECT ON SHIPPING_CONTACT TO shipping_clerk;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A view hides rows just as well as it hides columns. Suppose the Brookville territory gets its own account, and that account should see only the customers of rep 65 - which in the shipped data is 1420, Whiskers & Wags Boutique.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      WHERE REP_NUM = '65' belongs inside the view definition. Put it there and one row comes back. Writing it on the outer SELECT instead would show the same single row today, but it would be the account's own query doing the filtering - and an account can always delete its own WHERE clause. Inside the view, the restriction is not the account's to remove.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Engine note: changing data through a view

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      MySQL will let an account UPDATE a simple view like SHIPPING_CONTACT and pass the change through to CUSTOMER, which is why granting UPDATE on a view deserves the same care as granting it on a table. SQLite refuses: UPDATE SHIPPING_CONTACT SET CITY = 'Akron' WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120'; answers cannot modify SHIPPING_CONTACT because it is a view. That is why the statement is quoted here rather than put in a sandbox. Creating views and reading from them works the same way in both.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Give each account the smallest set of privileges its work requires, and stop there.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Grant on a view rather than the table whenever the account needs only some columns or some rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Reserve Oracle's PUBLIC for data any employee could see, and remember it reaches accounts created later.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • In MySQL there is no PUBLIC - create a role, grant the privilege to the role, then grant the role.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Write the REVOKE on the day the access stops being needed, not at the next audit.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Check every route - direct grant, PUBLIC, role - before you declare an account's access removed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      🔍 Check yourself: security

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q1KimTay's shipping desk

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The shipping desk needs every customer's name and street address to print labels, and must never see BALANCE or CREDIT_LIMIT. The account shipping_clerk currently holds no privileges at all. Which approach gives the desk exactly what it needs and nothing more?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. This puts the rule in a person's good intentions rather than in the DBMS, which is exactly what privileges exist to avoid.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. ALL includes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on customer records - far beyond reading an address, and hard to unwind later.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔c. Correct: the view fixes the column list, so a grant on the view cannot reach BALANCE or CREDIT_LIMIT at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. REVOKE only removes a privilege that was granted, and this account holds none yet. A later table-level GRANT SELECT on CUSTOMER would carry every column with it regardless.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: When an account needs part of a table, grant on a view that exposes that part and grant nothing on the table itself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q2A contractor leaves KimTay

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A contractor account named temp_analyst was granted SELECT on INVOICE directly last month, and the contract has now ended. No PUBLIC grant and no role touches INVOICE, so the direct grant is the account's only route to it. Which statement removes that read access and disturbs nothing else?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔a. Correct: REVOKE names the privilege, the object, and the account it is being taken from - and because the direct grant is the only route here, that one statement really does end the access.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. The keyword is FROM, not TO - privileges are granted to an account and revoked from one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. This destroys the three INVOICE rows and breaks the foreign key INVOICE_LINE depends on, all to solve an access problem that one statement solves.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. There is no NONE privilege in SQL; you remove access with REVOKE, not by granting something empty.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: REVOKE privilege ON object FROM account; is the mirror image of GRANT, with FROM in place of TO - and it ends the access only when the grant it names is the account's only route.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q3The ITEM catalog goes company-wide

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      KimTay wants every account in its Oracle database - including accounts created next year - to be able to read ITEM, while nobody outside the buying team may change it. Which single statement fits?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. ALL hands INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the catalog to every account in the database, which is the opposite of the requirement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. There is no every_user group; Oracle's reserved name for all accounts is PUBLIC.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. The order is reversed - ON names the object being protected and TO names who receives the privilege.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Correct: PUBLIC is Oracle's reserved name for all accounts, and the grant reaches accounts created afterwards too.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: In Oracle, PUBLIC means every account, now and in future - use it for data any employee could reasonably see.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q4The same rule on the MySQL server

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      KimTay now needs that same "everyone may read ITEM" rule on a MySQL server. The DBA types GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO PUBLIC; and MySQL rejects it. Why, and what works instead?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. There is no ALL_USERS keyword in MySQL either; the mechanism is missing, not the spelling.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔b. Correct: PUBLIC is Oracle's. MySQL 8 will not create an account as a side effect of GRANT, so it errors, and a role granted to every account is the equivalent - remember SET DEFAULT ROLE, since a role is inactive until it is made a default.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. Primary key indexes have nothing to do with privileges; every KimTay table has one and grants work fine.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Nothing has to be revoked before it is granted, and REVOKE against a non-existent PUBLIC account fails for the same reason the GRANT did.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: PUBLIC is Oracle's; in MySQL you reach every account with a role that you grant out and set as a default.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-5 Indexes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Look up one word in the back of a textbook and you find the page in a second. Without that index you would turn every page. A database index works the same way: it is a separate structure the DBMS maintains, holding the values of one or more columns in sorted order along with a pointer to the row each value came from. When a query filters or sorts on those columns, the DBMS can walk the small sorted structure instead of reading every row in the table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Index

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      An index is a database object built on one or more columns of a table, kept in sorted order, that lets the DBMS find matching rows without scanning the whole table. It holds no data of its own - drop it and every row is still there, exactly as it was.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Nothing is free. The index is a second copy of those column values, so it takes disk space. More important, it has to stay correct: every INSERT, every DELETE, and every UPDATE that touches an indexed column has to change the index too. That is the trade you are making each time you create one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What an index buys you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Faster WHERE lookups on the indexed columns, faster ORDER BY on them, and faster joins when the join column is indexed. On a five-row table you will not notice. On a table with two million invoice lines, the difference between a scan and an index lookup is the difference between a report that runs and one that times out.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What an index costs you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Extra storage, and slower writes. A table with four indexes does five pieces of work on every insert instead of one. An index nobody uses is pure cost - it slows every load and returns nothing. That is why dropping an unused index is a real optimization, not housekeeping.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-5a Creating an index

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You give the index a name, name the table, and list the columns in parentheses. The name matters only for dropping it later - no query will ever mention it. The same statement works in SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      KimTay's staff search ITEM by description all day, so that is the column to index. Run the sandbox and the catalog will show the new object sitting next to the table it belongs to.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The starter creates one index and lists it - one row. The solution adds a second one on CATEGORY, so two rows come back. Both boxes drop both names first, which is what lets you flip between starter and solution and still get the count each one promises. The NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%' filter hides the indexes SQLite built automatically for the primary keys - those are there whether you ask for them or not.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      An index can cover several columns. CREATE INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3 ON CUSTOMER (REP_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME); sorts by REP_NUM first and by CUSTOMER_NAME within each rep, which is exactly the shape of a query that filters on one rep and sorts the results by name. Order matters: this index helps a query that filters on REP_NUM alone, and does very little for one that filters on CUSTOMER_NAME alone.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You can watch the DBMS change its mind. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN asks SQLite how it intends to run a query without running it. In the starter below the index line is commented out, and the plan says SCAN CUSTOMER. Uncomment it - that is the solution - and the plan becomes SEARCH CUSTOMER USING INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Without the index the plan reads SCAN CUSTOMER plus USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY - every row read, then sorted. With it, the plan reads SEARCH CUSTOMER USING INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3 (REP_NUM=?), and the sort disappears because the index already holds the names in order. You are reading the plan here, not the two customers of rep 20 - EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN describes the query instead of running it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Engine note: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is SQLite's spelling

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is SQLite syntax, which is why it runs in the sandbox. MySQL asks the same question with EXPLAIN SELECT ...;, and Oracle with EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT ...; followed by SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);. All three print something different, and none of the three wordings is portable. The question you are asking never changes: did the optimizer choose the index, or read the whole table?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You never name an index in a query

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Notice that the SELECT is identical in both runs. Indexes are chosen by the query optimizer, not requested by you. There is no FROM CUSTOMER USING CUSTOMER_INDEX3 in standard SQL. Your job is to create the indexes that fit how the data is actually queried; the optimizer's job is to decide, query by query, whether using one beats reading the table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-5b Dropping an index

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      An index that the optimizer never chooses is costing you writes and space for nothing, so removing it is real work. DROP INDEX takes the index name. The data is untouched - the same rows are still in the table when the statement finishes, and every query still returns the same answer, just possibly by a slower route.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Only ITEM_INDEX1 is left in the catalog. The solution goes one step further and reads ITEM afterwards, so you get two result tables: the one-row catalog listing, then all five items. Dropping an index removes an access path, never data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Index statements across the three engines
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      TaskSQLiteMySQLOracle
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CreateCREATE INDEX ITEM_INDEX1 ON ITEM (DESCRIPTION);Same statementSame statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DropDROP INDEX ITEM_INDEX2;DROP INDEX ITEM_INDEX2 ON ITEM;DROP INDEX ITEM_INDEX2;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      List themSELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index';SHOW INDEX FROM ITEM;SELECT INDEX_NAME, TABLE_NAME FROM USER_INDEXES;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Show the planEXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT ...;EXPLAIN SELECT ...;EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT ...;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Name scopeUnique across the databaseUnique within one tableUnique across the schema

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      That SQLite listing statement has no NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%' filter on it, so run it as written and you also get the five sqlite_autoindex_* entries SQLite built for the primary keys of REP, CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE. The sandboxes on this page add the filter to keep the output to the indexes you created yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      7-5c Creating unique indexes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Add the word UNIQUE and the index does a second job. It still speeds up lookups, but it also refuses any INSERT or UPDATE that would put a duplicate value in the indexed column. This is how you enforce "no two of these may ever match" on a column that is not the primary key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Take a barcode table for the warehouse scanners. Two items sharing a barcode would mean the wrong product goes in the box, so the rule has to live in the database rather than in whichever program happens to be doing the insert.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The starter builds the table and the unique index and shows two rows. The solution adds a third row with a barcode nobody else has - 740039 - and it is accepted, because unique means no repeats, not no new rows. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS at the top takes the index with the table, so both boxes start clean every Run.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Now prove the rule bites. The sandbox below is the same setup with one extra statement at the end: an insert that reuses CF21's barcode. It is rejected, and the message names the index's column.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The starter stops with UNIQUE constraint failed: ITEM_BARCODE.BARCODE, and the error is all you see - the rows before it were stored, but nothing is displayed because the run never reached a SELECT. That is the index doing its job: the bad row never reaches the table. Change the value, as the solution does, and the insert goes through and three rows come back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      One more thing to expect: you cannot create a unique index on a column that already contains duplicates. The DBMS checks the existing rows first and refuses to build an index it would immediately violate. CITY in the shipped CUSTOMER data holds Maple Grove twice, so the attempt fails; CUSTOMER_NAME holds four different values, so that one succeeds.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The starter fails with UNIQUE constraint failed: CUSTOMER.CITY because customers 1120 and 1310 are both in Maple Grove. Nothing is created, so you can press Run on it as often as you like. The solution indexes CUSTOMER_NAME instead, where all four values differ, and the index appears in the catalog.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The primary key is already covered

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You never need a unique index on a primary key column - declaring the key made it unique, and most engines build the supporting index for you. Those are the sqlite_autoindex_* rows the sandboxes filter out. Reach for CREATE UNIQUE INDEX for the other columns that must not repeat: a barcode, an email address, an external order reference.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Index columns that appear often in WHERE, ORDER BY, or a join condition.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Leave small tables alone - scanning three REP rows is already as fast as it gets.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Count the writes before adding an index to a table that is loaded in bulk every night.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Use CREATE UNIQUE INDEX when a non-key column must never repeat, and clean the duplicates out first or the index will not build.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Drop any index the optimizer never chooses; it costs writes and space and returns nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Remember the name is only for DROP INDEX - queries never mention it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      🔍 Check yourself: indexes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q1The nightly INVOICE_LINE load

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      KimTay's nightly job inserts several hundred rows into INVOICE_LINE, and the table is read by exactly one month-end report that totals every row in it. A developer proposes adding four new indexes to the table. What should you expect?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. An index is extra work on insert, not a shortcut - the DBMS still has to place the row and then update each index.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔b. Correct: four indexes mean five structures to maintain per inserted row, which is the cost side of the trade.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. Maintaining an index on every write is precisely where the cost shows up; space is the smaller half of it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. A report that reads every row gains nothing from an index, because there is no subset to find.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: An index trades slower writes and extra space for faster reads - on a write-heavy, scan-once table you pay the cost and collect nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q2Barcodes in the KimTay warehouse

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Warehouse staff scan a six-character barcode stored in a table alongside ITEM_ID. Two different items must never carry the same barcode, but the barcode is not that table's primary key. Which action enforces the rule inside the DBMS?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. An ordinary index happily stores the same value many times; only the UNIQUE keyword refuses duplicates.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. A check in one program does not bind the next program, the reporting tool, or a hand-typed INSERT.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. Uniqueness can be enforced on any column with a unique index, key or not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Correct: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX makes the DBMS itself refuse the second row with UNIQUE constraint failed, whatever tool sends it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX is how you enforce no-duplicates on a column that is not the primary key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q3Dropping ITEM_INDEX2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      An index named ITEM_INDEX2 on ITEM (CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION) is never chosen by the optimizer, so the DBA runs DROP INDEX ITEM_INDEX2;. What happens to KimTay's data and queries?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔a. Correct: an index holds no data of its own, so dropping it removes only an access path.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. The index stores pointers to rows, not the rows - removing it cannot remove data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. That would be ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN; DROP INDEX does not change the table's structure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. No query ever names an index in its FROM clause, so no query can break when one disappears.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Dropping an index removes an access path and nothing else - the rows, the columns, and the answers all stay the same.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q4Making the optimizer use CUSTOMER_INDEX3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      After creating CUSTOMER_INDEX3 on CUSTOMER (REP_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME), a developer asks what has to change in the next query so that the new index actually gets used. What is the right answer?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. Standard SQL has no syntax for naming an index in a query - the FROM clause names tables and views.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. Nesting has nothing to do with index selection; the optimizer weighs every access path in every query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔c. Correct: you create indexes to fit the workload, and the optimizer picks one query by query - EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is how you check which way it went.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. Indexes are not objects you grant privileges on; access is controlled on the table or view.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: You choose which indexes exist; the optimizer chooses when to use them, and the query text never changes.
