                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              7-6 System Catalog

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Every database you have built in this course knows something about itself. When you ran CREATE TABLE ITEM, the DBMS did not only make room for rows. It also wrote down that a table called ITEM exists, that it has six columns, that ITEM_ID is four characters and is the primary key, and that REORDER_LEVEL holds a small integer. That record lives inside the database, in tables you can read with an ordinary SELECT. It is called the system catalog, and it is what lets a DBMS answer questions about its own contents.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              System catalog

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A set of tables the DBMS maintains about the database itself: which tables, columns, views, and indexes exist, and how each one is defined. It is also called the data dictionary. You read it with SELECT; you never write to it directly.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The catalog earns its keep on the job for three reasons. You will inherit databases you did not build and have to find out what is in them. You will need to know what a change is going to break before you make it, and the only reliable list of everything that stores a REP_NUM is the catalog. And the tools you already use are reading it for you: the schema strip on every sandbox on this page, the object list in MySQL Workbench, the migration script your team runs on a Friday afternoon.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What the catalog can tell you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Which tables exist in the database, and on the larger engines who owns them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Which columns each table has, in what order, of what type, and whether nulls are allowed
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Which views exist, and the defining query stored with each one
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Which indexes exist and which table and columns they were built on
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Which constraints are declared, including primary keys and foreign keys
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • On MySQL and Oracle, which users hold which privileges on which objects

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQL: INFORMATION_SCHEMA

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQL exposes the catalog as a database named INFORMATION_SCHEMA whose tables you query like any other. Two of them do most of the work. TABLES holds one row per table, and COLUMNS holds one row per column of every table. Both are filtered by TABLE_SCHEMA, which is the name of the database you are asking about. Leave that filter off and you get every database on the server, which is almost never what you meant.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- MySQL. INFORMATION_SCHEMA does not exist in SQLite, so neither of these runs on this page.
-- SELECT: the catalogue is queried with ordinary SQL - that is the whole point of
--   it. This asks for the names of the tables.
SELECT TABLE_NAME

-- FROM: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES holds one row per table in the server.
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES

-- WHERE: narrow it to one database, or you get every table on the server.
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'

-- ORDER BY: the catalogue makes no promise about order either.
ORDER BY TABLE_NAME;

-- SELECT: the second question - what does one particular table look like?
SELECT COLUMN_NAME, DATA_TYPE, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH, IS_NULLABLE

-- FROM: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS holds one row per COLUMN of every table.
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS

-- WHERE: which database...
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'

--   ...and which table inside it.
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP'

-- ORDER BY ORDINAL_POSITION: sorts the columns back into the order the table
--   declares them, rather than alphabetically.
ORDER BY ORDINAL_POSITION;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQL also gives you SHOW TABLES; and DESCRIBE REP;, which are short-hand for those same two queries. They are convenient at a command line and useless inside a program, because a SHOW result cannot be joined, filtered, or counted. Anything you want to compute with has to come from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Asking the same four questions of three engines
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              QuestionMySQLSQLite (this page)Oracle
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Which tables exist?SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table';SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM USER_TABLES;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Which columns does REP have?SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY' AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP';SELECT name FROM pragma_table_info('REP');SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM USER_TAB_COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_NAME = 'REP';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Which views exist?SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';SELECT VIEW_NAME FROM USER_VIEWS;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Which indexes exist?SELECT DISTINCT INDEX_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.STATISTICS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index';SELECT INDEX_NAME FROM USER_INDEXES;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQLite: sqlite_master and pragma_table_info

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQLite has no INFORMATION_SCHEMA. It keeps one catalog table, sqlite_master, holding a row for every table, view, index, and trigger in the database. The columns you will use are type, name, tbl_name (the object the entry belongs to), and sql (the exact statement that created it). Run the starter first, then narrow it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The unfiltered version also lists the indexes SQLite built on its own. Add a WHERE clause on type to keep tables and views only.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter returns ten rows: the five KimTay tables and five entries of type index whose names begin sqlite_autoindex_. Nobody typed a CREATE INDEX for those. SQLite built one for each primary key so it could enforce uniqueness, and it recorded them in the catalog exactly as faithfully as the objects you asked for. The filtered version comes back with the five tables and no views, because this database has none yet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              For columns, SQLite offers pragma_table_info, a function you put in a FROM clause and hand a table name. It returns one row per column, in table order.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              notnull is a keyword in SQLite, so it has to be wrapped in double quotation marks before the engine will read it as a column name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nine rows come back in the order the columns were declared. Any column the CREATE TABLE declared NOT NULL shows a notnull of 1; in REP those are LAST_NAME and FIRST_NAME, because a rep with no name is not a rep. pk reads 1 on REP_NUM, marking it as the first column of the primary key. Run the same query against INVOICE_LINE and you get 1 on INVOICE_NUM and 2 on ITEM_ID, which is how a two-column key is recorded.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One reading that will surprise you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              REP_NUM is the primary key, yet its notnull value is 0. In MySQL and Oracle a primary key column is automatically NOT NULL, and their catalogs say so. SQLite is the exception, and section 7-7 shows exactly what that lets through the door.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The question only the catalog can answer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay asks you to widen REP_NUM from two characters to three. Before you touch anything you need the list of every table that stores a REP_NUM. No query against the data can produce that list, because you would have to know where to look before you could look. The catalog produces it in one statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- MySQL: one row per column of every table, so a column name is searchable.
-- SELECT: the answer wanted here is a list of TABLES, even though the search is
--   being made on a column name.
SELECT TABLE_NAME

-- FROM: the columns catalogue, because that is where column names live.
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS

-- WHERE: restrict to one database...
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'

--   ...and to the column being hunted. This answers "where else does REP_NUM
--   appear?" - the question you ask before changing or dropping a column.
  AND COLUMN_NAME = 'REP_NUM'

-- ORDER BY: sorts the list of tables found.
ORDER BY TABLE_NAME;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter searches for PRICE and finds one table. Change the column name to REP_NUM and run it again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PRICE lives in ITEM alone. REP_NUM lives in CUSTOMER and REP, so the widening job is two ALTER TABLE statements and not one. Because pragma_table_info accepts the table name from the outer query, the subquery runs once per table, and the answer stays correct when somebody adds a sixth table next month.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              7-6a Update of the System Catalog

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nobody keeps the catalog current by hand. The DBMS updates it as part of carrying out the statement you ran. CREATE TABLE adds the rows that describe the new table, CREATE INDEX adds a row for the index, DROP TABLE removes every row belonging to that table, and ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO rewrites the stored definition under the new name. All of it happens inside the same statement, so the catalog is never out of step with the database it describes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You can watch it happen. Count the catalog, create something, count it again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nothing in this script writes to sqlite_master. Every change to it is a side effect of CREATE and DROP. The DROP TABLE IF EXISTS on line 1 is what lets you press Run twice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter reports ten entries before and twelve after, because it created a table and SQLite quietly added the index that enforces its primary key. The solution asks for a second index as well, so it reports thirteen, and its middle result lists all three entries side by side. Then one DROP TABLE takes the count back to ten, because dropping a table removes the catalog entries for its indexes as well. You never wrote a single INSERT or DELETE against the catalog.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Read the catalog; never write to it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              sqlite_master is a real table, and UPDATE sqlite_master SET name = 'ITEMS'; looks like it should work. Do not. SQLite refuses it outright with table sqlite_master may not be modified unless a dangerous pragma is set, MySQL refuses it too, and on an engine that allows it you end up with a database whose description no longer matches its contents, which is how a file becomes unopenable. The way to change what the catalog says is to run the statement that changes the thing it describes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What the catalog is good for

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Finding your way around an unfamiliar database, listing every place a column name appears, confirming that a CREATE or DROP did what you expected, and generating scripts. Because the entries are rows, you can filter, join, count, and order them like any other data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What it is not

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              It is not a backup and not a place to store notes about the database. It holds structure, not rows: the catalog knows CUSTOMER has a BALANCE column of type DECIMAL(9,2), and knows nothing whatever about Whiskers and Wags Boutique owing 4820.75.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can say what the system catalog is and why a DBMS keeps one
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can list a database's tables in MySQL and in SQLite
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can list one table's columns, types, and null settings in both engines
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can find every table that contains a given column name
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can say who updates the catalog, and when
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can explain why reading the catalog is safe and writing to it is not

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 🔍 Check yourself: the system catalog

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1KimTay's inherited MySQL database

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A contractor hands KimTay Pet Supplies a MySQL database and leaves. Before widening REP_NUM from two characters to three, the DBA has to know every table that stores a column named REP_NUM. Which approach produces that list reliably?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. This works only if you already know every table name, which is the thing you are trying to find out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct: the COLUMNS table holds one row per column of every table, so a column name is searchable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. DESCRIBE reports the columns of the one table you name and says nothing about any other table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Source code shows where a column is used, not where it is stored; an unused column still has to be changed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: The catalog is the only place that knows the whole schema, so schema questions go to the catalog.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2Listing views in the sandbox

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An analyst working in the SQLite sandbox on this page wants a list of every view that exists in the current database. Which statement returns it?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. INFORMATION_SCHEMA is MySQL's catalog and does not exist in SQLite at any version.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. SHOW is a MySQL command over its own catalog; SQLite has no SHOW statement to run.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. pragma_table_info takes a table name and returns its columns, and there is no table called VIEWS.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct: sqlite_master holds one row per object, and type tells you whether it is a table, view, index, or trigger.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: One catalog table, filtered by type, answers every what-exists question in SQLite.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3The audit table that registered itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A DBA at KimTay runs CREATE TABLE AUDIT_LOG, then immediately queries sqlite_master and finds a row describing AUDIT_LOG already there. Who put that row in the catalog?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct: updating the catalog is part of executing the statement, so the two can never disagree.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Writing to the catalog by hand is refused with 'table sqlite_master may not be modified', and on engines that permit it the result is a corrupt database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The catalog is stored, not derived; dropping the table is what removes the row, not a rescan.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. There is no delay and no scheduled refresh; the entry exists the moment the statement finishes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: CREATE, ALTER, and DROP update the catalog as part of their own work, which is why it is never stale.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              7-7 Integrity Constraints in SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A constraint is a rule about what data is allowed, written into the table definition and enforced by the DBMS. That last part is what makes it worth the trouble. You can check in your own program that nobody enters a negative price, and the check protects the one program you wrote it in. Put the rule in the table and it protects the data against every program, every import script, every person at a command line, permanently.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Integrity constraint

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A rule stored with the table that the DBMS applies to every insert, update, and delete. A statement that would break the rule is rejected with an error and nothing at all is changed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You have been declaring constraints since Module 3 without dwelling on them. Every CREATE TABLE in the KimTay schema names a PRIMARY KEY and marks some columns NOT NULL, and the three tables with a parent above them (CUSTOMER, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE) declare FOREIGN KEY clauses as well. This section takes the whole set seriously: what each one refuses, what the refusal looks like, and which engine enforces which rule and when.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The five constraints

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The constraints SQL gives you
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ConstraintThe rule it enforcesExample from KimTay
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PRIMARY KEYIdentifies each row uniquely. Values may not repeat, and on every engine except SQLite may not be null.ITEM_ID in ITEM; the pair INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID in INVOICE_LINE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              UNIQUENo two rows may hold the same value, but the column is still allowed to be null.A supplier's email address: one address belongs to one supplier
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              NOT NULLThe column must hold a value. A null is refused.LAST_NAME in REP; a rep with no surname is not a rep
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CHECKAn expression that has to be true for the row. Anything false is refused.A commission RATE has to fall between 0 and 0.25
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              FOREIGN KEYA value here must already exist in the parent table's key. This is referential integrity.INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID has to name an item that exists

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A primary key is a unique constraint and a not-null constraint at the same time, plus the declaration that this is the identifier for the row. UNIQUE is the weaker relative you reach for when a second column also has to be one of a kind but is allowed to be missing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declaring them in CREATE TABLE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Constraints are declared where the table is defined. A rule about a single column can be written on that column's line. A rule about more than one column, or one you want to give a name to, goes on its own line after the columns. Naming a constraint with the CONSTRAINT keyword costs one word and buys you an error message that says which rule you broke.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: this one is built to show constraints, so read the rules rather
--   than the columns.
CREATE TABLE SUPPLIER (

    -- PRIMARY KEY: unique and never null, enforced on every INSERT and UPDATE.
    SUPPLIER_ID    CHAR(3)      PRIMARY KEY,

    -- NOT NULL: this column must always hold a value.
    SUPPLIER_NAME  VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,

    -- UNIQUE: no two suppliers may share an email address. Unlike a primary key,
    --   a UNIQUE column is still allowed to be null.
    EMAIL          VARCHAR(40)  UNIQUE,

    -- Both rules on one column: a lead time must be present...
    LEAD_DAYS      SMALLINT     NOT NULL,

    -- CONSTRAINT ... CHECK: ...and it must make sense. CHECK tests a condition on
    --   every row written; naming the constraint means the error message tells
    --   you which rule was broken instead of leaving you to guess.
    CONSTRAINT LEAD_DAYS_POSITIVE CHECK (LEAD_DAYS > 0)
);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Add the named CHECK as a line of its own after LEAD_DAYS, then a second supplier, then read the catalog entries the table produced.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two suppliers come back. The catalog query is the point where 7-6 and 7-7 meet: SUPPLIER produced three entries, the table plus two automatic indexes named sqlite_autoindex_SUPPLIER_1 and sqlite_autoindex_SUPPLIER_2. One enforces the primary key and the other enforces the UNIQUE on EMAIL. A uniqueness rule is not a note in a manual; it is a structure the engine builds and maintains for you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What a violation looks like

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay's warehouse tries to add a supplier that promises same-day delivery and records the lead time as zero days. Zero is not greater than zero, so the CHECK refuses the row. Run the starter as it stands and read the message. The sandbox shows you the error and nothing else, because the statement that failed stopped the script where it stood.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter is meant to fail, so read the message before you change anything. Then give the rule the smallest lead time it will accept and run it again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The engine answers CHECK constraint failed: LEAD_DAYS_POSITIVE. That is what naming the constraint bought you. Leave the name off and SQLite reports the expression instead, as in CHECK constraint failed: LEAD_DAYS > 0, and some engines report only the table, which tells you a rule was broken but not which one. The solution changes the zero to a one, the smallest lead time this rule allows, and both suppliers go in. The other three refusals read the same way, and every one of them names the column it protected.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- Each of these is rejected. They assume SUPPLIER exists and already holds S10,
-- so build it with the CREATE TABLE above first, then paste ONE of these and run it.
-- Rejected by the PRIMARY KEY: S10 is already in the table, and a primary key
--   value can only be used once.
INSERT INTO SUPPLIER VALUES ('S10', 'Duplicate Co', 'new@duplicate.example', 4);

-- UNIQUE constraint failed: SUPPLIER.SUPPLIER_ID     (that primary key is taken)

-- Rejected by NOT NULL: the id is new and the email is new, but the name is
--   missing, and that column was declared NOT NULL.
INSERT INTO SUPPLIER VALUES ('S40', NULL, 'nameless@example.com', 4);

-- NOT NULL constraint failed: SUPPLIER.SUPPLIER_NAME

-- Rejected by UNIQUE: a brand new supplier id, but an email address another row
--   already holds. Each constraint is checked separately, and any one of them
--   failing stops the whole statement.
INSERT INTO SUPPLIER VALUES ('S50', 'Second Buckeye', 'orders@buckeyepet.example', 4);

-- UNIQUE constraint failed: SUPPLIER.EMAIL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A rejected statement changes nothing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The row is not written halfway. The INSERT is undone completely, the table is exactly as it was, and if you were inside a transaction the rest of it is still yours to COMMIT or ROLLBACK. That is the whole promise of a constraint: the database never holds data that breaks its own rules, not even for an instant.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Referential integrity, enforced for real

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Referential integrity is the rule that a foreign key has to point at a row that exists. INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID is declared REFERENCES ITEM(ITEM_ID) in the schema this page ships, so a line for item ZZ99 ought to be impossible. Watch what actually happens.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Ask the engine for the current setting first, then try the insert it should have stopped.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The pragma reports 0, and the insert is accepted. That is the explanation for both. SQLite parses foreign key declarations and stores them in the catalog, but it does not enforce them unless enforcement is turned on for the connection. The row you created is an orphan, an invoice line for an item that does not exist, and every inner join to ITEM will quietly leave it out: seven rows in INVOICE_LINE, six rows in the join. That is the shape of the bug, and it is a hard one to see.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Now turn enforcement on and run the identical insert.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter proves the switch flipped: it reports 1 instead of 0. Then add the same insert as the sandbox above and watch it be refused.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. Nothing was written. The engine looked for ZZ99 in ITEM, did not find it, and refused the row, not because a program remembered to check but because the rule is in the database. Every route into the table is covered by it at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The rule guards the other direction as well. A parent row that children point at cannot be deleted out from under them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CF21 is the grain-free dry food. The starter shows you which invoices ordered it; decide what should happen before you run the delete.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter returns two lines, on invoices 50710 and 50711. Removing the item would leave both pointing at nothing, so the engine refuses the delete with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. Deleting those two lines first and then the item works. So does declaring the foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE, which tells the engine to remove the children along with the parent. That is powerful and worth knowing, and worth respecting, because one short DELETE can then remove a great deal more than you had in mind.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The pragma is per connection, not per database

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON lasts for the current connection and is not stored in the file. Press Reset on the sandbox, or open the same database from another program, and enforcement is off again. MySQL with InnoDB and Oracle enforce foreign keys always, with no switch anyone can forget. Expect inserts that passed on this page to start failing when you move the work to MySQL, and be glad of it: the ones that fail were the ones building orphans.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Enforcement does not get in the way of correct work. Item DG04 exists, invoice 50712 exists, and the pair (50712, DG04) is not yet taken, so this row is legal with the pragma on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The starter shows the two lines invoice 50712 shipped with. Add the leash and three lines should come back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PRIMARY KEY does not imply NOT NULL in SQLite

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Here is the trap section 7-6 pointed at when notnull read 0 for REP_NUM. In MySQL and Oracle a primary key column is automatically NOT NULL; the engine adds the rule whether you write it or not. SQLite, for compatibility with databases written before the rule was enforced, lets a null into the primary key column of an ordinary table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This is a scratch table of your own, not KimTay's data, which ships with no nulls anywhere. Count the rows and count the keys separately, and Module 5 explains why the two numbers can differ.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One row stored, zero keys stored. COUNT(*) counts rows and COUNT(REP_NUM) skips the null, so the table holds a rep that nothing can identify or join to. The fix is two words in the right place. Write REP_NUM CHAR(2) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY and the same insert is refused with NOT NULL constraint failed: REP_PRACTICE.REP_NUM. It costs nothing on the engines that would have added the rule for you, so make it a habit.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Adding a constraint to a table that already exists

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything above was declared at creation time. Real work is rarely that tidy: the CHECK you needed becomes obvious a year after the table went into production. MySQL 8.0 and Oracle let you attach one to a live table.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- MySQL 8.0 and Oracle. SQLite answers 'near "CONSTRAINT": syntax error'.
-- ALTER TABLE: constraints can be added to a table that already exists.
ALTER TABLE ITEM

-- ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK: names the rule and states it. The engine tests every
--   existing row before accepting it - if any current price were zero or less,
--   the statement would be rejected until the data was fixed.
ADD CONSTRAINT PRICE_POSITIVE CHECK (PRICE > 0);

-- ALTER TABLE: a second table, a different kind of rule.
ALTER TABLE INVOICE

-- ADD CONSTRAINT: naming it makes it possible to drop it later by name.
ADD CONSTRAINT INVOICE_CUSTOMER_FK

-- FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES: says the column on the left must always hold a value
--   that exists in the column on the right - the rule that stops orphan invoices.
FOREIGN KEY (CUSTOMER_NUM) REFERENCES CUSTOMER(CUSTOMER_NUM);

-- ALTER TABLE: removing a rule.
ALTER TABLE ITEM

-- DROP CONSTRAINT: takes the rule off the table by name. The data stays exactly
--   as it is - only the checking stops, so new rows may now break the old rule.
DROP CONSTRAINT PRICE_POSITIVE;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQLite has no ADD CONSTRAINT at any version. Its ALTER TABLE expects a column definition after ADD, so it stops on the keyword CONSTRAINT and reports a syntax error there. A constraint has to be present when the table is created, so adding one means the rebuild pattern from 6-8a: create a replacement table with the constraint declared, copy the rows across, drop the original, rename the replacement, all inside one transaction. Exercise 5 walks that through on REP.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Check the data before you add the rule

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A constraint added to a table that already has rows is accepted only if the existing data obeys it. One item priced at 0.00 and ADD CONSTRAINT PRICE_POSITIVE fails on MySQL, and the copy INSERT fails on SQLite. That is correct and useful behaviour. Run the query that finds the offenders first: SELECT * FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE <= 0; returns no rows on the shipped data, so the rule is safe to add here.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • I can explain why a DELETE can be refused as well as an INSERT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 🔍 Check yourself: integrity constraints

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1Whiskers and Wags Boutique, entered twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A clerk at KimTay accidentally runs the insert for customer 1420, Whiskers and Wags Boutique, a second time. CUSTOMER_NUM is the primary key of CUSTOMER. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. NOT NULL is about missing values, and a rejected insert never stores a partial row anywhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. No CHECK constraint is declared on CUSTOMER_NUM, and a duplicate is not a range problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct: a primary key forbids duplicate values, so the engine rejects the statement outright.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. An INSERT never replaces an existing row; that would silently destroy the data already stored.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A primary key is a promise of uniqueness that the DBMS keeps on every insert, without being asked.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2Retiring the grain-free dry food

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay runs on MySQL with InnoDB. A buyer tries to delete item CF21 from ITEM, and CF21 still appears on invoice lines for 50710 and 50711. What does the engine do?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct: referential integrity guards the parent too, so the delete is rejected while children exist.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. No engine invents a replacement value; that would silently change what the invoices say was sold.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A foreign key constrains both sides: children may not point at nothing, and parents may not vanish.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. That happens only when the foreign key was declared ON DELETE CASCADE, which is a deliberate choice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Referential integrity blocks deletes as well as inserts, because both can leave a foreign key pointing at nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3Two students, one sandbox, two results

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In the sandbox on this page, one student inserts an invoice line for item ZZ99, which does not exist, and the row is accepted. A classmate runs the identical insert and it is refused with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. What explains the difference?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Enforcement has been optional in every SQLite version and is still off by default in this sandbox.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Both sandboxes run outside an explicit transaction, and the accepted row is genuinely in the table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. Having the clause is what makes enforcement possible; without it the pragma would change nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct: SQLite stores foreign keys always but enforces them only when the pragma is on for the connection.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: In SQLite a declared foreign key and an enforced foreign key are two different things, separated by one pragma.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q4Capping a KimTay commission rate

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay decides no sales rep may ever be recorded on a commission rate above 0.25. Reps are added by a web form, by a nightly import, and occasionally by hand at a command line. Where does the rule belong?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Validation in the form protects only the form, and here there are three ways in, not one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct: a constraint in the table is enforced on every statement from every source, permanently.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A report finds bad data after it is stored and after decisions have been made on it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. NOT NULL only requires a value to be present; 0.90 is present and would be accepted.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A rule that matters belongs in the table, because the table outlives every application that writes to it.
