                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-3 Concatenating Columns

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Concatenation joins two or more character values into one. The database stores a rep's first name and last name in separate columns, which is correct: they are separate facts, and storing them apart is what lets you sort by last name. A mailing label wants them together. Concatenation is how a query delivers one without disturbing the other.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            There are two spellings. CONCAT is a function and takes any number of arguments. The || operator joins exactly two values at a time, and you chain it for more. Both run in this sandbox.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A space is a value like any other. Pass ' ' as a middle argument: CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Concatenation

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Joining character values end to end to form a single value. Nothing is added between them unless you supply it, which is why the separators, spaces, commas and dashes have to appear as literals in the expression.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The || operator does the same job in a form many people find easier to read, because the separators sit where they will appear in the output. Build a mailing line out of the three address columns of REP.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Chain the operator: column, separator, column, separator, column. The comma and the spaces are literals in quotes. Reps 20 and 35 both give Maple Grove, OH 44601.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            For a longer label, CONCAT usually reads better than a chain of four or five operators, because the separators are arguments in a list rather than punctuation between operators.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Nine arguments in all: the five columns and the four separators between them. Watch the comma after the street but the plain space before the state.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The null problem

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Here is the part that costs people real time. Concatenating a value with null does not do the harmless thing you might expect, and what it does depends on the engine and on the spelling you chose. COALESCE(value, replacement) is the tool for the job: it hands back the first argument unless that argument is null, in which case it hands back the second. Run this and read all three columns.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONCAT_RESULT is the text Rep: with the null skipped. PIPE_RESULT is null, and this sandbox prints a null cell as the word NULL, so you will see NULL there rather than a blank. SAFE_RESULT is Rep: unassigned, because COALESCE replaced the null before the join happened.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What happens when a null joins the expression
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ExpressionMySQLSQLite (this sandbox)What to remember
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONCAT('Rep: ', NULL)NULL'Rep: 'The same call gives opposite answers in the two engines
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            'Rep: ' || NULLNULL, but only because || means OR there unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT is setNULLOne null makes the entire pipe expression null here
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            'Rep: ' || COALESCE(NULL, 'unassigned')'Rep: unassigned''Rep: unassigned'Handle the null yourself and both engines agree
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Three engines, three answers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            MySQL CONCAT returns null if any argument is null; this sandbox skips the null and returns the rest. In MySQL, || is the logical OR operator by default, not concatenation at all. Oracle does use || for concatenation the way this sandbox does, but Oracle treats a null as an empty string, so there the label survives instead of going null. Never carry a concatenation expression between engines without testing it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            None of the seeded KimTay rows contain a null, so where does a real null come from? From a query. Module 6 showed that an outer join manufactures nulls for the unmatched side, and Companion Care Clinic has no invoice. Run this and watch that one customer lose its whole label.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Four rows. Three customers look identical across all three label columns. Companion Care Clinic does not: PIPE_LABEL prints as NULL, CONCAT_LABEL trails off after the slash, and only SAFE_LABEL says what is going on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The lesson is not that concatenation is dangerous. It is that a label built from a column that might be null needs a decision from you about what the null should read as. COALESCE is where you record that decision, and it is portable across every engine in this course.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • CONCAT(a, ' ', b) and a || ' ' || b both join values in this sandbox
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • Separators are literals you supply; nothing appears between values on its own
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • In this sandbox || returns null if either side is null, while CONCAT skips the null
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • MySQL CONCAT returns null instead, and MySQL reads || as OR by default
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • A null result prints in this sandbox as the word NULL, which is the engine telling you there is no value, not a blank label
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • Wrap any nullable column in COALESCE before concatenating and both engines produce the same label
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • Outer joins are the usual source of nulls in otherwise complete data, as Companion Care Clinic shows

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q1Rep 20's name on a mailing label

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A label for rep 20 should read Valerie Kaiser, but CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME) returns ValerieKaiser. What went wrong?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. CONCAT accepts many arguments here; the call in the stem passed only two of them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. No blanks were stored to begin with, and TRIM was never applied to this expression.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. The order is correct; the names appear in the order they were listed, with nothing between them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔d. Correct: add ' ' as a middle argument, or write FIRST_NAME || ' ' || LAST_NAME.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Separators in a concatenated value are literals you write out, never something the engine adds.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q2Labeling KimTay customers with their invoice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A LEFT JOIN from CUSTOMER to INVOICE builds the label C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || I.INVOICE_NUM. Three labels read correctly and Companion Care Clinic's cell reads NULL. Why?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. The name is present; the SELECT shows CUSTOMER_NAME correctly in the neighboring column.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔b. Correct: one null anywhere in a || chain makes the entire result null, which this sandbox displays as the word NULL.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, which is exactly why the unmatched row is visible at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. BALANCE takes no part in this expression, and a zero balance is a value rather than a null.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: An outer join manufactures nulls, and a null anywhere in a || chain wipes out the whole label.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q3Moving KimTay's label query to MySQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A label expression written here as CONCAT(CUSTOMER_NAME, ' / ', INVOICE_NUM) is moved to MySQL, where some invoice numbers come back null. What should you expect?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. The two engines disagree on this exact point, which is why the expression is not portable as written.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. Nulls are legal arguments in both engines; neither raises an error for one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔c. Correct: MySQL CONCAT returns null on any null argument, while this sandbox skips it and returns the rest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. This sandbox does skip the null, but MySQL does not, so the outputs differ.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Wrap nullable columns in COALESCE before concatenating and the expression behaves the same on every engine.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-4 Stored Procedures Using MySQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A stored procedure is a named block of SQL that lives inside the database itself. You write it once, the server stores it, and from then on anyone with permission runs it by name. The SQL does not sit in a text file on somebody's laptop, and it is not pasted into four different application screens that slowly drift apart. It lives next to the data it operates on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Engine note - read this once

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Nothing in 8-4, 8-5, or 8-6 is a sandbox exercise, so there is no Run button in these three sections and that is expected. The sandbox is SQLite, and SQLite has no stored procedures at all: no CREATE PROCEDURE, no DELIMITER, no DECLARE, no CALL, and no GRANT. Everything below is MySQL, shown in plain code blocks for you to run in MySQL Workbench or the mysql client against the KimTay database. One caution: the two deliberate counter-examples in 8-6, a bare UPDATE and a bare DELETE with no WHERE clause, are ordinary SQL that any engine will happily run. That is exactly why they are dangerous, and exactly why they are labelled. Do not run them against data you care about.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why put SQL in the database

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            You already know how to write every statement a procedure contains. The question is where those statements should live. Moving them into the database buys you several things at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • One correct copy. The rule for adjusting a balance exists in exactly one place, so fixing it fixes it everywhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • Reuse by name. A report writer, a web application, and a nightly job can all issue the same CALL instead of each rewriting the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • Fewer round trips. Five statements sent one at a time is five conversations with the server; one CALL is one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • A safety boundary. An account can be allowed to run a procedure without being allowed to run raw DELETE against the table. 8-6 shows how that is arranged and what it depends on.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • A home for the hard parts. The tricky join, the exact WHERE clause, the error handling: written once by whoever knows the schema best.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What a procedure looks like

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Start with the smallest useful example. This one takes no parameters and reports how many sales reps KimTay has. The DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS line is there so you can edit and re-run the script as often as you like.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- DELIMITER //: switch the statement terminator so the semicolons inside the
--   procedure are not mistaken for the end of it.
DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable. Without it, the second
--   run fails because the procedure already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHOW_REP_COUNT //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the simplest possible one - empty parentheses mean it takes
--   no parameters at all.
CREATE PROCEDURE SHOW_REP_COUNT()

-- BEGIN ... END wrap the body.
BEGIN

    -- One ordinary statement. Its result is returned to the caller.
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS REP_COUNT FROM REP;
END //

-- Restore the normal semicolon.
DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Four parts matter. CREATE PROCEDURE SHOW_REP_COUNT() names the procedure and gives it an empty parameter list. BEGIN and END bracket the body. Inside the body, ordinary SQL statements each end with a semicolon. And the whole thing is wrapped in a pair of DELIMITER commands, which is the part that surprises everyone the first time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER is not SQL and the server never sees it. It is an instruction to your client program telling it which characters mark the end of a statement. Normally that is the semicolon. But a procedure body is full of semicolons, so a client using the default rule chops CREATE PROCEDURE into pieces and sends the first fragment on its own, which is a syntax error. DELIMITER // changes the rule to two slashes, so the client sends the entire CREATE PROCEDURE ... END as one statement. DELIMITER ; puts the rule back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Any character sequence that does not appear in your code will work, and // and $ are the two you will see most often. Avoid the backslash, which MySQL treats as an escape character, and avoid a sequence that is itself an operator, such as a single |. Whichever one you pick, remember two things: the statements between the two DELIMITER commands must end with that sequence instead of a semicolon, and you must set the delimiter back to ; at the end or every later statement in your session will look wrong to the client.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Running the procedure takes one word:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: runs the procedure. The empty parentheses are still required even though
--   there is nothing to pass, and the SELECT inside sends its result back.
CALL SHOW_REP_COUNT();

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The result is a single row with a single column, REP_COUNT, holding 3: Kaiser, Hull, and Perez. A procedure whose body ends in a bare SELECT sends that result set straight back to whoever called it, exactly as if you had typed the SELECT yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Parameters: IN, OUT, and INOUT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A procedure with no parameters can only ever do one thing. Parameters are how a caller says which customer, which item, how much. Each parameter is declared with a mode, a name, and a data type, in that order. Leave the mode off and MySQL assumes IN.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The three parameter modes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ModeDirection of travelExample declaration
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            INCaller to procedure. The body may change its own copy, but the caller never sees that change.IN i_customer_num CHAR(4)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            OUTProcedure to caller. MySQL sets the value to NULL as the procedure starts, whatever the caller passed.OUT o_balance DECIMAL(9,2)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            INOUTBoth directions. The body sees the value the caller supplied and hands back whatever it leaves there.INOUT io_commission DECIMAL(8,2)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            An OUT or INOUT argument has to be something that can be written to, so the caller passes a session variable such as @balance, never a literal. Passing 250.00 where an OUT parameter is expected is an error.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Never name a parameter after a column

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Inside a procedure body, when a name could mean either a declared parameter or a column, MySQL resolves it as the parameter. Name a parameter REP_NUM and the condition WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM becomes the parameter compared with itself, which is true for every row in the table. The prefixes used throughout these sections - i_ for IN, o_ for OUT, io_ for INOUT, v_ for a local variable - exist to make that collision impossible.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Here is the mistake made concrete, so that you recognize it when it happens to you:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- DELIMITER //: as always, so inner semicolons are safe.
DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: clears out any earlier BAD_REP_NAME so this script
--   can be re-run without erroring on a duplicate name.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS BAD_REP_NAME //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one is broken on purpose - watch the parameter name.
CREATE PROCEDURE BAD_REP_NAME(

    -- IN parameter named REP_NUM, which is ALSO the name of a column in REP.
    --   That collision is the bug.
    IN  REP_NUM     CHAR(2),

    -- OUT parameter: a value the procedure hands back to the caller.
    OUT o_last_name VARCHAR(20))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO: instead of returning a result set, the value found is put
    --   into a variable. It expects exactly one row.
    SELECT LAST_NAME
    INTO   o_last_name

    -- FROM: REP, the table whose REP_NUM column collides with the parameter above.
    FROM   REP

    -- BROKEN. Both sides of this comparison are read as the COLUMN REP_NUM, so
    --   the condition says "where the column equals itself" - true for every row.
    --   That is why parameters are conventionally prefixed i_ or p_: the prefix
    --   makes a collision like this impossible.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = REP_NUM;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: passing the rep number and a session variable to receive the answer.
--   Because of the name collision, the WHERE clause matched every rep, so the
--   procedure returns whichever last name the engine happened to reach - not
--   necessarily rep 35's.
CALL BAD_REP_NAME('35', @last);

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The procedure is created without complaint. The call fails with ERROR 1172 (42000): Result consisted of more than one row, because the WHERE clause matched all three rep rows, Kaiser, Hull, and Perez. Notice how the error blames the wrong thing: it reports too many rows, not the naming collision that produced them. Rename the parameter to i_rep_num and the procedure behaves.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-4a Retrieving a single row

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The most common job for a procedure is to look one thing up and hand it back. SELECT ... INTO does that: it runs an ordinary query, then copies each selected column into the variable named in the matching position of the INTO list. One column or several, it is built for a query that returns exactly one row. Zero rows and it assigns nothing; two or more rows and it raises an error. Both of those cases are the subject of 8-5.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: same re-runnability guard as before - drops any
--   earlier DISP_REP_NAME before the CREATE below runs.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DISP_REP_NAME //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the fixed version of the previous example.
CREATE PROCEDURE DISP_REP_NAME(

    -- The i_ prefix keeps the parameter name distinct from the column name.
    IN  i_rep_num    CHAR(2),

    -- Two OUT parameters: a procedure may hand back as many values as you like.
    OUT o_last_name  VARCHAR(20),
    OUT o_first_name VARCHAR(20))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO with two columns and two variables. They are matched by
    --   position, so the order of the two lists has to agree.
    SELECT LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME
    INTO   o_last_name, o_first_name

    -- FROM: REP, the table this corrected lookup reads.
    FROM   REP

    -- Now the comparison is genuinely column against parameter.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = i_rep_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Because REP_NUM is the primary key of REP, that WHERE clause can match at most one row, which is what makes SELECT ... INTO the right tool here. Two columns are selected and two variables are listed, in the same order. Call it, then read the session variables the same way you read any expression:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: the two @ variables are session variables, supplied as somewhere for the
--   OUT parameters to land. They need no declaration.
CALL DISP_REP_NAME('35', @last, @first);

-- SELECT: OUT parameters are not displayed automatically - reading the variables
--   back is how you see what the procedure produced.
SELECT @last AS LAST_NAME, @first AS FIRST_NAME;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The result is one row: LAST_NAME is Hull and FIRST_NAME is Richard. The CALL itself displays nothing. The procedure put its answers into @last and @first, and the SELECT that follows is what shows them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Tracing CALL DISP_REP_NAME('35', @last, @first) line by line
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            StepWhat runsWhat MySQL doesState afterward
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1CALL DISP_REP_NAME('35', @last, @first);Binds the literal '35' to i_rep_num, sets both OUT parameters to NULL, and reserves @last and @first as their destinationsi_rep_num = '35', o_last_name = NULL, o_first_name = NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2BEGINOpens the body; no local variables are declared hereNo change
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3SELECT LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME INTO o_last_name, o_first_name FROM REP WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num;Finds exactly one row, rep 35, then copies column one into the first variable and column two into the secondo_last_name = 'Hull', o_first_name = 'Richard'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            4ENDReturns, copying the OUT values into the caller's session variables@last = 'Hull', @first = 'Richard'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            5SELECT @last AS LAST_NAME, @first AS FIRST_NAME;Displays the two session variablesOne row: Hull, Richard

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Local variables and a computed answer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Sometimes the value you want is not stored anywhere and has to be worked out. A local variable gives the body somewhere to hold an intermediate result. Declare it with DECLARE, give it a type, and optionally a DEFAULT. Every DECLARE has to appear at the top of the block, before the first executable statement, and a local variable declared without a DEFAULT starts each call as NULL. Assign to it with SET, or by naming it in an INTO list.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            KimTay's credit department keeps asking how much room a customer has left. That is CREDIT_LIMIT minus BALANCE, and no column holds it:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: drops any earlier GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE so the CREATE
--   that follows doesn't fail on a name that already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one computes something rather than just fetching it.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_available    DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE: a LOCAL variable, visible only inside this procedure and gone the
    --   moment it ends. Every DECLARE must come before the first real statement
    --   of the body. Note there is no @ - that prefix marks session variables.
    DECLARE v_balance      DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- A second local, declared with the same type as the column it will hold.
    DECLARE v_credit_limit DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO: read both values from the row in one statement rather than
    --   querying the table twice.
    SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
    INTO   v_balance, v_credit_limit

    -- FROM: CUSTOMER, the table holding both BALANCE and CREDIT_LIMIT for this
    --   lookup.
    FROM   CUSTOMER

    -- WHERE: CUSTOMER_NUM is the primary key of CUSTOMER, so this matches exactly
    --   the one customer passed in - required for SELECT ... INTO to work.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- SET: assigns a value to a variable. The calculation is done in the
    --   procedure, not in SQL, and the answer goes into the OUT parameter.
    SET o_available = v_credit_limit - v_balance;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: a customer that owes money - the available credit is limit minus balance.
CALL GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE('1420', @avail);

-- SELECT: the CALL alone shows nothing - this reads the OUT value back through
--   @avail.
SELECT @avail AS CREDIT_AVAILABLE;

-- CALL: a customer with a zero balance, so the whole limit is still available.
--   Same procedure, different argument - which is the point of parameters.
CALL GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE('1310', @avail);

-- SELECT: same read-back, now showing the second call's result.
SELECT @avail AS CREDIT_AVAILABLE;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The first call reports 1179.25 for Whiskers & Wags Boutique, whose limit of 6000.00 stands against a balance of 4820.75. The second reports 10000.00 for Companion Care Clinic, which owes nothing against a limit of 10000.00. Two callers, two answers, one copy of the arithmetic.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Tracing CALL GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE('1420', @avail)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            StepWhat runsWhat MySQL doesState afterward
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1CALL GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE('1420', @avail);Binds '1420' to i_customer_num; o_available is set to NULL as the procedure startsi_customer_num = '1420', o_available = NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2DECLARE v_balance DECIMAL(9,2); DECLARE v_credit_limit DECIMAL(9,2);Creates two local variables that exist only until END, each starting as NULLv_balance = NULL, v_credit_limit = NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT INTO v_balance, v_credit_limit FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;Matches one row, Whiskers & Wags Boutique, and fills both localsv_balance = 4820.75, v_credit_limit = 6000.00
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            4SET o_available = v_credit_limit - v_balance;Evaluates 6000.00 - 4820.75 and stores the result in the OUT parametero_available = 1179.25
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            5END, then SELECT @avail AS CREDIT_AVAILABLE;Copies o_available back to the session variable and displays it@avail = 1179.25

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            INOUT: a value that goes in and comes back changed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            An INOUT parameter is the right choice when the procedure's job is to adjust a number the caller is already holding. A commission run works that way: it starts with a rep's running total and adds the effect of one more sale, at that rep's own rate.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: the same re-run guard as every script above -
--   removes any earlier ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION first.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: demonstrates the third parameter direction.
CREATE PROCEDURE ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION(
    IN    i_rep_num     CHAR(2),
    IN    i_sale_amount DECIMAL(9,2),

    -- INOUT: the caller passes a value IN, the procedure changes it, and the new
    --   value goes back OUT through the same parameter. Use it when the answer
    --   depends on what was there before.
    INOUT io_commission DECIMAL(8,2))
BEGIN

    -- A local to hold the rate looked up from the table.
    DECLARE v_rate DECIMAL(4,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO: fetch this rep's commission rate.
    SELECT RATE
    INTO   v_rate

    -- FROM: REP, the table that holds each rep's commission RATE.
    FROM   REP

    -- WHERE: matches the one rep passed in; REP_NUM is the primary key of REP,
    --   so SELECT ... INTO gets exactly the one row it needs.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = i_rep_num;

    -- SET: the INOUT parameter appears on BOTH sides - its incoming value is
    --   read on the right, and the updated total is written back on the left.
    SET io_commission = io_commission + (i_sale_amount * v_rate);
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- SET: give the session variable a starting value. An INOUT parameter must
--   already hold something, because the procedure reads it before writing it.
SET @comm = 39355.00;

-- CALL: the variable goes in holding the old commission and comes out holding
--   the new one.
CALL ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION('35', 1200.00, @comm);

-- SELECT: read the changed value back.
SELECT @comm AS NEW_COMMISSION;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            @comm starts at rep 35's stored commission of 39355.00. That rep's rate is 0.07, so a 1200.00 sale adds 84.00 and the procedure hands back 39439.00. Change that INOUT to OUT and the arithmetic breaks immediately: the incoming 39355.00 would be discarded when the procedure starts, leaving NULL plus 84.00, which is NULL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Seeing what is stored

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Procedures are objects in the database, so the catalog knows about them. In MySQL you can list the ones you have created:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- SELECT: the catalogue again, this time listing stored routines rather than
--   tables - procedures and functions both appear here.
SELECT ROUTINE_NAME, ROUTINE_TYPE

-- FROM: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES, one row per stored routine on the server.
FROM   INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES

-- WHERE: DATABASE() returns the name of the database you are currently connected
--   to, so this narrows the list to your own routines without hard-coding a name.
WHERE  ROUTINE_SCHEMA = DATABASE()
ORDER  BY ROUTINE_NAME;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            That query is another place the two engines part company. MySQL keeps this metadata in INFORMATION_SCHEMA. SQLite has no INFORMATION_SCHEMA at all, and its catalog, sqlite_master, lists tables, indexes, views, and triggers because those are the only object types it has. There is no row there for a procedure, because SQLite cannot store one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            To see the text of one procedure rather than a list of names, ask for its definition:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE: prints the full text of a procedure as the server
--   stored it. This is how you read code somebody else wrote, or recover your
--   own when the script that created it has been lost.
SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE DISP_REP_NAME;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Open a connection to the KimTay database

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In MySQL Workbench, open a SQL tab against the schema that holds REP, CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, and INVOICE_LINE. In the command line client, run USE followed by the database name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Run the whole script, DELIMITER lines included

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Select the entire block from DELIMITER // through DELIMITER ; and execute it as one script. Running only the CREATE PROCEDURE portion is what produces the classic syntax error at the first semicolon inside the body.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Confirm that it was stored

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Run the INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES query above, or SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE with the procedure name, and check that the name appears.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Call it, then read the output variables

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Issue the CALL, then SELECT the session variables you passed. The CALL alone shows nothing when every result travels through OUT parameters.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can say in one sentence what a stored procedure is and where it lives.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I know why DELIMITER is needed and that the server never sees it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can choose between IN, OUT, and INOUT for a given parameter and defend the choice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I never give a parameter the same name as a column.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can write SELECT ... INTO for a lookup on a primary key and read the answer back through a session variable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            🔍 Check yourself: procedures, parameters, and CALL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q1Access Pet Center's credit check

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            KimTay wants one place that reports how much credit a customer has left. The procedure declares IN i_customer_num CHAR(4) and OUT o_available DECIMAL(9,2). What does the OUT mode actually change about the call?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. Backwards. An OUT parameter is set to NULL as the procedure starts, so anything the caller passed is discarded; INOUT is the mode that carries a starting value in.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔b. Correct. OUT means the value travels from the procedure to the caller, which is why the argument has to be a writable session variable such as @avail rather than a literal.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. A CALL displays nothing on its own. Only a bare SELECT inside the body returns a result set; an OUT parameter has to be selected afterward to be seen.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. Confuses returning a value with storing one. Nothing in this procedure changes the database; CREDIT_LIMIT minus BALANCE is computed fresh on every call.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: OUT is a one-way channel out of the procedure, and the caller reads it by selecting the session variable it named in the CALL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q2A rep lookup that matches everybody

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A developer names a parameter REP_NUM, the same as the column, and writes WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM in the body. Calling it with '35' fails with ERROR 1172, result consisted of more than one row. What happened?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔a. Correct. When a name could mean a parameter or a column, MySQL resolves it as the parameter, so the condition reduces to a value equal to itself and every row in REP qualifies.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. The resolution goes the other way, and a column compared with itself would match every row rather than none, since every REP_NUM in the shipped data holds a value.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. No cast is involved. Comparing two CHAR(2) values is ordinary, and a type problem would not produce a row-count error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. SELECT ... INTO is the normal way to fetch one row inside a procedure. A cursor is for stepping through many rows, which is a different problem.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Prefix parameter names so they can never collide with column names, because the error MySQL reports describes a symptom rather than the cause.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q3KimTay's first procedure in Workbench

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A student pastes a CREATE PROCEDURE whose body holds three statements into the mysql client and gets a syntax error at the first semicolon inside the body. What fixes it?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. The body needs those semicolons; every statement between BEGIN and END must be terminated. Removing them produces a different syntax error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. A transaction groups changes to data. It says nothing about where the client believes one statement ends and the next begins.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔c.
