Correct. The client, not the server, is splitting the text at the first semicolon, so changing the terminator makes it send the whole CREATE PROCEDURE as one statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. A procedure normally lives in the same schema as the tables it uses, and its location has nothing to do with a statement terminator.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: DELIMITER is a client instruction that keeps a semicolon-filled procedure body from being chopped into fragments before it reaches the server.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-5 Error Handling

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A procedure that fails loudly costs you ten minutes. A procedure that fails silently costs you a month, because nobody knows it failed. Error handling is what turns the second kind into the first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The trouble starts with SELECT ... INTO, which expects exactly one row. When it finds none, MySQL does not raise an error. It raises warning 1329, No data - zero rows fetched, selected, or processed, and the procedure carries on to the next statement as though nothing had happened. Warnings are easy to miss, and most application code never looks at them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Here is a lookup with no handler at all. It is correct for every customer that exists, which is exactly why the flaw survives testing:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE: makes the script re-runnable. Without it, the second run
--   fails because the procedure already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: written the obvious way, with no error handling at all -
--   which is exactly what makes it unsafe.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_balance      DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO: fine when the customer exists. When it does not, the
    --   SELECT finds no row, MySQL raises a NOT FOUND warning rather than an
    --   error, and o_balance is left holding whatever it held before. The caller
    --   is never told that anything went wrong.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- SET: clear the variable so the next result is unambiguous.
SET @bal = 0;

-- CALL: a customer that exists. The balance comes back correctly.
CALL GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE('1120', @bal);

-- SELECT: reads back @bal, the correct balance for a customer that exists.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND;

-- CALL: a customer that does NOT exist. No error is raised.
CALL GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE('9999', @bal);

-- SHOW WARNINGS: the only evidence that anything happened - a NOT FOUND warning
--   that a program would have to go looking for.
SHOW WARNINGS;

-- SELECT: the variable still holds the PREVIOUS customer's balance, now being
--   reported as if it belonged to customer 9999. A wrong answer, silently.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The first SELECT @bal reports 3512.50, the balance for Access Pet Center. There is no customer 9999, so the second call assigns nothing, SHOW WARNINGS displays warning 1329, and @bal comes back NULL, because an OUT parameter was set to NULL when the procedure started. Nothing stopped, nothing was recorded, and the only clue is a warning the caller had to ask for.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            NULL is at least visibly wrong. The dangerous version returns a number that looks perfectly reasonable. An INOUT parameter is not blanked: it arrives holding whatever the caller put in it, and if the lookup assigns nothing, that incoming value is what travels straight back out. A local variable behaves the same way within a single execution: DECLARE gives it NULL at the start of every call, but once you have assigned to it, a later failed lookup leaves the earlier value sitting there untouched.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE: same reason as before - without it, re-running the script
--   fails because the procedure already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS STALE_DEMO //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the same trap, made even easier to fall into by using INOUT.
CREATE PROCEDURE STALE_DEMO(
    IN    i_customer_num CHAR(4),

    -- INOUT means the parameter arrives holding the caller's old value, so a
    --   failed lookup leaves that stale value sitting in place.
    INOUT io_balance     DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- No handler, so a miss changes nothing and says nothing.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   io_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- SET: reset @bal so a leftover value from the previous demo can't be
--   mistaken for real output.
SET @bal = 0;

-- CALL: a real customer, so the variable is filled correctly.
CALL STALE_DEMO('1120', @bal);

-- SELECT: reads back @bal, filled in correctly for a customer that exists.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND;

-- CALL: a customer that does not exist.
CALL STALE_DEMO('9999', @bal);

-- SELECT: the previous customer's balance is still there, and nothing in the
--   output distinguishes a real answer from a leftover one. This is why a
--   procedure must report what happened, not just what it found.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Both SELECT statements report 3512.50. The second one is a lie: @bal still held Access Pet Center's balance from the first call, the INOUT parameter carried it into the body, nothing overwrote it, and it came back out as the answer for a customer that does not exist. A credit check built on that answer approves an order for nobody.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The rule worth memorizing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A wrong answer that looks right is worse than an error message. An error stops the work and names the problem. A stale value travels quietly into an invoice, a report, and a decision.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DECLARE ... HANDLER

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A handler is a standing instruction: when this condition occurs anywhere in the block, run this statement. You declare it once, at the top of the block, and MySQL applies it for the rest of the block. The shape is DECLARE, then an action, then HANDLER FOR, then a condition, then one statement, or a BEGIN ... END group of statements.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The action is CONTINUE or EXIT. CONTINUE runs the handler statement and then resumes with the statement after the one that raised the condition. EXIT runs the handler statement and then leaves the enclosing BEGIN ... END block, which for a top-level block means the procedure returns.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Now the same balance lookup, written so that a missing customer is reported instead of hidden:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE: clears out any earlier version so the script can run again.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the safe version of the lookup.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUST_BALANCE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_balance      DECIMAL(9,2),

    -- A second OUT parameter carrying a plain-language status, so the caller
    --   learns what happened as well as what was found.
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE ... HANDLER: registers what to do when a condition arises. CONTINUE
    --   means "run this, then carry on with the next statement"; NOT FOUND is the
    --   condition raised when a SELECT ... INTO matches no row.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND

        -- CONCAT builds a message that names the customer that was missing.
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num);

    -- Set the OUT parameters to known values BEFORE the lookup, so nothing stale
    --   can survive. This line is what kills the previous example's bug.
    SET o_balance = NULL;

    -- The optimistic default, overwritten by the handler if the lookup misses.
    SET o_status  = 'OK';

    -- The lookup itself. If it finds nothing, the handler fires and o_status
    --   changes; if it succeeds, o_status stays 'OK'.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: a customer that exists - balance filled in, status 'OK'.
CALL GET_CUST_BALANCE('1120', @bal, @status);

-- SELECT: reads @bal and @status back through the session variables the
--   CALL wrote to.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND, @status AS STATUS;

-- CALL: a customer that does not - balance NULL, status explaining why. The
--   caller can now tell the two cases apart without guessing.
CALL GET_CUST_BALANCE('9999', @bal, @status);

-- SELECT: same read-back, now showing the NULL balance and the handler's
--   status message.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND, @status AS STATUS;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The first call reports 3512.50 with status OK. The second reports NULL with status No customer numbered 9999. The caller now has something it can test. Notice the two SET statements before the query: establishing a known starting state is what makes the outcome unambiguous, whichever path the body takes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Tracing CALL GET_CUST_BALANCE('9999', @bal, @status)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            StepWhat runsWhat MySQL doesState afterward
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1BEGIN, then the DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER lineRegisters the handler for the rest of the block; declaring it executes nothing yetHandler armed for NOT FOUND
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2SET o_balance = NULL; SET o_status = 'OK';Establishes a known starting stateo_balance = NULL, o_status = 'OK'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3SELECT BALANCE INTO o_balance FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '9999';Matches zero rows, assigns nothing, and raises the NOT FOUND condition, SQLSTATE class 02o_balance still NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            4The handler firesRuns SET o_status = CONCAT(...) because the condition matchedo_status = 'No customer numbered 9999'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            5CONTINUE takes effect, then ENDResumes at the statement after the SELECT; there is none, so the procedure returns@bal = NULL, @status = 'No customer numbered 9999'

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Which conditions you can handle

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Handler conditions in MySQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ConditionWhat it namesFires when
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            NOT FOUNDSQLSTATE class 02A SELECT ... INTO matched no rows. The same condition also covers a cursor fetched past its last row, though no cursors appear in these three sections.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQLWARNINGSQLSTATE class 01The statement completed but raised a warning, such as a value truncated on its way into a column
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQLEXCEPTIONEvery SQLSTATE class other than 00, 01, and 02A genuine error: a constraint violation, a duplicate key, or more than one row for a SELECT ... INTO
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            One named failureA single MySQL error number, written FOR 1451, or a SQLSTATE value, written FOR SQLSTATE '23000'You want that failure handled differently from everything else. An error number names exactly one error; a SQLSTATE value names a family, so '23000' catches a duplicate key as well as a foreign key violation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The three general conditions cover different SQLSTATE classes and do not overlap, so one procedure can safely declare a NOT FOUND handler and a SQLEXCEPTION handler at the same time. A missing row goes to the first, a constraint violation to the second. Class 00 means success and needs no handler.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONTINUE or EXIT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONTINUE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Note the problem and keep going. Right when the rest of the body is still safe to run: recording that a lookup came up empty, then finishing a report. Wrong when the statements that follow depend on the value that never arrived, because they will run anyway, on nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            EXIT

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Note the problem and stop. Right when the failed statement was a precondition for everything after it: if the customer does not exist, do not update, do not delete, do not log a payment. This is the safer default for any procedure that changes data.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SQLEXCEPTION: catching a real error

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SELECT ... INTO is equally unhappy with too many rows, but that case is an error rather than a warning: ERROR 1172 (42000), Result consisted of more than one row. With no handler, the procedure stops there and the error surfaces to whoever called it. With a handler, you decide what the caller sees.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            This procedure looks a balance up by city, a design that only works while each city holds one customer. KimTay has two in Maple Grove, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE: re-runnable script, same reasoning as the earlier examples.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one looks up on a NON-key column, which is where the
--   other failure mode lives - too many rows rather than none.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY(
    IN  i_city    VARCHAR(20),
    OUT o_balance DECIMAL(9,2),
    OUT o_status  VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE EXIT HANDLER: EXIT means "run this, then STOP the procedure" -
    --   unlike CONTINUE, nothing after the failing statement runs. SQLEXCEPTION
    --   catches any error, including a SELECT ... INTO that matched several rows.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION

        -- CONCAT builds a message that names the city where the lookup failed.
        SET o_status = CONCAT('Lookup failed for ', i_city, ' - check the city');

    -- Known starting values again.
    SET o_balance = NULL;

    -- The optimistic default, overwritten by the EXIT handler if SQLEXCEPTION
    --   fires.
    SET o_status  = 'OK';

    -- One city holds one customer and works; another holds two, the INTO cannot
    --   choose between them, and the EXIT handler takes over.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CITY = i_city;
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: Northfield has exactly one customer, so the lookup succeeds.
CALL GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY('Northfield', @bal, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back @bal and @status - the balance found, and status 'OK'.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND, @status AS STATUS;

-- CALL: Maple Grove has two, so SELECT ... INTO fails and the EXIT handler
--   reports it instead of returning one of the two at random.
CALL GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY('Maple Grove', @bal, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back @bal and @status - NULL balance, and the message the
--   EXIT handler set.
SELECT @bal AS BALANCE_FOUND, @status AS STATUS;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Northfield holds one customer, Downtown Aquarium & Pets, so the first call reports 1200.00 with status OK. Maple Grove holds two, so the second raises error 1172, the handler catches it, and the caller sees NULL with status Lookup failed for Maple Grove - check the city. The session stays alive and the client sees no error at all. That is the point of catching it, and also the responsibility that comes with catching it: if you swallow an error, you have to report it some other way, or you have rebuilt the silent failure you set out to remove.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Declaration order is fixed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Inside a BEGIN ... END block MySQL requires a strict order: DECLARE for variables and conditions first, then any cursor declarations, then handler declarations, and only then executable statements. Nothing in these sections uses a cursor, but the slot exists between the two kinds of declaration. Putting a DECLARE after a SET is a syntax error, and the message points at the DECLARE rather than explaining the rule.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Give every procedure a status parameter

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            An OUT o_status costs one line and turns a procedure into something a caller can check. Set it to a known value at the top of the body, overwrite it in each handler, and overwrite it once more when the work finishes successfully. The caller then never has to guess whether anything happened.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can explain why SELECT ... INTO finding no rows is a warning rather than an error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I know that an OUT parameter starts as NULL, that an INOUT parameter arrives holding the caller's value, and that a local variable starts NULL on every call but keeps whatever it was last assigned during that call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can write a NOT FOUND handler and a SQLEXCEPTION handler and say which one fires when.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can choose CONTINUE or EXIT for a given procedure and defend the choice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I set a status value at the top of the body so the caller always learns what happened.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            🔍 Check yourself: handlers and silent failure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q1A balance lookup for a customer who is not there

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE has no handler at all. It runs SELECT BALANCE INTO o_balance for customer 9999, which does not exist in KimTay's data. What does the caller get?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. Zero rows raises a warning, not an error. Too many rows is the error case; too few passes by quietly and the body keeps running.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. That is the hazard with an INOUT parameter, which arrives holding whatever the caller passed, or with a local variable already assigned earlier in the same execution. This OUT parameter was set to NULL when the procedure started.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔c. Correct. Nothing is assigned, the OUT parameter keeps the NULL it started with, and MySQL raises warning 1329 that no data was fetched.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. MySQL never invents a value. A missing row and a balance of 0.00, which is what Companion Care Clinic actually has, are different facts.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Without a handler, a lookup that finds nothing reports nothing, and the only trace is a warning almost no caller checks.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q2Two customers in Maple Grove

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A procedure runs SELECT BALANCE INTO o_balance FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CITY = i_city and is called with 'Maple Grove', which matches both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. Which handler catches that?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. NOT FOUND covers SQLSTATE class 02, which means zero rows. Two rows is the opposite problem and belongs to a different class entirely.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. SQLWARNING covers class 01. Too many rows for SELECT ... INTO is error 1172, SQLSTATE 42000, which is not a warning and would slip past this handler.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. MySQL refuses rather than picking one, which is the safe choice; silently keeping an arbitrary row would produce a plausible wrong answer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔d. Correct. SQLEXCEPTION covers every SQLSTATE class other than 00, 01, and 02, which includes the more-than-one-row error.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: NOT FOUND, SQLWARNING, and SQLEXCEPTION cover different SQLSTATE classes, so one procedure can declare several handlers without them overlapping.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q3A delete routine that keeps going after it fails

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A procedure that removes a customer declares a CONTINUE handler for SQLEXCEPTION that sets a status message, and three more statements follow the DELETE. What is the risk of choosing CONTINUE here?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔a. Correct. CONTINUE resumes at the statement after the one that failed, so anything written on the assumption that the DELETE worked runs anyway, against unchanged data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. Handlers assign to OUT parameters routinely; that is how a status message reaches the caller in every example in this section.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. No handler rolls a transaction back on its own. A ROLLBACK happens only if you write one, which is why the SHIP_ITEM handler includes it explicitly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. Neither CONTINUE nor EXIT retries anything. CONTINUE moves forward and EXIT leaves the block; MySQL has no retry action.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Use EXIT when the statements that follow depend on the one that failed, and save CONTINUE for cases where the rest of the body is still safe to run.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-6 Using Update Procedures

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Everything so far has read data. Procedures that change data are where the case for putting SQL in the database stops being about convenience and starts being about safety. The reason is short: the procedure carries the WHERE clause. It is written once, by someone who knew what they were doing, and it cannot be forgotten at four in the afternoon.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-6a Changing data with a procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Consider the everyday task of adding a charge to a customer's balance. Typed by hand it is one statement. Typed by hand with the last line missing it is a very different statement:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- The accident. Read it, do not run it: every worked example below
-- assumes the shipped balances are still intact.
-- UPDATE: the table.
UPDATE CUSTOMER

-- SET with no WHERE: every customer's balance goes up by 250. The statement is
--   perfectly valid SQL, which is precisely the danger - wrapping this logic in
--   a procedure that always carries its own WHERE clause is how you stop a
--   missing line from reaching production.
SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + 250.00;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            That succeeds. MySQL reports Query OK, 4 rows affected, and every KimTay customer has been charged: Access Pet Center rises to 3762.50, Downtown Aquarium & Pets to 1450.00, Companion Care Clinic to 250.00 for an order it never placed, and Whiskers & Wags Boutique to 5070.75. There is no syntax error to catch it, and outside a transaction there is nothing to roll back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Now the same operation as a procedure. The WHERE clause is part of the stored definition and the customer number is a required parameter, so there is no version of this that runs without a target:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable - without it, the
--   second run fails because UPD_CUST_BALANCE already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS UPD_CUST_BALANCE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: an UPDATE wrapped safely, so the WHERE clause can never be
--   forgotten and a missing customer is reported rather than ignored.
CREATE PROCEDURE UPD_CUST_BALANCE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    IN  i_amount       DECIMAL(9,2),
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- A local to hold the customer's name, used in the status message.
    DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35);

    -- EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND: if the customer does not exist, stop before the
    --   UPDATE ever runs and say so. EXIT rather than CONTINUE is deliberate.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num, ' - nothing changed');

    -- The lookup does double duty: it fetches the name AND proves the customer
    --   exists. A miss here fires the handler and the procedure ends.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME
    INTO   v_name
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- The change itself, reached only when the customer is known to exist.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER

    -- SET: adds the caller's i_amount to the customer's current balance.
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + i_amount

    -- The WHERE clause is written into the procedure once and cannot be left off
    --   by a caller in a hurry.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- Report exactly what was done, naming the customer and the amount.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Balance for ', v_name, ' changed by ', i_amount);
END //

DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The lookup at the top is doing real work. It fetches the name for the status message, but more importantly it is an existence test. If the customer is not there, NOT FOUND fires, and because the handler is an EXIT handler the UPDATE never runs at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: a real customer. The status names them and the amount.
CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('1120', 250.00, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message the successful call set.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

-- SELECT: proof that exactly one row moved and the other three did not.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- CALL: a customer that does not exist. The handler stops the procedure before
--   the UPDATE, so nothing at all is changed and the caller is told why.
CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('9999', 250.00, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message explaining why nothing changed.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The first call reports Balance for Access Pet Center changed by 250.00, and the listing that follows shows 1120 at 3762.50 while 1225, 1310, and 1420 sit untouched at 1200.00, 0.00, and 4820.75. The second call reports No customer numbered 9999 - nothing changed, and no row anywhere moved. This example does change the shipped data; the cleanup at the end of the section puts 1120 back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Tracing CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('9999', 250.00, @status)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            StepWhat runsWhat MySQL doesState afterward
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35); DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND ...Creates the local variable and arms the handlerv_name = NULL, handler armed
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME INTO v_name FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '9999';Matches zero rows and raises NOT FOUNDv_name still NULL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3The handler firesSets o_status to the message naming 9999o_status = 'No customer numbered 9999 - nothing changed'
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            4EXIT takes effectLeaves the BEGIN ... END block at once, skipping the UPDATE and the final SETThe UPDATE never executes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            5Control returns to the callerCopies the OUT value back into the session variable@status holds the message; all four balances unchanged

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            An update procedure with a transaction

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            When a procedure changes data, a handler is the natural place to undo partial work. This one reduces stock as an item ships, wraps the change in a transaction, and rolls back if anything goes wrong. Notice the declaration order: the local variable first, then the handlers, then the executable statements.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: same re-runnability guard, now for SHIP_ITEM.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHIP_ITEM //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: a procedure that changes data inside a transaction, with two
--   different handlers for two different kinds of failure.
CREATE PROCEDURE SHIP_ITEM(
    IN  i_item_id     CHAR(4),
    IN  i_qty_shipped SMALLINT,
    OUT o_status      VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN
    -- A local to hold the item's description, used in the success message.
    DECLARE v_description VARCHAR(30);

    -- EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION with a BEGIN ... END block: a handler can run
    --   several statements, not just one, when it is wrapped like this.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
    BEGIN

        -- ROLLBACK first: undo any half-finished change before reporting.
        ROLLBACK;

        -- SET: reports the failure back through the status parameter.
        SET o_status = 'Shipment failed - stock left unchanged';
    END;

    -- A second handler for a different condition. NOT FOUND is not an error, so
    --   it needs its own handler; SQLEXCEPTION would never catch it.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No item numbered ', i_item_id);

    -- Look up the item, which also proves it exists before anything is changed.
    SELECT DESCRIPTION
    INTO   v_description
    FROM   ITEM
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = i_item_id;

    -- START TRANSACTION: open the safety net around the change.
    START TRANSACTION;

    -- The change itself.
    UPDATE ITEM

    -- SET: reduces on-hand stock by the quantity shipped.
    SET    ON_HAND = ON_HAND - i_qty_shipped

    -- WHERE: the same one-row guarantee - only this item's stock changes.
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = i_item_id;

    -- COMMIT: reached only if the UPDATE raised nothing. If it had, the
    --   SQLEXCEPTION handler would have rolled back and ended the procedure
    --   before this line.
    COMMIT;

    -- The success message, built from the description looked up earlier.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Shipped ', i_qty_shipped, ' of ', v_description);
END //

DELIMITER ;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: a real item. Stock falls by three and the status says so.
CALL SHIP_ITEM('CF21', 3, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message confirming the shipment.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

-- SELECT: confirm the new stock figure.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';

-- CALL: an item id that does not exist. The NOT FOUND handler stops the
--   procedure before the transaction is even opened.
CALL SHIP_ITEM('ZZ99', 1, @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message explaining why nothing shipped.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The first call reports Shipped 3 of Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb and leaves ON_HAND at 45, down from 48. The second reports No item numbered ZZ99 and never opens a transaction, because the EXIT handler for NOT FOUND returns before START TRANSACTION is reached.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The SQLEXCEPTION handler is the insurance policy, and it is worth being exact about when it earns its keep. KimTay's ON_HAND is a plain SMALLINT, so shipping more units than exist would quietly produce a negative number rather than an error, which is a data-quality problem this procedure does not solve. Declare the column SMALLINT UNSIGNED instead and the same subtraction raises ERROR 1264, out of range value, under MySQL's default strict SQL mode. Then the handler does its job: the ROLLBACK undoes the change and the caller is told the shipment failed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            8-6b Deleting data with a procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Everything true of UPDATE is more true of DELETE. An UPDATE that hits every row can sometimes be reasoned back out of, because the old values are often recoverable from somewhere. A DELETE that hits every row leaves nothing to reason with.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- The accident. Read it, do not run it.
-- DELETE with no WHERE: every customer row is removed in one statement. Nothing
--   warns you, and outside a transaction nothing brings them back. This is the
--   statement the procedure below exists to make impossible.
DELETE FROM CUSTOMER;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Against the KimTay data this one fails, with ERROR 1451 (23000), Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails, because invoices 50710, 50711, and 50712 point at customers 1120, 1420, and 1225. The whole statement is rolled back and no rows are removed. That is a foreign key doing its job, and it is not a rescue to count on: on any table with no children, the same statement empties it without complaint.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The procedure version takes the customer number as a parameter, confirms that the customer exists, and turns the foreign key error into a sentence a person can read:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: and again for DEL_CUSTOMER, so this script can run
--   more than once.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DEL_CUSTOMER //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: a delete that can only ever remove one named row, and that
--   explains itself whichever way it ends.
CREATE PROCEDURE DEL_CUSTOMER(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(70))
BEGIN
    -- A local to hold the customer's name, used later in the status message.
    DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35);

    -- Handler 1 - an actual error. The likeliest one here is a foreign key
    --   violation: the customer still has invoices pointing at it.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
        SET o_status = CONCAT('Could not delete ', i_customer_num, ' - invoices still reference it');

    -- Handler 2 - not an error at all, just nothing found. Two conditions, two
    --   handlers, two different messages.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num);

    -- Fetch the name, and in doing so confirm the customer exists.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME
    INTO   v_name
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- The delete, with its WHERE clause built in permanently.
    DELETE FROM CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- Reached only when the delete succeeded.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Deleted ', v_name);
END //

DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Two handlers, two different failures. NOT FOUND belongs to SQLSTATE class 02 and SQLEXCEPTION covers the classes outside 00, 01, and 02, so they cannot both claim the same condition.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CALL: a customer with no invoices - the delete succeeds.
CALL DEL_CUSTOMER('1310', @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message confirming the delete.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

-- CALL: a customer that DOES have invoices. The foreign key refuses the delete,
--   the SQLEXCEPTION handler catches it, and the row survives.
CALL DEL_CUSTOMER('1120', @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message explaining the foreign key refusal.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

-- CALL: a customer that never existed. The NOT FOUND handler answers this one.
CALL DEL_CUSTOMER('9999', @status);

-- SELECT: reads back the status message for the missing customer.
SELECT @status AS STATUS;

-- SELECT: three outcomes, and the table shows exactly one row gone.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Three calls, three endings. Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so 1310 is removed and the status reads Deleted Companion Care Clinic. Access Pet Center appears on invoice 50710, so the DELETE raises the foreign key error, the SQLEXCEPTION handler catches it, and the status reads Could not delete 1120 - invoices still reference it, with the row still in place. Customer 9999 never existed, so NOT FOUND fires before the DELETE is reached. The final listing shows 1120, 1225, and 1420 remaining.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Put Companion Care Clinic back before you move on, so that the rest of the course's examples still match:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- INSERT INTO with no column list: put the deleted customer back, supplying a
--   value for all nine columns in the table's own order. This is the tidy-up
--   step, so the rest of the module works against the shipped data.
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER
VALUES ('1310', 'Companion Care Clinic', '89 River Rd.', 'Maple Grove', 'OH',
        '44601', 0.00, 10000.00, '20');

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The safety argument, stated plainly

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Typed by hand

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The WHERE clause is rewritten every time, by whoever is at the keyboard. A missing line, a stray semicolon, or the wrong window changes every row in the table. Existence is never checked, failures arrive as raw error codes, and the only record of what was intended is in somebody's memory.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Run as a procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The WHERE clause is stored once and cannot be dropped. The key is a required parameter, so nothing runs without a target. Existence is verified before the change, failures come back as sentences through a status parameter, and the definition can be reviewed and version controlled like any other code.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            There is a second, sharper version of the argument that has nothing to do with typing. Privileges in MySQL can be granted on a procedure rather than on a table. Give an account the right to execute DEL_CUSTOMER and withhold DELETE on CUSTOMER, and that account can retire a closed account through the checked, single-row path and has no way to issue a bare DELETE at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS: make the account, skipping quietly if it is already
--   there. MySQL identifies accounts as user@host.
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'billing_clerk'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'change_me';

-- GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE: the clerk may RUN the procedure. Notice what is not
--   granted - no DELETE on CUSTOMER at all, so the only way this account can
--   remove a customer is through the procedure, with all its checks in place.
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE KIMTAY.DEL_CUSTOMER TO 'billing_clerk'@'localhost';

-- GRANT SELECT: read access to the table, so the clerk can see the list. Reading
--   and deleting are separate privileges, and only one of them is given here.
GRANT SELECT ON KIMTAY.CUSTOMER TO 'billing_clerk'@'localhost';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why that actually works: SQL SECURITY DEFINER

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The arrangement depends on a default worth saying out loud. Unless you write otherwise, MySQL creates a procedure with SQL SECURITY DEFINER, so the body runs with the privileges of the account that defined it, not the account that called it. That is why the clerk needs EXECUTE and nothing more: the DELETE inside the procedure is performed on the definer's authority. Create the same procedure with SQL SECURITY INVOKER and the clerk would need DELETE on CUSTOMER after all, which is precisely the privilege you were trying to withhold.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Engine note

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            GRANT, REVOKE, and CREATE USER are MySQL and Oracle. SQLite has no user accounts and no privilege system whatsoever, so none of these statements exist there - permission in SQLite is whatever the operating system says about the database file. Replace KIMTAY with the name of your own schema before running them, and use a real password rather than the placeholder.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Cleaning up

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Two of the examples in this section changed real rows: UPD_CUST_BALANCE added 250.00 to customer 1120, and SHIP_ITEM took 3 units off item CF21. Put both back to their shipped values, so that every later example in the course still matches. Writing the restore as an assignment rather than an adjustment makes it safe to run twice:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- UPDATE: restore the balance the worked examples changed, so the shipped data
--   is back where it started.
UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = 3512.50 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- UPDATE: and the stock figure the SHIP_ITEM example reduced.
UPDATE ITEM     SET ON_HAND = 48      WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Procedures persist until you drop them. When you have finished working through these three sections, remove the ones you created:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            -- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: clean up every procedure this lesson created. IF
--   EXISTS on each line means the whole script runs to the end even if some of
--   them were never created or have already been dropped.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHOW_REP_COUNT;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS BAD_REP_NAME;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DISP_REP_NAME;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS STALE_DEMO;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS UPD_CUST_BALANCE;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHIP_ITEM;
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DEL_CUSTOMER;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can write an update procedure whose WHERE clause uses a required parameter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I use an EXIT handler so that a missing row prevents the change instead of quietly matching nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can wrap a change in a transaction and ROLLBACK from inside a SQLEXCEPTION handler.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can explain why a foreign key error is a better outcome than a successful delete.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I can state the privilege argument, EXECUTE on the procedure rather than DELETE on the table, and I know it works because MySQL defaults a procedure to SQL SECURITY DEFINER.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • I restore any row an example changed before moving on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            🔍 Check yourself: update and delete procedures

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q1A charge posted to Access Pet Center

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Against the shipped data, a clerk runs CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('1120', 250.00, @status). What is Access Pet Center's balance afterward, and what makes this safer than typing the UPDATE by hand?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. The body adds: BALANCE = BALANCE + i_amount. Pass a negative amount to reduce a balance; the direction is the caller's choice, not the procedure's.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔b. Correct. 3512.50 plus 250.00 is 3762.50, and the stored WHERE clause on the required parameter is what keeps the change to one customer.
