                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. The arithmetic is right but the reason is wrong. A procedure may change every row in a table; being stored places no limit on the row count.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. That would be an assignment rather than an adjustment. This procedure adds to the existing balance, so 3512.50 is the starting point, not something discarded.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: The safety comes from the WHERE clause living in the stored definition beside a required key parameter, not from anything MySQL enforces on its own.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q2Retiring Companion Care Clinic

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DEL_CUSTOMER is called for 1310, then for 1120. Companion Care Clinic has no invoice; Access Pet Center appears on invoice 50710. What do the two calls report?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. A procedure does run with the definer's privileges by default, but privileges and constraints are different things. A foreign key is enforced no matter who issues the statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. MySQL commits each statement on its own unless you open a transaction, so the delete of 1310 takes effect immediately and permanently.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔c. Correct. The unreferenced row goes, the referenced one raises ERROR 1451, and the handler converts that error into the readable status the caller receives.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘d. NOT FOUND is about the lookup finding no customer, not about invoices, and nothing here cascades: the invoice for 1120 is exactly what blocks the delete.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: A foreign key stops the delete and the SQLEXCEPTION handler explains it, so the caller learns why nothing was removed instead of guessing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Q3Locking down KimTay's billing clerk

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            KimTay wants a clerk to be able to remove a closed customer account through the checked path, but never to be able to issue a bare DELETE against CUSTOMER. Which arrangement delivers that?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘a. This is exactly the exposure to remove. Once DELETE on the table is granted, one forgotten line empties it, and no amount of care makes that impossible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘b. SELECT alone cannot delete anything, so the clerk could not do the job at all; the account still has to be permitted to run the procedure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✘c. A transaction helps only if the mistake is noticed before the COMMIT, and it does nothing to stop a bare DELETE from being issued in the first place.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • ✔d. Correct. The privilege is attached to the procedure, and because MySQL creates procedures with SQL SECURITY DEFINER by default, the DELETE inside runs on the definer's authority, so the only delete available to that account is the one that takes a customer number and checks it first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Remember: Granting EXECUTE on a procedure instead of DELETE on a table turns a policy about how deletes should be done into a rule the server enforces, provided the procedure keeps the default SQL SECURITY DEFINER.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            🧩 Anatomy of a stored procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Each card is one line taken from the KimTay procedures in 8-4 through 8-6. Drop each line into the part of the procedure it belongs to. Every card fits exactly one zone.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      0 / 8 placed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7 Selecting Multiple Rows with a Procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Every procedure you have written so far has worked on one row. You passed in a customer number, the procedure ran a SELECT ... INTO, and one set of values landed in the variables. That works because the query could only ever match one row: CUSTOMER_NUM is the primary key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Real requests are rarely that tidy. "Review every customer in rep 20's territory" matches two rows in the KimTay data, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. "Log every line on invoice 50710" matches two rows. A procedure that has to look at each of those rows in turn needs a different tool, and that tool is a cursor.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Engine note, said once

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Cursors, handlers, and loops are MySQL stored-program features. None of the procedure code in this section runs in this page's sandbox, because the sandbox is SQLite and SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE, no DECLARE, and no cursors. Read the procedure code in the code blocks and run it in MySQL Workbench. What the sandboxes in this section do run is ordinary SQL: the queries the cursors are built on, and at the end the set-based statements that replace one of the loops entirely.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7a Using a Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Start from what already works. Inside a procedure, this statement copies one row into two variables:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- SELECT ... INTO: the one-row form you have already used. It works only when
--   the query returns exactly one row, which is why it is safe on a primary key
--   lookup and dangerous on anything else.
SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

    -- INTO: two columns land in two variables, matched by position.
    INTO v_balance, v_credit_limit

    -- FROM: the customer table this lookup reads.
    FROM CUSTOMER

    -- Filtering on the key is what guarantees the single row.
    WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Now change the condition from a primary key to a rep number. The query is still legal SQL, but it no longer returns one row:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two rows come back: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic. Ask yourself which one a single set of variables could hold.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two rows come back. Put that same query behind SELECT ... INTO in a MySQL procedure and the procedure stops with ERROR 1172: Result consisted of more than one row. There is no partial credit and no silent first row. SELECT ... INTO demands exactly one row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor is a named pointer into the result set of a SELECT. Instead of assigning a whole result to variables at once, a cursor holds the rows and hands them to you one at a time, in order, on demand. Think of it as a bookmark that starts above the first row and moves down one row every time you ask for the next one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You declare a cursor by giving it a name and the query it stands for. Declaring does not run the query. It records the definition so the procedure can open it later:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor is a query held ready, so the procedure can
--   walk its rows ONE AT A TIME. This line only defines it - nothing runs yet,
--   and the SELECT below is not executed until OPEN.
DECLARE cust_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- The query the cursor will walk. Four columns, so four variables will be
    --   needed to receive each row.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

    -- FROM: the customer table the cursor's query reads.
    FROM CUSTOMER

    -- A cursor query may use a parameter exactly like any other query.
    WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num

    -- ORDER BY matters more than usual here: it fixes the order the rows will be
    --   handed to you in, one by one.
    ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two details in that declaration earn their keep. The query refers to i_rep_num, the procedure's own parameter, so one cursor definition serves every rep. And it carries ORDER BY. A loop reads rows in the order the cursor produces them, so if the order matters to your logic or to a report, say so in the cursor query.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Declaration order is a rule, not a style

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      MySQL requires every DECLARE to sit at the top of the BEGIN block in a fixed order: variables and conditions first, then cursor declarations, then handler declarations. Put the handler above the cursor and the procedure will not compile. Name variables so they cannot collide with column names, which is why these examples use the v_ prefix for local variables and i_ for IN parameters.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7b Opening a Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Declaring a cursor is paperwork. Opening it is the moment the work happens:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- OPEN: runs the cursor's query and positions it just BEFORE the first row.
--   Nothing has been read yet; the cursor is simply ready to start.
OPEN cust_cursor;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • MySQL runs the cursor's SELECT, using whatever values the parameters and variables hold right now.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • The result set is built and held for this cursor.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • The cursor position is set just above the first row, not on it. Nothing has been copied into your variables yet.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • If the query matches no rows at all, OPEN still succeeds. You find out that the result is empty on the first FETCH, not here.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Open once, then close

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Opening a cursor that is already open raises ERROR 1325: Cursor is already open, and fetching from a cursor that was never opened raises ERROR 1326: Cursor is not open. One OPEN, one loop, one CLOSE. If a procedure needs to walk the same rows twice, close the cursor and open it again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7c Fetching Rows from a Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      FETCH moves the cursor down one row and copies that row's column values into variables:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- FETCH ... INTO: moves the cursor on by one row and copies that row's values
--   into the listed variables. The variables must match the cursor's SELECT list
--   in number, order and type. One FETCH gets exactly one row, which is why a
--   loop is needed to reach them all.
FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                       v_balance, v_credit_limit;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The match is positional. The variable list must have exactly as many variables as the cursor query has columns, in the same order, with compatible types. The cursor above selects four columns, so the FETCH names four variables. Get the count wrong and MySQL reports ERROR 1328: Incorrect number of FETCH variables. Get the order wrong and the procedure runs happily while writing a balance into a name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      One FETCH gives you one row. To reach them all, the FETCH goes inside a loop, and the loop needs a way to know it has run out of rows. That is what the NOT FOUND handler does. When a FETCH is attempted past the last row, MySQL raises the NOT FOUND condition; the handler catches it and sets a flag you control:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DECLARE ... DEFAULT: a flag variable, starting at 0 meaning "not finished".
DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

-- CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND: when a FETCH runs past the last row, NOT FOUND
--   is raised. This handler sets the flag and lets execution carry on, which is
--   how the loop learns that the rows have run out.
DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

-- LOOP with a LABEL: cust_loop names the loop so it can be left by name.
cust_loop: LOOP

    -- Read the next row into the variables.
    FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                           v_balance, v_credit_limit;

    -- Test the flag IMMEDIATELY after the fetch. If the fetch failed, the
    --   variables still hold the PREVIOUS row, so processing them here would
    --   duplicate the last row - a classic off-by-one in cursor code.
    IF v_done = 1 THEN

        -- LEAVE: jumps out of the named loop. Without it this runs forever.
        LEAVE cust_loop;
    -- END IF: when the flag is still 0, there is no LEAVE, so control falls
    --   straight through to the row-processing step below.
    END IF;

    -- work on the row that was retrieved goes here
-- END LOOP: sends control back to the top for the next row.
END LOOP cust_loop;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Read that loop the way MySQL runs it. LOOP repeats forever until something leaves it. The label cust_loop gives LEAVE a target. CONTINUE on the handler means "after handling the condition, carry on with the next statement" rather than abandoning the block, which is what lets the very next IF see the flag and exit cleanly.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Test the flag immediately after FETCH

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A failed FETCH does not blank out your variables. They still hold the previous row's values. If you do the work first and test v_done at the bottom of the loop, the last row gets processed twice: once for real, once from the leftovers of the FETCH that found nothing. The test belongs on the line right after the FETCH, before any use of the fetched values.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Use a CONTINUE handler here, not an EXIT handler. An EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND ends the enclosing block the moment the rows run out, which skips your CLOSE and any summary work you meant to do after the loop.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7d Closing a Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      When the loop ends, release the result set:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- CLOSE: releases the cursor and the resources the server was holding for it.
--   Always close what you open, so a long-running procedure does not accumulate
--   open cursors.
CLOSE cust_cursor;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • The memory holding the rows is freed and the cursor name becomes available to OPEN again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • MySQL closes a cursor automatically at the end of the block that declared it, but write the CLOSE anyway: it documents the lifecycle and it matters in long procedures that open several cursors.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Closing a cursor that is not open raises ERROR 1326, so do not put a CLOSE in a path that may run twice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • After CLOSE, the variables keep the values from the last successful FETCH. That is fine to use for a summary line, as long as you know that is where the values came from.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7e Writing a Complete Procedure Using a Cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Now assemble the pieces against KimTay. The goal: for one rep, walk that rep's customers, work out how much credit each one has left, mark anyone with less than $5,000 of room for a follow-up call, and record the results so the DBA can read them back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A MySQL procedure has nowhere to "print" a row, so the procedure writes its findings to a table. Create that table first:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: clear out any table left behind by an earlier run, so
--   this script can be re-run from the top.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS CUST_REVIEW;

-- CREATE TABLE: somewhere for the procedure to write its results. A stored
--   procedure that loops over rows usually has to put its output somewhere, and
--   a small result table is the simplest place.
CREATE TABLE CUST_REVIEW
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),

     -- The computed figure the procedure will work out per customer.
     AVAILABLE_CREDIT DECIMAL(9,2),

     -- The verdict, chosen by an IF inside the loop.
     REVIEW_NOTE VARCHAR(10));
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 1: the shell

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Parameter, variables, cursor, handler, OPEN and CLOSE. It compiles and runs and does nothing. That is exactly the point: get the declarations legal before adding logic.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 2: the loop

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Add the labelled LOOP, the FETCH, and the LEAVE test. Now the procedure walks every row and still produces no output, so any error you see is a cursor error, not a logic error.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 3: the work

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Put the per-row calculation and the INSERT inside the loop. Only now is there anything to get wrong about the business rule.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 1. Note the declaration order: variables, then the cursor, then the handler.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable. Without it, the
--   second run fails because REP_CREDIT_REVIEW already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS REP_CREDIT_REVIEW //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: stage one of building a cursor procedure - declarations only,
--   with an OPEN and CLOSE and nothing in between. Build it in stages like this
--   and each piece can be checked before the next is added.
CREATE PROCEDURE REP_CREDIT_REVIEW (IN i_rep_num CHAR(2))
BEGIN

    -- The finished flag.
    DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

    -- One variable per column the cursor returns, declared with matching types.
    DECLARE v_customer_num CHAR(4);
    DECLARE v_customer_name VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE v_balance DECIMAL(9,2);
    DECLARE v_credit_limit DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- Two more for values the procedure will calculate rather than fetch.
    DECLARE v_available DECIMAL(9,2);
    DECLARE v_note VARCHAR(10);

    -- The cursor declaration. MySQL demands a strict order inside a procedure:
    --   variables first, then cursors, then handlers. Get it wrong and the
    --   procedure will not compile.
    DECLARE cust_cursor CURSOR FOR

        -- The same four columns walked through earlier in this section.
        SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

        -- FROM: the customer table this procedure reviews.
        FROM CUSTOMER

        -- WHERE: the rep parameter, so one procedure serves every rep.
        WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num

        -- ORDER BY: keeps the fetch order predictable, as before.
        ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- The handler comes last of the three, and arms the finished flag.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

    -- Open and close with nothing between them: this version does no work, but it
    --   proves the declarations are correct.
    OPEN cust_cursor;
    CLOSE cust_cursor;
END //

DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 2. Add the loop between the OPEN and the CLOSE. Only the middle of the procedure changes:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- OPEN: run the query and get ready to read.
    OPEN cust_cursor;

    -- The loop skeleton: fetch, test, leave. Stage two adds the walking, still
    --   without doing anything to the rows.
    cust_loop: LOOP

        -- FETCH: read the next row into the variables, same call as before.
        FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                               v_balance, v_credit_limit;

        -- The exit test goes straight after the FETCH and before any processing.
        IF v_done = 1 THEN
            LEAVE cust_loop;
        -- END IF: with the flag still 0, there is no row work yet in this stage,
        --   so control falls straight through to the bottom of the loop.
        END IF;
    -- END LOOP: sends control back to the top for the next FETCH; stage three
    --   will add row-processing work before this line.
    END LOOP cust_loop;

    -- CLOSE: tidy up once the rows are exhausted.
    CLOSE cust_cursor;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stage 3. Fill in the loop body and the procedure is finished:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable, same reason as
--   every earlier version of this procedure.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS REP_CREDIT_REVIEW //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the finished version - declarations, cursor, loop, and real
--   work inside the loop.
CREATE PROCEDURE REP_CREDIT_REVIEW (IN i_rep_num CHAR(2))
BEGIN

    -- The finished flag, starting at 0.
    DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

    -- One variable per cursor column...
    DECLARE v_customer_num CHAR(4);
    DECLARE v_customer_name VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE v_balance DECIMAL(9,2);
    DECLARE v_credit_limit DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- ...plus two for the values computed inside the loop.
    DECLARE v_available DECIMAL(9,2);
    DECLARE v_note VARCHAR(10);

    -- The cursor: the set of rows to be walked, one at a time.
    DECLARE cust_cursor CURSOR FOR

        -- The same four columns as the earlier stages, ready for the FETCH below.
        SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

        -- FROM: the customer table, same as every version of this cursor.
        FROM CUSTOMER

        -- WHERE: this call's rep parameter.
        WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num

        -- ORDER BY: keeps the walk order predictable, as before.
        ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- The handler that trips the flag when the rows run out.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

    -- Run the query and position before the first row.
    OPEN cust_cursor;

    -- The walking loop.
    cust_loop: LOOP

        -- Read one row into the variables.
        FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                               v_balance, v_credit_limit;

        -- Stop as soon as the fetch fails, before processing stale values.
        IF v_done = 1 THEN
            LEAVE cust_loop;
        -- END IF: with the flag still 0, control falls through to the row work
        --   below instead of leaving the loop.
        END IF;

        -- Row-at-a-time work, part 1: a calculation.
        SET v_available = v_credit_limit - v_balance;

        -- Row-at-a-time work, part 2: a DECISION. This is what a cursor buys you -
        --   plain SQL can compute the number, but choosing different actions per
        --   row is procedural logic.
        IF v_available < 5000 THEN
            -- SET: under $5,000 of available credit, so this row gets flagged
            --   for a follow-up call.
            SET v_note = 'Call rep';
        -- ELSE: everyone else clears the $5,000 threshold, so no follow-up is
        --   logged.
        ELSE
            SET v_note = 'No action';
        -- END IF: the verdict now sits in v_note, ready for the INSERT below.
        END IF;

        -- Row-at-a-time work, part 3: write the verdict out. One INSERT per pass
        --   of the loop, so one result row per customer.
        INSERT INTO CUST_REVIEW
               (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, AVAILABLE_CREDIT, REVIEW_NOTE)
        VALUES (v_customer_num, v_customer_name, v_available, v_note);
    -- END LOOP: sends control back to the top for the next customer.
    END LOOP cust_loop;

    -- Release the cursor.
    CLOSE cust_cursor;
END //

DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Run it for rep 20 and read the results back:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- CALL: run the review for one rep. The procedure returns nothing directly -
--   its output is the rows it wrote into CUST_REVIEW.
CALL REP_CREDIT_REVIEW('20');

-- SELECT: read the results table to see what the loop produced, one row per
--   customer the cursor walked.
SELECT * FROM CUST_REVIEW

-- ORDER BY: the same customer order the cursor walked, for an easy check.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CUST_REVIEW after CALL REP_CREDIT_REVIEW('20')
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CUSTOMER_NUMCUSTOMER_NAMEAVAILABLE_CREDITREVIEW_NOTE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1120Access Pet Center3987.50Call rep
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1310Companion Care Clinic10000.00No action

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two rows in, two rows out, each one the product of a separate trip through the loop. Access Pet Center has 7500.00 minus 3512.50, which is 3987.50 of room and lands under the threshold. Companion Care Clinic has spent nothing against a 10000.00 limit and needs no action.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Why DELIMITER wraps all of this

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The procedure body is full of semicolons, and the MySQL client would otherwise treat the first one as the end of the CREATE PROCEDURE statement. DELIMITER // tells the client to end statements at // instead, and DELIMITER ; puts it back afterward. It is a client instruction, not SQL, so it never appears inside the procedure.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7f Using More Complex Cursors

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Nothing about a cursor restricts it to one table. The cursor query is an ordinary SELECT, so joins, calculated columns, GROUP BY, and HAVING are all fair game. Here is a cursor over a four-table join that also computes a line total:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor's query can be as complex as any other. This
--   one joins four tables, and the procedure still walks the result one row at a
--   time exactly as before.
DECLARE line_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- Three stored columns and one calculated column. A cursor column does not
    --   have to correspond to anything stored.
    SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION,
           L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE

    -- FROM: the customer table, aliased C for the joins below.
    FROM CUSTOMER C

    -- Hop 1 - customer to invoice.
    JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM

    -- Hop 2 - invoice to line item.
    JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

    -- Hop 3 - line item to item.
    JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID

    -- The parameter filters the joined rows.
    WHERE C.REP_NUM = i_rep_num

    -- Fixes the order the rows will be fetched in.
    ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Four tables are needed because the four selected columns live in three of them and INVOICE_LINE ties them together: CUSTOMER_NAME comes from CUSTOMER, INVOICE_NUM from INVOICE, DESCRIPTION from ITEM, and the line total is computed from INVOICE_LINE. The FETCH for this cursor needs four variables, and the fourth one receives a calculated value rather than a stored column, so declare it wide enough for the product: DECLARE v_line_total DECIMAL(9,2);.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Run the underlying query to see the rows the loop would walk. The cursor's parameter is written out as a literal, so the statement is plain SQL and runs here:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Rep 20 gives two rows, both on invoice 50710: Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb at 127.5 and Nylon Dog Leash 6ft at 23.98. Rep 65 also gives two rows, both on invoice 50711: Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb at 85.0 and Small Animal Grooming Kit at 15.25. Drop the ITEM join and the query fails, because DESCRIPTION has nowhere to come from.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor query can also read more than one parameter. This procedure takes a rep and a minimum line total, so the same code answers "every line over $50 in rep 65's territory" and "every line over $10 in rep 20's":

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: make the script re-runnable.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS BIG_LINE_LOG;

-- CREATE TABLE: the destination for whatever the procedure finds. Its columns
--   match the four the cursor returns.
CREATE TABLE BIG_LINE_LOG
    (CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),
     INVOICE_NUM CHAR(5),
     DESCRIPTION VARCHAR(30),
     LINE_TOTAL DECIMAL(9,2));

DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable. Without it, the
--   second run fails because BIG_LINE_ITEMS already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS BIG_LINE_ITEMS //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: two parameters this time, and both are used inside the
--   cursor's query rather than in the loop.
CREATE PROCEDURE BIG_LINE_ITEMS (IN i_rep_num CHAR(2),
                                 IN i_min_total DECIMAL(7,2))
BEGIN

    -- The finished flag.
    DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

    -- One variable per cursor column, in the same order.
    DECLARE v_customer_name VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE v_invoice_num CHAR(5);
    DECLARE v_description VARCHAR(30);
    DECLARE v_line_total DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- The cursor over a four-table join.
    DECLARE line_cursor CURSOR FOR

        -- The same three stored columns and one calculated column as the
        --   walkthrough above.
        SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION,
               L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE

        -- FROM: the customer table, aliased C, same starting point as before.
        FROM CUSTOMER C

        -- Hop 1 - customer to invoice.
        JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM

        -- Hop 2 - invoice to line item.
        JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

        -- Hop 3 - line item to item.
        JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID

        -- WHERE: the rep parameter, same as the earlier cursors.
        WHERE C.REP_NUM = i_rep_num

        -- The second parameter filters on the CALCULATION, not on a stored
        --   column. Doing the filtering here rather than inside the loop means
        --   fewer rows are ever fetched - the database is better at discarding
        --   rows than your loop is.
          AND L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE >= i_min_total

        -- ORDER BY: fixes the fetch order for the loop, same as the earlier
        --   cursors.
        ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION;

    -- The handler that ends the loop.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

    -- Run the query.
    OPEN line_cursor;

    -- Walk the rows.
    line_loop: LOOP

        -- FETCH: read the next row into the four variables, matched by position.
        FETCH line_cursor INTO v_customer_name, v_invoice_num,
                               v_description, v_line_total;

        -- Test the flag right after the FETCH, before the possibly stale values
        --   get used.
        IF v_done = 1 THEN
            LEAVE line_loop;
        -- END IF: with the flag still 0, control falls through to the row work
        --   below.
        END IF;

        -- The only work per row: copy it into the log table. Because the cursor
        --   already filtered, no IF is needed here.
        INSERT INTO BIG_LINE_LOG
               (CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE_NUM, DESCRIPTION, LINE_TOTAL)
        VALUES (v_customer_name, v_invoice_num, v_description, v_line_total);
    -- END LOOP: sends control back to the top for the next line item.
    END LOOP line_loop;

    -- Tidy up.
    CLOSE line_cursor;
END //

DELIMITER ;

-- CALL: rep 65, lines worth 50.00 or more. Change either argument and the same
--   procedure answers a different question.
CALL BIG_LINE_ITEMS('65', 50.00);

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Rep 65 covers Whiskers & Wags Boutique, and exactly one of that customer's lines clears $50. Run the cursor's query with both parameter values filled in to confirm which row the loop would write:
