                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      One row: invoice 50711, Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb, 2 at 42.50, a line total of 85.0. Change 50 to 10 and a second line appears, Small Animal Grooming Kit at 15.25.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor can also walk grouped results. Each FETCH then delivers one group, not one base-table row:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      -- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor over a GROUPED query. Each row the cursor
--   hands back is a summary of several underlying rows, which is fine - the
--   cursor neither knows nor cares how its query was built.
DECLARE invoice_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- Two grouping columns and one aggregate.
    SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
           SUM(L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE)

    -- FROM: the invoice table this grouped query starts from.
    FROM INVOICE I

    -- Hop 1 - invoice to customer, for the name.
    JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM

    -- Hop 2 - invoice to its line items, for the money.
    JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

    -- GROUP BY: one row per invoice, so the cursor walks invoices rather than
    --   lines. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list appears here.
    GROUP BY I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME

    -- ORDER BY: fixes the invoice order the cursor will walk, same as any
    --   other cursor query.
    ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Three rows, one per invoice: 50710 at 151.48, 50711 at 100.25, 50712 at 120.49. A cursor over this query would loop three times.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Complexity lives in the query, not the loop

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Whether the cursor selects from one table, four joined tables, or a GROUP BY, the loop code is identical: OPEN, FETCH into a matching list of variables, test the flag, do the work, CLOSE. Push as much filtering and calculating as you can into the cursor query so the loop stays short and the database does what it is good at.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      8-7g Advantages of Cursors

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Cursors buy you real things:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • A procedure can process an unknown number of rows, from zero to thousands, with the same code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Each row can take a different path: an IF on the fetched values can write to one table or another, skip a row, or call a different procedure per row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Values from the row are held in variables, so you can carry a running total, compare this row with the previous one, or build a message that names the customer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Row-level error handling becomes possible: a handler can log the one row that failed and let the loop continue with the rest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • The work happens inside the database. A caller sends one CALL instead of pulling every row across the network and looping in application code.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Now the honest caution. A cursor loop is still a loop, and SQL is at its best when it operates on a whole set at once. The REP_CREDIT_REVIEW procedure above is a fine teaching example and a poor production design, because the rule it applies is expressible in plain SQL. The two INSERT ... SELECT statements in the sandbox below produce the same CUST_REVIEW contents that the entire loop produced, and because they are ordinary SQL the whole script runs here:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      You should get the same two rows the procedure produced: 1120 with 3987.5 and 'Call rep', 1310 with 10000 and 'No action'. The leading DROP TABLE IF EXISTS is what lets you press Run a second time without an error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Set-based first

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      With four customers the difference is invisible. With four hundred thousand it is not. A cursor pays per-row overhead on every FETCH and holds its result set open for the life of the loop, which means locks and memory held longer. The optimizer can plan one INSERT ... SELECT as a single operation; it cannot optimize across the iterations of your loop. Write the set-based statement first, and reach for a cursor only when the set-based statement cannot express the work.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor earns its place when

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Each row needs a decision that SQL cannot express in one statement: calling another procedure per row, writing to a different table depending on the values, walking rows in order to carry state from one row to the next, or logging and skipping individual failures while the rest continue.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stay set-based when

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The rule is a filter, a calculation, or a conditional value that a WHERE clause or a pair of statements can express. UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT ... SELECT already operate on every matching row. If your loop body is one INSERT with no per-row branching, the loop is doing nothing the engine could not do faster.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • SELECT ... INTO requires exactly one row; more than one raises error 1172.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Declare in order: variables, then cursors, then handlers, all at the top of the BEGIN block.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • OPEN runs the query and positions above the first row; opening it twice raises error 1325.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • FETCH copies one row into a variable list that matches the cursor's columns in count, order, and type.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1; gives the loop its exit signal.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Test the flag on the line right after the FETCH, before using any fetched value.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • LEAVE the labelled loop, then CLOSE the cursor; closing a cursor that is not open raises error 1326.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Put joins, filters, calculations, and ORDER BY in the cursor query; keep the loop body small.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Before writing a cursor, ask whether one set-based statement would do the same job faster.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      🔍 Check yourself: cursors in procedures

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q1Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic in one review

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A KimTay procedure must review every customer assigned to rep 20, which in the current data means Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. The developer writes SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, BALANCE INTO v_customer_num, v_balance FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num; and calls the procedure with '20'. What happens, and what belongs there instead?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. SELECT INTO has no loop of its own; it assigns one row's values one time and then stops
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. ORDER BY changes the order of rows, never the count, so the two-row result is unchanged
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔c. Correct: more than one row breaks SELECT INTO, and a cursor hands the loop one row per FETCH
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. A variable holds one value; the problem is the number of rows returned, not the width of a column

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: SELECT INTO is a one-row tool, so the moment a query can match many rows the procedure needs a cursor.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q2Compiling the Companion Care Clinic report procedure

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A procedure for the KimTay credit report declares the NOT FOUND handler first, then the cursor over CUSTOMER, then the local variables. MySQL refuses to create it. Which arrangement inside BEGIN does MySQL require?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔a. Correct: MySQL enforces this exact sequence, and a misplaced DECLARE is a compile-time error
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. The handler is declared last even though it can fire at the first FETCH; declaration order is not run order
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. MySQL is strict here, and it also requires every DECLARE to precede the first executable statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. The FETCH variable list does depend on the cursor query, but the declarations still go variables first

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Declaration order in a MySQL block is a syntax rule: variables and conditions, then cursors, then handlers.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q3Whiskers & Wags Boutique logged twice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor loop over invoice lines does its INSERT into the log table first and tests IF v_done = 1 THEN LEAVE line_loop; END IF; at the very bottom of the loop body. The log ends up with an extra copy of the last line for Whiskers & Wags Boutique. Why?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. The join is fine; the duplicate comes from the loop structure, which processes one iteration too many
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. FETCH begins above the first row and the first FETCH retrieves it, so no row is skipped or repeated there
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. A CONTINUE handler is the right choice; it sets the flag and lets the next statement run normally
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔d. Correct: a failed FETCH does not clear the variables, so work done before the flag test repeats the last row

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Test the done flag on the line immediately after FETCH, before any statement uses the fetched values.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q4Walking Downtown Aquarium & Pets invoice lines

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A developer is tracing a cursor procedure that reports the lines on invoice 50712 for Downtown Aquarium & Pets. Which statement actually executes the cursor's SELECT, and which one moves values into the local variables?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘a. DECLARE only records the cursor definition; no rows exist until the cursor is opened
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔b. Correct: OPEN runs the query once and sets the position, and each FETCH advances one row and assigns variables
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. FETCH advances through a result set that already exists; it does not re-run the query each time
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. CLOSE releases the result set; walking the rows again requires a second OPEN after the CLOSE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: DECLARE defines, OPEN runs the query and positions the cursor, FETCH assigns one row, CLOSE releases it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Q5KimTay's nightly available-credit run

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A cursor procedure loops over every KimTay customer, computes CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE, and inserts one row per customer into a review table with a fixed note. There is no other per-row logic, and the customer table has grown large. What should the DBA do?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✔a. Correct: with no per-row branching, one INSERT ... SELECT does the same work as a single optimized operation
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘b. An open cursor holds its result set and its locks for the whole loop, which is not the cheaper option here
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘c. INSERT ... SELECT is standard SQL and is exactly the replacement this workload calls for
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • ✘d. A view stores a query, not data, and selecting from it never writes rows into another table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Remember: Use a cursor only when a row needs a decision SQL cannot express; otherwise the set-based statement wins.
