                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-8 Using PL/SQL in Oracle

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You have already written this procedure once. In MySQL you named a parameter, declared a couple of local variables, filled them with a SELECT ... INTO, and wrapped the whole thing between BEGIN and END. Oracle's procedural language is called PL/SQL, and it does those same four things. The reason to write the procedure a second time is not that Oracle needs a different idea. It is that the idea is easier to see once you have watched it survive a change of dialect.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Read the table below before you read any code. Almost every line in the PL/SQL versions that follow is one of these rows in action. Two entries are genuinely new thinking rather than new punctuation, and both are in the last two rows: PL/SQL treats a query that returned the wrong number of rows as an error you are expected to catch, and it gives that error a name.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The same procedure ideas, spelled for MySQL and for Oracle PL/SQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What you need to doMySQLOracle PL/SQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Stop the client from splitting the body at each semicolonDELIMITER // before, DELIMITER ; afterA single / on its own line after END;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declare a local variableDECLARE L_NAME VARCHAR(35); inside the bodyL_NAME CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE; before BEGIN
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Accept an input parameterIN I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4)I_CUSTOMER_NUM IN CHAR
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Fill variables from one rowSELECT col INTO L_VAR FROM ...SELECT col INTO L_VAR FROM ...
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Send a line of text back to the screenSELECT L_NAME;DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(L_NAME);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Replace a procedure you already createdDROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS, then CREATECREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Run itCALL GET_CUSTOMER('1225');EXECUTE GET_CUSTOMER('1225');
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              React when the query found no rowDECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUNDEXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              React when the query found too many rowsNothing built in; you check by handEXCEPTION WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nothing in this lesson runs in the sandbox at the bottom of the page

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The browser engine on this page is SQLite, and SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE, no PL/SQL, and no DBMS_OUTPUT. Every PL/SQL block here is labelled Oracle and is meant to be read, and to be typed into Oracle SQL Developer or SQL*Plus if you have access to one. Where a lesson has a runnable neighbour, there is a sandbox showing that neighbour, and it says what it is showing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-8a Error Handling in PL/SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Here is the MySQL procedure again, so the comparison is in front of you rather than in your memory. It takes a customer number, reads that customer's name and balance into two local variables, and prints them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- MySQL, for comparison with the Oracle and SQL Server versions below.
DELIMITER //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: MySQL puts the direction (IN) BEFORE the parameter name.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER (IN I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE, with the type written out in full.
    DECLARE L_NAME    VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE L_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO fills the two locals.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    INTO   L_NAME, L_BALANCE
    -- FROM: the customer table this lookup reads.
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    -- WHERE: filters to the one row this call targets - the customer number
    --   passed in as I_CUSTOMER_NUM.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- MySQL has no print statement, so output is produced by SELECTing the
    --   variables - the result comes back as a one-row result set.
    SELECT L_NAME AS CUSTOMER_NAME, L_BALANCE AS BALANCE;
END //
DELIMITER ;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              That procedure is correct for the case it was written for, which is a customer number that exists and identifies exactly one row. It is silent about the two cases that will eventually happen: somebody passes a number that is not in the table, and somebody changes the WHERE clause so more than one row qualifies. Oracle refuses to be silent about either.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- Oracle PL/SQL. CREATE OR REPLACE: no separate DROP is needed - this replaces
--   any existing procedure of the same name in one statement.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER (I_CUSTOMER_NUM IN CHAR) AS

    -- %TYPE: declare the variable as "whatever type that column is". If the
    --   column is widened later, the variable follows automatically. Note there
    --   is no DECLARE keyword here - in Oracle, declarations simply sit between
    --   AS and BEGIN. Oracle also puts the direction AFTER the parameter name.
    L_NAME     CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE;
    L_BALANCE  CUSTOMER.BALANCE%TYPE;
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO works the same way as in MySQL.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    INTO   L_NAME, L_BALANCE
    -- FROM: same customer table as the MySQL version.
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    -- WHERE: filters to the single row identified by the parameter.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE: Oracle's print. || joins strings, and TO_CHAR formats
    --   the number to a fixed picture so columns line up.
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(L_NAME || '  ' || TO_CHAR(L_BALANCE, '99999.99'));

-- EXCEPTION: Oracle's error handling is a block at the END of the procedure,
--   rather than handlers declared at the top as in MySQL.
EXCEPTION

    -- NO_DATA_FOUND: the named condition for a SELECT ... INTO that matched
    --   nothing - Oracle's equivalent of MySQL's NOT FOUND.
    WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('No customer numbered ' || I_CUSTOMER_NUM);

    -- TOO_MANY_ROWS: the opposite failure - the INTO matched more than one row.
    --   Oracle gives this its own name; MySQL lumps it under SQLEXCEPTION.
    WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('That condition matched more than one customer.');

    -- WHEN OTHERS: the catch-all, and it must come last. SQLERRM holds the text
    --   of whatever actually went wrong.
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Unexpected error: ' || SQLERRM);
END;

-- The lone / on its own line is what tells SQL*Plus to send the block to the
--   server - Oracle's equivalent of MySQL's DELIMITER dance.
/

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything above the word EXCEPTION is the happy path. Everything below it is what to do instead when the happy path fails. Oracle calls a failure an exception, and it hands you three named ones for free. NO_DATA_FOUND means the SELECT ... INTO matched zero rows. TOO_MANY_ROWS means it matched two or more. OTHERS means anything else at all, and SQLERRM is the message Oracle would have printed if you had not caught it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Exception

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A named run-time failure. In PL/SQL an exception stops the normal flow of a block at the statement that caused it and jumps straight to the block's EXCEPTION section, skipping every statement in between. If the block has no matching handler, the exception is passed back to whatever called the block.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The two failure cases are shapes of a result set, not exotic events, and you can watch all three shapes in SQLite even though SQLite does not name them. Run the box below. The first query returns one row, which is the case GET_CUSTOMER was written for. The second returns none, which is NO_DATA_FOUND. The third returns two, which is TOO_MANY_ROWS.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three queries, three shapes of answer: one row, no rows, two rows. SQLite reports all three as ordinary results. Oracle gives the last two names and expects you to handle them. Case 2 shows an empty area rather than a table, because no row qualified.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why %TYPE is worth the extra typing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              L_NAME CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE; means "whatever type CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME is declared as, give me one of those." If someone widens that column next year, your procedure follows along without being edited. Writing L_NAME VARCHAR2(35); instead pins a copy of today's decision into your code, and copies drift.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Raising an exception of your own

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The three built-in exceptions cover mistakes the database can detect. They cannot cover a rule that exists only in KimTay's head, such as never letting a balance climb past its credit limit. For a rule like that you declare an exception, raise it yourself, and handle it in the same section as the built-in ones.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- Oracle PL/SQL: a procedure that changes data and refuses to leave the database
--   in a state it considers invalid.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE ADD_TO_BALANCE (
    I_CUSTOMER_NUM  IN CHAR,
    I_AMOUNT        IN NUMBER) AS

    -- Declaring your OWN exception. It is not an error the database raises - it
    --   is a name for a business rule you are about to enforce yourself.
    OVER_LIMIT   EXCEPTION;

    -- Two locals typed from the columns they will hold.
    L_BALANCE    CUSTOMER.BALANCE%TYPE;
    L_LIMIT      CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT%TYPE;
BEGIN

    -- The change is made first, then checked. Everything is inside a transaction
    --   until COMMIT, so it can still be taken back.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER
    -- SET: adds the signed amount to the current balance - the caller controls
    --   the sign, so this same line handles a charge or a payment.
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + I_AMOUNT
    -- WHERE: targets only the customer named by the parameter.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- SQL%ROWCOUNT: how many rows the last statement affected. Zero means the
    --   customer number was wrong - an UPDATE that matches nothing is not an
    --   error, so you have to detect it yourself.
    IF SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 THEN

        -- RAISE: trigger a condition deliberately, sending control to the
        --   EXCEPTION block below.
        RAISE NO_DATA_FOUND;
    END IF;

    -- Read the row back to see what the update actually produced.
    SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
    INTO   L_BALANCE, L_LIMIT
    -- FROM: the same customer table the UPDATE just changed.
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    -- WHERE: the same customer the UPDATE targeted, so the values read back are
    --   the ones the change just produced.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- The business rule. Nothing in the database forbids this, so the procedure
    --   enforces it.
    IF L_BALANCE > L_LIMIT THEN
        RAISE OVER_LIMIT;
    END IF;

    -- COMMIT: reached only when both checks passed. Until this line, nothing is
    --   permanent.
    COMMIT;
-- EXCEPTION: catches both the built-in NO_DATA_FOUND case and the OVER_LIMIT
--   rule this procedure raises on itself.
EXCEPTION

    -- Every handler rolls back first, so a rejected change leaves no trace.
    WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
        ROLLBACK;

        -- RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR: hands a numbered error and a readable message
        --   back to the calling program. Numbers from -20000 to -20999 are
        --   reserved for your own application errors.
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001,
            'No customer numbered ' || I_CUSTOMER_NUM);

    -- The custom exception declared at the top is caught by name here.
    WHEN OVER_LIMIT THEN
        ROLLBACK;
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20002,
            'That charge would push the balance past the credit limit.');

    -- The catch-all for anything unforeseen, still rolling back.
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        ROLLBACK;
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20003, 'Unexpected error: ' || SQLERRM);
END;
/

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Notice the order of events. The UPDATE runs first, then the check, then COMMIT. That is deliberate. Because nothing has been committed when OVER_LIMIT is raised, the ROLLBACK in the handler puts the balance back exactly as it was. This is the transaction discipline from Module 6, now living inside a procedure instead of inside a session.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              WHEN OTHERS goes last, always

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PL/SQL tries the handlers in the order you wrote them and stops at the first one that matches. WHEN OTHERS matches everything, so any handler placed after it is unreachable. If you put WHEN OTHERS first, your careful NO_DATA_FOUND message never prints and every failure looks the same. Numbers passed to RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR must fall between -20000 and -20999; those are the ones Oracle reserves for you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-8b Writing a Complete Procedure Using a Cursor in PL/SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A SELECT ... INTO handles one row. When the answer is a list, you need a cursor: a name for a query that the procedure can walk through one row at a time, doing whatever it likes at each stop. The task here is the one you wrote in MySQL: given a rep number, list that rep's customers.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The query underneath the cursor is nothing special, and you can run it right now. This is the exact SELECT that the PL/SQL cursor below is built on, and rep 20 is Valerie Kaiser's record.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two rows come back: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic. A cursor does not change what this query returns. It changes who reads the rows and how many at a time. Try changing '20' to '65' to see a one-row list.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- Oracle PL/SQL: the cursor loop, Oracle style.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST (I_REP_NUM IN CHAR) AS

    -- CURSOR ... IS: Oracle's cursor declaration. Same idea as MySQL's
    --   DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR, different wording.
    CURSOR CUSTGROUP IS
        -- SELECT: the three columns each FETCH below will copy into the loop's
        --   variables, in this order.
        SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
        -- FROM: the same customer table the sandbox version above queried.
        FROM   CUSTOMER
        -- WHERE: the parameter stands in for the literal '20' used in the
        --   sandbox - one cursor definition serves every rep.
        WHERE  REP_NUM = I_REP_NUM
        -- ORDER BY: keeps the rows in customer-number order as they're fetched.
        ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- One variable per cursor column, typed from the columns themselves.
    L_CUSTOMER_NUM   CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM%TYPE;
    L_CUSTOMER_NAME  CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE;
    L_BALANCE        CUSTOMER.BALANCE%TYPE;
BEGIN

    -- Run the query and position before the first row.
    OPEN CUSTGROUP;

    -- A plain LOOP, exited by the test inside.
    LOOP

        -- Read one row into the three variables.
        FETCH CUSTGROUP INTO L_CUSTOMER_NUM, L_CUSTOMER_NAME, L_BALANCE;

        -- EXIT WHEN with %NOTFOUND: Oracle asks the cursor directly whether the
        --   last fetch got anything, so no flag variable and no handler are
        --   needed - simpler than the MySQL equivalent.
        EXIT WHEN CUSTGROUP%NOTFOUND;

        -- The work for this row: print it.
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(L_CUSTOMER_NUM || '  ' || L_CUSTOMER_NAME ||
                             '  ' || TO_CHAR(L_BALANCE, '99999.99'));
    END LOOP;

    -- Release the cursor on the normal path.
    CLOSE CUSTGROUP;
-- EXCEPTION: a single catch-all for this listing - nothing here raises a
--   business exception of its own, so there is only one failure shape to name.
EXCEPTION
    -- WHEN OTHERS: the only handler; anything that goes wrong during the fetch
    --   loop ends up here.
    WHEN OTHERS THEN

        -- %ISOPEN: if the failure happened mid-loop the cursor is still open, so
        --   check before closing - closing a closed cursor is itself an error.
        IF CUSTGROUP%ISOPEN THEN
            CLOSE CUSTGROUP;
        END IF;
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20004, 'Listing failed: ' || SQLERRM);
END;
/
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declare

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CURSOR CUSTGROUP IS ... names the query. Nothing runs yet. The parameter I_REP_NUM is allowed inside the cursor's WHERE clause, which is what makes one cursor serve every rep.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Open

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OPEN CUSTGROUP; runs the query and positions the cursor just before the first row. This is the moment the database actually does the work.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Fetch

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              FETCH CUSTGROUP INTO ... copies the current row into your three variables and steps forward one row. The variables must match the SELECT list in number, order, and type.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Exit

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              EXIT WHEN CUSTGROUP%NOTFOUND; is tested immediately after the FETCH. %NOTFOUND turns true on the fetch that ran off the end, so put this line directly under the FETCH and above the work, or you will process the last row twice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              5

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Close

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CLOSE CUSTGROUP; releases the cursor. The handler closes it too, because a block that fails halfway leaves the cursor open otherwise.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              For a loop that does nothing but read every row, PL/SQL offers a shorter form that declares the cursor, opens it, fetches, tests, and closes it for you. There are no local variables to declare and no way to forget CLOSE.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- Oracle PL/SQL: the same listing, written the way Oracle programmers actually
--   write it.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST (I_REP_NUM IN CHAR) AS
BEGIN

    -- FOR ... IN (query) LOOP: a cursor FOR loop. Oracle declares the cursor,
    --   opens it, declares a record to hold each row, fetches, tests for the end
    --   and closes it - all implicitly. Compare it with the version above: the
    --   same job, with every place a mistake could hide taken away.
    FOR C IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
              -- FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY: the same query as the CUSTGROUP cursor
              --   above, unchanged - only how it's opened, walked, and closed
              --   is different here.
              FROM   CUSTOMER
              WHERE  REP_NUM = I_REP_NUM
              ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM)
    LOOP

        -- C is the loop record, and its fields are named after the query's
        --   columns. Nothing had to be declared for it.
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(C.CUSTOMER_NUM || '  ' || C.CUSTOMER_NAME);
    END LOOP;
END;
/

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              C is a record with one field per column in the SELECT list, so you write C.CUSTOMER_NAME instead of a separately declared variable. Use the long form when you need to do something unusual, such as reading two cursors in step with each other. Use this form the rest of the time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Seeing the output at all

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE writes to a buffer, not to your screen. In SQL*Plus and SQL Developer you have to ask for that buffer to be displayed, once per session, with SET SERVEROUTPUT ON;. A procedure that appears to print nothing is very often a procedure that ran perfectly into a buffer nobody read.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What travels between engines

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A procedure is a named, stored, parameterised block of logic. A cursor is opened, fetched from in a loop, and closed. A failure is trapped in one place rather than checked after every statement. Learn these three and you can read procedural code in any of the engines in this module.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What does not travel

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Where you declare variables, how you end the block, how you print, and what the failure cases are called. Oracle names NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS; MySQL and SQL Server do not. Never paste a PL/SQL block into a different engine and expect a small edit to fix it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Declare local variables above BEGIN, not inside the body, and prefer %TYPE over a hand-copied data type.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Put EXCEPTION after the last statement of the happy path and before END;.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • List WHEN OTHERS last, because it matches everything ahead of any handler placed after it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Test %NOTFOUND immediately after the FETCH and before you use the fetched values.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Close the cursor in the handler as well as at the end of the happy path.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Turn on SET SERVEROUTPUT ON; before you decide your procedure printed nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Check Yourself: PL/SQL in Oracle

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1A customer number KimTay has never issued

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay's GET_CUSTOMER procedure runs SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE INTO L_NAME, L_BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM; and is called with '1999', which is not in the table. What does Oracle do next?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct. A SELECT ... INTO promises exactly one row. Zero rows breaks that promise, and Oracle names the break NO_DATA_FOUND so a handler can decide what the caller sees.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. TOO_MANY_ROWS is the opposite failure: two or more rows matched. Zero and many are different problems with different names and usually different responses.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. This is the MySQL habit applied to Oracle. MySQL leaves the variables alone unless you declared a NOT FOUND handler; Oracle refuses to continue at all and raises an exception instead.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. SELECT ... INTO is the normal way a PL/SQL block reads a single row. It is legal inside a procedure and nowhere else in Oracle SQL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: In PL/SQL a SELECT ... INTO that matches no row raises NO_DATA_FOUND; it never quietly leaves the variables as they were.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2Listing Valerie Kaiser's two customers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              REP_CUSTOMER_LIST opens a cursor over rep 20's customers and fetches into three variables inside a LOOP. What stops the loop after the second customer?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. %FOUND is true while fetches are succeeding, so exiting on it would end the loop before the first customer was printed. It is the attribute you test to continue, not to stop.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. The third FETCH runs past the last row, %NOTFOUND turns true, and the EXIT WHEN immediately below the FETCH ends the loop before the stale variable values are used again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. CLOSE is written after the loop and cannot run until the loop has already ended. Closing a cursor releases it; it is not a loop-control statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. The cursor visits only the rows its query returned, which is two here because of WHERE REP_NUM = I_REP_NUM. CUSTOMER holding four rows is irrelevant.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Put EXIT WHEN cursor%NOTFOUND; immediately after the FETCH and above the work, or the loop processes the last row a second time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3A charge that would push Whiskers & Wags past its limit

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ADD_TO_BALANCE runs the UPDATE first, then checks the new balance against CREDIT_LIMIT and raises a user-defined OVER_LIMIT exception. What must the handler do so KimTay never keeps the over-limit balance?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Handlers are tried in the order written and WHEN OTHERS matches everything, so putting it first makes every handler below it unreachable and every failure look identical.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. PL/SQL does not roll back a transaction because a block raised an exception. The UPDATE is still sitting uncommitted, and something has to undo it explicitly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct. Nothing was committed, so ROLLBACK restores the balance exactly, and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR with a number in the -20000 to -20999 range tells the caller why in plain words.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. A procedure guessing at a smaller amount invents data nobody asked for. The correct response to a refused business rule is to refuse and say so, not to substitute a value.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: An exception stops the block but does not undo the transaction; roll back inside the handler and report the refusal with RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9 Using T-SQL in SQL Server

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Third dialect, same five tasks. Microsoft SQL Server's procedural language is Transact-SQL, universally shortened to T-SQL. It reaches the same destinations as MySQL and PL/SQL and takes a visibly different road: every local variable name starts with @, you assign to a variable inside the SELECT list rather than with INTO, and there is no EXCEPTION keyword because errors are trapped with BEGIN TRY and BEGIN CATCH.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One row of this table matters more than the rest. Read the fourth row twice. T-SQL's SELECT @L_VAR = col does not object when the query matches the wrong number of rows, which means the safety net Oracle gave you for free is a net you have to weave yourself.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The same procedure ideas, spelled for MySQL and for T-SQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What you need to doMySQLSQL Server T-SQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Mark the end of the routine for the clientDELIMITER // before, DELIMITER ; afterGO on its own line after the last statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Open the bodyBEGIN ... ENDAS, then the statements
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declare a local variableDECLARE L_NAME VARCHAR(35);DECLARE @L_NAME VARCHAR(35);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Fill a variable from one rowSELECT col INTO L_VAR FROM ...SELECT @L_VAR = col FROM ...
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Set a variable to a literal valueSET L_TOTAL = 0;SET @L_TOTAL = 0;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Accept an input parameterIN I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4)@I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Send a line of text back to the screenSELECT L_NAME;PRINT @L_NAME;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Find out how many rows that statement touchedROW_COUNT()@@ROWCOUNT
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Run itCALL GET_CUSTOMER('1225');EXEC GET_CUSTOMER '1225';
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Trap an errorDECLARE ... HANDLER FOR ...BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Raise an error of your ownSIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'THROW 50001, 'message', 1;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nothing in this lesson runs in the sandbox at the bottom of the page

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE, no @ variables, no PRINT, and no cursors. Every block in this lesson is labelled SQL Server and is written to be read, or to be typed into SQL Server Management Studio or Azure Data Studio. Each subsection has a sandbox running the plain SQL statement that the procedure wraps, so you can still see the data the procedure would be working on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9a Retrieving a Single Row and Column in T-SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Same task as 8-8a: given a customer number, report that customer's name and balance.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL. CREATE PROCEDURE with no parentheses around the parameter
--   list, and every parameter and variable name starting with @.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER
    @I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4)

-- AS: opens the body. T-SQL does not require BEGIN ... END around it.
AS

-- DECLARE: the @ prefix is part of the name here, not a marker for something
--   special as it is in MySQL.
DECLARE @L_NAME    VARCHAR(35);
DECLARE @L_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2);
DECLARE @L_ROWS    INT;

-- SELECT @variable = column: T-SQL's way of loading variables from a query -
--   assignments inside the SELECT list, with no INTO clause at all.
SELECT @L_NAME    = CUSTOMER_NAME,
       @L_BALANCE = BALANCE
-- FROM: the customer table this lookup reads.
FROM   CUSTOMER
-- WHERE: the parameter value passed in as @I_CUSTOMER_NUM. Nothing here
--   guarantees exactly one match - that is what @L_ROWS checks below.
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- @@ROWCOUNT: how many rows the previous statement touched. Capture it
--   immediately - the very next statement overwrites it.
SET @L_ROWS = @@ROWCOUNT;

-- T-SQL raises nothing when this SELECT matches no row, so the procedure has to
--   test the count itself. Zero rows means no such customer.
IF @L_ROWS = 0

    -- PRINT: T-SQL's print statement. + joins strings here, where Oracle used ||.
    PRINT 'No customer numbered ' + @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- More than one row means the variables hold the LAST row read, silently.
ELSE IF @L_ROWS > 1

    -- No CAST needed here - the message is plain text, unlike the ELSE branch
    --   below.
    PRINT 'That condition matched more than one customer.';

-- Exactly one row: the normal path.
ELSE

    -- CAST is required, because T-SQL will not join a number to a string.
    PRINT @L_NAME + '  ' + CAST(@L_BALANCE AS VARCHAR(20));

-- GO: not SQL at all, but a batch separator the client uses to decide where one
--   piece of work ends. It plays the same role as MySQL's DELIMITER and Oracle's /.
GO
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- EXEC: SQL Server's way of running a procedure - MySQL says CALL, Oracle uses
--   the procedure name on its own. Arguments follow with no parentheses.
EXEC GET_CUSTOMER '1420';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The IF block is not decoration. Without it, a customer number that is not in CUSTOMER leaves @L_NAME holding whatever it held before, which is NULL on the first call and yesterday's customer on a later one. A condition matching two rows leaves @L_NAME holding the last row the query happened to return, in whatever order the engine chose. Neither case raises anything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              @@ROWCOUNT is how you find out, and it is a moving target: every statement resets it, including an IF that does nothing but test it. That is why the procedure copies it into @L_ROWS on the very next line and then tests @L_ROWS twice. Written the tempting way, as IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 ... ELSE IF @@ROWCOUNT > 1, the second test would be reading the count left behind by the first IF rather than the count from the SELECT, and the two-row case would never be reported.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The single most portable-looking difference that is not portable

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SELECT ... INTO means two completely different things. In MySQL and Oracle it copies column values into local variables. In T-SQL, SELECT col INTO NEW_TABLE FROM ... creates a brand-new table and fills it, which is the CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT behaviour from 6-1. Assigning to a T-SQL variable is always SELECT @var = col or SET @var = (SELECT ...).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This is the query the T-SQL procedure runs; the procedure adds a parameter and two variables around it. One row comes back: Whiskers & Wags Boutique with a balance of 4820.75. Change 1420 to 1999 and the box shows an empty result, which is the case the @@ROWCOUNT test is there to catch.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9b Changing Data with a Stored Procedure in T-SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Reading is the easy half. A procedure that changes data has to decide what to do when the change does not apply, and it has to leave the database in a sane state when something fails halfway. Here is a procedure that adds an amount to a customer's balance, refuses to touch a customer number that does not exist, and rolls back rather than committing a half-finished change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL: a data change wrapped in a transaction with structured
--   error handling.
CREATE PROCEDURE ADD_TO_BALANCE
    @I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
    @I_AMOUNT       DECIMAL(9,2)
AS

-- BEGIN TRY: everything up to END TRY is protected. If any statement inside
--   fails, control jumps straight to the CATCH block.
BEGIN TRY

    -- Open the transaction so a failure can be undone.
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;

    -- The change itself.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER
    -- SET: adds the amount to the existing balance rather than replacing it.
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + @I_AMOUNT
    -- WHERE: the customer number passed in - the one row this call is allowed
    --   to touch.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- An UPDATE that matched nothing is not an error, so check the count and
    --   turn it into one deliberately.
    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0

        -- THROW: raise an error with your own number and message. Anything from
        --   50000 up is yours to use. This sends control to CATCH.
        THROW 50001, 'No customer with that number. Nothing was changed.', 1;

    -- Reached only when the update touched a row.
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
-- END TRY: marks the end of the protected block. If nothing failed, execution
--   continues after END CATCH, skipping the CATCH block entirely.
END TRY

-- BEGIN CATCH: runs only when something in the TRY block failed.
BEGIN CATCH

    -- @@TRANCOUNT: how many transactions are open. Test it before rolling back -
    --   a ROLLBACK with no open transaction is itself an error.
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0

        -- Undoes the update - reached only when TRY's error triggered CATCH
        --   with a transaction still open.
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

    -- ERROR_MESSAGE(): the text of whatever went wrong, available only inside a
    --   CATCH block.
    PRINT 'ADD_TO_BALANCE failed: ' + ERROR_MESSAGE();
-- END CATCH: closes the error-handling block that BEGIN CATCH opened.
END CATCH;
GO
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- EXEC: two arguments, separated by a comma, in the order the procedure declares
--   them. A customer that exists, so the update commits.
EXEC ADD_TO_BALANCE '1225', 350.00;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Here @@ROWCOUNT is read once, on the statement immediately after the UPDATE, so it needs no variable. THROW raises an error, which sends control straight to BEGIN CATCH, exactly the way RAISE sends a PL/SQL block to its EXCEPTION section. Numbers at or above 50000 are the ones reserved for your own errors. @@TRANCOUNT is checked before the rollback because a ROLLBACK with no open transaction is itself an error, and an error inside a CATCH block has nowhere left to go.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Downtown Aquarium & Pets ends at 1550.00 against a credit limit of 5000.00. The first UPDATE exists so that pressing Run a second time gives the same answer rather than 1900.00. The stored procedure adds the parameter, the transaction, and the @@ROWCOUNT test around the middle statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9c Deleting Data with a Stored Procedure in T-SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A delete procedure has the same shape and one extra hazard. A row that other rows still point at cannot be deleted, and the database will say so. That is the foreign key doing its job, and a procedure that ignores the possibility will hand a raw engine error to whoever called it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL: a delete that reports all three of its possible outcomes.
CREATE PROCEDURE DELETE_ITEM
    @I_ITEM_ID CHAR(4)
AS

-- BEGIN TRY: same protected-block pattern as ADD_TO_BALANCE - a failure
--   inside jumps straight to CATCH below.
BEGIN TRY

    -- The delete, with its WHERE clause built into the procedure.
    DELETE FROM ITEM
    -- WHERE: the one item number the caller passed in.
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = @I_ITEM_ID;

    -- Outcome 1: nothing matched. Not an error, so it is detected by the count.
    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0

        -- No CAST needed here - @I_ITEM_ID is already a string, unlike
        --   @L_BALANCE back in GET_CUSTOMER.
        PRINT 'No item numbered ' + @I_ITEM_ID + '. Nothing was deleted.';

    -- Outcome 2: the row was removed.
    ELSE

        -- Confirms the delete succeeded - the mirror image of Outcome 1's
        --   message.
        PRINT 'Item ' + @I_ITEM_ID + ' deleted.';
-- END TRY: closes the protected block. Getting here means neither outcome
--   above threw, so CATCH below is skipped entirely.
END TRY
-- BEGIN CATCH: reached only if the DELETE above raised an error - a normal
--   "no rows matched" is not one.
BEGIN CATCH

    -- Outcome 3: the delete was refused - typically by a foreign key, because
    --   invoice lines still point at the item. ERROR_MESSAGE() reports which.
    PRINT 'Could not delete ' + @I_ITEM_ID + ': ' + ERROR_MESSAGE();
-- END CATCH: closes the error-handling block; GO ends the batch right after it.
END CATCH;
GO
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- EXEC: DG04 appears on an invoice line, so the foreign key refuses the delete
--   and the CATCH block explains why. The item survives.
EXEC DELETE_ITEM 'DG04';

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DG04 is the Nylon Dog Leash, and invoice 50710 still lists it. SQL Server refuses the delete, CATCH receives control, and the caller gets a sentence in English instead of a stack trace. Note the two distinct outcomes the procedure now distinguishes: an item that could not be deleted, and an item that was never there. Those are different problems and they deserve different messages.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This page's engine will enforce the same rule if you ask it to. PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; turns enforcement on for the session, and then the delete below fails with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. That statement is shown rather than run because the error would replace everything else in the output.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON: SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless you ask
--   it to, and the setting lasts only for this connection.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- DELETE: the same attempt, in the sandbox on this page. INVOICE_LINE holds rows
--   referring to DG04, so the delete is refused and you see the error the SQL
--   Server CATCH block above was reporting.
DELETE FROM ITEM
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';
