The second result has four rows instead of five: the working copy carried no foreign key over from ITEM, so nothing stopped the delete there. Checking before deleting is the habit worth keeping.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9d Using a Cursor in T-SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Same task as 8-8b: list one rep's customers, one row at a time. T-SQL cursors have four moving parts that PL/SQL hides, and all four have to be right.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL: the cursor loop, third dialect.
CREATE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST
    @I_REP_NUM CHAR(2)
AS

-- One variable per cursor column, all declared up front.
DECLARE @L_CUSTOMER_NUM  CHAR(4);
DECLARE @L_CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35);
DECLARE @L_BALANCE       DECIMAL(9,2);

-- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: the query to be walked.
DECLARE CUSTGROUP CURSOR FOR
    -- SELECT: the three columns the loop below will print.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    -- FROM: the customer table this cursor walks.
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    -- WHERE: limits the cursor to customers belonging to the rep passed in as
    --   @I_REP_NUM.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = @I_REP_NUM
    -- ORDER BY: fixes the order the cursor visits rows in - without it, the
    --   engine could hand rows back in any order it likes.
    ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- Run the query and get ready to read.
OPEN CUSTGROUP;

-- FETCH NEXT FROM ... INTO: T-SQL spells out the direction. The FIRST fetch
--   happens BEFORE the loop - that is what makes a WHILE loop possible here.
FETCH NEXT FROM CUSTGROUP
    INTO @L_CUSTOMER_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_BALANCE;

-- @@FETCH_STATUS: 0 means the last fetch worked. Testing it at the TOP of the
--   loop replaces MySQL's flag-and-handler arrangement entirely.
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
-- BEGIN: opens the loop body. T-SQL's WHILE, like its IF, needs BEGIN ... END
--   around anything longer than a single statement.
BEGIN

    -- The work for this row.
    PRINT @L_CUSTOMER_NUM + '  ' + @L_CUSTOMER_NAME + '  ' +
          CAST(@L_BALANCE AS VARCHAR(20));

    -- The SECOND fetch, at the bottom of the loop. Forget this line and the
    --   loop repeats the same row forever - the classic T-SQL cursor bug.
    FETCH NEXT FROM CUSTGROUP
        INTO @L_CUSTOMER_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_BALANCE;
-- END: closes the loop body. Control returns to the WHILE line above, which
--   re-tests @@FETCH_STATUS against the fetch that just ran.
END

-- CLOSE releases the rows...
CLOSE CUSTGROUP;

-- ...and DEALLOCATE releases the cursor's name. T-SQL needs both; MySQL and
--   Oracle need only the close.
DEALLOCATE CUSTGROUP;
GO
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The priming fetch

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The FETCH NEXT above the WHILE exists so that @@FETCH_STATUS has a value the first time the loop condition is tested. Without it the loop is testing the status of some earlier, unrelated fetch.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The fetch at the bottom

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The second FETCH NEXT is the last statement inside the loop. Leave it out and @@FETCH_STATUS never changes, the condition stays true, and the procedure prints the first customer forever.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              @@FETCH_STATUS is global

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              It reports on the most recent fetch on any cursor in the session, not on CUSTGROUP specifically. Test it immediately after the fetch you care about, before any other statement can overwrite it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CLOSE then DEALLOCATE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CLOSE releases the rows. DEALLOCATE releases the name, so CUSTGROUP can be declared again. Skip DEALLOCATE and the second call to the procedure fails with a complaint that a cursor with that name already exists.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Reach for a set before you reach for a cursor

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A cursor processes one row per trip through the loop. A single UPDATE or SELECT processes all the matching rows in one statement, and the engine is free to optimise it. Write a cursor when each row needs its own decision that SQL cannot express, and not because looping feels more familiar than thinking in sets.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two rows, in the order the cursor would visit them: 1120 first, then 1310. The ORDER BY is what makes a cursor's visiting order predictable. Without it the engine may hand back rows in any order it likes, and a report built on that order becomes unreliable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-9e Using More Complex Cursors in T-SQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nothing about a cursor requires its query to be simple. The query can join four tables, compute a column, and sort the result, and the loop does not change shape at all. Here is a cursor over every invoice line belonging to one rep's customers, keeping a running total as it goes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL: a cursor over a four-table join, keeping a running total as
--   it goes - something a single SELECT cannot do as it walks.
CREATE PROCEDURE REP_INVOICE_LINES
    @I_REP_NUM CHAR(2)
AS

-- One variable per cursor column.
DECLARE @L_INVOICE_NUM   CHAR(5);
DECLARE @L_CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35);
DECLARE @L_DESCRIPTION   VARCHAR(30);
DECLARE @L_LINE_TOTAL    DECIMAL(9,2);

-- An accumulator, declared WITH a starting value. It must begin at 0 rather than
--   NULL, because NULL + anything is NULL and the total would never build.
DECLARE @L_RUNNING_TOTAL DECIMAL(9,2) = 0;

-- The cursor: three stored columns and one calculated one, across four tables.
DECLARE LINEGROUP CURSOR FOR
    -- SELECT: the calculated column (NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE) is what
    --   @L_LINE_TOTAL receives below; the other three columns copy straight
    --   across.
    SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION,
           IL.NUM_ORDERED * IL.QUOTED_PRICE
    -- FROM: CUSTOMER is the base table each hop below joins outward from.
    FROM   CUSTOMER C

           -- Hop 1 - customer to invoice.
           JOIN INVOICE I       ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM

           -- Hop 2 - invoice to line item.
           JOIN INVOICE_LINE IL ON I.INVOICE_NUM  = IL.INVOICE_NUM

           -- Hop 3 - line item to item.
           JOIN ITEM IT         ON IL.ITEM_ID     = IT.ITEM_ID
    -- WHERE: limits the join to the rep's own customers.
    WHERE  C.REP_NUM = @I_REP_NUM
    -- ORDER BY: invoice first, then description within it - the order the
    --   cursor will print and total rows in.
    ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, IT.DESCRIPTION;

-- OPEN: runs the four-table query above and positions the cursor before the
--   first row.
OPEN LINEGROUP;

-- The priming fetch, before the loop.
FETCH NEXT FROM LINEGROUP
    INTO @L_INVOICE_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_DESCRIPTION, @L_LINE_TOTAL;

-- The same fetch-and-test loop as REP_CUSTOMER_LIST, now walking the
--   four-table cursor above.
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN

    -- Add this row's total to the accumulator. The variable survives from one
    --   pass of the loop to the next, which is how the running total builds.
    SET @L_RUNNING_TOTAL = @L_RUNNING_TOTAL + @L_LINE_TOTAL;

    -- Print the detail line.
    PRINT @L_INVOICE_NUM + '  ' + @L_CUSTOMER_NAME + '  ' +
          @L_DESCRIPTION + '  ' + CAST(@L_LINE_TOTAL AS VARCHAR(20));

    -- Advance to the next row.
    FETCH NEXT FROM LINEGROUP
        INTO @L_INVOICE_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_DESCRIPTION, @L_LINE_TOTAL;
END

-- CLOSE: releases the rows this cursor was holding, same as in
--   REP_CUSTOMER_LIST.
CLOSE LINEGROUP;
DEALLOCATE LINEGROUP;

-- The grand total, printed once after the loop - the accumulator's final value.
PRINT 'Total for rep ' + @I_REP_NUM + ': ' +
      CAST(@L_RUNNING_TOTAL AS VARCHAR(20));
GO

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Run the cursor's query yourself and you can predict the procedure's output exactly. For rep 20 it prints two lines and a total of 151.48.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two lines on invoice 50710 for Access Pet Center: 127.50 and 23.98. The second query is the same total the cursor builds up in @L_RUNNING_TOTAL, done in one statement instead of a loop. When SUM can answer the question, SUM is the better answer. Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so it contributes nothing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A cursor that changes the row it is sitting on

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declaring a cursor FOR UPDATE OF a column lets the loop modify the row it has just fetched, using WHERE CURRENT OF instead of a WHERE clause that has to find the row all over again.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SQL Server T-SQL: an UPDATABLE cursor - one that changes the rows it walks.
DECLARE @L_ITEM_ID CHAR(4);
-- @L_ON_HAND: holds the quantity column this cursor is about to update.
DECLARE @L_ON_HAND SMALLINT;

-- DECLARE ITEMGROUP CURSOR FOR: the query to be walked, made updatable by
--   the FOR UPDATE OF clause below.
DECLARE ITEMGROUP CURSOR FOR
    -- SELECT: the item id and the quantity the loop will adjust.
    SELECT ITEM_ID, ON_HAND
    -- FROM: the item table this cursor updates.
    FROM   ITEM
    -- WHERE: limits the cursor to the Habitat category - the two items the
    --   loop below will touch.
    WHERE  CATEGORY = 'Habitat'

-- FOR UPDATE OF: declares which column the loop intends to change, and tells the
--   engine to hold the rows so they can be updated in place.
FOR UPDATE OF ON_HAND;

-- OPEN: runs the query and locks the matching rows for update.
OPEN ITEMGROUP;

-- The priming fetch.
FETCH NEXT FROM ITEMGROUP INTO @L_ITEM_ID, @L_ON_HAND;

-- WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0: the same loop test as the earlier cursors - keep
--   going while the last fetch found a row.
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
    -- The update this cursor exists to make - to the row it just fetched.
    UPDATE ITEM
    -- SET: increases ON_HAND by 10 for that row.
    SET    ON_HAND = ON_HAND + 10

    -- WHERE CURRENT OF: "the row this cursor is sitting on" - no key comparison
    --   is needed, because the cursor already knows which row that is. Worth
    --   knowing, and worth avoiding: a single UPDATE ... WHERE CATEGORY =
    --   'Habitat' does the same job in one statement and far more quickly.
    WHERE  CURRENT OF ITEMGROUP;

    -- Advances the cursor - required every pass, or @@FETCH_STATUS never
    --   changes and the loop never ends.
    FETCH NEXT FROM ITEMGROUP INTO @L_ITEM_ID, @L_ON_HAND;
END

-- CLOSE: releases the rows this cursor was holding.
CLOSE ITEMGROUP;
DEALLOCATE ITEMGROUP;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              That loop touches the two Habitat items, AV07 and FT88, and adds 10 to each. It is also a good example of a cursor that should not have been written, because one UPDATE ITEM SET ON_HAND = ON_HAND + 10 WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat'; does the identical job in a single statement. Reserve WHERE CURRENT OF for the case where the new value depends on a decision you can only make row by row.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Declaring the cursor honestly makes it cheaper

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DECLARE LINEGROUP CURSOR LOCAL FAST_FORWARD FOR ... tells SQL Server the cursor is read-only, moves forward only, and is not visible outside the routine that declared it. That is what most reporting cursors actually are, and saying so lets the engine skip the machinery a scrollable, updatable cursor needs. Do not add FOR UPDATE OF to a cursor that never updates anything.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Every local variable name begins with @, and so does every parameter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Assign with SELECT @var = col, never SELECT col INTO var, which builds a table in T-SQL.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Read @@ROWCOUNT on the statement immediately after the one you are asking about, and copy it into a variable if you need to test it more than once.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Write the priming FETCH above the loop and the advancing FETCH as the loop's last statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • End with CLOSE and then DEALLOCATE, so the cursor name is free for the next call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Trap failures in BEGIN CATCH, and check @@TRANCOUNT before rolling anything back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Check Yourself: T-SQL in SQL Server

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1Two of Valerie Kaiser's customers at once

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A T-SQL procedure runs SELECT @L_NAME = CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20';. Both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic match. What ends up in @L_NAME?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. This is Oracle's behaviour, where the same situation raises TOO_MANY_ROWS. T-SQL has no equivalent and treats the multi-row case as ordinary.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. An assignment stores one value. Combining several rows into one string is something you would have to write deliberately with STRING_AGG or similar.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct. The assignment is repeated for every matching row, so the last row processed wins, and the order is whatever the engine chose. Capture @@ROWCOUNT into a variable on the very next statement if that matters.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Nulling the variable would at least be a visible signal. T-SQL gives you a plausible-looking value from a row you never asked for, which is harder to notice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: SELECT @var = col silently keeps the last matching row, so save @@ROWCOUNT on the next statement whenever exactly one row is required.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2Walking a rep's customers one at a time

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A T-SQL cursor loop is controlled by WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0. Why does FETCH NEXT appear once above the loop and again as the loop's last statement?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct. Without the priming fetch the WHILE tests the status of some earlier fetch; without the one inside, the status never changes and the loop repeats the first row forever.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. There is no such requirement. The two fetches are there because of how WHILE evaluates its condition, not because of a rule about cursors.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A single FETCH NEXT both retrieves the current row and advances. Counting rows is a separate job for @@ROWCOUNT or an aggregate query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. FETCH NEXT only moves forward. Reading backward needs a cursor declared SCROLL and an explicit FETCH PRIOR, neither of which appears here.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A T-SQL cursor loop needs a priming FETCH before WHILE and an advancing FETCH as the loop's final statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3Retiring the Nylon Dog Leash from the catalog

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DELETE_ITEM is called with 'DG04', which invoice 50710 still lists as an ordered item. The body sits inside BEGIN TRY and BEGIN CATCH. What happens?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A foreign key exists precisely to stop this. Allowing the delete would leave invoice line 50710 pointing at an item id that no longer exists.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. The engine refuses the delete, control passes to BEGIN CATCH, and ERROR_MESSAGE() gives the caller a sentence instead of a raw engine error.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The statement never completes, so there is no successful row count to read. @@ROWCOUNT is the test for the different case where the item id simply was not in the table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Cascading deletes happen only when the foreign key was declared ON DELETE CASCADE. Nothing here declares that, and silently deleting invoice lines would be a poor default anyway.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Wrap a delete in TRY/CATCH so a foreign key refusal becomes a readable message, and use @@ROWCOUNT for the separate case of a row that was never there.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              8-10 Using a Trigger

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything in 8-8 and 8-9 had to be called. Somebody typed EXECUTE or EXEC or CALL, and the procedure ran. A trigger is the opposite arrangement: it is stored code that nobody calls, attached to a table, that the database itself runs whenever a particular kind of change hits that table. This is the one topic in the module that runs in the sandbox on this page, so you can watch it happen instead of taking it on faith.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Trigger

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A block of code stored in the database and attached to one table, which the database executes automatically when a row of that table is inserted, updated, or deleted. It has no name at the call site because there is no call site. The statement that caused it does not mention it and cannot see it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Triggers exist in all four engines in this module, with the same idea and four different spellings. Two things vary: how you name the row being changed, and whether the trigger runs once per row or once per statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Trigger syntax across the four engines in this module
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              EngineHow the trigger is declaredHow it refers to the row
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQLCREATE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW, wrapped in DELIMITER //NEW.col and OLD.col
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OracleCREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW:NEW.col and :OLD.col, with the colon
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL ServerCREATE TRIGGER n ON t AFTER INSERT AS -- no FOR EACH ROWThe inserted and deleted tables, holding every affected row at once
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQLite (this page)CREATE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROWNEW.col and OLD.col
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The SQL Server row is a real difference, not a spelling difference

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQL, Oracle and SQLite run a row-level trigger once for every row the statement touched. SQL Server runs the trigger once for the whole statement and hands you two tables, inserted and deleted, containing all the affected rows. Code written as though inserted holds exactly one row is correct until the day somebody inserts two rows in one statement, and then it silently processes only one of them.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An audit log, end to end

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay wants a permanent record of every invoice line as it is added: which invoice, which item, how many, and when. Nobody is going to remember to write that second INSERT every time, and a rule that depends on everybody remembering is not a rule. Run the box below and watch the log row appear without anything asking for it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One row comes back: 50712, GR15, 4, and whatever date you pressed Run. Read statement 3 again and notice it says nothing about INVOICE_LINE_LOG. That is the whole point of a trigger, and also the whole danger. Delete statement 2, press Run again, and the log comes back empty.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Read statement 3 one more time. It is an ordinary INSERT into INVOICE_LINE. It does not name INVOICE_LINE_LOG, does not know the log exists, and would be written identically by somebody who had never heard of the trigger. The log row appeared anyway, because the database ran the trigger between the row landing and the statement finishing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why the box opens with three lines of housekeeping

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The sandbox keeps its database between one press of Run and the next. A second CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE_LOG would fail because the table already exists, a second CREATE TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE would fail for the same reason, and a second INSERT of the same invoice line would fail on the primary key. DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS, DROP TABLE IF EXISTS, and a targeted DELETE put the sandbox back to a known state so the box gives the same answer every time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OLD and NEW

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Inside the trigger body, NEW is the row as it will be after the change and OLD is the row as it was before. An INSERT has a NEW and no OLD, a DELETE has an OLD and no NEW, and an UPDATE has both. That is what makes an update trigger the natural place to record a before-and-after audit trail.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Exactly one log row: 1120, 3512.5, 3762.5. Two UPDATE statements ran but only one was a real change, and the WHEN clause is what kept the second one out of the log. Delete the WHEN line and press Run again to see the noise it was filtering.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two features are doing work in that trigger. AFTER UPDATE OF BALANCE narrows it to updates that name the BALANCE column, so an address correction never wakes it up. WHEN OLD.BALANCE <> NEW.BALANCE narrows it further to updates that actually moved the number. Without them the log fills with entries recording that nothing happened, and a log nobody trusts is a log nobody reads.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              BEFORE and AFTER

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The timing word decides when the trigger runs relative to the change, and that decides what it is capable of.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              BEFORE

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Runs while the row is still a proposal. The change has not been applied and no other trigger has seen it. This is the timing that can refuse the statement outright, and in some engines it can adjust the incoming values. Use it for validation and normalisation: rules about whether a row is allowed in at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              AFTER

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Runs once the row is on file and every constraint has been satisfied. The change is real, so the trigger can safely act on it: write an audit row, adjust a total in another table, queue a notification. Use it for consequences, meaning things that should follow from a change that has already been accepted.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A BEFORE trigger refuses a row by raising an error. On this page the call is RAISE(ABORT, 'message'), wrapped in a SELECT because SQLite trigger bodies contain statements. Oracle uses RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR, SQL Server uses THROW, MySQL uses SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'. All four cancel the statement and hand the message back to whoever wrote it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              As written the insert succeeds and Harbor Pet Supply appears with a credit limit of 9000. Now change 9000.00 to 15000.00 and press Run again: the WHEN clause turns true, RAISE(ABORT) cancels the statement, and the box reports the message instead of a table. Nothing was stored, which is what BEFORE buys you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The cost: effects you cannot see at the call site

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A trigger can change a table nobody mentioned. That is genuinely useful and it is also the reason triggers get a bad reputation. Run the box below, then read the two statements in it and try to explain from them alone why ON_HAND moved.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The Small Animal Grooming Kit ends at 18, down from its seeded 22. The INSERT names INVOICE_LINE and only INVOICE_LINE, yet a row in ITEM changed. The UPDATE at the top resets ON_HAND to 22 so the box gives 18 every time rather than 14, then 10, then 6.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A trigger is invisible from the statement that fires it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Somebody debugging that INSERT sees one statement touching one table. They will not find the UPDATE by reading the application, because it is not in the application. They will not find it by reading the INSERT, because it is not there either. Two rules keep this manageable: write down in the schema documentation every trigger you create, and never write a trigger whose job could have been done by a constraint, a default, or a plain statement in the calling code.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              There is a second, quieter hazard. A trigger that updates a table which has its own trigger will fire that one too, and a chain of triggers can end up doing far more work than the original statement suggests, or in the worst case circle back to the table it started from. Keep bodies short, keep the chain shallow, and prefer one trigger doing one thing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Finding and removing triggers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because a trigger is invisible at the call site, being able to list the ones a database holds is not optional. On this page they live in sqlite_master alongside tables, views and indexes. MySQL and SQL Server use INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERS, and Oracle uses USER_TRIGGERS.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One row: LOG_NEW_LINE, trigger, INVOICE_LINE. That third column is the one that matters when you are trying to work out why a table keeps changing on its own. To watch the listing empty out, add DROP TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE; immediately ABOVE the SELECT and press Run again. Putting it after the SELECT changes nothing you can see, because the catalog is read before the drop happens.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DROP TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE; removes it, in every engine here. Dropping the table a trigger is attached to removes the trigger with it, which is worth knowing before you rebuild a table using the copy-and-rename pattern from 6-8a and wonder later why the audit log went quiet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Choose BEFORE to refuse or adjust a row, and AFTER to act on a row that has been accepted.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Use NEW for the incoming values and OLD for the values being replaced; an INSERT has no OLD and a DELETE has no NEW.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Narrow the trigger with UPDATE OF column and a WHEN clause so it does not fire on changes it does not care about.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Write DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS above CREATE TRIGGER in any script you expect to run twice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • In SQL Server, write the body against the inserted and deleted tables as sets, because it fires once per statement, not once per row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Document every trigger you create, because nobody will find it by reading the statement that fires it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Check Yourself: Triggers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1The grooming kit that lost four units

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A clerk inserts one row into INVOICE_LINE for GR15 with NUM_ORDERED of 4. Afterwards ITEM.ON_HAND for GR15 reads 18 instead of 22. The INSERT statement mentions only INVOICE_LINE. What explains the change?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A foreign key restricts what values are allowed; it never copies or adjusts data in the parent table. Nothing about INSERT propagates changes across a relationship.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. ON_HAND is a stored column holding a number, not a computed one. Nothing recomputes it when the table is read.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A CHECK constraint can only accept or reject a value in the row being written. It cannot change a value, and it cannot touch a different table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct. The trigger is attached to INVOICE_LINE, fires after the row lands, and issues an UPDATE ITEM ... WHERE ITEM_ID = NEW.ITEM_ID that no one reading the INSERT would ever see.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A trigger is the usual explanation when a table changes without any statement naming it, which is exactly why triggers must be documented.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2Harbor Pet Supply's oversized credit limit

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay wants a new customer row carrying a credit limit above 10000 refused outright, not written and then removed afterwards. Which trigger timing does that job?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct. A BEFORE trigger runs before the row is stored, so raising an error there cancels the statement and nothing is ever written.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. The proposed values are fully available to a BEFORE trigger through NEW. Waiting until after the row exists means writing it and then undoing it, which is what the requirement rules out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The requirement is about a customer arriving for the first time, which is an insert. An update trigger would not fire at all on a new row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Timing is exactly what differs. Cancelling from AFTER means the row was already written, and recovering from that is the transaction rollback problem the requirement was trying to avoid.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Use BEFORE for rules about whether a row may enter at all, and AFTER for consequences of a row that has already been accepted.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3Auditing a balance change at Access Pet Center

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An AFTER UPDATE OF BALANCE trigger on CUSTOMER writes an audit row each time a balance moves. Which reference gives the balance as it stood before the UPDATE?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. NEW always means the incoming version of the row. The timing word changes when the trigger runs, not which version each name refers to.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. OLD is the row as it was and NEW is the row as it will be, which is what lets a single audit row record 3512.50 and 3762.50 side by side.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. An unqualified column inside a trigger body is ambiguous at best and refers to whatever table the surrounding statement addresses. Audit code should always say OLD. or NEW. explicitly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. The whole purpose of OLD is to keep the previous version available to the trigger. It is present for updates and deletes and absent only for inserts.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: OLD and NEW name the before and after versions of the row; an insert has no OLD and a delete has no NEW.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q4Rebuilding KimTay's audit setup a second time

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A sandbox box creates INVOICE_LINE_LOG and the trigger LOG_NEW_LINE, then inserts one invoice line. Why does the box open with DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS and DROP TABLE IF EXISTS?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A trigger fires every time its event happens, indefinitely. Nothing about firing consumes or disables it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. A table created in an earlier run is perfectly readable later; that persistence is the reason the drops are needed, not a reason they would not help.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct. The sandbox keeps its database from one press of Run to the next, so without the drops the second run fails on the existing table, the existing trigger, and the duplicate primary key.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE_LOG; would empty it without dropping it. The table is dropped because the script recreates it, not because emptying it is impossible.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Any script you expect to run more than once should open with DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS and DROP TABLE IF EXISTS for everything it creates.
