                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Summary What You Learned in Module 8

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      This module took one small set of tasks and wrote them out in three procedural dialects: MySQL, Oracle PL/SQL, and SQL Server T-SQL, with the trigger written once more in this page's own SQLite. Fetch one customer's name and balance. Change a balance safely. Delete an item that other rows may still reference. Walk a list one row at a time. Do something automatically when a row arrives. The tasks did not get harder as you moved between engines. Only the spelling changed, and noticing which parts were spelling and which parts were ideas is the actual skill.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Three things are ideas. A stored procedure is named, parameterised logic that lives in the database rather than in an application, so every caller gets the same rules. A cursor is a way to hand a query's rows to your own logic one at a time, for the cases where a single statement cannot express the decision. A trigger is logic the database runs for you, attached to a table rather than to a caller. Those three transfer to any engine you meet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The module's tasks in three procedural dialects
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      TaskMySQL / Oracle PL/SQLSQL Server T-SQL
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Declare a variableDECLARE L_NAME VARCHAR(35); / L_NAME CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE;DECLARE @L_NAME VARCHAR(35);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Fill it from one rowSELECT col INTO L_VAR FROM ... in bothSELECT @L_VAR = col FROM ...
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Notice the query found nothingDECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND / WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THENIF @@ROWCOUNT = 0
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Loop over a listOPEN, FETCH, EXIT WHEN %NOTFOUND, CLOSEOPEN, priming FETCH, WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0, CLOSE, DEALLOCATE
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Trap a failure in one placeDECLARE ... HANDLER / EXCEPTION WHEN ...BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      React automatically to a rowAFTER INSERT ... FOR EACH ROW, NEW.col / :NEW.colON t AFTER INSERT, the inserted table, once per statement
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • PL/SQL names its failure cases. NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS are raised for you; WHEN OTHERS catches the rest and must be listed last.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • You can declare and raise an exception of your own for a business rule the database cannot know about, and report it with RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR using a number between -20000 and -20999.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • T-SQL raises nothing when an assignment matches zero rows or many. @@ROWCOUNT, read on the very next statement and copied into a variable if you need to test it more than once, is how you find out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • A T-SQL cursor needs a priming FETCH before the loop, an advancing FETCH as the loop's last statement, and both CLOSE and DEALLOCATE at the end.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • A cursor is the right tool only when each row needs its own decision. When SUM, a single UPDATE, or a join can answer the question, they are faster and shorter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Triggers run without being called. BEFORE can refuse a row; AFTER acts on a row already accepted. NEW and OLD name the incoming and outgoing versions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • SQL Server triggers fire once per statement and read the inserted and deleted tables, so trigger bodies written for one row are quietly wrong for a multi-row statement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • Nothing at the call site reveals that a trigger exists, which is why every trigger belongs in the schema documentation and why a constraint is the better tool whenever one will do.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What this page could and could not show you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Triggers ran here for real, in SQLite, and so did every query underneath the procedures. Stored procedures, PL/SQL, and T-SQL did not, because SQLite implements none of them. That is not a gap in the material; it is the reason the dialect tables exist. When you next sit in front of Oracle or SQL Server, the table for that engine is the translation key, and the ideas underneath it are already yours.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can explain the difference between a stored procedure and a trigger in terms of who calls it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can say what NO_DATA_FOUND means and name the T-SQL test that does the same job.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can write a cursor loop in either dialect and say where the loop stops and why.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can choose between BEFORE and AFTER for a stated requirement and defend the choice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can predict what OLD and NEW hold for an insert, an update, and a delete.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • I can name two reasons a trigger is harder to debug than the same code written in the caller.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Every term below appeared in this module. The third column is the one to check before you use a term in an exam answer, because half of these are correct in exactly one engine and wrong in the other two.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Review Module 8 Review

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The quiz below is cumulative. Some questions are about the procedures, cursors, and triggers you met in this module; others reach back to joins, grouping, nulls, and functions, because a procedure is only ever as good as the SQL inside it. Answer each one before you look at the note under the options, and pay attention to the questions where two options look almost the same. That is usually where the real distinction lives.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How to read a wrong answer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Every option carries a note naming the specific misconception behind it, not simply the word "incorrect". If you picked an option, read its note first and the correct option's note second. Working out why the wrong idea was tempting is worth more than confirming the right one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Use the sandbox to settle any question about what the data actually contains. Both databases are loaded, so you can test a claim about KimTay or StayWell without leaving the page.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQL Sandbox · SQLite engine
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Four customers come back, from 1120 to 1420. Every column of every row is filled in; nothing in the shipped data is missing. Companion Care Clinic sits at 1310 with a balance of 0 and no invoice anywhere in the database, which makes it the row to reach for whenever a question is about something that has no match. Replace the query with anything you want to check.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Procedures and cursors: what a parameter buys you, where a cursor loop stops, and why SUM often beats a loop.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Error handling: which failures Oracle names for you, which ones T-SQL leaves you to detect, and where the handler goes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Triggers: BEFORE against AFTER, OLD against NEW, and why the calling statement gives no hint that one exists.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Carried forward: outer joins for unmatched rows, HAVING after GROUP BY, IS NULL rather than = NULL, and which functions survive a change of engine.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Module 8 Review Quiz

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1The clinic with no invoice

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay wants a list of every customer alongside their invoice numbers, and Companion Care Clinic must appear even though it has no invoice at all. Which approach produces that?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. An inner join keeps only rows that matched on both sides, so Companion Care Clinic is dropped entirely. It never invents a zero for a row it discarded.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. A left outer join keeps every row of the left table whether or not it matched, filling the right table's columns with null when there was nothing to match.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The inner join has already removed the clinic before the WHERE clause runs, so there is no row left for IS NULL to find. This condition returns nothing at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. UNION stacks results with matching column lists on top of each other. CUSTOMER and INVOICE have different columns, and stacking would not pair a customer with its invoices anyway.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: When a question says a row must appear even with nothing to match, it is asking for an outer join.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2KimTay's categories with more than one item

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ITEM holds five rows spread across four categories. Which clause narrows a grouped result down to only the categories holding more than one item?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. WHERE is evaluated row by row before any group exists, so COUNT(*) has nothing to count yet and the engine rejects the condition.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. ORDER BY decides the order rows are returned in. It never removes a row, so every category would still be listed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from a result. It has no notion of how many rows went into each category and cannot filter on a count.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct. HAVING runs after GROUP BY has built the groups and their aggregate values, which is the only point at which COUNT(*) for a category is available to test. Only Habitat qualifies, with AV07 and FT88.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping, and only HAVING can test an aggregate.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3The clinic's missing invoice number

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Nothing in KimTay's shipped data is missing, but a query can still produce a null. A left outer join from CUSTOMER to INVOICE gives Companion Care Clinic a row whose INVOICE_NUM is null, because there was nothing on the right to match. Which condition keeps only the customers whose INVOICE_NUM came back null?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct. Null means unknown, and a comparison with an unknown is itself unknown rather than true, so SQL provides IS NULL as the only way to test for it. Run it in the sandbox and exactly one row comes back: 1310, Companion Care Clinic.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. This comparison evaluates to unknown for every row, including the null one, so the query returns nothing at all. It is the single most common null mistake.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. An empty string is a known value of zero length; null is the absence of any value. An unmatched outer join column is null and does not match = ''.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. NOT expects a condition, not a column. Even where an engine tolerates the syntax, a null operand makes the result unknown rather than true.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Test for a missing value with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; = NULL matches nothing, ever.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q4Printing a rep's full name on a KimTay report

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You need LAST_NAME and FIRST_NAME combined into one column, and the same statement has to work in MySQL and in this page's engine. Which expression does that?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. + joins text in SQL Server but means numeric addition elsewhere, so the same expression gives a number, a null, or an error depending on the engine.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. There is no ADD function in any of these engines. Addition is an operator, and it is arithmetic rather than text handling.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct. CONCAT behaves the same way in MySQL and SQLite, which is why it is the safe choice when a statement has to survive a change of engine. The || operator also works in both.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. JOIN combines rows from two tables. It has nothing to do with combining two columns of one row into a single value.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: CONCAT and || join text the same way in MySQL and SQLite; + is SQL Server's spelling and does not travel.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q5Dating KimTay's audit rows

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An audit trigger has to stamp each log row with the current date. Which pairing is correct for the two engines named?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. TODAY() is not a function in either engine. Date handling is in fact where these engines diverge most, not where they agree.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. SYSDATE is Oracle's spelling. MySQL has a SYSDATE() function with different behaviour from CURDATE(), and SQLite has nothing of the kind.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. GETDATE() is SQL Server's spelling and is available in neither MySQL nor SQLite. There is no portable spelling of the current date across all four engines.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct. CURDATE(), NOW(), YEAR(), DATEDIFF() and DATE_ADD() are MySQL; SQLite uses DATE('now'), strftime('%Y', col), julianday(a) - julianday(b) and DATE(col, '+30 days').

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Date functions are the least portable part of SQL; look up the spelling for the engine you are on every single time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q6One procedure for four KimTay customers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              GET_CUSTOMER is written once but has to work for 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420. What makes a single stored procedure serve all four?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A view is a stored query with a fixed definition. It does not accept a value from the caller, so it cannot change which customer is returned from one call to the next.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. The parameter is substituted into the WHERE clause on every execution, which is exactly what makes one stored routine reusable instead of single-purpose.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A cursor is about processing many rows one at a time. This procedure deliberately handles a single row; the varying part is which row, and that is the parameter's job.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Storing one procedure per customer would mean a new procedure every time KimTay signs a customer. Parameters exist precisely so that never has to happen.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A parameter is what turns stored code from a single-purpose script into something worth storing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q7Handling one rep's customers one at a time

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A single SELECT already returns both of rep 20's customers in one result. Why would a procedure use a cursor over that query instead?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A cursor is generally slower, because the engine gives up set-based optimisation and hands rows over one at a time. Speed is a reason to avoid cursors, not to choose them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. A SELECT inside a procedure is an ordinary SELECT with every clause available. Nothing about being stored restricts the query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct. The cursor exists so that code can run between rows, making a decision or performing an action per row that a single statement could not express.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Column count has nothing to do with it. A one-column query can drive a cursor and a twenty-column query can be returned as an ordinary result set.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Choose a cursor only when each row needs its own decision; when a single statement can answer the question, it is both shorter and faster.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q8A customer number that is not on file

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In Oracle, a SELECT ... INTO inside a procedure matches no row. What happens immediately afterwards?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct. SELECT ... INTO promises exactly one row, so zero rows is a failure with a name, and control jumps to the handlers you wrote.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. A procedure using SELECT ... INTO is not producing a result set at all; it is filling variables. There is no empty result to hand back.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. This describes what MySQL does when no NOT FOUND handler was declared. Oracle deliberately refuses to continue on values that were never retrieved.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. No engine silently broadens a query you wrote. Returning an arbitrary customer instead of the requested one would be far worse than raising an error.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Oracle names its two single-row failures and expects a handler; silence is not one of the options.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q9An update at KimTay that changed nothing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A T-SQL procedure updates CUSTOMER using a customer number that is not in the table. How does the procedure find out that no row changed?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. @@FETCH_STATUS reports on the most recent cursor FETCH. It has nothing to say about an UPDATE and would hold a stale value here.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. An UPDATE that matches no row is a complete success that happened to affect nothing. SQL Server raises no error, which is exactly why the check is needed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The row count of CUSTOMER does not change when an UPDATE matches nothing, and it does not change when an UPDATE succeeds either. A cursor adds work without adding information.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct. @@ROWCOUNT holds the number of rows the preceding statement affected, and every following statement overwrites it, so it must be read straight away and saved if it is needed twice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: @@ROWCOUNT is T-SQL's answer to "did that actually do anything", and it must be read on the very next statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q10Keeping KimTay's stock figures honest

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Every new row in INVOICE_LINE must reduce ITEM.ON_HAND by the quantity ordered, and nobody wants to depend on each programmer remembering to write the second statement. What handles this?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. A CHECK constraint accepts or rejects a value in the row being written. It cannot change a value and it cannot reach into a different table.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct. The trigger is attached to INVOICE_LINE, fires once per inserted row, and runs the UPDATE no matter which program did the insert or whether its author knew the rule existed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. A view is a stored query. Reading it can compute a current figure, but it cannot change the stored ON_HAND column that the rest of the system reads.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. An index affects how quickly rows are located. It stores no logic and changes no data, so it cannot enforce a rule of any kind.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: A rule that must hold no matter who writes the statement belongs in the database, and a trigger is the tool when a constraint cannot express it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Practice Hands-On Exercises

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The first two exercises run in the sandbox. The rest are written to be read, reasoned about, and if you have access to the engine named, typed in and executed there. Where an exercise names Oracle or SQL Server, write the answer out in full even though you cannot run it here; being able to produce correct PL/SQL or T-SQL from a specification is exactly what is being asked of you.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Start with the runnable ones. StayWell wants a permanent record of every payment as it arrives, written by the database rather than by whoever happens to be at the keyboard. Run the box, then answer the two questions in the checklist below it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In this databaseclick a table to see its rows
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One log row: L004 for 465.00. The INSERT names only PAYMENT, and PAYMENT_LOG filled itself in. Try adding a second INSERT with PAYMENT_ID 98 for lease L003 at 725.00 and predict the result before you press Run. Remember to add a matching DELETE at the top if you want the box to stay re-runnable.

Those columns are on LEASE, not on PAYMENT, so the trigger body needs a subquery against LEASE using NEW.LEASE_ID. Add the two columns to the CREATE TABLE first, then rewrite the trigger's INSERT. Remember DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS at the top.

INTO, and prints the description together with ON_HAND * PRICE. Handle NO_DATA_FOUND with a message naming the id that was not found, and finish with WHEN OTHERS reporting SQLERRM. Declare the variables with %TYPE.

Write it once with the explicit OPEN / FETCH / EXIT WHEN %NOTFOUND / CLOSE form and once as a cursor FOR loop, and say in one sentence which you would keep and why.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Exercise 5 (SQL Server, write it out)

Use BEGIN TRY and BEGIN CATCH, open an explicit transaction, THROW an error numbered 50010 if @@ROWCOUNT is 0, and THROW 50011 if the new limit would exceed 20000.00. Save @@ROWCOUNT into a variable if you test it more than once, and roll back in the CATCH block only after testing @@TRANCOUNT.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Before you hand in a trigger

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Check three things every time. Does the script open with DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS so it can be run twice? Does the trigger fire only on the changes it cares about, using UPDATE OF and WHEN rather than firing on everything and filtering later? And is there a line in your documentation saying the trigger exists, on which table, and what it does? A trigger nobody wrote down is a bug waiting for a new colleague.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • After running the payment box: name the statement that put a row in PAYMENT_LOG, and say why it is not the INSERT you can see.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • After running the payment box: predict what PAYMENT_LOG would hold if the trigger said BEFORE INSERT instead of AFTER INSERT, then change it and check.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Exercise 3: my procedure declares every variable with %TYPE and lists WHEN OTHERS last.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Exercise 4: my explicit cursor closes the cursor in the handler as well as on the happy path.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Exercise 5: my CATCH block tests @@TRANCOUNT before it rolls anything back.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Exercise 6: my cursor loop has a priming FETCH, an advancing FETCH, and both CLOSE and DEALLOCATE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Exercise 7: my SQL Server trigger body would still be correct if two invoice lines were inserted by one statement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              S-1 Why Supabase, and what you are actually getting

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This section answers the question you should ask before signing up for anything: what is Supabase, why does this course use it, and what does it cost you. By the end you will know where Supabase fits next to the other two ways this course lets you run SQL, what the free plan actually gives you, what it does not give you, and what to have ready before you start the sign-up in the next section.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Dashboard paths and service limits in this guide were verified on August 3, 2026. If the interface changes, use Supabase's current project-pausing, Data API, and database-connection guides as the source of truth.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What Supabase is, in plain terms

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Supabase is a company that runs PostgreSQL databases for you. You create an account in a web browser, you create a project, and Supabase starts a real PostgreSQL database on its own servers. You then open SQL Editor in the left-hand sidebar of your project, type SQL into the editor, and click the Run button (or press Ctrl+Enter on Windows, Cmd+Enter on a Mac). Results appear in a panel below the editor. There is nothing to download, nothing to install, no server to start on your laptop, and no port numbers to type. For classwork it is free, and the Free plan does not ask for a credit card.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The word you will see everywhere in Supabase is project. For our purposes one project is one database, plus some extras this course does not need (an auto-generated web API, a login system, file storage). When the documentation says "your project," read it as "your database." Projects are grouped under an organization. Supabase creates a default organization for you automatically the first time you create an account, and assigns you the Owner role in it, so this is not something you have to set up.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PostgreSQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PostgreSQL (often shortened to "Postgres") is a free, open-source relational database. It belongs to the same category of software as MySQL, Oracle Database, and Microsoft SQL Server -- they are all relational databases that speak SQL, though they are separate products from different vendors and only PostgreSQL and MySQL are open source. PostgreSQL stores tables, enforces primary and foreign keys, and speaks SQL -- everything Modules 1 and 2 describe applies to it without change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three places you can run SQL in this course

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You now have three options, and they are good at different things. None of them replaces the others.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The three ways to run SQL in this course
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Where you type SQLWhat it actually isHow long it lastsBest for
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The sandbox on this pageSQLite running inside your browser tabUntil you reload the pageTrying one statement quickly, with zero setup
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A local installMySQL or PostgreSQL installed on your own computerUntil you uninstall it or reformat the machineWorking offline, and matching Module 3's MySQL exactly
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SupabasePostgreSQL running on Supabase's serversUntil you delete the project (an idle project pauses, but the data stays)Homework you want to keep and reach from any computer

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The in-page sandbox is deliberately throwaway. It is the fastest way to test whether a SELECT returns what you expected, and the safest place to make a mistake, but the moment you reload the page your tables are gone. A local install is permanent but it lives on exactly one machine: if you write your KimTay tables on a lab computer, they are not there when you get home, and a reformat takes them with it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Supabase sits in between. The database is real, it keeps your data, and you reach it from any computer that has a web browser -- you sign in to the Supabase dashboard with your Supabase account (your sign-up email and password, or your GitHub login). If your laptop dies the week before an assignment is due, your REP and CUSTOMER tables are still sitting on Supabase's server exactly as you left them, and you can open them from a lab machine or a library computer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One honest catch: it is Postgres, not MySQL

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Module 3 teaches MySQL-flavoured SQL. Supabase gives you PostgreSQL. The great majority of what you have learned transfers untouched -- CREATE TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, INSERT INTO, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, and the VARCHAR, CHAR, DECIMAL, SMALLINT, and DATE types all exist in PostgreSQL and behave the same way for everything this course asks you to do. A small number of things differ. You will not use CREATE DATABASE: PostgreSQL does have that statement, but your project already is the database, and the statement will fail in the SQL Editor anyway because the editor wraps what you run in a transaction and PostgreSQL forbids CREATE DATABASE inside one. DESCRIBE is a MySQL command that PostgreSQL does not have at all. And PostgreSQL quietly lowercases unquoted table and column names, so CREATE TABLE REP actually creates a table named rep -- harmless as long as you never wrap a name in double quotes, which is why this course does not.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Where the differences are listed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Do not try to memorize the differences now. Section S-6 puts the MySQL statement and the PostgreSQL statement side by side for every case Module 3 uses, including the full KimTay DDL rewritten for Postgres and the replacement for DESCRIBE. Work through the setup first, then use S-6 as your reference sheet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What the free plan gives you

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The Supabase Free plan is genuinely free, needs no credit card, and is more than enough for this course. Three limits are worth knowing before you start.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Free plan limits that matter for this course
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              LimitWhat it means for you
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              2 active projectsYour account can have two free projects running at the same time. This is a total across every organization where you are an Owner or Administrator -- it is not two per organization. Paused projects do not count against it, so plan on one project for KimTay and keep the second slot free.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              500 MB database size per projectEach project gets its own half gigabyte of database storage. The whole KimTay database is a few kilobytes, so you will not come close.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Paused after 1 week of inactivityIf a free project goes seven days without database activity, Supabase pauses it to save resources. Supabase emails the project owner a warning roughly a week beforehand, and again once the project has actually been paused.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pausing is not deletion

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A paused project stops serving requests, but your tables, rows, and settings are preserved. To bring it back, open the Supabase dashboard, select the organization and paused project, then click Resume project and confirm. You have a one-year window to restore it from the dashboard. Supabase evaluates user database activity across the previous seven days and says a few database requests each day are typically enough to avoid a pause. After a warning email, visiting the project in the dashboard can also generate activity and prevent that pending pause.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The Free plan does not back up your data

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Automatic daily backups are a paid-plan feature; Free plan projects have none. Supabase keeping your database running is not the same as Supabase keeping a copy of it. Before you submit any assignment, save your own copy of the SQL that builds and fills your tables -- keep the CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements in a text file on your computer or in cloud storage. If anything ever goes wrong, you can rebuild the whole KimTay database by pasting that file back into the SQL Editor.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One security label you will see, and why it is fine here

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              "Unrestricted" is expected for coursework
