                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Q1The window that remembers too much

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    On Windows, a classmate runs the EDB installer with Command Line Tools checked and confirms psql.exe sits in C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin. They switch back to a PowerShell window they had open all along and get 'psql' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘a. PATH is the list of folders Windows searches for programs, not the install location, so reinstalling elsewhere changes nothing about being found.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✔b. Correct - the installer does not add that folder to the path, and a window opened earlier kept the old PATH, so a fresh window plus the entry is the fix.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘c. Command Line Tools is the component that provides psql, and they already confirmed psql.exe exists; the server component is optional because the database lives at Supabase.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘d. The entry must have no quotation marks and no trailing backslash, so adding either is how a correct-looking Path edit still fails.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Remember: Prove a Path edit worked with where.exe psql in a newly opened PowerShell window - never in the window that was already sitting there.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Q2The password with punctuation in it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A student's Supabase database password contains a $ and an &. Pasted into PowerShell with no quotation marks, the line never reaches psql at all - PowerShell answers The ampersand (&) character is not allowed. Wrapped in double quotation marks, the command runs but the connection is refused as an authentication failure instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘a. PowerShell accepts either kind, and double quotes are the trouble: inside them anything starting with $ is expanded, which is why the password silently arrived wrong.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘b. Unquoted, & is reserved and produces that error, ; ends the command, # starts a comment, and a space splits the argument in two.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘c. Two mistakes at once: pgAdmin's Password field is not a URL and takes the password literally, and the characters this section has you percent-encode are @ : / ? # [ ] % - the fix for $ is quoting, not encoding.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✔d. Correct - single quotes stop $ expansion and neutralise &, ;, #, and spaces; a literal single quote inside is written twice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Remember: Single quotes in PowerShell, every time - or skip the URL entirely with the -h -p -d -U flag form and type the password at the prompt.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Q3The tree with nothing in it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A student opens pgAdmin 4 for the first time on the lab computer. The Object Explorer on the left shows only a Servers node with nothing under it, and their connection string is sitting in Notepad next to the window.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✔a. Correct - that is the path (some builds read Create then Server...), and the host, port, maintenance database, username, and password all come out of the one string.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘b. pgAdmin wants the pieces separately: the host is only what sits between @ and the last :, such as aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘c. Name on the General tab is just a label for you with no effect on the connection; the database name goes in Maintenance database on the Connection tab.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • ✘d. The master password only protects saved server passwords on that computer; the Password field needs your Supabase database password, typed literally.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Remember: Registering a server is just the connection string taken apart into five labelled boxes, and pgAdmin's labels differ slightly from the words in the string.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    🧩 Match the Windows error to what actually caused it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Click a card, then click where it belongs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Every message below is one a Windows student in this section really hits: PowerShell, psql, or pgAdmin refusing to cooperate. Drop each card into the bucket that names its cause. Read the whole card - the detail buried at the end, not the first few words, is what decides the answer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              0 / 7 placed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              S-6 Postgres vs. MySQL: what changes from Module 3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Module 3 taught you SQL in MySQL. Supabase gives you Postgres. This section is the translation sheet: by the end of it you will know exactly which lines from your Module 3 script you can paste into the Supabase SQL Editor unchanged, which four or five lines need a small edit, why one of those edits (quoting) causes almost every error a student hits in their first Postgres hour, and how to read the error message when it happens anyway.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Before you start

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You need two things open: your Module 3 .sql script (the one with CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, and the KimTay INSERT statements), and your Supabase project dashboard from the earlier sections of this module. Everything in this section can be done in the browser. A terminal is optional and is only mentioned where it is genuinely optional -- it is never the only way to do something.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The important thing to understand first: MySQL and Postgres are two products that both speak SQL. The language is standardized, so the parts you spent Module 3 on -- SELECT, WHERE, INSERT, table design, keys -- are the same in both. What differs is a thin layer of housekeeping around the edges: how you get a database, how you look at a table, how you spell an auto-numbered column, what quotation marks mean, and one Supabase-specific security switch that MySQL has no equivalent for. That is the whole list. It is shorter than it feels.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Module 3 (MySQL) to Supabase (Postgres): the whole difference list
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What you want to doModule 3 (MySQL)Supabase (Postgres)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Create a databaseCREATE DATABASE KimTay; then USE KimTay;Already done -- your project is the database. Tables go in the public schema.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              See a table's columnsDESCRIBE REP;Click the table in the Table Editor, or run the information_schema query below. (\d rep if you have psql.)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              List all tablesSHOW TABLES;The Table Editor sidebar, or query information_schema.tables. (\dt if you have psql.)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Auto-numbered keyID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEYid INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Quote a column or table namebackticks: REP_NUM double quotes: "REP_NUM" -- but usually do not quote at all
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Quote a piece of text'Kaiser' worked, and so did "Kaiser" under MySQL's default settings'Kaiser' only. Double quotes always mean a column or table name.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Return the first 5 rowsSELECT * FROM REP LIMIT 5;Identical: SELECT * FROM rep LIMIT 5;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Skip rows then return someLIMIT 20, 10 or LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 only -- Postgres rejects the comma form
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Column types used by KimTayCHAR, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATE, SMALLINTSame names, no edits needed (one small CHAR display quirk is noted below)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Let the outside world read the tableNot applicable -- MySQL has no built-in web APISupabase exposes public over an auto-generated API, so you must turn on Row Level Security. See the warning below.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You do not create the database -- you already have one

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In Module 3 the first line of your script was CREATE DATABASE. In Supabase, creating the project created the database, and the connection you set up earlier in this module already points at it. So delete the CREATE DATABASE and USE lines from your Module 3 script. Start straight at CREATE TABLE.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How to run a statement, and how to know it worked

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In the Supabase dashboard, open SQL Editor in the left sidebar, paste your SQL into the editor pane, and click Run (or press Ctrl+Enter, Cmd+Enter on a Mac). A statement like CREATE TABLE returns no rows, so a successful run shows a green success message reading Success. No rows returned. That message is what "it worked" looks like -- it is not an error. A failed run shows a red panel with the Postgres error text; read the first line of it, then check the troubleshooting table at the end of this section. To see the table you just made, open Table Editor in the left sidebar; if a brand-new table is not listed yet, reload the page.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              New tables land in a schema called public. A schema is a named folder for tables inside one database. Postgres uses schemas heavily; MySQL treats the word SCHEMA as a plain synonym for DATABASE, which is why the same idea was called a database in Module 3. You can leave everything in public for this course. If you want the KimTay tables kept apart from anything else you build later, you can make your own folder:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- CREATE SCHEMA: a schema is a named folder for tables inside one database.
--   Supabase gives you several already, and public is the one it exposes.
CREATE SCHEMA kimtay;

-- CREATE TABLE kimtay.rep: the schema name in front of the table name says which
--   folder the table goes in. A table outside public is NOT reachable through
--   Supabase's auto-generated API, which is exactly why this is worth knowing -
--   it is either a feature or a trap depending on what you wanted.
CREATE TABLE kimtay.rep (
  rep_num    CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY,
  last_name  VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL
);
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Stick with public

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The Table Editor and the auto-generated API look at public by default. A table in a schema of your own will not appear in the Table Editor until you change the schema dropdown at the top of the table list, and it will not be reachable through the Supabase API until you expose the schema under Integrations > Data API and grant the appropriate roles access. That is real work for no benefit in this course. Use public.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Supabase-only step: turn on Row Level Security

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This has no MySQL equivalent, and skipping it is the single most consequential mistake you can make here. Supabase publishes every table in the public schema through an auto-generated web API. A table you create with the Table Editor gets Row Level Security (RLS) switched on for you. A table you create by running CREATE TABLE in the SQL Editor -- which is what you are about to do with your Module 3 script -- does not. Until you enable RLS and write a policy, the dashboard flags the table as unrestricted, and depending on your project's settings its rows may be readable by anyone holding your project's public key. Run the statements below immediately after creating each table. Enabling RLS with no policy denies all API access, which is the safe starting point -- your own SQL Editor queries keep working, because they do not go through the API.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- run this right after every CREATE TABLE in the SQL Editor
-- ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY: with RLS on, no row is readable or
--   writable through Supabase's public API until a policy explicitly allows it.
--   Any table you create in public is exposed to the internet until you run this,
--   so treat it as part of the CREATE TABLE, not as an optional extra.
ALTER TABLE public.rep ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- check it: rowsecurity should be true for every table you made
-- SELECT: the verification query. Never assume the setting took - look.
SELECT tablename, rowsecurity

-- pg_tables: PostgreSQL's catalogue of tables, queried like any other table.
FROM pg_tables

-- Narrow it to the schema Supabase exposes.
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY tablename;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Inspecting a table: DESCRIBE has two replacements

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DESCRIBE REP; does not exist in Postgres. There are two replacements, and the browser one needs nothing installed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The browser way: open Table Editor from the left sidebar and click rep. The columns, types, and NOT NULL settings are on screen. That is your DESCRIBE. If you would rather have a query you can paste into the SQL Editor, this one works on any Postgres anywhere:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- SELECT: the portable way to inspect a table's structure - the same
--   INFORMATION_SCHEMA you met in Module 7, and it works on any modern engine.
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable

-- information_schema.columns: one row per column of every table.
FROM information_schema.columns

-- Which schema...
WHERE table_schema = 'public'

--   ...and which table. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to LOWER case, so the
--   catalogue stores 'rep' even if you typed REP - which is why the value here
--   is lower case.
  AND table_name   = 'rep'

-- ORDER BY ordinal_position: restores the column order the table declares,
--   instead of alphabetical order.
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why table_schema is in that query

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Without the table_schema = 'public' line, the query returns the columns of every table named rep in every schema you can see, so you would get each column listed more than once as soon as you had a second rep anywhere. Note also that both values are lowercase and in single quotes: information_schema stores identifiers as text, and Postgres stored your unquoted table name folded to lowercase. Searching for 'REP' returns zero rows -- which is a confusing way to be told your table exists.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The terminal way, for reference: psql is the command-line Postgres client, and it has shortcuts called meta-commands. They begin with a backslash. They are psql features rather than SQL, so they take no semicolon, they are never sent to the server, and they will not work in the Supabase SQL Editor in the browser.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- \dt: list tables on your current search path (public, by default).
\dt

-- \d rep: show the columns, types and keys of one table.
\d rep

-- \d+ rep: the same, plus storage and description details. These three are psql
--   shorthands for catalogue queries - faster to type, but only available in
--   psql, whereas the INFORMATION_SCHEMA query above works anywhere.
\d+ rep
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You do not need psql for this course

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              psql is the PostgreSQL command-line client. It can be installed by itself on macOS with Homebrew's libpq package, or with PostgreSQL command-line tools on Windows; you do not need to run a local database server. If you try it, copy the direct string from Connect when IPv6 works, or the Session pooler string on an IPv4-only network. Everything this section asks you to do can also be done in the browser.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Auto-numbering: AUTO_INCREMENT becomes IDENTITY

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              KimTay does not use auto-numbering -- REP_NUM and CUSTOMER_NUM are CHAR codes that the business assigns. But you will want it in your own tables, and AUTO_INCREMENT is a MySQL-only keyword that Postgres rejects with a syntax error. The modern, standard spelling is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY. An identity column is automatically NOT NULL, so you do not add that yourself:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: a table whose key the database fills in for you.
CREATE TABLE note (

  -- GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY: PostgreSQL supplies the next number itself,
  --   and ALWAYS means you are not allowed to supply one by hand. This is the
  --   standard SQL replacement for the older SERIAL type.
  note_id  INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  body     VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL
);

-- Turn on row level security the moment the table exists, as always.
ALTER TABLE public.note ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- leave note_id out of the INSERT and Postgres fills it in
-- INSERT with a partial column list: only body is supplied. The key is generated.
INSERT INTO note (body) VALUES ('Called customer 1120 about invoice.');

-- A second row, and a second generated key - no coordination needed on your part.
INSERT INTO note (body) VALUES ('Mailed replacement part.');

-- proof it worked: you should get note_id 1 and 2, which you never typed
SELECT note_id, body FROM note ORDER BY note_id;

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ALWAYS means Postgres owns the number: if you try INSERT INTO note (note_id, body) VALUES (7, '...') it refuses, which is exactly the accident you want blocked. (There is an escape hatch, OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, for the rare times you need it.) If you want MySQL's more permissive behaviour, where supplying your own value is allowed and only a missing value is generated, write GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY instead.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              You will also see SERIAL in older tutorials (note_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY). It still works and produces a similar auto-numbered column, but it is a Postgres-specific shorthand that creates a separate sequence object and lets anyone insert their own value. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the one to learn: it is the SQL standard, and it is what current Postgres documentation steers you toward.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Quoting: the difference that causes the most confusion

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In MySQL, backticks protect a name and everything keeps the case you typed. Postgres has a different rule, and it is worth reading twice: an identifier that is not quoted is folded to lowercase. REP_NUM, Rep_Num, and rep_num all become rep_num. An identifier that is wrapped in double quotes keeps its case exactly and must be double-quoted every single time you mention it afterwards. (Postgres folds down; the SQL standard actually says to fold up. Nobody agrees, which is the real reason the safe advice is to never quote and always type lowercase.)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The case-folding trap

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              If you create a table as CREATE TABLE "REP" ("REP_NUM" CHAR(2)); then SELECT * FROM REP; fails with relation "rep" does not exist -- Postgres folded your query to lowercase, but the table is genuinely named uppercase REP. From then on you must write SELECT "REP_NUM" FROM "REP"; forever. Fix: never put double quotes around table or column names when you create them. Type them unquoted, in lowercase, and Postgres will let you refer to them in any case you like. If you have already done it, the repair is ALTER TABLE "REP" RENAME TO rep; -- and note you must quote the old name to say it, and must not quote the new one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              So when you port the Module 3 DDL, drop the backticks and do not replace them with double quotes. This is the safe version, and after it every one of SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP;, SELECT rep_num FROM rep; and SELECT Rep_Num FROM Rep; returns the same rows:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- CREATE TABLE: the full REP table on PostgreSQL, in lower case. Unquoted names
--   are folded to lower case by the server, so rep and REP are the same table -
--   picking one style and sticking to it saves confusion later.
CREATE TABLE rep (
  rep_num    CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY,
  last_name  VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,
  street     VARCHAR(20),
  city       VARCHAR(15),
  state      CHAR(2),
  zip        CHAR(5),
  commission DECIMAL(8,2),
  rate       DECIMAL(4,2)
);

-- And immediately lock the table down, before any data goes into it.
ALTER TABLE public.rep ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two kinds of quote

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In Postgres, single quotes mean "this is a piece of text" and double quotes mean "this is the name of a table or column". They are not interchangeable. MySQL, under its default settings, let you write "Kaiser" as a string; Postgres reads that as a column named Kaiser and answers column "Kaiser" does not exist. Backticks are neither -- Postgres does not use them at all and reports a syntax error the moment it sees one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              -- correct
-- INSERT with SINGLE quotes around the text values. In PostgreSQL a single quote
--   means "this is a text value" - which is what you want here.
INSERT INTO rep (rep_num, last_name, first_name)
VALUES ('20', 'Kaiser', 'Valerie');

-- wrong in Postgres: double quotes make these column names
-- ERROR:  column "20" does not exist
-- The same statement with DOUBLE quotes. PostgreSQL reads a double-quoted string
--   as an IDENTIFIER - a table or column name - so it goes looking for a column
--   called 20, cannot find one, and refuses. MySQL and SQLite are more forgiving
--   here, which is exactly how the habit gets picked up.
INSERT INTO rep (rep_num, last_name, first_name)
VALUES ("20", "Kaiser", "Valerie");

-- proof the correct one worked
SELECT rep_num, last_name, first_name FROM rep;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Apostrophes inside text

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              This part did not change. To store a name like O'Brien, double the apostrophe: 'O''Brien'. Those are two single quotes in a row, not one double quote. It works the same way in MySQL and Postgres.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Data types: most of them carry over untouched

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Every type in the KimTay schema exists in Postgres under the same name: CHAR(2), VARCHAR(35), DECIMAL(9,2), DATE, and SMALLINT. You can copy those column definitions across with no edits at all. DECIMAL is simply another name for Postgres's NUMERIC, so your money columns keep their exactness. SMALLINT holds -32768 to 32767, the same range you learned. Dates still go in as '2026-09-14', year first -- that year-first ISO form is the one Postgres documents as unambiguous.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQL types that need a different name in Postgres
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              MySQLPostgresWhy
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              INT AUTO_INCREMENTINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITYAUTO_INCREMENT is a MySQL-only keyword; Postgres reports a syntax error
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DATETIMETIMESTAMP, or better TIMESTAMPTZThere is no datetime type in Postgres. TIMESTAMPTZ (short for timestamp with time zone) is the Supabase default and the safer choice for real events. DATE is unchanged.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              TINYINT(1) for yes/noBOOLEAN with TRUE / FALSEPostgres has a real boolean type
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              DOUBLEDOUBLE PRECISIONPostgres does not accept bare DOUBLE. Naming only -- but keep money in DECIMAL, which the Postgres docs recommend for exact amounts.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              One CHAR quirk worth knowing

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CHAR(n) pads short values with spaces in both products, but they hand the value back differently: MySQL strips the trailing spaces when you read the column, while Postgres stores and displays them. For KimTay this changes nothing you can see, because rep_num is exactly 2 characters and zip is exactly 5, so there is no padding. It matters the day you put 'Kaiser' in a CHAR(20): Postgres returns it with fourteen trailing spaces. If that ever bites you, use VARCHAR -- which is what the Postgres documentation recommends for most columns anyway.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What does not change

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Almost everything. SELECT, FROM, WHERE, AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, joins, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, DEFAULT -- identical, character for character. LIMIT 5 behaves the same in both. NULL still means "no value recorded" and still refuses to equal anything, so you still test it with IS NULL rather than = NULL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Everything from Module 2 carries over completely, because none of it was ever about a particular product. Functional dependence, candidate keys, primary keys, foreign keys, first, second, and third normal form, ER diagrams -- those are properties of the relational model itself. A design that is in 3NF in MySQL is in 3NF in Postgres. The reason Module 2 came before Module 3 is exactly this: the thinking outlasts the tool.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              When it goes wrong: the five errors you will actually see

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Postgres error messages are blunt but honest. Read the first line, find it here, apply the fix, and re-run. Nothing in this table requires starting over.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              First-hour error messages, translated
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Postgres saysWhat you actually didFix
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              syntax error at or near ""`Left a backtick in the scriptDelete the backticks. Do not replace them with anything.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              relation "rep" does not existEither the table was never created, or you created it with double quotes around an uppercase nameConfirm it exists in the Table Editor. If it is listed as REP, run ALTER TABLE "REP" RENAME TO rep;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              column "Kaiser" does not existUsed double quotes around a piece of text in an INSERTChange the double quotes to single quotes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              syntax error at or near "AUTO_INCREMENT"Pasted the MySQL auto-numbering keywordReplace with GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              type "datetime" does not existPasted a MySQL DATETIME columnReplace with TIMESTAMPTZ
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              syntax error at or near "\\"Typed a psql meta-command such as \d rep into the browser SQL EditorUse the Table Editor or the information_schema query instead

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              So the honest summary of your port is: delete two lines at the top, drop the backticks, add one ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; per table, keep the rest. If you built the KimTay tables in the in-browser SQL sandbox during Module 3, that sandbox is a third SQL engine again, so treat your MySQL script -- not the sandbox session -- as the thing you are porting, and expect the same short edit list.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • You removed CREATE DATABASE and USE from the top of your Module 3 script
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Your CREATE TABLE statements have no backticks and no double quotes around table or column names
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • All table and column names are typed in lowercase
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Every piece of text in your INSERT statements is wrapped in single quotes, never double quotes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • CHAR, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATE, and SMALLINT were left exactly as Module 3 wrote them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • Each statement returned Success. No rows returned (or a result grid) rather than a red error panel
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • You ran ALTER TABLE public.<name> ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; for every table, and the pg_tables check shows rowsecurity true for all of them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • You can see the columns of rep in the Table Editor, and the information_schema query returns the same list
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP; and SELECT rep_num FROM rep; both return rows -- that proves you did not quote your identifiers at creation time
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rep; returns the number of reps you inserted, so you know the data landed and not just the table

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              🔍 Check yourself: porting Module 3 SQL to Postgres

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q1The whole-script paste

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A student opens the Module 3 .sql script, selects all of it, and pastes it straight into the Supabase SQL Editor. Before pressing Run they stop and ask what actually has to be edited. According to this section, what is the honest edit list?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. MySQL and Postgres both speak standard SQL, so the query work from Module 3 carries over character for character.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. Creating the Supabase project already created the database, and your connection points straight at it, so both lines come out and the script starts at CREATE TABLE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔c. Correct -- the section summarizes the port as exactly this: delete two lines at the top, drop the backticks, add one ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; per table, keep the rest.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. Every type KimTay uses -- CHAR, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATE, SMALLINT -- exists in Postgres under the same name and needs no edit.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Porting the Module 3 script is a short edit list at the edges, not a rewrite of your SQL.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q2The table that exists but cannot be found

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A student creates their table with CREATE TABLE "REP" ("REP_NUM" CHAR(2)); because the Module 3 script used capitals everywhere. The Table Editor shows a table called REP. Then SELECT * FROM REP; fails with relation "rep" does not exist. What happened?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔a. Correct -- a quoted identifier keeps its case exactly, an unquoted one folds to lowercase, so the query looked for rep and the table is genuinely REP; the repair is ALTER TABLE "REP" RENAME TO rep;.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. The query already was in capitals -- Postgres folded it down to rep anyway, which is precisely why it failed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. The CREATE TABLE succeeded; the Table Editor is listing the table, which is the proof that quoting created it rather than blocking it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. RLS controls the auto-generated web API, not the SQL Editor -- your own SQL Editor queries keep working with RLS on and no policy.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Never put double quotes around a table or column name when you create it; type it unquoted and lowercase.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q3There is no DESCRIBE here

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A student needs to check the columns, types and NOT NULL settings of rep for a homework answer. They are working entirely in the browser and have nothing installed on the lab computer. What does this section tell them to do?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. \d is a psql meta-command, never sent to the server, and typing it in the browser editor gives syntax error at or near "\".
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘b. DESCRIBE is a MySQL statement that does not exist in Postgres, so it is not standard SQL and will not run here.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. information_schema stores the folded lowercase name, so searching for 'REP' returns zero rows -- a confusing way to be told your table exists.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔d. Correct -- these are the two options the section gives you in the browser: the Table Editor, and that information_schema.columns query with both values lowercase and in single quotes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: DESCRIBE does not exist in Postgres -- in the browser, use the Table Editor or an information_schema.columns query.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Q4The lines nobody had to touch

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two classmates are arguing over a printout of the Module 3 script, marking which lines survive the move to Postgres untouched. One of them is right about a whole group of lines. Which claim matches what this section says does NOT change?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘a. Postgres rejects the comma form; only LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 works there, so this line is one of the few that must be edited.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✔b. Correct -- the section calls the query keywords, aggregates and joins identical character for character, and says the KimTay column types exist under the same names with no edits needed; everything conceptual from Module 2 carries over too.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘c. AUTO_INCREMENT is a MySQL-only keyword and Postgres answers syntax error at or near "AUTO_INCREMENT"; the standard spelling is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • ✘d. In Postgres double quotes always mean a table or column name, so this gives column "Kaiser" does not exist -- text needs single quotes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Remember: Almost all of your Module 3 querying, and all of Module 2's design thinking, transfers to Postgres unchanged.
