Drop it on the Supabase Postgres equivalent from this section's translation sheet.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 / 6 placed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        S-7 Keeping your database safe

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Your project now holds real data on a real server on the internet, which means it has secrets attached to it. This section gets you to the point where you can name every secret Supabase gave you, say out loud which one is allowed to appear in code other people can read, fix a password you accidentally pasted somewhere public, and keep a copy of your own work that survives anything that happens to the project. None of this takes long, and doing it once now saves you a bad afternoon later.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        You were given three different secrets, and they do not do the same job

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        People new to this tend to treat every long random string as one thing called "the key". Supabase hands you three, and the difference between them is the difference between a safe project and a project anyone can empty. Here is what each one is for.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The three credentials on a Supabase project
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CredentialWhat it actually isMay it appear in code a user can see?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Database passwordThe password for the Postgres postgres user -- it is the part you paste into the connection string you use in psql, pgAdmin, or TablePlus.No. It belongs in your connection tool and nowhere else.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Publishable key (starts with sb_publishable_; older docs and older projects call this the anon key)A public, low-privilege key that identifies your project to the outside world. What it is allowed to read or change is decided by Row Level Security.Yes. This is the only one designed to be shipped in a browser app.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Secret key (starts with sb_secret_; older docs and older projects call this the service_role key)A key that bypasses Row Level Security completely and can read, change, or delete every row in every table.Never. Not in a browser app, not in a public repository, not in a screenshot.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two naming systems, same two jobs

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Supabase is in the middle of renaming its API keys. Projects created recently show sb_publishable_... and sb_secret_.... Older projects and most tutorials show anon and service_role, which are JSON Web Tokens (long strings with two dots in them). Both systems work today, and Supabase has said the legacy anon and service_role keys will be deprecated by the end of 2026. Whichever pair your project shows, the rule is identical: the low-privilege one (publishable / anon) is public, the high-privilege one (secret / service_role) is not.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        These three things live in three different places, and this trips people up:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Connection strings come from the Connect button at the top of your project dashboard. Note that the string it gives you has [YOUR-PASSWORD] in it as a placeholder -- Supabase does not put your real password there.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • API keys (publishable and secret, or anon and service_role) are under Settings -> API Keys. Newer projects split them across a Publishable and secret API keys tab and a Legacy API keys tab. The publishable key also appears inside the Connect dialog's framework code snippets.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • The database password is not displayed anywhere, ever. Supabase shows it to you once when you create the project and never again. If you do not have it written down, your only option is to reset it, which you do at Database -> Settings.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If a tutorial sends you somewhere that does not exist

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Older tutorials tell you to look under Project Settings -> Database for a connection string. Supabase reorganized the dashboard, so connection strings now come from the Connect button and password resets live at Database -> Settings. If a tutorial's menu path does not match what you see on screen, the tutorial is out of date, not your project.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The secret key is the whole database

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Treat the secret key (sb_secret_..., or service_role on an older project) exactly the way you would treat your own bank login. It ignores every security rule you set up, so anyone holding it can read your CUSTOMER table, empty your INVOICE table, or drop your schema. It is meant only for code running on a server you control, read from an environment variable that is not committed. If you paste it into front-end JavaScript, into a public GitHub repo, or into a Discord message asking for help, assume it is compromised. Go to Settings -> API Keys and revoke or rotate it right away -- for legacy service_role keys this is the Legacy API keys tab; for new-style keys you can revoke the one key that leaked and create a replacement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Row Level Security, in one sentence

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📖
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Row Level Security (RLS)

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Row Level Security is a Postgres feature that decides, row by row, whether the person asking is allowed to see or change that row -- so two users hitting the same SELECT can get different results.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Two things surprise students here. First, whether RLS is on depends on how you made the table: tables created through the dashboard Table Editor get RLS enabled for you, while tables you create by running CREATE TABLE in the SQL Editor do not. Second, RLS turned on with no policies written means nobody gets any rows through the public API -- that is the correct, safe default, not a bug.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        That explains the classic confusion: you connect with psql using the database password, run SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER;, and see all four customers -- but a web page using the publishable key shows an empty list. Two separate reasons let psql through. You are connected as the postgres role, which owns those tables, and Postgres exempts a table's owner from that table's RLS policies unless the table was explicitly set to FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. On top of that, the postgres role on Supabase carries the BYPASSRLS attribute. The web page has neither: it arrives as the low-privilege public role, and there is no policy telling Postgres to let it through.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Good enough for coursework, not for anything real

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        For this course you are the only person touching the KimTay tables, you are reaching them over psql or the SQL Editor, and nothing is exposed to the public. Leaving RLS off on your assignment tables is fine. The moment a table holds someone else's information, or a browser app can reach it with the publishable key, RLS off means anyone on the internet can read and rewrite that table. The difference is not the software -- it is who else can reach it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If a password leaks, rotate it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Leaking happens in ordinary ways: you paste a connection string into a class chat to ask why it fails, you commit a .env file, you screen-share your terminal. There is no undo for a leaked secret -- the only real fix is to replace it so the old one stops working.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Open the database settings

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        In your project, go to Database -> Settings in the left sidebar. This is where the database password lives, separately from the Connect panel where you copy connection strings.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        2

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Reset the password

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Find the Database password section and choose Reset database password. Let Supabase generate a strong one, then copy it into a password manager or a note before you close the dialog. You cannot read it back later -- if you lose it, your only move is to reset again. A generated password can contain characters like @, #, /, : or ?, which is fine, but see the note below about what that means for connection strings.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        3

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Wait a minute, then rebuild your connection string

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The reset can take a couple of minutes to take effect, so do not panic if the first attempt still fails. Then go back to Connect at the top of the dashboard, copy the session pooler string again, and replace the placeholder [YOUR-PASSWORD] with your new password. Delete the square brackets too -- leaving them in is the single most common reason this step fails. The old string is dead the moment the reset finishes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        4

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Test the new string before you rely on it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Run psql "YOUR-NEW-CONNECTION-STRING" (quotes included) and then SELECT 1; at the postgres=> prompt. If you get back a table with a 1 in it, the string is good. Type \q to quit. If you get password authentication failed, re-read the previous step -- brackets, or an un-encoded special character, are almost always the cause.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        5

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Update every place that stored the old one

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Saved connections in pgAdmin or TablePlus, any .env file, and any note on your machine. If a tool suddenly says authentication failed, this is why.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        6

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Clean up the leak itself

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Delete the chat message, and if the secret went into a Git commit, remember that deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from history -- anyone can still read the old commit. Rotating is what makes it harmless.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        ⚠️
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Special characters in a password must be percent-encoded

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A connection string is a URI, and Postgres requires characters with special meaning in a URI to be percent-encoded inside it. If your generated password contains @, :, /, ?, #, %, & or a space, you must replace it in the string: @ becomes %40, : becomes %3A, / becomes %2F, # becomes %23, % becomes %25, and a space becomes %20. A password of p@ss/word goes into the string as p%40ss%2Fword. Symptom when you get this wrong: password authentication failed even though you pasted the right password, or a confusing could not translate host name error, because everything after an un-encoded @ was read as a server address. If you would rather not deal with this, reset the password and pick your own using only letters, digits, - and _.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep passwords out of your shell history

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        When you type a full connection string on the command line, the whole thing -- password included -- gets written to a plain text history file. On a Mac with zsh that is ~/.zsh_history; on bash it is ~/.bash_history; in Windows PowerShell it is %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt. Separately, anything you type at the postgres=> prompt inside psql is saved to ~/.psql_history. Prefer saving the connection in pgAdmin or TablePlus, or storing the string in a file you do not commit, rather than retyping it in the terminal all day.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Stop Git from ever seeing your secrets

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If your project folder is a Git repository, create a file named .gitignore in the top of that folder with these three lines in it, before you create any file that holds a secret: 

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        # .gitignore - each line is a pattern for files git must never track.
# .env: the usual name for the file holding connection strings and passwords.
.env

# *.env: the same protection for .env.local, .env.production and friends. The *
#   matches any run of characters.
*.env

# A specific file by name. Anything listed here stays on your machine - which is
#   what keeps a database password out of a public repository.
secrets.txt
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Git only ignores files it is not already tracking, so this has to happen first. To confirm it worked, run git status -- your .env file should not appear in the list. If it does appear, it is already tracked, and you need git rm --cached .env and then a commit.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Your real backup is a .sql file you own

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A Supabase Free plan project is paused after 7 days of inactivity, and the Free plan allows only 2 active projects at a time. Supabase keeps your data while a project is paused and gives you up to 1 year to restore it from the dashboard, so this is not an emergency -- but you still do not want your only copy of a graded assignment sitting somewhere you do not control, behind a login that could be down the night before it is due. This is exactly what Module 3-9, "Saving SQL Commands", was preparing you for -- now you are doing it for a real reason.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep one plain text file, in your own notes folder, containing every CREATE TABLE and INSERT you ran, in the order you ran them. That file is your backup, your rebuild script, and your submission all at once.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- kimtay-setup.sql
-- KimTay Pet Supplies -- rebuild from empty
-- Last run: 2026-08-02
-- A header comment naming the file, what it builds and when it last ran. Three
-- lines, and they answer the questions you will have in six months.

-- CREATE TABLE comes first, and parent tables come before the tables that
-- reference them - the order in the file IS the build order.
CREATE TABLE REP (
    REP_NUM     CHAR(2)         PRIMARY KEY,
    LAST_NAME   VARCHAR(15)     NOT NULL,
    FIRST_NAME  VARCHAR(15)     NOT NULL,
    STREET      VARCHAR(20),
    CITY        VARCHAR(15),
    STATE       CHAR(2),
    ZIP         CHAR(5),
    COMMISSION  DECIMAL(8,2),
    RATE        DECIMAL(4,2)
);

-- No column list here, so the values must be in exactly the
-- same order as the columns above. If you ever reorder the
-- CREATE TABLE, this INSERT breaks silently or loudly.
INSERT INTO REP VALUES
    ('20','Kaiser','Valerie','624 Randall','Grove','FL','33321',20542.50,0.05);

-- ...then CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE in that order,
-- because each one references the tables above it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Order matters. A table with a REFERENCES clause cannot be created before the table it points at, so REP comes before CUSTOMER, and INVOICE and ITEM both come before INVOICE_LINE. Writing the file in run order is what makes it work on a fresh project.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Prove the backup is real by running it

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A backup you have never restored is a guess. Test it against an empty database -- and it has to be empty, because CREATE TABLE REP on a project that already has a REP table stops with relation "rep" already exists. Do not test it against the project holding your graded work.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The easiest way: create a second project (the Free plan allows 2 active ones), wait the minute or two it takes to provision, open the SQL Editor, paste the whole file in, and press Run. If you already have 2 active projects, pause one you are not using from its dashboard first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        If you have psql installed, you can do the same from a terminal. Two things to get right: you must be in the folder that holds the file, and you must add -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1. By default psql prints an error and keeps going, so a broken script can scroll a failure off your screen and still finish looking successful. That flag makes it stop at the first error, which is the whole point of a test.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        # 1. Move into the folder that holds the file.
#    On Mac/Linux, type `cd ` (with the space), then drag the
#    folder from Finder onto the terminal window and press Enter.
# cd: changes the shell's working directory, so the file name below can be
#   written on its own instead of as a long path.
cd ~/Documents/database-course

# 2. Confirm the file is actually here before you run anything.
# ls: lists the file if it exists and reports an error if it does not - a
#   two-second check that saves a confusing psql error later.
ls kimtay-setup.sql          # Mac/Linux

# dir kimtay-setup.sql       # Windows PowerShell

# 3. Run it. The quotes around the connection string are required.
# -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 is the important flag: without it psql keeps going after a
#   failed statement and leaves you with a half-built database. With it, the
#   script stops at the first error, where the problem actually is.
# -f names the file to run.
psql "YOUR-SESSION-POOLER-CONNECTION-STRING" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f kimtay-setup.sql

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How you know it worked: psql echoes one line per statement -- CREATE TABLE for each table, INSERT 0 1 for each single-row insert -- and returns you to your normal shell prompt with no red ERROR: text. In the SQL Editor, a green success message and no error panel means the same thing. Either way, do not take the absence of an error as proof. Ask the database what it actually has:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        -- Which tables exist now?
-- SELECT: ask the catalogue what was actually created, rather than trusting that
--   the script did what you expected.
SELECT table_name
FROM   information_schema.tables

-- public is the schema Supabase exposes, and the one your script wrote into.
WHERE  table_schema = 'public'
ORDER  BY table_name;

-- Did the rows land?
-- COUNT(*) per table: the second half of the check. A table can exist and still
--   be empty if the INSERTs failed, so structure and data are worth checking
--   separately.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM REP;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why your tables come back lowercase

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        That first query lists customer, invoice, invoice_line, item, rep -- all lowercase, even though you typed CREATE TABLE REP. Postgres folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase. Nothing is wrong, and SELECT * FROM REP; still works, because that name gets folded the same way. You would only need to care if you had wrapped a name in double quotes when you created it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What must never go in that file

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The .sql file holds SQL only. No password, no connection string, no keys. Then it is safe to email to yourself, drop in cloud storage, or commit to a repository -- which is the entire point of keeping the secrets somewhere else.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You can say which of the three secrets is safe in front-end code, and it is the publishable key (the anon key on an older project) -- not the database password, not the secret / service_role key.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Your secret / service_role key exists only in the Supabase dashboard, or in a server-side file you have never committed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You know the three different locations: connection strings from Connect, API keys at Settings -> API Keys, password reset at Database -> Settings -- and that the password itself is never displayed anywhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • Your database password is written down somewhere you will still have it next month, because Supabase will not show it to you again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You can explain in one sentence why psql shows rows that a browser app using the publishable key does not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • RLS being off on your KimTay tables is a decision you made knowingly, not a default you never looked at.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • A kimtay-setup.sql file with every CREATE TABLE and INSERT, in run order, is saved in your own notes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • You have run that file once against an empty database with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 (or in a fresh project's SQL Editor) and then confirmed with a COUNT(*) that the rows are really there -- not just that nothing turned red.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • No file you have shared, committed, or pasted into a chat contains a password or a connection string, and git status does not list your .env.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        🔍 Check yourself: keys, leaks and backups

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pick an answer — the explanation opens right away.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q1The key that ships to the browser

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A classmate is building a small web page that lists KimTay items, and the page's JavaScript is downloaded by anyone who visits. They have three strings from the dashboard in front of them and ask which one belongs in that JavaScript. Which credential is designed for this?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. The database password belongs in your connection tool and nowhere else -- it is for psql, pgAdmin or TablePlus, never for code a user can see.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔b. Correct -- the publishable key is a public, low-privilege key that identifies your project, and the table says it is the only one designed to be shipped in a browser app.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. It returns rows every time precisely because it bypasses Row Level Security entirely, which is why it must never appear in browser code, a public repo, or a screenshot.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. A private repository is not protection: browser JavaScript is downloaded by every visitor, so whatever is in it is public regardless of where the source lives.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Exactly one Supabase credential is meant to be public: the publishable / anon key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q2The connection string in the class chat

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A student cannot get psql to connect, so they paste their whole session pooler connection string -- real password included -- into the class group chat asking what is wrong. Ten minutes later they realize what they have done. What is the fix?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘a. Deleting the message does not un-see it -- the section says there is no undo for a leaked secret, and the old password keeps working until it is replaced.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. A Postgres connection string is not tied to one computer, which is exactly why the section treats a pasted string as compromised.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. Supabase shows the database password once when you create the project and never displays it again, so nobody can read it back to you -- the only move is a reset.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔d. Correct -- this is the rotation sequence in the section: reset the password, wait a moment, rebuild the string from Connect replacing [YOUR-PASSWORD], update pgAdmin/TablePlus/.env, then clean up the leak.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Rotating the secret is what makes a leak harmless; deleting the message is only the last step.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Q3The night before it is due

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A student wants to be sure that a broken project, a paused project, or a Supabase login problem cannot cost them their graded KimTay work. They list four things they could call a backup. Which one is the real backup this section describes?

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✔a. Correct -- the section calls that file your backup, your rebuild script and your submission at once, and tells you to prove it by running it against an empty project.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘b. Supabase really does keep paused data and give you up to a year to restore it, but that copy still sits behind a login you do not control on the night it is due.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘c. A screenshot cannot be run, so it rebuilds nothing -- and it captures the rows without the CREATE TABLE statements that define them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • ✘d. That test project is one more copy behind the same login, and the section builds it *from* the .sql file -- the file is the source, the second project is only the proof that it runs.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Remember: Your backup is a .sql file you own, written in run order, and tested once against an empty database.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Real-World Project & Database Setup

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A capstone brief that exercises all six course objectives, plus a concrete plan for giving students a real database to build on — via Supabase, a local install, or both.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Map Objective coverage map

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The capstone below is designed so a student cannot finish it without touching every one of the six course objectives — including the two the Module 1–3 table of contents didn't reach on its own.

File system vs. databaseEvery phase — a student can't justify a real database to a real client without articulating this.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                2. Database models & entity relationshipsThe conceptual ER diagram phase requires modeling real entities and relationships end to end.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                3.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 4. Oracle / Access / MySQL differencesStudents choose (or are assigned) an implementation engine and must note at least one place their syntax diverged from what this site's SQLite sandbox showed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Project Real-World Capstone Project BriefObjective 1 Objective 2 Objective 3 Objective 4 Objective 5 Objective 6

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Every course objective, delivered as one project you build a piece at a time. You are not writing this the week before it is due — each lesson adds the next piece to the same project, so by the last class the thing is already finished and you are only presenting it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Where your requirements come from

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Choose an organization you already know from the inside — a job, a family business, a club you belong to, a team you play on, a side project of your own — and work from the records it already produces: its spreadsheets, sign-up forms, receipts, schedules, price lists, its website. Those artifacts are the requirements, the same way KimTay’s paper invoices are the requirements behind the database in Module 1. If you cannot see a piece of information anywhere in them, it does not belong in your database.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Choosing your organization

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pick something real and small. Five to eight entities is the right size; fewer than four will not exercise normalization, and more than eight turns into a term of data entry. The test is simple: can you describe, from memory or from a document you already have, what one row of every table would contain? If yes, the scope is right.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Good scopes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A coffee shop’s drinks, ingredients, and daily sales. A youth league’s teams, players, games, and scores. A tutoring service’s tutors, students, subjects, and sessions. A small landlord’s properties, units, tenants, and rent payments.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Scopes that go wrong

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                “A social network.” “An airline.” “Amazon.” These have no natural edge, so the design never finishes. Also avoid anything whose real data you would not be comfortable putting in a class assignment — use invented names and rounded numbers wherever real people are involved.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What you add, session by session

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The course meets three times a week for four hours, for one month: twelve sessions covering all eight modules. This table is the whole project, one row per session. Each row builds directly on the one above it — the schema you normalize in session 3 is the one you designed in session 2, the tables you build in sessions 4 and 5 are that same design in SQL, and every query from session 6 onward runs against the data you loaded yourself. Roughly the last 45 minutes of each session is set aside for this work, with your instructor in the room, so most of it gets done in class.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                📝
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why the sessions are not evenly split

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The modules are not the same size, so the sessions are weighted to match. Module 2 gets two and a half sessions because normalization is the hardest thinking in the course and the rest of the project depends on getting it right. Module 4 gets three because lesson 4-1 alone covers eight separate topics. Modules 5 through 8 get one session each, which is tight — expect to finish some reading outside class, and lean on the fact that every lesson on this site is self-contained enough to work through on your own.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                💡
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Keep one folder from day one

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Make a single project folder in the first week and never start a second one. Your build script grows in place, your ERD gets redrawn in place, your notes accumulate in one document. The reason the last row of that table says “assemble the portfolio” rather than “write the project” is that if you have kept the folder, the last session is assembly and a demo, not a scramble.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Final portfolio

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Everything below already exists if you kept up with the table above. Hand it in as one folder.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Scope paragraph and entity list (session 1)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • ER diagram with keys and crow’s-foot cardinality on every relationship (session 3)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Normalization walkthrough showing each violation, the rule it broke, and the fix — the reasoning, not just the final tables (session 3)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Data dictionary: every column with its type and its null policy (sessions 4 and 8)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • One .sql build script that rebuilds the whole database from empty, in dependency order (session 5)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Seed data with the awkward cases included — a genuine NULL, a repeat customer, a cancelled or refunded row (session 5)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A second .sql file with every query the project requires, each with its captured output: three single-table SELECT queries (session 6), a sorted report and an aggregate (session 7), a grouped report using GROUP BY and HAVING (session 8), two multi-table JOIN queries and one gap-finding query (session 9), and an UPDATE and DELETE inside a transaction (session 10)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • Evidence it runs on a deployed database, reached from your own machine (sessions 4 and 10)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A view, an index, and the integrity constraints that stop your database accepting bad data (session 11)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A trigger, or a stored procedure written out and explained, plus a note on anything you had to change between database engines (session 12)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • A short written reflection: how would a data warehouse use this same data differently for reporting?
